stories.title: Saskatoon bus riders worry 10-minute rapid transit service promise is slipping
stories.summary: Saskatoon's transit director says 10-minute bus rapid transit service is not off the table as network redesign options show more infrequent service than previously promised.
stories.author: Vanessa Tiberio
stories.content:
A bus rider advocate is raising concerns that Saskatoon’s long-held promise of introducing a bus rapid transit (BRT) system with 10-minute service is slipping away.

Robert Clipperton says he was surprised to see information boards displayed at recent public engagement sessions held by the city showing BRT wait times ranging from 15 to 30 minutes.

“It never crossed our mind. 10 was always the figure used,” Clipperton told Global News in an interview.

“With 15-minute service, I don’t know where you’re going to put all these people. And of course, the whole idea is to increase ridership.”

But Mike Mollenbeck, Saskatoon’s transit director, says the frequencies on the presentation boards are meant to show the difference between two network options with different routing and service priorities, adding that concerns about frequency will be used in the next stage of the design process.

“So if that’s a comment that we’re hearing, or if that becomes a comment we’re hearing, then definitely something that could be taken into account,” Mollenbeck said in an interview.

Patricia Lewis attended the city’s final engagement session on Saturday and said she stopped riding the bus because of its infrequent service.

“Currently the bus system requires me to take two buses and allocate two hours to myself to get to my workplace if I want to get there on time,” Lewis said, adding that more frequent and reliable service would mean she would use the system more often.

“People will not have confidence in the public transport system if frequency is not guaranteed,” Lewis said.

But the potential increase in wait times is not the only thing surprising Saskatoon bus riders. Earlier this month, the city announced it would delay the full launch of the BRT by another year and is planning to slowly implement changes along the network as it approaches that July 2029 completion date.

Clipperton said he was disappointed to hear this news.

“But we would rather that when the system is up and running, it’s up and running in a position that can offer good service as opposed to something that has detours and stuff because of construction on the routes,” he said.

The city previously said it would begin rolling out improvements in phases, with the first to take effect in January. However, it did not specify what service improvements will be made first.

Mollenbeck says they are looking to increase service in the Aspen Ridge neighbourhood in the city’s northeast in January by introducing regular weekday service.

The city is also planning seasonal changes and will communicate to riders how they can see them in the coming weeks, he said.

While open house sessions on a redesign of the bus network’s priorities are now over, the city is still seeking feedback from residents on what level of service they would like to see alongside proposed changes to bus sign designs and the future of a loop at Confederation Mall.

The online survey deadline has been extended and now closes at the end of this month, according to Mollenbeck.

stories.title: 2 people hurt in train derailment near Terrace
stories.summary: Ashley Michnowski, a spokesperson for CN, said the derailment happened around 1:10 p.m., approximately 16 kilometres southwest of Terrace.
stories.author: Amy Judd
stories.content:
Two people were taken to the hospital in serious but stable condition after a train derailment near Terrace.

Ashley Michnowski, a spokesperson for CN, said the derailment happened around 1:10 p.m., approximately 16 kilometres southwest of Terrace.

“Preliminary reports indicate that a CN locomotive and five rail cars have derailed,” she said.

“There are no fires, no dangerous goods and no impact to public safety.”

Michnowski did not elaborate on who was injured or how they were injured.

Highway 16 was shut down for a time, but has since reopened.

B.C. Emergency Health Services confirmed that they were called at 1:02 p.m. about a motor vehicle incident involving a train.

“Two ambulances with primary care paramedics and a paramedic supervisor attended the scene,” Brian Twaites, Bcehs Paramedic public information officer, said in a statement.

“Paramedics provided emergency medical care and transported two patients to hospital, both in serious, but stable condition.”

stories.title: ‘It was something you never forget’: Annual Kettle Campaign kicks off in London
stories.summary: The Salvation Army’s 2026 Christmas Kettle Campaign officially kicked off Tuesday and runs until Dec. 24.
stories.author: Lauren Stallone
stories.content:
The Salvation Army’s 2026 Christmas Kettle Campaign officially kicked off Tuesday and runs until Dec. 24.

“Kettles started appearing at various retail locations across London,” said Nancy Kerr, executive director of Salvation Army London. “We’ll have over 40 different locations this year.”

The campaign is aiming to raise $650,000, after falling short last year.

“Our goal last year was $650,000 and that’s our goal this year and it was higher than it had been in the past, but we brought in $624,000,” said Kerr. “We were really quite happy even though it wasn’t what we needed.”

If individuals wanting to donate don’t have cash on hand, you can also pay by tapping your card.

Kerr said about 15 per cent of last year’s donations were made via “tip tap.”

“A big portion of the funds raised go towards our Christmas assistance program,” said Kerr. “We’ve already got about 3,200 families registered for just this year.”

The Kettle Campaign is the Salvation Army’s largest public fundraising campaign of the year, with volunteers playing a big part.

“The Salvation Army helped my family when I was growing up,” said Marilyn Page, a volunteer with the Kettle Campaign. “It was something that you never forget.”

Page has been a volunteer for 10 years.

“I feel wonderful,” said Page. “Sometimes I wish I could do more days.”

Page encourages other people to give back this holiday season.

She said she knows firsthand even a small amount makes a big difference.

“People are just wonderful and generous,” said Page. “They are happy to drop a coin or bill.”

stories.title: CN Rail train derails in northern B.C., sends five cars off tracks
stories.summary: Terrace, British Columbia - A CN Rail train travelling in northern B.C. has derailed, sending several cars off the track.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A spokeswoman for the company says it happened around 1:10 p.m., about 16 kilometres southwest of Terrace.

Ashley Michnowski says in an emailed statement that preliminary reports indicate that a CN locomotive and five railcars went off the tracks.

The company did not directly respond to a question about how many people were injured, but the statement says there was no fire, no dangerous goods were involved and there is no public safety risk.

It says Highway 16 was temporarily closed by local authorities.

Terrace RCMP and BC Emergency Health Services did not immediately respond to a request for details.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 17, 2026.

SYDNEY - Rachel Homan is no stranger to the Grand Slam of Curling National stop, with four of her record 20 GSOC women’s titles recorded in this city.

Nov. 17, 2026

New subscriber benefit!

Copied to clipboard

A gifted article has been claimed.

Out of gifts for the month

Unfortunately you've used all of your gifts this month. Your counter will reset on the first day of next month.

Misper Apawu[](https://www.thestar.com/news/canada/nova-scotia/homan-einarson-open-with-wins-at-grand-slam-of-curling-national-stop/article_26034f94-4be4-5b37-a49a-e901d88f6195.html)

By The Canadian Press

Homan’s Ottawa-based team, aiming for a third straight win at the National, opened the round robin segment with an 8-5 win over Selena Sturmay’s Edmonton crew at Centre 200 on Tuesday morning.

Homan, with third Tracy Fleury, second Emma Miskew and lead Sarah Wilkes, were trailing 4-3 after five ends against Sturmay, but counted five in the sixth end to grab full control of the game.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Angine de Poitrine debut third member in Toronto

Another familiar name at this event, 2016 champion Kerri Einarson and her crew from Gimli, Man., opened with a 6-3 win over Anne O’Hara’s team from the United States.

Einarson, who won her seventh Grand Slam title last month at the Co-op Invitational in Victoria, B.C., had to borrow brooms from the Sydney Curling Club for the game after discovering three of their brooms had snapped in an equipment bag while travelling.

Einarson scored two in the first end, went ahead 3-2 in the fourth and counted a big three in the seventh for the win.

In other women’s games on Tuesday, Anna Hasselborg of Sweden rolled past Satsuki Fujisawa of Japan 6-3, Miku Nihira of Japan beat You-Been Park of South Korea 8-1, and Isabella Wrana defeated Kyeong-Ae Kim of South Korea 8-1.

In Tuesday’s late draw, Switzerland’s Xena Schwaller played Christina Black’s team from Halifax, N.S., while Alina Paetz of Switzerland faced Mina Kobayashi of Japan.

In opening day men’s action, coach Giacomo Colli filled in for ailing lead Cesare Spiller and the Italian squad skipped by Stefano Spiller edged Matt Dunstone’s hot Canadian crew 4-3.

Brad Jacobs of Calgary, the reigning Olympic gold medallists, beat Jordan McDonald’s Winnipeg foursome 9-2, Yannick Schwaller’s Switzerland squad edged Takumi Maeda of Kitami 7-6 and Oskar Eriksson of Sweden beat Grant Hardie of Scotland 7-3.

Philipp Hoesli of Switzerland rolled past Brendan Bottcher of Edmonton 7-4, and American Daniel Casper rocked Kyle Waddell of Scotland 12-3.

In Tuesday’s late draw, three-time GSOC National champion Bruce Mouat of Scotland faced Tsuyoshi Yamaguchi of Japan, and John Epping’s Winnipeg-based squad played American John Shuster.

Play continues all week in this third stop on the GSOC schedule — the Co-op Invitational and P&H Masters in Medicine Hat, Alta., have already been completed. The playoffs are scheduled for Saturday and the finals are set for Sunday.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 17, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Windsor’s new mayor is part of a wave of electoral change in Ontario border cities
stories.summary: Voters ousted incumbent mayors in Windsor, Niagara Falls and Sarnia amid economic uncertainty and growing frustration over local issues
stories.author: Patrick White
stories.content:
Listen to this article

Learn more about audio

As Scotland the Brave blared from the bagpipes, hundreds of well-dressed Windsorites twisted to watch their new city council walk down the aisle to be sworn in.

Nine of the 11 council members drew polite applause. The crowd saved a full-throated Windsor salute for Councillor Darcie Renaud, the sole woman on council, and Mayor Fred Francis.

In his dark suit and skin-tight crewcut, the new boss looks a whole lot like an old boss. Mr. Francis’s brother Eddie held the mayor’s job from 2003 to 2014.

And the policies Mr. Francis laid out during a 15-minute inaugural speech had a familiar ring here: fiscal conservatism, downtown revitalization, a vow to stand firm in the face of U.S. tariffs and other economic challenges.

“Over the next four years,” he told a packed Capitol Theatre on Monday, “our work will be guided by a shared vision of a city that is financially responsible, economically competitive, safe, affordable, welcoming and full of opportunity.”

Despite his local familiarity, Mr. Francis is the face of a particular strain of change sweeping through local councils this week as new mayors are sworn in across Ontario. Voters in the province’s cities – and border cities in particular – issued an unusual rejection of incumbent leadership in last month’s elections. Among mayoral incumbents who ran in municipalities with more than 25,000 residents, about 52 per cent lost – a rate roughly double that of recent historical averages.

In border cities hit hard by Donald Trump’s tariffs and testy U.S.-Canada relations, the carnage was more pronounced. The mayors of Windsor, Niagara Falls and Sarnia all suffered defeat by nine or more percentage points.

Of the 26 Ontario members of the Border Mayors Alliance, a coalition formed last year as a unified voice in the fight against U.S. tariff threats, only eight are returning to office. It’s a trend that politicians at all levels need to watch, said Martin Horak, an associate professor of political science at the University of Western Ontario who specializes in comparative urban politics.

“The voters who bothered to turn out municipally are clearly in a bad mood and that usually spells bad news for incumbents,” he said. “And we might see some reflection of that when we get to federal and provincial elections down the road.”

The Windsor election might offer hints of the complex voter dynamics at play. Incumbent mayor Drew Dilkens’s loss by 14 percentage points surprised even the most obsessive of city hall junkies. He had served in the chair since 2014. In his final term, he helped break ground on a new hospital and participated in ribbon cuttings for a $6-billion battery plant and an international bridge that nearly became collateral damage in the larger trade dispute.

As U.S. tariffs targeted Canadian automobiles, the Windsor region’s chief export, Mr. Dilkens became the face of municipal resistance, appearing on CNN and other U.S. networks. Early in 2025, he spearheaded the formation of the Border Mayors Alliance and ran the organization out of his office.

“If I look at my three terms, my most productive was my last term,” he said in an interview.

Municipal World, a national trade publication for local government, agreed, naming Mr. Dilkens the 2026 Mayor of the Year.

“The irony is not lost on me,” he said nearly two weeks after the disappointing election results. “But it just speaks to the fact that it was not about me. I don’t take it personally. It just was about the need to seek a different situation than the one we find ourselves in.”

He ascribes the loss, and others like it across the province, to “a spell of uncertainty” cast by the Trump presidency. The spell is deepest in border communities where residents rely on U.S. exports, cheer U.S. sports teams and, in many cases, work U.S. jobs.

The economic data isn’t as gloomy as most people think. While the regional unemployment rate snuck past 11 per cent last summer, it has since retreated to around 7 per cent.

“The sentiment publicly is that the economy is struggling,” said Ryan Donally, president and chief executive officer of the Windsor Essex Chamber of Commerce. “But the data and the feeling are not aligning.”

Part of the sentiment could come from Windsor’s downtown street life. As civic-minded residents spilled out of the swearing-in ceremony on Monday night, scenes of human crisis were evident all over the core. A security guard outside a Salvation Army used his foot to nudge a man sprawled on the sidewalk. A screaming match between a man and a woman descended into a fist fight. A group of people left an empty morphine sulfate bottle behind on a park bench.

Pat Papadeas, co-host of the Rose City Politics podcast, which is devoted to local concerns, said downtown issues were “a big part” of both the Dilkens and Francis campaigns.

“I think what really resonated with voters is Francis saying Dilkens had 12 years to address this,” Ms. Papadeas said. “I think absolutely that local issues, downtown being one of them, was actually more prominent than the broader border context for people.”

In short, all politics are local.

There was one notable exception to the turnover in border-city mayors. Sault Ste. Marie Mayor Matthew Shoemaker won a second term with 50 per cent of the vote. The local electorate was uneasy over layoffs at Algoma Steel, U.S. tariffs and increasing challenges around addictions and homelessness, he said.

He’d spent the previous four years dealing with those issues head-on and offering up a healthy dose of hope in the form of a massive port project. The city is still looking for provincial and federal assistance with the $250-million first phase. The finished project could bring 4,000 jobs and $900-million in annual GDP.

“That was critical,” Mr. Shoemaker said of his hopeful message. “It was critical because of the history of our community. We have faced these ups and downs before.”

He’d spent the previous four years dealing with those issues head-on and offering up a healthy dose of hope in the form of a massive port project. The city is still looking for provincial and federal assistance with the $250-million first phase. The finished project could bring 4,000 jobs and $900-million in annual GDP.
“That was critical,” Mr. Shoemaker said of his hopeful message. “It was critical because of the history of our community. We have faced these ups and downs before.”

stories.title: Canada, India close to finalizing free trade deal, envoy says
stories.summary: Defence agreement likely to be signed during Modi’s trip to Ottawa in December, says Indian high commissioner to Canada
stories.author: Catherine Morrison
stories.content:
Listen to this article

Learn more about audio

India’s high commissioner to Canada says the two countries are on the cusp of finalizing a free-trade agreement, 16 years after talks first began.

Prime Minister Mark Carney and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi formally revived trade negotiations almost a year ago on the sidelines of the G20 leaders summit in South Africa.

Modi is set to visit Canada next month, making stops in Toronto and Ottawa on Dec. 11 and 12, just ahead of this year’s G20 summit in Miami.

Speaking at an event held by the Centre for Strategic Statecraft and the Canadian International Council in Ottawa on Tuesday, Dinesh Patnaik, the Indian high commissioner to Canada, said it’s likely a defence agreement will be signed during the trip.

International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu has said Canada is looking to sign a trade agreement with India before the end of the year.

The Liberals have set out to double non-U.S. exports over the next decade and have also set a goal of doubling two-way trade with India to $70-billion annually by 2030. In 2025, two-way goods and services trade between Canada and India amounted to $30.4-billion.

The two countries have been in trade talks since 2010. But those talks were shut down in 2023 after the federal government accused New Delhi of playing a role in the assassination of a Canadian Sikh activist in Surrey, B.C.

Canada and India are now working to rebuild their diplomatic relationship, though there have been tensions in the bilateral relationship for decades over the activities of Sikh separatists in Canada who call for the creation of an independent country, to be called Khalistan, out of India’s Punjab region.

India has long accused Canada of not doing enough to quiet the separatist movement, while Canada has defended the freedom of those to express themselves while condemning any violence.

Those tensions clouded then-prime minister Justin Trudeau’s first visit to India in 2018, but erupted into a full-blown diplomatic dispute in September, 2023 when Trudeau said Canada had evidence linking Indian government agents to the murder of a Canadian Sikh activist in British Columbia.

In 2024, the RCMP said there was evidence of a wider campaign of intimidation and violence by agents with links to the Indian government and expelled the high commissioner and five diplomats when they would not co-operate in the investigations. India also expelled Canadian diplomats.

Carney made the first move to restore ties when he invited Modi to the G7 summit in Alberta in June, 2025, where the two agreed to reappoint high commissioners.

The two met again at the G20 summit in South Africa last November, where they agreed to launch formal trade talks to cover a wide range of goods and services, including agriculture and agri-food, digital trade, mobility and sustainable development.

Carney later visited Mumbai and New Delhi in March, marking the first visit there by a Canadian prime minister in eight years.

That trip concluded with a meeting with Modi and the signing of a series of agreements – including a $2.6-billion deal to supply India with about 22 million pounds of uranium for energy generation and 10 commercial agreements worth more than $5.5-billion.

Trade talks between Canada and India have since steadily advanced, with Sidhu and Indian Industry Minister Piyush Goyal meeting 10 times since May, 2025.

Patnaik said that as Canada and India have been working to rebuild trust, the countries can’t allow “fringe issues” to derail the progress that has been made.

Victor Thomas, president and CEO of the Canada-India Business Council, said at the event Tuesday that business between Canada and India has never reached its full potential.

He said that while people May think finalizing a trade agreement is the finish line, it’s only the starting point for businesses across both countries.

stories.title: House unanimously passes Conservative MP’s bill honouring son who died by suicide
stories.summary: The Quebec MP has been championing the legislation while grieving the loss of his son who died by suicide after struggling with addiction and encounters with the justice system.
stories.author: Émilie Bergeron
stories.content:
Warning: This story deals with a sensitive issue that some readers May find upsetting. Please read at your own discretion.

The House of Commons has unanimously adopted a bill introduced by Conservative MP Luc Berthold, in memory of his son, that aims to help young people struggling with addiction.

The Quebec MP, who also serves as deputy House leader for the Official Opposition, has been championing the legislation while grieving the loss of his son David, who died by suicide after struggling with addiction and encounters with the justice system.

Bill C-231 was given the alternate title “For the Friends of David Law.” It would allow youth courts, in certain circumstances, to delay sentencing for a young person found guilty of an offence, allowing them to participate in a substance abuse treatment program or another type of treatment program.

The bill would amend the Youth Criminal Justice Act to give courts that option.

Shortly before the Commons unanimously adopted the bill on Monday, Berthold addressed his son during an emotional speech that noted it would have been David’s 30th birthday.

“Today, David, the House of Commons is unanimous. Your life, your experiences, your joys, your sorrows, none of it will have been in vain,” he said.

“Your life will serve as an example to perhaps help other young people avoid going through all the hardships you went through, perhaps make different choices, and help young people choose a path that will allow them to be here for their 30th birthday.”

Before Bill C-231 can become law, it must pass through the Senate and receive royal assent from the Governor General.

Speaking to reporters alongside his wife, Caroline, and daughter, Justine, Berthold said he was taking his grief “one day at a time,” with some days more difficult than others.

Berthold, a former mayor of Thetford Mines, Que., was first elected to Parliament in 2015.

“I think we started out with the idea of doing something, of giving meaning to something that makes no sense, in order to help other people,” Caroline said.

Both of David’s parents said that during a period when he was doing better, their son had expressed a desire to help “his friends.”

“He even had plans with his father to give talks to help young people, so I think this bill is, in a way, making the help David wanted to provide a reality,” Caroline said.

Berthold said he hopes the Senate will move more quickly than the House of Commons in advancing Bill C-231.

At the same time, the Conservative MP welcomed the collaboration among lawmakers from all parties during the bill’s consideration.

He also thanked public servants, noting that his original proposal had been broadened to give young people access not only to addiction treatment but also to other forms of care, including mental health treatment.

“We really had great collaboration from everyone to make this bill something that will, I hope, change the lives of many young people,” Berthold said.

Asked what would be needed to ensure provincial and municipal governments have the resources to provide appropriate addiction treatment programs, the Quebec MP said the bill was a first step.

“Our goal is to raise awareness among people, but also among governments, so that when a judge tells a young person to go to a treatment centre, there will be one available to them, and access won’t depend on their parents’ financial means,” he said.

Berthold criticized what he described as a “two-tier system,” in which lower-income families struggle to help their children access the resources and support they need.

He said raising awareness would be “the next step once we’ve completed all the stages of the legislative process here.”

For immediate mental health support, call 988. For a directory of support services in your area, visit the Canadian Association for Suicide Prevention at suicideprevention.CA.

stories.title: Traditional instruments and dance feature at Western’s Cultural Showcase
stories.summary: Betty Liu introduced Western University students and staff to the guzheng, a Chinese traditional plucked "zith...
stories.author: Samantha Luis
stories.content:
Betty Liu introduced Western University students and staff to the guzheng, a Chinese traditional plucked “zither,” at the school’s Cultural Showcase this week.

Liu wore nail-like finger picks to pluck the 21 strings of the instrument she’s been playing since she was five, the same one her mom played.

She performed at Western’s Mustang Lounge, where hundreds gathered to experience culture through music, dance, and food at the event co-organized by the University Student’s Council and Western International for the school’s International Week.

Food booths at the Cultural Showcase (Credit: Sam Luis/ XFM News)

“Internationalization at Western has been an ongoing and dynamic way of getting students engaged with the actual efforts that we do here,” said USC President Steve Xia.

As guests filtered in Monday, the Antonio Alas Mariachi band opened with traditional Mexican music. The band has been performing for more than 20 years, members told the audience.

Instrumentals could be heard throughout the halls of the UCC building.

Dance performances included K-pop, traditional Chinese, and traditional South Asian styles. Dancers were wearing traditional clothing to match their culture.

Guzheng performance (Credit: Sam Luis/ XFM News)

Many stood to get a better view and camera angles for their personal photo galleries.

Robin Dangol took the stage and strung multiple songs to a background melody on his sitar, a traditional Indian string instrument. He said one of the songs was difficult to play. Not because it’s difficult to perform, but because it’s easy to get lost in song and get carried away.

Between acts, the audience members were clapping and cheering for the performers.

Traditional Chinese dance (Credit: Sam Luis/ XFM News)

Beyond the performances themselves, the showcase also gave students a chance to see representation from their own cultures.

“One of the performances was from my culture… Seeing that performed and represent my culture. I’m really happy about it,” said Akshaya Premkumar, one of the main hosts of the night. “To see that other people are getting to know about the culture, the significance of it, and to see that that exchange is happening and I get to be a part of it, makes it very special for me.”

The food booths gave attendees a variety of popular cuisines to try from all over the world. A few popular ones were to-go containers of ramen, Jamaican patties, and coxinha.

The remainder of International Week was set to feature a Dating Across Differences workshop, Global Café, and Cooking Showdown, concluding with Songs of Many Lands.

stories.title: Militia leaders under UN sanctions spoke at meetings in Canadian cities
stories.summary: Officials of the group formerly known as M23 reportedly met with members of the Congolese diaspora
stories.author: Geoffrey York
stories.content:
Leaders of a Rwandan-backed rebel militia visited Canada this month and spoke at public meetings in several cities without eliciting government action, sparking calls for Ottawa to take stronger steps to enforce United Nations sanctions against the armed group.

The militia, once known as M23 and now rebranded as the FRN, is under UN sanctions for a range of atrocities, including the rape and killing of civilians in eastern regions of the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

Two senior officials of the FRN visited Canada in early November and attended meetings in Hamilton, Toronto and Gatineau, Que., according to photos and videos on social media that have been independently verified by a Congo expert.

One of the officials, Manzi Willy Ngarambe, is a Canadian citizen who was appointed by the militia as the deputy governor of North Kivu province, a key region of eastern Congo that was captured by the group with assistance from thousands of Rwandan troops last year.

A state-run Congolese news agency, Agence Congolaise de Presse (ACP), reported last week that Congo’s government sent a diplomatic note to Ottawa to raise concerns about the presence of the militia’s leaders in Canada, including Mr. Ngarambe.

The Congolese government wants Canada to bring charges against any Canadians or residents of Canada who have joined the group, the news agency said, and has requested “judicial co-operation” from Ottawa on the issue.

A legal analysis, to be released Wednesday by a Canadian human-rights group and two Congolese groups, concludes that Mr. Ngarambe should be subject to criminal prosecution by Canadian authorities for violating the UN sanctions.

The sanctions are fully applicable under Canadian law, and Mr. Ngarambe’s actions in support of the militia are a clear violation of the sanctions, the report says.

“Given Ngarambe’s leadership role within M23, his conduct is fundamentally embedded within the operational activity of the sanctioned entity itself,” says the report, which is co-authored by Canadian Lawyers for International Human Rights, the Congo Accountability Network and Conseil Canadien de Représentation des Communautés Congolaises.

The report recommends that Ottawa ask the RCMP to launch a criminal investigation of Mr. Ngarambe for violations of UN sanctions and possible complicity in war crimes and crimes against humanity.

Mr. Ngarambe did not respond to several attempts by The Globe and Mail to contact him via phone numbers and social media pages that are associated with him.

The other militia leader who attended the Canadian meetings, Freddy Kaniki, is a senior FRN official who has been quoted in Rwandan media as the militia’s deputy co-ordinator for economic affairs.

A media outlet in North Kivu, the Kivu Morning Post, reported that Mr. Kaniki and Mr. Ngarambe attended public meetings in Toronto, Ottawa and Hamilton this month, with Mr. Kaniki speaking and talking with members of the Congolese diaspora on the subject of “rebuilding the Congolese nation.”

Social media videos showed the two men at a conference at McMaster University in Hamilton in early November.

Jason Stearns, a Congo expert and Simon Fraser University political scientist who founded the Congo Research Group, said the videos show Mr. Ngarambe and Mr. Kaniki in the room where the McMaster conference was held.

“I’m surprised and disappointed that M23 representatives were able to hold events in Canada,” Prof. Stearns told The Globe.

“The M23 is under UN sanctions, and Canadian law prohibits knowingly making funds or other property available to the group. Even if there was no overt fundraising or recruitment, I would expect the M23 to use these visits to build political sympathy and cultivate relationships that could translate into material support.”

As a longstanding champion of the multilateral system, the federal government “should take the enforcement of UN sanctions at home as seriously as it takes their adoption abroad,” Prof. Stearns said.

Andrea Lawson, a spokesperson for McMaster University, said the conference was an academic discussion that included people from local communities who were affected by the 1994 genocide in Rwanda.

“McMaster University regularly hosts conferences that explore complex global issues. Organizers are expected to follow university policies and guidelines, and the use of university facilities by external speakers or attendees does not constitute endorsement of their views, affiliations or activities,” she told The Globe in response to questions.

Aditee Kissoon, a spokesperson for Global Affairs Canada, said the department does not comment on alleged sanctions violations or potential investigations or enforcement actions.

“The assessment of potential criminal liability is based on the facts of each case and the applicable legal framework,” she said in response to queries about the militia leaders and their activities in Canada.

Asked about the reported Congolese government request for Canadian charges against the militia leaders, Ms. Kissoon said Canada does not comment on “confidential diplomatic communications with foreign governments.”

stories.title: How cell phone bans in schools are reversing learning losses
stories.summary: Harvard-led researchers have studied cell phone bans in elementary and high schools and say they are giving the policy a good grade.
stories.author: Genevieve Beauchemin
stories.content:
Quebec - Harvard-led researchers have studied cell phone bans in elementary and high schools and say they are giving the policy a good grade.

The large-scale study in classrooms across the United States found implementing rules forcing students to put phones away throughout the school day, reverses some learning losses. This improvement points to some of the benefits of policies in place in provinces across Canada, including Quebec.

The study looked at a 10-year period starting in 2013, when student test scores began to tumble. That year also coincides with the rapid rise of students using smartphones. Harvard’s Center for Education Policy Research noted that Grade 8 math and reading achievements fell by roughly one grade equivalent and that students lost two to three weeks of learning every year.

The study analyzed test scores of 3.3 million students at 4,600 U.S. schools and found bans that cut access to cell phones during the school day reversed roughly half of the learning losses. In other words, students that put their phones in pouches on school grounds added an equivalent of one or two weeks of learning over a full year.

“These kinds of strict cell phone bans, by putting them out of reach, greatly reduce distractions,” said Tom Kane, Harvard faculty director.

Kane says the impact is modest but that the benefits add up over time. The study also concluded the positive effects were consistent across schools and student demographics. Kane also says early evidence shows that the “bell-to-bell” cellphone bans also improved student achievement.

Breaking students’ phone addiction

In Quebec, this is the second school year with a full cell phone ban in place in elementary and high schools. Many teachers have noted changes in learning and behaviour in their classrooms.

Adam Wiltzer teaches math and science at Royal West Academy in Montreal West. He noted a significant drop in the quality of his students’ work in the first two years after the pandemic. He says while his students take formal assessments seriously, they had a tendency to tune out of other class activities.

“The cell phone was the easiest source of distraction, that had the widest breadth of distraction,” he said.

He also says the biggest difference with the cell phone bans plays out in the cafeteria.

“Our ban extends to lunch and recess,” he said. “Prior to the ban, the cafeteria was silent, everyone was staring at their phone. The cafeteria is loud again because people are talking to each other again.”

“I really feel we have done some pretty good work at breaking an addiction. We are not there yet, because when it’s 3 p.m. and the bell rings, everyone immediately goes to get their phone. It’s unfortunate and I don’t necessarily know what to do about that,” said Wiltzer.

Kane says he hopes that the Harvard study showing some positive improvements will lead schools to continue with strict cell phone bans and that more studies will be done on smartphone and social media use outside the classroom.

“We are 13 years in on this and we don’t have strong evidence (of) the impact on students,” he said.

He adds it is key to have strong data to paint a full picture of how hanging up on cell phones in and out of the classroom could help.

stories.title: Krampus excluded from Strathroy Santa Claus Parade amidst community controversy
stories.summary: Organizers of the annual Strathroy Santa Claus Parade have decided to exclude the Krampus figure from this year’s festivities, reversing a decision that would have seen the creature, which debuted last year, participate again.
stories.author: Gerry Dewan
stories.content:
Organizers of the annual Strathroy Santa Claus Parade have decided to exclude the Krampus figure from this year’s festivities, reversing a decision that would have seen the creature, which debuted last year, participate again. The move follows a public debate sparked by concerns over the figure’s inclusion in the event.

The parade, organized by a committee with the Strathroy Lions Club, typically features local first responders, businesses, politicians, and community organizations. Last year, a float sponsored by Coven House, a downtown tattoo parlour, introduced Krampus, a figure from Alpine folklore.

Tanya Griffin, owner of Coven House, described the reaction to the Krampus float last year as manageable.

“We didn’t have any crying children,” Griffin stated. “We did have children holding their parents a little tighter and asking questions.”

She noted that parents were actively explaining the figure to their children.

In many Central and Eastern Alpine countries, Krampus is a companion to Saint Nicholas. While Saint Nicholas rewards good children, Krampus is said to punish the naughty, traditionally with a bundle of birch sticks.

Griffin commented on the cultural context, “They still use Santa and Krampus in conjunction to sort of terrify children into being good for the Christmas holidays.”

Griffin expressed surprise when her Krampus float received the runner-up award for best costume last year. However, shortly thereafter, a campaign emerged opposing its presence.

Griffin identified members of the Calvary Church in Strathroy as spearheading the opposition.

“They had signed a petition with, I think, 34 signatures explaining that we had introduced a demon into the Christ-centered children’s parade, which is called the ‘Santa Claus Parade’ in our town,” Griffin recounted.

In response to the opposition, Griffin’s supporters launched their own petition, gathering approximately 500 signatures. Despite this, and after receiving initial acceptance for this year’s parade, Griffin was informed that the Krampus float was no longer welcome.

Rev. Dr. Brad Morrison, a minister with the Strathroy United Church, voiced his displeasure with the decision.

“I was disappointed by the decision when I heard about it,” Morrison said, advocating on behalf of Griffin.

He expressed broader concerns about community inclusivity, “Really a concern about what might happen next. Who’s going to be eliminated from a community event simply because a small group of people complain about it.”

Gerry Smithers, president of the Strathroy Lions Club, declined to comment further on the decision, confirming only that it will stand for this year’s parade, though future discussions May occur.

The Krampus-free Strathroy Santa Claus Parade is scheduled to proceed this Saturday, beginning at 1:00 p.m.

The parade will pass by her Frank Street shop. She says she will remain at Coven House during the parade and invites anyone interested to visit her and her Krampus figure there.

The move follows a public debate sparked by concerns over the figure’s inclusion in the event.

The parade, organized by a committee with the Strathroy Lions Club, typically features local first responders, businesses, politicians, and community organizations. Last year, a float sponsored by Coven House, a downtown tattoo parlour, introduced Krampus, a figure from Alpine folklore.
Tanya Griffin, owner of Coven House, described the reaction to the Krampus float last year as manageable.
“We didn’t have any crying children,” Griffin stated. “We did have children holding their parents a little tighter and asking questions.”
She noted that parents were actively explaining the figure to their children.

content_blocks.text: In many Central and Eastern Alpine countries, Krampus is a companion to Saint Nicholas. While Saint Nicholas rewards good children, Krampus is said to punish the naughty, traditionally with a bundle of birch sticks.
Griffin commented on the cultural context, “They still use Santa and Krampus in conjunction to sort of terrify children into being good for the Christmas holidays.”
Griffin expressed surprise when her Krampus float received the runner-up award for best costume last year. However, shortly thereafter, a campaign emerged opposing its presence.
Griffin identified members of the Calvary Church in Strathroy as spearheading the opposition.

“They had signed a petition with, I think, 34 signatures explaining that we had introduced a demon into the Christ-centered children’s parade, which is called the ‘Santa Claus Parade’ in our town,” Griffin recounted.

In response to the opposition, Griffin’s supporters launched their own petition, gathering approximately 500 signatures. Despite this, and after receiving initial acceptance for this year’s parade, Griffin was informed that the Krampus float was no longer welcome.

stories.title: P.E.I. nurses rally as province leans on costly private agency staff
stories.summary: Prince Edward Island nurses took their contract fight outside the legislature Tuesday, calling on the province to invest in its public health-care workforce and reduce spending on private staffing agencies.
stories.author: Maria Sarrouh
stories.content:
Charlottetown – Prince Edward Island nurses took their contract fight outside the legislature Tuesday, calling on the province to invest in its public health-care workforce and reduce spending on private staffing agencies.

More than 1,600 registered nurses, registered psychiatric nurses and nurse practitioners have been without a collective agreement for more than a year and a half. Their rally comes as the cost of relying on temporary agency workers climbs. According to the P.E.I. Nurses’ Union, Health P.E.I. spent approximately $44 million on agency staff in 2025–26.

“What it means for our members is the focus is purely on filling the gaps and not the causes of why those vacancies are there,” said union President Kim Sears. “The focus needs to be on retention. Recruitment alone isn’t going to help when you can’t retain the nurses.”

Sears said she’s also hearing that spending could approach $60 million in the current fiscal year, though that projection has not been confirmed.

The union wants the health authority to prioritize working conditions for permanent staff, pointing to what it describes as unsafe staffing ratios, inadequate recognition of specialized nursing roles and compensation that falls behind other provinces.

Wages could push nurses to leave P.E.I.

P.E.I. general-duty registered nurses have the lowest base hourly wages in Atlantic Canada, according to a November comparison by the Canadian Federation of Nurses Unions.

For nurse practitioner Laurie Thomas, the concern is that pay hasn’t kept pace with growing responsibilities.

“Our role and responsibility in the system has grown exponentially, and our wages haven’t,” she said.

Thomas, who has worked as a nurse practitioner on the Island since 2013, worries more of her colleagues could leave Health P.E.I. for opportunities elsewhere if a new agreement doesn’t reflect the work they do.

P.E.I. ’s fall fiscal update forecasts the province’s health authority will run $74.3 million over its 2026–27 operating budget, with agency staffing listed as one of several pressures, but not the sole cause.

According to reporting by The Guardian , Health P.E.I. spent more than $27 million on private agency staff between Jan. 1 and July 10, 2026. The figures were detailed in a freedom of information request received by the Charlottetown newspaper.

Region-wide ban on travel nurses

Health Minister Cory Deagle said the Island is working to reduce its reliance on nurses supplied by private agencies, adding taxpayers can’t afford the cost. But for now, several facilities can’t operate without them, and they also allow permanent nurses to take vacations.

“The reality is we’d have to close beds if we reduce those staff,” he said. “Our system can’t handle that overnight.”

He added that it will take time for staffing reductions to show up in spending figures.

Deagle also plans to meet with counterparts in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, ideally before year’s end, to advocate for a region-wide ban on travel nurses.

“Our goal should always be zero. Will it get there? My hope is yes,” he said.

The pressure on pay extends beyond the Island. Statistics Canada found that registered nursing employees aged 25 to 54 earned 1.4 per cent less per hour in 2025 than before the pandemic, once inflation is factored in.

Meanwhile, hours purchased from private staffing agencies by Canadian hospitals more than doubled between 2019–20 and 2023–24, according to the Canadian Institute for Health Information .

The nurses’ union says it walked away from negotiations in September after 32 days of bargaining, citing a lack of meaningful counterproposals from Health P.E.I.

“We felt we were being stonewalled at the bargaining table and had no choice but to walk,” Sears said.

She added that it was the first time in 24 years the union had taken that step.

“We did not take this lightly.”

The two sides are scheduled to meet with a conciliation officer on Dec. 21 and 22, in an effort to resolve the outstanding issues and reach a new agreement.

stories.title: Preston Manning-led report says Western Canada can unite, gain power within Confederation
stories.summary: The report's recommendations broadly push for more sovereignty across the four westernmost provinces and suggest ways they can better communicate their demands to Ottawa.
stories.author: Dayne Patterson
stories.content:
A report examining the future of Western Canada suggests provinces should seek more sovereignty and provincial control rather than consider leaving Canada.

The report stems from a two-day video conference in mid-September with the Alberta and the West Assembly group.

The conference came a month before Albertans voted in a provincewide referendum to keep the province in Canada and avoid holding a second, binding vote on separation.

Dozens of delegates looked at how to address the divide between Ottawa and Western Canada. The report says there were tens of thousands of online views of the sessions.

Preston Manning, a conservative elder statesman leading the report, said it makes two important points.

One is “unite the West and leave the rest.” The other is that there can be sovereign provinces within Confederation.

“I actually think one of the biggest problems the current federal government’s got is in this whole area of federal-provincial relations,” Manning said Tuesday in Calgary.

“You’ve got Newfoundland, you’ve got Quebec, you got the Western provinces that are alarmed by federal intrusions in areas of provincial responsibility.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "You've got Newfoundland, you've got Quebec, you got the Western provinces that are alarmed by federal intrusions in areas of provincial responsibility."

Manning, founder of the Reform Party and former federal Opposition leader, chaired the assembly with former Liberal B.C. premier Gordon Campbell.

The report’s recommendations broadly push for more provincial sovereignty across the four westernmost provinces, particularly in Alberta, and suggest ways provinces can better communicate their demands to Ottawa and the roles each government has in agreements.

It says a large part of that is all working toward the same goal line as a team in a united West.

It also suggests using Quebec as a yardstick to see how willing the federal government is to bend to provincial pushback.

“I think there’s lot that could be imitated with respect to Quebec’s pushing for sovereignty within the federation, but not going so far as the (Parti Québécois) government is now to advocate secession,” Manning told reporters.

The report says it took Alberta’s Oct. 19 referendum question on separation into account. Separatist leaders argued the province was better on its own than having to work with federal leadership.

In one reference, the report suggests Alberta use the 1991 Canada-Quebec Immigration Accord as a template for its own, similar agreement.

There were nine other questions on immigration and the Constitution in the Alberta referendum, and the majority of voters said Alberta should take more control over immigration.

The report encourages a jurisdictional audit to examine federal and provincial authority and where they overlap, as well as consider how Charter and Indigenous rights play into federal and provincial agreements.

It also encourages provinces, especially in the West, to pick up on Alberta’s steps toward sovereignty.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith has said the province is doing well to address what she called the nine bad laws imposed by the federal government, largely on energy-related rules.

Manning said he plans to ask members of Parliament and the legislatures in B.C., Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba to respond to the report’s recommendations.

British Columbia’s recently elected majority Conservative government is more likely to be on the same page as their conservative counterparts in Alberta and Saskatchewan, Manning added.

“I think it strengthens the possibility for this, ‘unite the West and leave the rest.'” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "I think it strengthens the possibility for this, 'unite the West and leave the rest.'"

stories.title: Canada, India on the cusp of finalizing free trade deal, says high envoy
stories.summary: Ottawa - India's high commissioner to Canada says the two countries are on the cusp of finalizing a free trade agreement.
stories.author: Catherine Morrison The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi formally launched trade negotiations almost a year ago on the sidelines of the G20 leaders summit in South Africa.

Modi is set to visit Canada next month, and envoy Dinesh Patnaik says it’s likely a defence agreement will be signed during the trip.

Article continues below

Angine de Poitrine debut third member in Toronto

Canada and India have been working to rebuild a diplomatic relationship that came to a screeching halt in recent years over accusations about India’s involvement in acts of violence and intimidation targeting Canadian Sikhs.

There have been tensions in the bilateral relationship for decades over the activities of Sikh separatists in Canada who call for the creation of an independent country, to be called Khalistan, out of India’s Punjab region.

Speaking at an event in Ottawa, Patnaik says Canada and India have been working to rebuild trust, adding that the countries can’t allow “fringe issues” to derail the progress that has been made.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 17, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Ontario Premier Doug Ford touts stronger ties with Quebec in Montreal speech
stories.summary: The premier used the appearance to highlight the combined economic strength of Ontario and Quebec, describing the two provinces as Canada's economic drivers.
stories.author: Alessia Simona Maratta, Timothy Sargeant
stories.content:
Ontario Premier Doug Ford called for closer economic ties between Ontario and Quebec during a speech in Montreal on Tuesday, arguing the country’s two largest provinces need to work together to confront U.S. tariffs and strengthen Canada’s economy.

Ford addressed nearly 1,000 people at a business luncheon hosted by Montreal’s chamber of commerce, in what organizers described as the first appearance by an Ontario premier in the business organization’s 200-year history.

“I’m just so honoured to be here and I’m very, very grateful for the amount of people who came out,” Ford said.

The premier used the appearance to highlight the combined economic strength of Ontario and Quebec, describing the two provinces as Canada’s economic drivers.

“Quebec and Ontario make up 61 per cent of Canada’s population and 58 per cent of our economy,” Ford said. “Our two provinces would be ranked the 17th largest economy in the entire world.”

Ford argued that closer co-operation between the provinces has become increasingly important in the face of tariffs imposed by U.S. President Donald Trump.

“I think there’s two great things that Trump did. He woke us up and united us as a country like we’ve never been united before,” Ford said.

“Given this reality, we have no choice, we have to continue working together.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "Given this reality, we have no choice, we have to continue working together."

Ford did not directly address his relationship with Quebec’s new premier, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, or the issue of Quebec sovereignty. Instead, he spoke about his admiration for Quebecers and their willingness to get things done.

“When Ontario and Quebec work together, there is nothing we can’t build and no market we can’t compete in,” Ford said.

During a question-and-answer period following his speech, Ford also focused on interprovincial trade barriers and argued they should be reduced.

“You can’t ship a bottle of wine from one province to another but we’re knocking down those barriers,” he said.

Quebec Liberal Leader Charles Milliard said Tuesday he would be watching the direction of the new Quebec government.

“We’ll see what the premier Plamondon has in mind as to his first decisions in his inaugural speech in two weeks,” Milliard told reporters.

Two Quebec cabinet ministers who were present did not speak to the media about Ford’s comments, leaving questions about how the relationship between the Ontario and Quebec governments will develop as Ford continues pushing for fewer barriers to interprovincial trade.

stories.title: Nutrien signs lease for new Washington State terminal
stories.summary: Saskatchewan potash producer to invest up to US$1-billion for export site
stories.author: Kate Helmore
stories.content:
Listen to this article

Learn more about audio

Saskatchewan fertilizer giant Nutrien Ltd. NTR-T has signed the lease for a new export terminal in Longview, Wash., an investment that could reach as much as US$1-billion.

The company signed the agreement with the Washington port on Monday night, Nutrien spokesperson Simon Scott told The Globe and Mail. Nutrien selected the U.S. site in November of last year after reviewing a number of locations across the Pacific Northwest, including the Port of Vancouver and the Port of Prince Rupert.

When construction in Washington is completed – slated for as early as 2032 – the terminal would annually export between five and eight million tonnes of potash, a fertilizer used in agriculture worldwide. The potash to be exported from Longview is mined in Saskatchewan and will ship to fast-growing agricultural markets in the Indo-Pacific, including China, India and Japan.

The terminal will lead to 432 direct jobs and a total of 1,082 indirect jobs in the county where Longview is located, according to an economic analysis commissioned by the port.

Last week The Globe reported that the project was moving ahead after the company and Longview staff presented the development plan and commercial terms to the port’s board. A decision was expected by the end of the month.

The move is a “procedural step” in advancing the project, Mr. Scott told The Globe last week. The lease is not a binding agreement. A final investment decision will be made in 2028, after the port has completed work to prepare the berth for the terminal.

Longview will spend US$110-million on developing the berth for Nutrien’s terminal, according to a Nov. 10 presentation to the port’s staff. Some of this funding will be provided by Nutrien, which will be reimbursed through credit on future cargo fees.

The Port of Vancouver is making a last-ditch effort to convince Nutrien to change its mind, saying it now offers many of the same perks that drew the company to a site in Washington State.

In an interview with The Globe before Nutrien confirmed it had signed the Longview lease, Vancouver Fraser Port Authority President Peter Xotta said the newly available Sterling Shipyards in Burrard Inlet could handle the fertilizer giant’s export needs. The site meets Nutrien’s requirements for port depth and size, and it can handle expansion, he said.

Mr. Xotta also pointed to Ottawa’s July decision to add the port’s growth strategy to the Major Projects Office, and the port is working with the MPO to “clearly articulate” to Nutrien the benefits of selecting Vancouver.

Bill C-39 which - if passed - will also make changes to the Canadian labour code that will allow the Jobs and Families minister to “take any measure” to end a strike or lockout of workers. (The Port of Vancouver has contended with numerous strikes in recent years that affected exports out of Nutrien’s Neptune terminal.)

Changes to the labour code and new space at the port should encourage Nutrien to reconsider, said Mr. Xotta, who also added that the company would save transportation costs. The Port of Vancouver is closer to its Saskatchewan mines than the U.S. port.

“I think they May be missing something that could be important to them and their shareholders, and of course to the longshoremen and other workers of Vancouver that would like those jobs.”

stories.title: Actions of the accused highlight testimony at murder trial looking into death of man who was set on fire
stories.summary: A man with close ties to both the victim and the accused resumed with his testimony on Tuesday under cross-examination from defence lawyer Alexandra Mamo.
stories.author: Nick Paparella
stories.content:
A man with close ties to both the victim and the accused resumed with his testimony on Tuesday under cross-examination from defence lawyer Alexandra Mamo.

Robert Beasley testified that he was with the victim, Jonathan Graham, 29, and the accused, Bradley Joudrey, 26, in the early morning hours of July 12, 2022.

The court has heard the pair ended up getting into a fight and before the night was out, one man was set on fire and the other was arrested and charged.

Beasley said he was at his sister’s place on Hilton Avenue when Joudrey returned on foot because he had crashed his Dodge Journey.

Joudrey asked Beasley to return to the crash site with him, saying, “He (Joudrey) crashed it ... he said he wanted to go find his Journey, he wanted to go find his belongings.”

Later, London Police Const. Brenda Racher testified that she was at the crash site along Royal Crescent and saw the two men.

When she saw the accused, she said, “I noticed he was unsteady on his feet, I could tell he had been drinking.”

After being arrested for impaired driving and aggravated assault, she added, “He (Joudrey) started throwing up inside my police cruiser, he was having a hard time breathing ... he needed his inhaler.”

It’s the Crown’s theory that Joudrey was upset with Graham that night because he was punched. The two would meet at a convenience store parking lot at Admiral Drive and Trafalgar Street in the early morning hours.

Graham died after being set on fire after having gasoline poured on him.

Following that, Joudrey was charged with first-degree murder. He has pleaded not guilty.

The court also heard from Craig Bryant, an expert from the Centre of Forensic Sciences in Toronto. He testified that he examined several pieces of evidence seized from the scene by police, including Graham’s burnt clothing and a Pepsi bottle the Crown claims contained gas.

He said, “Gasoline was identified in that particular item.”

Bryant also examined the driver seat section of Graham’s white Jeep for the same accelerant.

The Crown’s case continues.

stories.title: Judge refuses ‘disproportionately lenient’ sentence so Afghan carjacker can dodge deportation
stories.summary: 'Collateral consequences cannot be used to justify a disproportionate sentence,' said the judge
stories.author: Chris Lambie
stories.content:
An Afghan man who pleaded guilty to three Toronto knifepoint robberies, including a carjacking, has failed to convince a judge he should be sentenced to six months less a day for each of his crimes so he can dodge deportation.

The Crown argued in Ontario’s Superior Court of Justice that Mohammed Nadim Shofa should be imprisoned for a decade for the robberies. Those include a 3 a.m. carjacking on June 7, 2024, where Shofa brandished a knife, held it to the torso of the driver, Sachin Sharma, and said, “drive now.” When the victim didn’t comply, Shofa started slashing at him, stabbing Sharma in the hand. When Sharma got out of his car, Shofa drove off in it.

“I find that a sentence of less than six months is disproportionately lenient for the three robberies and the assault on Mr. Sharma,” Justice Breese Davies wrote in a Nov. 6 decision.

“I also find that apportioning Mr. Shofa’s sentence as he suggests would result in an artificial sentence that circumvents the will of Parliament and violates several established principles of sentencing.”

The judge said she appreciates that Shofa “will face very serious immigration consequences if he receives a sentence of six months or more on any offence.”

But the penalty he argued for “is an improper, artificial sentence,” Davies said.

Sentences for carjacking typically range from three and a half to five years, she said.

“In some cases, the collateral consequences can justify a significant adjustment in the sentence or even a departure from the appropriate range,” she said. “However, the further the sentence strays from the established range, the less likely it is that it will be proportionate to the gravity of the offence and the responsibility of the offender. And collateral consequences cannot be used to justify a disproportionate sentence.”

The court heard that around 4 a.m. on May 20, 2024, Shofa “robbed the lone employee of a restaurant at knifepoint.”

The worker handed over $100 and Shofa also stole their iPhone.

Two weeks later, Shofa walked into a Yonge Street store around 9:50 p.m., grabbed the clerk, brandished a knife and demanded money. After trying unsuccessfully to open the cash register, Shofa left the store without taking anything.

“Shofa was on probation (for an earlier armed robbery) when each incident occurred and was prohibited from possessing any weapon as defined by the Criminal Code,” said the decision.

Shofa, who pleaded guilty to 13 charges, argued for a sentence of six months less a day for each of them “so he will retain a right of appeal if the government seeks to deport him,” said the decision.

“Mr. Shofa argues that even if a sentence of six months less a day is outside the range for a particular offence, a global sentence in the range of six and a half years is proportionate.”

Shofa, 29, was born in Iran and raised in Afghanistan. He worked about 18 months as a nurse in Afghanistan until moving to Canada with his parents in August 2021.

“Mr. Shofa experienced significant trauma in Afghanistan. In addition to the violence and political instability in Afghanistan that contributed to the family’s decision to immigrate to Canada, Mr. Shofa was the victim of a shooting,” said the decision. “He was also seriously injured during a robbery at his family’s home.”

One of Shofa’s brothers was killed in 2022 by the Taliban in Afghanistan, said the decision. “And Mr. Shofa’s parents were both killed in a car accident in Canada about a year ago.”

He was “homeless and addicted to drugs in May and June 2024, which very likely contributed to his decision to commit the carjacking (and the other robberies),” said the decision.

Shofa was diagnosed with a “severe substance use disorder,” it said. “Mr. Shofa started drinking when he was a teenager, and by the time he left Afghanistan, he was drinking almost every day. Mr. Shofa started using crystal meth after he arrived in Canada and his drug use escalated quickly. Eventually, Mr. Shofa was injecting crystal meth on a daily basis and was using heroin and fentanyl to counteract the effects of the methamphetamine.”

Davies sentenced Shofa to five and a half years in prison, noting Shofa is not a Canadian citizen.

“He is a citizen of Afghanistan. He came to Canada in August 2021 after the Taliban seized control in Afghanistan,” said the judge. “Mr. Shofa’s immigration status in Canada is not clear, but it is likely he entered Canada on a temporary resident permit and was later given permanent resident status because his father assisted the Canadian Armed Forces in Afghanistan.”

Shofa “will be inadmissible in Canada and will lose his permanent resident status once I convict him of robbery,” Davies said. “A permanent resident becomes inadmissible to Canada on the basis of ‘serious criminality’ if they are convicted of a crime with a maximum sentence of 10 years or more.”

The judge pointed out that robbery is punishable by a maximum sentence of life imprisonment.

“Because Mr. Shofa is inadmissible in Canada, a removal order will likely be issued regardless of the sentence I impose,” she said. “However, there is some doubt about whether Canada would return Mr. Shofa to Afghanistan. If Mr. Shofa is a ‘protected person,’ a deportation order will not be carried out unless (Immigration Minister Sean Fraser) forms the opinion that he poses a danger to the public in Canada.”

A temporary suspension of removal orders to Afghanistan has been in place since 1994 “because the conditions in Afghanistan pose a risk to its entire civilian population,” Davies said. “But the removal of non-citizens who are inadmissible for serious criminality is not automatically stayed under that temporary suspension. Despite the uncertainty, according to the legal opinion given to Mr. Shofa, his deportation is a ‘real possibility.’”

Chris Lambie is Atlantic bureau chief for National Post. He has worked for news organizations from Newfoundland to the Northwest Territories and is a three-time National Newspaper Award nominee, with a win for local reporting.
paragraphs: An Afghan man who pleaded guilty to three Toronto knifepoint robberies, including a carjacking, has failed to convince a judge he should be sentenced to six months less a day for each of his crimes so he can dodge deportation.

The Crown argued in Ontario’s Superior Court of Justice that Mohammed Nadim Shofa should be imprisoned for a decade for the robberies. Those include a 3 a.m. carjacking on June 7, 2024, where Shofa brandished a knife, held it to the torso of the driver, Sachin Sharma, and said, “drive now.” When the victim didn’t comply, Shofa started slashing at him, stabbing Sharma in the hand. When Sharma got out of his car, Shofa drove off in it.
“I find that a sentence of less than six months is disproportionately lenient for the three robberies and the assault on Mr. Sharma,” Justice Breese Davies wrote in a Nov. 6 decision.

“I also find that apportioning Mr. Shofa’s sentence as he suggests would result in an artificial sentence that circumvents the will of Parliament and violates several established principles of sentencing.”
The judge said she appreciates that Shofa “will face very serious immigration consequences if he receives a sentence of six months or more on any offence.”
But the penalty he argued for “is an improper, artificial sentence,” Davies said.
Sentences for carjacking typically range from three and a half to five years, she said.

“In some cases, the collateral consequences can justify a significant adjustment in the sentence or even a departure from the appropriate range,” she said. “However, the further the sentence strays from the established range, the less likely it is that it will be proportionate to the gravity of the offence and the responsibility of the offender. And collateral consequences cannot be used to justify a disproportionate sentence.”
The court heard that around 4 a.m. on May 20, 2024, Shofa “robbed the lone employee of a restaurant at knifepoint.”
The worker handed over $100 and Shofa also stole their iPhone.

Two weeks later, Shofa walked into a Yonge Street store around 9:50 p.m., grabbed the clerk, brandished a knife and demanded money. After trying unsuccessfully to open the cash register, Shofa left the store without taking anything.
“Shofa was on probation (for an earlier armed robbery) when each incident occurred and was prohibited from possessing any weapon as defined by the Criminal Code,” said the decision.

Shofa, who pleaded guilty to 13 charges, argued for a sentence of six months less a day for each of them “so he will retain a right of appeal if the government seeks to deport him,” said the decision.
“Mr. Shofa argues that even if a sentence of six months less a day is outside the range for a particular offence, a global sentence in the range of six and a half years is proportionate.”
Shofa, 29, was born in Iran and raised in Afghanistan. He worked about 18 months as a nurse in Afghanistan until moving to Canada with his parents in August 2021.

“Mr. Shofa experienced significant trauma in Afghanistan. In addition to the violence and political instability in Afghanistan that contributed to the family’s decision to immigrate to Canada, Mr. Shofa was the victim of a shooting,” said the decision. “He was also seriously injured during a robbery at his family’s home.”
One of Shofa’s brothers was killed in 2022 by the Taliban in Afghanistan, said the decision. “And Mr. Shofa’s parents were both killed in a car accident in Canada about a year ago.”
He was “homeless and addicted to drugs in May and June 2024, which very likely contributed to his decision to commit the carjacking (and the other robberies),” said the decision.

Shofa was diagnosed with a “severe substance use disorder,” it said. “Mr. Shofa started drinking when he was a teenager, and by the time he left Afghanistan, he was drinking almost every day. Mr. Shofa started using crystal meth after he arrived in Canada and his drug use escalated quickly. Eventually, Mr. Shofa was injecting crystal meth on a daily basis and was using heroin and fentanyl to counteract the effects of the methamphetamine.”
Davies sentenced Shofa to five and a half years in prison, noting Shofa is not a Canadian citizen.

“He is a citizen of Afghanistan. He came to Canada in August 2021 after the Taliban seized control in Afghanistan,” said the judge. “Mr. Shofa’s immigration status in Canada is not clear, but it is likely he entered Canada on a temporary resident permit and was later given permanent resident status because his father assisted the Canadian Armed Forces in Afghanistan.”

Shofa “will be inadmissible in Canada and will lose his permanent resident status once I convict him of robbery,” Davies said. “A permanent resident becomes inadmissible to Canada on the basis of ‘serious criminality’ if they are convicted of a crime with a maximum sentence of 10 years or more.”
The judge pointed out that robbery is punishable by a maximum sentence of life imprisonment.

“Because Mr. Shofa is inadmissible in Canada, a removal order will likely be issued regardless of the sentence I impose,” she said. “However, there is some doubt about whether Canada would return Mr. Shofa to Afghanistan. If Mr. Shofa is a ‘protected person,’ a deportation order will not be carried out unless (Immigration Minister Sean Fraser) forms the opinion that he poses a danger to the public in Canada.”

A temporary suspension of removal orders to Afghanistan has been in place since 1994 “because the conditions in Afghanistan pose a risk to its entire civilian population,” Davies said. “But the removal of non-citizens who are inadmissible for serious criminality is not automatically stayed under that temporary suspension. Despite the uncertainty, according to the legal opinion given to Mr. Shofa, his deportation is a ‘real possibility.’”

Chris Lambie is Atlantic bureau chief for National Post. He has worked for news organizations from Newfoundland to the Northwest Territories and is a three-time National Newspaper Award nominee, with a win for local reporting.

stories.title: B.C. First Nation, Nanaimo Forest Products sign partnership agreement
stories.summary: The agreement involves Nanaimo Forest Products, which operates Harmac Pacific and has been operating in the Nation's territory for more than 75 years.
stories.author: Kylie Stanton, Amy Judd
stories.content:
Snuneymuxw First Nation and Nanaimo Forest Products Limited have signed an agreement to strengthen their relationship and create new economic opportunities in the Nanaimo area.

The agreement involves Nanaimo Forest Products, which operates Harmac Pacific and has been operating in the Nation’s territory for more than 75 years.

“What we are signing here today is much more than an agreement on paper,” Mike Crucil, with Nanaimo Forest Products Ltd., said.

Nanaimo-Lantzville MLA George Anderson also welcomed the agreement, saying it demonstrated what could be achieved through partnerships based on “respect, trust and shared commitment to the future.”

B.C.’s Premier-designate, Lorne Doerkson, applauded the new partnership, saying it is amazing to see the collaboration.

But the announcement comes as relations between the province and some First Nations leaders are under strain.

After the provincial election, the Union of B.C. Indian Chiefs warned against ripping up B.C.’s Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act (Dripa) and instead urged using it as a framework for reconciliation.

On the campaign trail, the BC Conservatives repeatedly said that repealing Dripa was a top priority.

Now that they are forming a majority government , First Nations warned it can’t happen.

“We’re not going to stand idly by while the government-elect does, in fact, rip it up,” Grand Chief Stewart Phillip, president of the Union of British Columbia Indian Chiefs, said.

“That’s a declaration of war.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "That's a declaration of war."

But Snuneymuxw First Nation Chief Michael Wyse said they are just looking to strengthen their relationships with partners and local businesses.

The new partnership’s initiatives and tangible benefits have not yet been detailed.
