stories.title: A Canadian teen was blackmailed after sending nude images. How AP found his scammer in Nigeria
stories.summary: Lagos, Nigeria (AP) — The teenage boy felt his heart drop. His mind went blank.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Erika Kinetz, The Associated Press,

Posted November 17, 2026 8:35 am.

Last Updated November 17, 2026 9:14 am.

LAGOS, Nigeria (AP) — The teenage boy felt his heart drop. His mind went blank.

He’d sent the nude photo the girl wanted, and now she was demanding money. She threatened to post the picture to his family, friends and boss and effectively destroy his life.

“My mind couldn’t think anymore,” he told The Associated Press. “It couldn’t even comprehend the situation I was in.”

He no longer believed there was a buxom brunette with a sweet smile on the other side of his phone. But he never imagined that one day he’d find out who was.

The teen was trapped in a scam that increasingly targets young men: Sextortion. The FBI has warned of a surge in financially motivated sextortion of minors – threatening to expose people’s private images unless they send money. This year is on track to be the worst ever.

By August, the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC) had received more than 40,000 reports of financial sextortion , against a total of 50,000 for all of last year. The impact can be lethal: Dozens of young people have taken their own lives after being sextorted.

Most sextortion crimes are never solved. But the AP and FRONTLINE met the teen’s scammer in Lagos: A soft-spoken Nigerian student named Ayomide.

“Scamming is not good,” said Ayomide, who in his early 20s is not much older than his victim. “I do feel bad. But as a man, you have to make money.”

Ayomide shared chat histories of some of his successful scams, including with his victim in Canada. The AP does not publish the names of underage victims, and reached out to the teen after he turned 18. He spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss traumatic events he had not even discussed with his family.

Ayomide told him that if he didn’t want his photo posted, he’d have to pay. Panicked, the teen said he sent $500.

“Are we done now?” he remembers asking. “Let’s go our separate ways.”

The response is seared on his brain: “Not just yet. This isn’t that simple.”

‘There’s no shame in being a Yahoo Boy’

Ayomide is part of a thriving subculture in Nigeria, in which scamming has been normalized — fueled, some say, by the legacy of colonialism. Yahoo Boys — as online scammers are known locally — are helping drive a global surge in sextortion by exploiting Western social media and payment infrastructure to blackmail their victims, the AP and FRONTLINE found. Even as sextortion rates reach record highs, steps some major social media platforms have taken to increase privacy have only made teens more vulnerable, data shows.

“These perpetrators are becoming more and more aggressive,” said Charles Smith, the FBI’s law enforcement attaché in Abuja. “It can happen to any of our children, any child with access to a computer or online.”

The share of U.S. middle and high school students who say they have been victims of sextortion has tripled in the last decade, to nearly 15%, according to researchers at the University of Wisconsin-Eau Claire and Florida Atlantic University. They also found that sextorted teens are nine times more likely to attempt suicide. More than 60 teens under 18 years old from around the world have killed themselves after being financially sextorted since the end of 2021, according to Paul Raffile, a cybersecurity analyst.

EDITOR’S NOTE: This story includes discussion of suicide. If you or someone you know needs help, the national suicide and crisis lifeline in the U.S. is available by calling or texting 988.

Like other Yahoo Boys the AP and FRONTLINE met, Ayomide said he learned how to use his phone to blackmail foreigners from his friends. All the scammers spoke on condition that their full names not be published because of their illegal work.

Some aspiring scammers in Nigeria join so-called Hustle Kingdoms — groups of young men who live and work together under the guidance of an experienced scammer who takes a cut of earnings. Universities have also become training grounds for scammers.

Sextortion has proven so profitable it is drawing the attention of organized criminal groups in West Africa and Southeast Asia, according to Interpol and the nonprofit International Justice Mission, which traced reports of child sextortion to scam compounds in Cambodia, Laos and Myanmar.

“There’s no shame in being a Yahoo Boy,” said Adedeji Oyenuga, a professor of criminology at Lagos State University. “There is pride.”

For many in Nigeria, scamming is just another hustle in a country where more than 90% of workers don’t have stable, formal jobs. Hit songs celebrate Yahoo Boys and videos on social media show scamming rich Westerners as a way to quick, flashy wealth.

But Ayomide seems out of place in the nightclubs that rise from dark, dirt streets on the outskirts of Lagos, where young men spray crisp paper money at the throbbing, beautiful crowd to prove how much they have to waste.

He described himself as a “soft boy” and said he was apprenticing at a barbershop while pursuing a degree in computer science. He said he’d rather cut hair than scam, but the math was not working in his favor.

His parents sell clothes in a local market, he said. It was up to him to squeeze 110,000 naira ($82) for school fees and 250,000 naira ($186) for his annual rent from an economy where 70% of people lived on less than $4.20 a day last year, according to the World Bank.

Some Nigerian parents see cybercrime as an appealing career opportunity for their kids, according to Oyenuga and others. Parents have pushed their sons into Hustle Kingdoms and arranged for their daughters to marry Yahoo Boys, he said.

Oyenuga got a call late one night from a student’s father, who asked the professor to help his son become a Yahoo Boy, he said. Oyenuga tried — and failed — to steer the engineering student toward foreign exchange trading instead.

“For the parents it’s poverty,” he said. “They just want their children to be successful.”

For Yahoo Boys themselves, scamming is often a temporary stage, a way to earn enough to get a foothold in the legitimate economy.

Ayomide said he hadn’t told his mother about his work because he knows she’d disapprove. He vowed to stop scamming within a year and figured he’d eventually earn enough as a barber to stay afloat. His dream, he said, is to be an engineer and work on planes out at the airport.

“Everything in Nigeria is all about money,” Ayomide said. “But I pray everything works out.”

Sextortionists use American tech to blackmail kids

Ayomide’s method was simple: impersonate a beautiful woman, follow hundreds of foreign men and boys on TikTok and chat up the ones who followed him back: What’s your name? Are you alone today? Do you want to have fun? Then he’d move the conversation to a private messaging app.

For every 50 people Ayomide follows on TikTok, he said, around 10 follow him back, and five of those are willing to chat.

Once he hooks someone, Ayomide said, he has them buy Apple or Steam gift cards, which he cashes out in local currency using CardBrother, a gift card resale app that markets to Nigerian users.

Steam said that it was phasing out physical gift cards this year, in part as a response to abuse by scammers.

Apple said it educates users about risks of gift card scams, including a warning on its gift card landing page. Apple said it removed CardBrother from its app store this year after finding it was connected to another account engaged in fraudulent activity.

The app was still available on Google Play, where it had gotten more than 1 million downloads. CardBrother’s developer did not respond to emailed requests for comment.

Google said it runs 10,000 safety checks on every app and scans 350 billion apps a day. Google removed the CardBrother app after AP flagged its fictitious US address and a dead phone number.

Ayomide also exploited PayPal, paying money mules he found on WhatsApp to use their accounts.

The AP provided PayPal with three accounts Ayomide used to extort his victims. PayPal said the accounts had been restricted shortly after they were created. The company said it is committed to providing a safe platform and invests in systems to disrupt suspicious activity. Meta said it has systems in place to detect malicious behavior on WhatsApp and bans millions of accounts each year.

One of Ayomide’s most successful characters was Ava, an attentive young woman with an extraordinary body.

The Canadian teen said he was 15 when Ava followed him on TikTok.

Just exchanging messages seemed harmless. And it was easy to avoid TikTok’s ban on direct messaging for under-16 accounts by inventing a birthday when he signed up.

Ava asked the teen to move their conversation to an encrypted messaging app called Zangi.

He said he called Ava but never managed to get through for one reason or another. Sometimes she tried him back, but when he picked up, all he heard was a woman saying “hello … hello … hello.”

Later, he would realize that he shouldn’t have followed Ava to Zangi and that the voice was likely a recording.

Ava told him it was hard for a girl to trust people online. Could he send a copy of his driver’s license?

Yes, he could.

Ayomide now had a weapon in his hands: A copy of the teen’s learner’s permit, with his address and date of birth.

Ayomide copied a naked photo he’d found online and sent it to the teen, telling him it was Ava.

“Of course, in my 15-year-old mind, I wanted more,” he told AP.

Then Ava asked for one in return. One evening, he sent it.

“Wow, that was nice,” Ayomide replied.

He’d sent the nude photo the girl wanted, and now she was demanding money. She threatened to post the picture to his family, friends and boss and effectively destroy his life.
“My mind couldn’t think anymore,” he told The Associated Press. “It couldn’t even comprehend the situation I was in.”
He no longer believed there was a buxom brunette with a sweet smile on the other side of his phone. But he never imagined that one day he’d find out who was.

The teen was trapped in a scam that increasingly targets young men: Sextortion. The FBI has warned of a surge in financially motivated sextortion of minors – threatening to expose people’s private images unless they send money. This year is on track to be the worst ever.

By August, the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC) had received more than 40,000 reports of financial sextortion , against a total of 50,000 for all of last year. The impact can be lethal: Dozens of young people have taken their own lives after being sextorted.
Most sextortion crimes are never solved. But the AP and FRONTLINE met the teen’s scammer in Lagos: A soft-spoken Nigerian student named Ayomide.
“Scamming is not good,” said Ayomide, who in his early 20s is not much older than his victim. “I do feel bad. But as a man, you have to make money.”

Ayomide shared chat histories of some of his successful scams, including with his victim in Canada. The AP does not publish the names of underage victims, and reached out to the teen after he turned 18. He spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss traumatic events he had not even discussed with his family.
Ayomide told him that if he didn’t want his photo posted, he’d have to pay. Panicked, the teen said he sent $500.
“Are we done now?” he remembers asking. “Let’s go our separate ways.”
The response is seared on his brain: “Not just yet. This isn’t that simple.”

Yahoo Boys — as online scammers are known locally — are helping drive a global surge in sextortion by exploiting Western social media and payment infrastructure to blackmail their victims, the AP and FRONTLINE found. “These perpetrators are becoming more and more aggressive,” said Charles Smith, the FBI’s law enforcement attaché in Abuja. “It can happen to any of our children, any child with access to a computer or online.”

The share of U.S. middle and high school students who say they have been victims of sextortion has tripled in the last decade, to nearly 15%, according to researchers at the University of Wisconsin-Eau Claire and Florida Atlantic University. They also found that sextorted teens are nine times more likely to attempt suicide. More than 60 teens under 18 years old from around the world have killed themselves after being financially sextorted since the end of 2021, according to Paul Raffile, a cybersecurity analyst.

“These guys they feed off of fear. They feed off of your own fear and they love the feeling of power,” he told AP.
Now it was Ayomide’s turn for desperation. PayPal had blocked the account he was using and he couldn’t cash out.
Ayomide’s goal had never been to post the photo. Posting the photo would mean defeat. He pummeled the teen with more than 100 WhatsApp messages over the course of 11 days.
“No matter how many thoughts go through your head and how much fear you are feeling, every time he tries to message or talk to you, just ignore it completely,” the teen told himself.
He strained to hold tight to his silence.
One ultimatum after the next pinged into silence. Ayomide had lost his power.
The teenage boy had won.

Ayomide said he never posted the Canadian’s picture. He said he had taken a few hundred dollars, but the teen told AP it was closer to $2,000. Neither had comprehensive records of the payments, and AP had no way to verify the amounts.
Ayomide and other scammers told AP and FRONTLINE that if victims don’t pay, they leave them alone.

The FBI and child safety advocates say this is sound advice: The best way to defeat sextortionists is to ignore them. They urge kids and teens at risk to talk with someone who can help — a parent, teacher, friend or child safety hotline — and report the crime .

“If kids pay, the threats inevitably continue,” said Lindsay Lobb, director of support services at the nonprofit Canadian Centre for Child Protection (C3P). “These people are only looking for money. They are not interested in sharing your image.”

Fewer than 1 in 10 young people who were financially sextorted reported to C3P that their images had been shared. When a photo is posted, Lobb added, it’s now possible to get those images taken down .
Ayomide said he felt bad about what he’d done to the Canadian teen and if he had the chance would apologize.
“Maybe we should just be friends,” he told AP and FRONTLINE. “I was sorry for the hurt.”
The teen told AP that he could not take an apology from a master manipulator seriously.
“I doubt he felt bad,” he said. “You can’t show these guys any pity because that’s all they feed off.”
Nearly two years after he escaped the scam, the teen is haunted by what happened. He said his heart still skips a beat when he gets random requests to talk.
He was recently targeted by another scammer, he said – someone pretending to be a Japanese woman asking if he lived nearby. This time round he knew exactly what to do.
“I just said no, never have, said I had no business with them and blocked the number,” he told AP.
A year after Ayomide vowed to stop, he had fallen in with a group of other Yahoo Boys at his university.
He declined to comment on why he is still scamming.
Bukola Omoseni and Grace Ekpu in Lagos, Nigeria; Simon Reef in Abuja, Nigeria; and Jesse Bedayn in Denver contributed to this report.

Carney said that Canada plans to increase its overall trade with China by 50 per cent by 2030

Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney (C) arrives at the Shenzhen Bao'an International Airport ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summiton November 16, 2026 in Shenzhen, China. (Pool / Getty Images)

November 17, 2026 at 8:35 a.m.

Ottawa — The Canadian and Chinese governments continued their rapprochement Tuesday, with China agreeing to provide tariff relief on roughly $400-million of Canadian pork, fish and seafood while Canada opened the door to more Chinese steel and aluminium.

Prime Minister Mark Carney’s office made the announcement Tuesday morning after he met with Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in Shenzhen, China.

“Exchanges between our two countries have increased significantly and we have greater capability and stability,” Carney told Xi during opening remarks to the meeting, adding that Canada plans to increase its overall trade with China by 50 per cent by 2030.

According to the federal government, China agreed to extend until 2028 an agreement that provided tariff relief on imports of Canadian frozen pork cuts as well as certain fish and seafood products such as frozen cold-water shrimp and prawns, molluscs and Greenland halibut. The deal — first signed when Carney visited China in January — was set to expire at the end of the year.

In exchange, Canada agreed to extend and expand its tariff remission program on certain Chinese steel and aluminium products until 2028. The Canadian release says that new Chinese products covered by the remissions are “items for which Canadian supply is insufficient or unavailable.”

The remission program allows importers to get a refund of the 25 per cent surtax imposed on Chinese steel and aluminium since 2024.

The extension and slight expansion of tariff relief between both countries appears to be a small step towards further rapprochement between both countries after years of frosty relations. Efforts to boost trade between both countries began in earnest after a key bilateral meeting between Carney and Xi in Beijing in January.

Canadian exports to China have surged just over 40 per cent since then, hitting $4.4 billion in September from $3.1 in January, according to Statistics Canada.

Ahead of the meeting, a key advisor to American President Donald Trump and frequent critic of Canada warned that a closer relationship between Carney and Xi could be seen as a step away from the U.S.

“Are u really threatening to play China off the U.S.? This is offensive in the extreme. You should be far more worried China is going to eat Canada alive — as it is already doing,” Peter Navarro wrote on X on Monday.

In a readout of the meeting, Carney’s office said he and Xi explored ways to deepen cooperation in “clean and conventional energy industries, including oil and gas, low-carbon technologies, and electric vehicles,” but did not provide further detail.

The prime minister has frequently signaled that he’s interested in having Chinese electric vehicle manufacturers set up assembly lines in Canada. Ahead of the bilateral with Xi, he said that Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade talks with the U.S. fail and American automakers continue reshoring their production South of the border.

But the Chinese companies would have to set up significant manufacturing operations and use Canadian labour, materials and critical minerals rather than simply send “kits” from China and assemble the cars in Canada.

During the meeting, Carney promised to send another “major” trade delegation to China in 2027 and announced Air Canada would launch new flights from Vancouver to Guangzhou by mid-2027.

“We both recognize that the enduring ties between the Canadian and Chinese people provide an exceptionally strong foundation for practical, respectful collaboration,” Carney told Xi at the onset of the meeting.

Christopher Nardi is a senior parliamentary reporter in Ottawa. He has worked in both French and English media, speaks Italian and writes about politics, national security, justice and how things work (or don't) in government. Reach him on Signal: ChrisNardi.01 cnardi@postmedia.com

Prime Minister Mark Carney’s office made the announcement Tuesday morning after he met with Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in Shenzhen, China.

“Exchanges between our two countries have increased significantly and we have greater capability and stability,” Carney told Xi during opening remarks to the meeting, adding that Canada plans to increase its overall trade with China by 50 per cent by 2030.

According to the federal government, China agreed to extend until 2028 an agreement that provided tariff relief on imports of Canadian frozen pork cuts as well as certain fish and seafood products such as frozen cold-water shrimp and prawns, molluscs and Greenland halibut. The deal — first signed when Carney visited China in January — was set to expire at the end of the year.

In exchange, Canada agreed to extend and expand its tariff remission program on certain Chinese steel and aluminium products until 2028. The Canadian release says that new Chinese products covered by the remissions are “items for which Canadian supply is insufficient or unavailable.”
The remission program allows importers to get a refund of the 25 per cent surtax imposed on Chinese steel and aluminium since 2024.

The extension and slight expansion of tariff relief between both countries appears to be a small step towards further rapprochement between both countries after years of frosty relations. Efforts to boost trade between both countries began in earnest after a key bilateral meeting between Carney and Xi in Beijing in January.
Canadian exports to China have surged just over 40 per cent since then, hitting $4.4 billion in September from $3.1 in January, according to Statistics Canada.
Ahead of the meeting, a key advisor to American President Donald Trump and frequent critic of Canada warned that a closer relationship between Carney and Xi could be seen as a step away from the U.S.

“Are u really threatening to play China off the U.S.? This is offensive in the extreme. You should be far more worried China is going to eat Canada alive — as it is already doing,” Peter Navarro wrote on X on Monday.

In a readout of the meeting, Carney’s office said he and Xi explored ways to deepen cooperation in “clean and conventional energy industries, including oil and gas, low-carbon technologies, and electric vehicles,” but did not provide further detail.

The prime minister has frequently signaled that he’s interested in having Chinese electric vehicle manufacturers set up assembly lines in Canada. Ahead of the bilateral with Xi, he said that Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade talks with the U.S. fail and American automakers continue reshoring their production South of the border.

But the Chinese companies would have to set up significant manufacturing operations and use Canadian labour, materials and critical minerals rather than simply send “kits” from China and assemble the cars in Canada.
During the meeting, Carney promised to send another “major” trade delegation to China in 2027 and announced Air Canada would launch new flights from Vancouver to Guangzhou by mid-2027.

“We both recognize that the enduring ties between the Canadian and Chinese people provide an exceptionally strong foundation for practical, respectful collaboration,” Carney told Xi at the onset of the meeting.

Christopher Nardi is a senior parliamentary reporter in Ottawa. He has worked in both French and English media, speaks Italian and writes about politics, national security, justice and how things work (or don't) in government. Reach him on Signal: ChrisNardi.01 cnardi@postmedia.com

stories.title: Toronto’s Promise Robotics raises $40-million to automate more homebuilding
stories.summary: Startup has already landed Mattamy Homes and D.R. Horton as early customers and set up factories in Calgary and outside Edmonton
stories.author: Murad Hemmadi
stories.content:
Promise Robotics Inc., a Toronto-based artificial intelligence startup, has raised $40-million in fresh financing to scale up an automated approach to homebuilding that’s attracting interest from major residential developers.

Founded in September 2020, the company is applying AI to the construction sector, where productivity growth has long been slow and skilled workers are in short supply .

“We don’t have enough industrial capacity in construction to build all the homes we need,” said Ramtin Attar, Promise’s chief executive and co-founder, in an interview.

The company has developed software that breaks up dwelling designs into pieces that robots can produce in a factory. It then ships the parts to developers’ residential projects and hires construction crews to stand them up as finished houses.

Promise has set up factories in Calgary and just outside Edmonton. And it has plans for a new facility in Phoenix, the start of a big push into the U.S.

The company has built about 200 homes to date, and it is currently working to scale its production to 700 homes a year. It has contracts to supply more than 2,500 to clients. Half of that volume is through a deal the company landed last month with D.R. Horton, an Arlington, Tex.-based company that is the largest homebuilder in the U.S.

Promise has also signed up the Alberta division of Mattamy Homes, one of Canada’s largest residential developers.

“There’s a lot more pressure on home builders – on their margins, ON their ability to build more consistently,” said Mr. Attar.

Promise first developed an AI system that controls off-the-shelf industrial machines to produce the frame, roof, floors and other major components for any house design. Each cell consists of two robots that share a worktable; together, they can produce a home in eight hours, Mr. Attar said. The company can also add Hvac systems and plumbing, and it has plans to expand into electrical wiring.

It distinguishes its approach from modular houses, which are also produced in factories, but are purpose-designed for mass manufacturing. By contrast, Promise follows clients’ existing designs.

The company now follows the house out the factory gate. For some projects, it uses its own construction crews, after realizing that challenges with labour scheduling were lengthening building timelines. “All the components were arriving at the site and then sitting there for a week for a crew to come,” said Mr. Attar.

White Star Capital, a London-based venture firm with Canadian operations, led Promise’s Series B round, which closed in the second quarter. Returning backers in the financing included the Public Sector Pension Investment Board; Radical Ventures, a prominent AI investor based in Toronto; and Horizons Ventures, a Hong Kong investment firm backed by billionaire Li Ka-shing.

“Home construction is a massive industry that needs a new way to keep up with demand,” Sanjay Zimmermann, a Toronto-based general partner at White Star, said in a statement.

Promise will spend its new capital on technology research and development, and expanding its 85-person work force to more than 100 staff. It’s also working on a new financial model for its factories, essentially warehouses into which Promise installs its robotic cells. They cost between $3-million and $15-million each. That’s cheaper than a modular housing factory, Mr. Attar said.

The company aims to make every facility a profitable, self-contained business, paid for through a combination of its own cash as well as financing from clients, banks or government agencies.

Significant sums have flown into startups developing general-purpose AI models for robots or sci-fi machines like humanoids . But Promise needs less capital than some other companies in physical AI, and developers want assurances that it’s not just burning cash, according to Mr. Attar.

“If I’m directing my supply chain at you, I want to see you stick around,” he said. “So, we are being very disciplined about how much we raise.”

Promise previously raised a US$15-million Series A, in October 2023, led by Horizons.

The company would like to participate in Ottawa’s efforts to boost residential construction in Canada and reduce housing costs. But technology companies like Promise aren’t eligible for federal homebuilding policies and programs, Mr. Attar said.

The country cannot simply “count on just how many hands can hold hammers,” he said. “That’s just not going to scale – we need to build that industrial capacity.”

stories.title: For its newest home collection, Hermès gets crafty
stories.summary: Hermès’ latest collection for the home paints a vibrant picture of a design team infatuated with material, craft and colour
stories.author: Andrew Sardone
stories.content:
A caravan of chauffeured cars quietly crawls through a warren of narrow streets in downtown Toronto. They arrive at a private laneway and deposit their passengers, who make their way down a cobblestone path to the motor court of a red brick Georgian estate perched on the edge of the Don Valley. Through the front door, glasses of champagne are being passed out to the curious crowd, who schmooze and snoop from room to handsome room, taking in the latest furniture and housewares from Hermès.

For a few days in the early fall, this private home has been reimagined by the Parisian house as Maison 24, a showcase that demonstrates how living with Hermès can extend well beyond a walk-in closet lined with Birkin and Kelly bags. Its latest decor releases are the standouts of the night.

In the wood-panelled dining room, a box with a top in marquetry squares of moody-hued leather sits on a sideboard surrounded by silver goblets. The den is lined with stacks of folded blankets including cashmere throws with bands of equestrian webbing that add texture and graphic interest to their edges. On one shelf, a cylindrical basket called Confetti in pink calfskin is cut-out like a game of Connect 4, revealing an array of vibrant dots.

Taking in the scene are customers, a gaggle of Toronto starchitects and Charlotte Macaux Perelman and Alexis Fabry, the artistic directors of the house’s Home Universe. Since 2014, when CEO Axel Dumas and artistic director Pierre-Alexis Dumas paired up the creative duo to oversee Hermès’ home products as well as Saint-Louis crystal and Puiforcat tableware, the architect (Macaux Perelman) and the photography curator (Fabry) have elevated its profile in the design world. Seeing their contemporary, tailored and often colourful aesthetic styled in a space that grandly represents the coziness of a historic Canadian home reinforces the versatility of Hermès’s work, especially when you consider the much more spare environment in Milan where the newest objects were unveiled earlier in the year.

During the week of the annual Salone del Mobile furniture fair each spring, design and fashion brands compete for exhibition space in the northern Italian city. Securing exclusive use of the most recently unearthed hidden courtyard, pedigreed villa or abandoned military hospital is essential for increasing buzz and visitor attendance. But Hermès, in its slow-and-steady style, has been returning to the same space since 2021. La Pelota, a former sports court in the Brera district, is reinvented every year as a frame for the new collection. In 2022, furniture vignettes were staged within four glowing structures that resembled the forms of water towers. In 2024, a dark space focused visitors’ attention downwards to a patchwork of wood, stone, slate and terracotta flooring meant to conjure a feeling of being grounded.

The 2026 installation, From Object to Space, was a landscape of white plaster cubes inlayed with slivers of beechwood that emphasized a rawness of material. Hand-written labels in graphite pencil identified showpiece debuts including the Stadium d’Hermès dining table by Brits Edward Barber and Jay Osgerby, its curved Carrara Venato top edged in a circle of Verde Alpi marble. Hammered metal, the elemental focus of the year, was incorporated as a centrepiece dish with edges wrapped in blue and purple leather laces, and a tubular vase nestled in tiers of sharply chopped horsehair. Overall, the message was harmony between style and substance.

“I believe that we’re very much attached to materiality,” said Macaux Perelman through a translator at the exhibition preview. “We give a lot of attention to the reality of craftsmanship, the fact that things are done by hand, that they’re all unique.” While the palladium-finish metal could feel cold, Macaux Perelman said its hammered texture gives it a warmth and duality by connecting it to the manual work involved in its creation. “The material used is important because it’s at the very heart of the product.”

Macaux Perelman and Fabry describe their role at Hermès as editors, overseeing teams who specialize in different product categories, establishing guidelines and helping designers and artisans course-correct through the creative process. “This is a small team, but it works hard,” Fabry said. “There are some things that are negotiable. The things that are not negotiable are creativity and the freedom of expression and quality.”

A very specific eye for colour is also essential. Hermès’s most iconic hues are the rich orange of its shop boxes and the gold skins used in its leather goods. The tones incorporated into its design pieces evoke a similar earthiness. “They’re not something fossilized, something that remains unchanged,” Fabry said of the house’s preferred spectrum. “Some years, we’ve changed the palette of colours more definitely than in other years. This year, perhaps, the change was more sudden. We opted more for muted colours.”

Hermès’s back catalogue includes furniture pieces by Jean-Michel Frank (a saddle-stitched leather Club armchair), Barber & Osgerby (the porcelain Halo table lamp) and Noé Duchaufour-Lawrance (who highlighted leather and cane in the frame of his Sellier sofa). Though these pieces were conceptualized across decades, what they have in common is a contemporariness in the moment they’re introduced, as well as years later.

“We don’t really think of our objects inside a Hermès boutique or in the home of someone. We ask ourselves instead, ‘is this object going to be passed on to the next generation,’” Macaux Perelman said. “Is this going to survive its era?”

As the Maison 24 house installation in Toronto illustrated, the design team wants their pieces to transcend space as much as time. “Each person is going to mix our objects through a kind of porosity with the environment where the object stays,” Fabry said. Pieces are meant to reflect, he noted, “the life of the person who’s bought the object, the trips, the travels this person does, and the evolution of a person’s taste.”

The Globe and Mail Style Magazine travelled as a guest of Hermès, which did not review or approve this article. Stories are based on merit; The Globe does not guarantee coverage.

content_blocks.text: During the week of the annual Salone del Mobile furniture fair each spring, design and fashion brands compete for exhibition space in the northern Italian city. Securing exclusive use of the most recently unearthed hidden courtyard, pedigreed villa or abandoned military hospital is essential for increasing buzz and visitor attendance. But Hermès, in its slow-and-steady style, has been returning to the same space since 2021. La Pelota, a former sports court in the Brera district, is reinvented every year as a frame for the new collection. In 2022, furniture vignettes were staged within four glowing structures that resembled the forms of water towers. In 2024, a dark space focused visitors’ attention downwards to a patchwork of wood, stone, slate and terracotta flooring meant to conjure a feeling of being grounded.

Hand-written labels in graphite pencil identified showpiece debuts including the Stadium d’Hermès dining table by Brits Edward Barber and Jay Osgerby, its curved Carrara Venato top edged in a circle of Verde Alpi marble. Hammered metal, the elemental focus of the year, was incorporated as a centrepiece dish with edges wrapped in blue and purple leather laces, and a tubular vase nestled in tiers of sharply chopped horsehair. stories.title: Mohawk teacher, 73, earns McGill’s first PhD in Indigenous Language Revitalization
stories.summary: Mary Onwá:ri Tekahawákhwen McDonald has taught the Mohawk language to thousands of students over the past decades, from elementary school all the way to university level.
stories.author: Morgan Lowrie
stories.content:
By her own estimate, Mary Onwá:ri Tekahawákhwen McDonald has taught the Mohawk language to thousands of students over the past decades, from elementary school all the way to university level.

But when someone suggested she might pursue a PhD, the idea of returning to class in her 70s was a daunting prospect.

“(I said) ‘no, why would I want to do that?'” the now-73-year-old says with a laugh. ” … How do I compete with 20-year-olds? Can I really do this?”

Today, the Mohawk educator, linguist and elder can add the title of “doctor” to her list of accomplishments. Earlier this year, she became the first person to graduate from McGill University with a PhD in Indigenous Language Revitalization.

McDonald said she was eventually convinced to apply to the program out of a desire to write down the knowledge she’s accumulated over 45 years of teaching and studying language.

McDonald, who is from the Akwesasne community that straddles Quebec, Ontario and New York, is a native Mohawk speaker who only learned to speak English in second grade.

She went on to study Iroquoian linguistics, with a concentration in Mohawk, in university in Albany, N.Y., and later got a teaching certification in Ontario.

Over the years, she said, she became interested in studying how native speakers learn the language as children.

“Kinship words” used to describe close relatives come first, she said, followed by the words used to describe other people close to them. Pronouns, commands, and nouns follow, as children learn increasingly complex sentences.

She said she learned that this knowledge can help to teach second-language students, too. “If you follow this pattern, you’re coming very close to duplicating a natural learning pattern,” she said.

McDonald summed up part of her research in her dissertation, entitled “Kanien’kéha Through the Eyes of a First-Language Speaker.”

And along the way, she also became a peer mentor to some of those twenty-something-aged students who she was once intimidated to join.

She recently invited reporters to meet some of her young peers, who were gathering to discuss their research. She chatted with a young man in Mohawk, and gave advice to another student who was presenting to the group. McDonald jokingly refers to the group as fellow “super-nerds.”

Jessica Coon, the program director for the ad hoc graduate program in Indigenous language revitalization, was one of McDonald’s supervisors. Coon said McDonald’s contribution to the program is “hard to overstate.”

“As a thesis supervisor, I think we always get to learn something from our students, but this has never been more true than in the case of working with Mary because she just knows so much about the language,” she said in an interview.

She said the program was created in part to accommodate students whose interest in language revitalization spans different disciplines — such as linguistics and education, in McDonald’s case.

“We really want the program to be broad enough to accommodate students approaching language revitalization of their languages from a variety of different perspectives and to have the flexibility built in to do that across different disciplines,” she said.

She says another student graduated with McDonald at the Master’s level, and there are four more students who started this fall, including two more PhD candidates. McDonald “is the first, but she won’t be the last,” she said.

While McDonald now describes herself as “retired,” she is clearly keeping busy. She travels back to McGill every two weeks, where she serves as an elder in residence and meets with the research group.

She also still works with more advanced Mohawk language-learners, pushing them to expand the bounds of their abilities and express themselves with not only accuracy, but “pizzazz.”

She said she plans to keep building on her thesis, and writing down the concepts she has spent a lifetime studying.

“I’ll do this till the day I pass because it’s a lot of fun,” she said.

stories.title: Canadian film powerhouse Rhombus Media acquired by nascent player Skywild Pictures
stories.summary: The deal has the potential to alter the country’s film and TV landscape
stories.author: Barry Hertz
stories.content:
When Niv Fichman co-founded Rhombus Media in 1979, the Canadian film and television landscape was, while not exactly easy to navigate, at least somewhat predictable. With an initial focus on documentaries and films that pivoted around music ( Yo-Yo Ma: Inspired By Bach , Don Giovanni Unmasked ), the production company benefited from an era in which broadcasters like the CBC had serious money to spend on sales, and the Canadian Television Fund (now part of the Canada Media Fund) threw its weight behind performance-art projects.

Flash forward five decades, and Rhombus has managed to weather the tectonic shifts in the screen sector by going bigger and glitzier while never sacrificing its art-house bona fides, forging deep ties with top-tier filmmakers both domestic (Atom Egoyan, Matt Johnson, Brandon Cronenberg, Patricia Rozema) and foreign (Park Chan-wook, Andrew Haigh, Fernando Meirelles). And now, Fichman’s small but mighty powerhouse is entering an entirely new, somewhat unexpected chapter: acquisition.

On Tuesday, Skywild Pictures, the Toronto-based production company launched last year by industry veterans Angela Jennings and Travis Farncombe, announced that it has acquired Rhombus in the company’s bid to scale up its footprint in the global marketplace. Fichman will remain the lead producer of the company under the Skywild banner, while Rhombus’s longtime lead producers Fraser Ash and Kevin Krikst will join Skywild’s team as senior vice-president, content, and vice-president, production, respectively.

“One thing that’s crucial about this is that the Rhombus brand is retained, and it’s business as usual for us,” Fichman says in an interview alongside Jennings. “When Angela and I first got together and she spoke about what their creative goal is – and in these kinds of situations, how often do you talk about a creative goal? – we talked about creating high-end content with the highest-end Canadian creators and to take that to the world. If you look at our website, which no one does, but that’s basically what it says. We wrote each other’s creative mandate.”

The deal has the potential to significantly alter the country’s film and TV landscape, given Rhombus’s storied history and robust active-development slate. Fichman co-founded Rhombus with director Barbara Willis Sweete, and filmmaker Larry Weinstein joined shortly thereafter. That partnership, which came to include Sheena Macdonald, was officially dissolved in 2015, leaving Fichman to head the company solo, delivering such hits as Johnson’s 2023 comedy BlackBerry and Park’s 2024 HBO miniseries The Sympathizer . Skywild, meanwhile, is a self-financed and relatively untested outfit, albeit one with ambitious plans.

“Skywild has never been interested in being the biggest. But we want to be important, and that’s what Rhombus has been for so many years,” says Jennings, who was previously president of the production company MEM, which specialized in unscripted, reality and lifestyle entertainment. “While we have growth plans, it’s not about going out and acquiring a bunch of businesses. We’re looking to build organically, and this was such a hand-in-glove fit with what Niv and his team have built over the last 50 years.”

Both Fichman and Jennings insist that the deal was born not out of any kind of strategic zeal but happy and accidental timing, with the former noting that a mutual colleague initially connected the two companies.

“In my whole life I’ve never thought about acquisition, it just came very spontaneously. Here’s an emerging company that’s been developing projects with a voracious appetite, and here’s this company that’s very mature but with a need for someone like Angela who oversees things,” says Fichman. “We’ve run our company on a project-by-project basis. We’ve never had a one-year plan, let alone a five-year plan. We’ve never thought about maximizing this thing called growth. But the opportunity of having Angela come on board and seeing the potential of what we can do and the markets we can go to is great.”

Such expansions include further exploiting Rhombus’s catalogue of titles, which is rich in such Criterion-flavoured hits as The Red Violin and Thirty Two Short Films About Glenn Gould , as well as focusing attention on the company’s small-screen work, which has in the past yielded such homegrown hits as Slings & Arrows , Michael: Tuesdays and Thursdays , and Sensitive Skin , the latter of which arrived via Don McKellar and Kim Cattrall, who are currently working together on a new series for Rhombus.

“We’re looking at the premium projects, with an added lens of commercial opportunities,” says Jennings. “Rhombus will certainly continue on their slate to be heavily feature films and the Skywild slate will continue to be heavily television, but there will be crossover between the two.”

Following Fichman’s close collaboration with Korean auteur Park on the Emmy-nominated series The Sympathizer , Rhombus is involved in developing a number of projects with the country’s top filmmakers, relationships that will benefit from the modernized audiovisual coproduction treaty that Ottawa signed with Seoul this past spring.

“There’s this crazy situation where I think we’re developing more Korean projects right now than anyone in Korea,” Fichman says.

The company is also currently in production on two promising new features: Child’s Play , a Canada-U.K. co-production directed by Chinese filmmaker Wang Xiaoshuai and starring Sandra Oh that is shooting in Toronto; and a yet-to-be-titled Toronto-set journalism thriller from Johnson, which stars Finn Wolfhard and is now in postproduction.

Still, one might think that after half a century spent at the top of his own company, Fichman might have a difficult time adjusting to a new hierarchy of sorts. Not so, according to the producer.

“I’m actually looking forward to having someone else help take responsibility, to be honest,” says Fichman. “But I’m ready. The time has come. I’m not hierarchical. In terms of making our year, I will still take responsibility for that. That’s my pride.”

“It also allows Niv to do the part that he’s very best at and most passionate of as a film producer,” adds Jennings. “It relieves him of the more day-to-day business parts of it. He’ll of course be a key element in the financing and the relationships and all of that. But we really will just offer the stability and runway in which Niv can do more of what he’s very best at.”
paragraphs: When Niv Fichman co-founded Rhombus Media in 1979, the Canadian film and television landscape was, while not exactly easy to navigate, at least somewhat predictable. With an initial focus on documentaries and films that pivoted around music ( Yo-Yo Ma: Inspired By Bach , Don Giovanni Unmasked ), the production company benefited from an era in which broadcasters like the CBC had serious money to spend on sales, and the Canadian Television Fund (now part of the Canada Media Fund) threw its weight behind performance-art projects.

Flash forward five decades, and Rhombus has managed to weather the tectonic shifts in the screen sector by going bigger and glitzier while never sacrificing its art-house bona fides, forging deep ties with top-tier filmmakers both domestic (Atom Egoyan, Matt Johnson, Brandon Cronenberg, Patricia Rozema) and foreign (Park Chan-wook, Andrew Haigh, Fernando Meirelles). And now, Fichman’s small but mighty powerhouse is entering an entirely new, somewhat unexpected chapter: acquisition.

On Tuesday, Skywild Pictures, the Toronto-based production company launched last year by industry veterans Angela Jennings and Travis Farncombe, announced that it has acquired Rhombus in the company’s bid to scale up its footprint in the global marketplace. Fichman will remain the lead producer of the company under the Skywild banner, while Rhombus’s longtime lead producers Fraser Ash and Kevin Krikst will join Skywild’s team as senior vice-president, content, and vice-president, production, respectively.

“One thing that’s crucial about this is that the Rhombus brand is retained, and it’s business as usual for us,” Fichman says in an interview alongside Jennings. “When Angela and I first got together and she spoke about what their creative goal is – and in these kinds of situations, how often do you talk about a creative goal? – we talked about creating high-end content with the highest-end Canadian creators and to take that to the world. If you look at our website, which no one does, but that’s basically what it says. We wrote each other’s creative mandate.”

The deal has the potential to significantly alter the country’s film and TV landscape, given Rhombus’s storied history and robust active-development slate. Fichman co-founded Rhombus with director Barbara Willis Sweete, and filmmaker Larry Weinstein joined shortly thereafter. That partnership, which came to include Sheena Macdonald, was officially dissolved in 2015, leaving Fichman to head the company solo, delivering such hits as Johnson’s 2023 comedy BlackBerry and Park’s 2024 HBO miniseries The Sympathizer . Skywild, meanwhile, is a self-financed and relatively untested outfit, albeit one with ambitious plans.

“Skywild has never been interested in being the biggest. But we want to be important, and that’s what Rhombus has been for so many years,” says Jennings, who was previously president of the production company MEM, which specialized in unscripted, reality and lifestyle entertainment. “While we have growth plans, it’s not about going out and acquiring a bunch of businesses. We’re looking to build organically, and this was such a hand-in-glove fit with what Niv and his team have built over the last 50 years.”

Both Fichman and Jennings insist that the deal was born not out of any kind of strategic zeal but happy and accidental timing, with the former noting that a mutual colleague initially connected the two companies.

“In my whole life I’ve never thought about acquisition, it just came very spontaneously. Here’s an emerging company that’s been developing projects with a voracious appetite, and here’s this company that’s very mature but with a need for someone like Angela who oversees things,” says Fichman. “We’ve run our company on a project-by-project basis. We’ve never had a one-year plan, let alone a five-year plan. We’ve never thought about maximizing this thing called growth. But the opportunity of having Angela come on board and seeing the potential of what we can do and the markets we can go to is great.”

Such expansions include further exploiting Rhombus’s catalogue of titles, which is rich in such Criterion-flavoured hits as The Red Violin and Thirty Two Short Films About Glenn Gould , as well as focusing attention on the company’s small-screen work, which has in the past yielded such homegrown hits as Slings & Arrows , Michael: Tuesdays and Thursdays , and Sensitive Skin , the latter of which arrived via Don McKellar and Kim Cattrall, who are currently working together on a new series for Rhombus.

“We’re looking at the premium projects, with an added lens of commercial opportunities,” says Jennings. “Rhombus will certainly continue on their slate to be heavily feature films and the Skywild slate will continue to be heavily television, but there will be crossover between the two.”

Following Fichman’s close collaboration with Korean auteur Park on the Emmy-nominated series The Sympathizer , Rhombus is involved in developing a number of projects with the country’s top filmmakers, relationships that will benefit from the modernized audiovisual coproduction treaty that Ottawa signed with Seoul this past spring.
“There’s this crazy situation where I think we’re developing more Korean projects right now than anyone in Korea,” Fichman says.

The company is also currently in production on two promising new features: Child’s Play , a Canada-U.K. co-production directed by Chinese filmmaker Wang Xiaoshuai and starring Sandra Oh that is shooting in Toronto; and a yet-to-be-titled Toronto-set journalism thriller from Johnson, which stars Finn Wolfhard and is now in postproduction.
Still, one might think that after half a century spent at the top of his own company, Fichman might have a difficult time adjusting to a new hierarchy of sorts. Not so, according to the producer.

“I’m actually looking forward to having someone else help take responsibility, to be honest,” says Fichman. “But I’m ready. The time has come. I’m not hierarchical. In terms of making our year, I will still take responsibility for that. That’s my pride.”

“It also allows Niv to do the part that he’s very best at and most passionate of as a film producer,” adds Jennings. “It relieves him of the more day-to-day business parts of it. He’ll of course be a key element in the financing and the relationships and all of that. But we really will just offer the stability and runway in which Niv can do more of what he’s very best at.”

stories.title: This Canadian company gives used EV batteries new life, but the pull of the U.S. is strong
stories.summary: Moment Energy offers an alternative solution to landfills or recycling plants
stories.author: Jared Lindzon
stories.content:
It’s a critical time for Canada’s economy and its business community. The country needs innovation and growth more than ever, yet businesses across a wide range of industries are facing trade disruptions, rising costs and technological change, among other challenges. This series profiles forward-thinking Canadian companies that are growing their markets by re-examining their business practices and trying new things.

Moment Energy is solving two of Canada’s biggest energy challenges but its CEO wonders if it will be able to reach its full potential without leaving the country.

Founded in 2019 by four Simon Fraser University engineering classmates, Vancouver-based Moment Energy helps divert used electric vehicle batteries away from landfills by repurposing them to solve local energy supply needs.

Properly disposing of a battery big enough to power a car can cost automakers thousands, and in places that don’t enforce sustainability standards – including Canada and most U.S. states – many are instead shipped to foreign landfills for a fraction of the cost.

“Recycling batteries is a very difficult process,” says Eddy Chiang, co-founder and chief executive officer. “You grind up these batteries into this black mass of materials and chemicals, and then hopefully refine the minerals out of it after.”

Moment Energy offers an alternative solution to landfills or recycling plants. Partnering automakers send batteries removed from EVs after the vehicle reaches its end-of-road-life – often from commercial fleets that swap out batteries once they’re no longer under warranty – with most retaining 70 to 90 per cent of their original capacity. Battery packs are dismantled and tested, and underperforming cells are removed. The remainder are reconfigured into modular racks and connected to Moment Energy’s AI-powered battery management system.

The repurposed batteries get a second life powering neighbourhoods, hospitals, manufacturing plants, airports and other places whose power needs aren’t being met by the existing grid.

Customers include power utilities that use the backup power to prevent blackouts, as well as end users such as the Vancouver International Airport, which uses Moment Energy’s battery energy storage system (Bess) to charge its fleet of electric vehicles. The system can store power at off-peak times when rates are low and discharge it during costly peak times.

Mr. Chiang explains that Canada’s energy infrastructure is over a century old and struggling to meet current demands, much less those of a more power-hungry future. Between artificial intelligence data centres, advanced manufacturing facilities and at-home EV charging stations, Canada is expected to fall short of its future energy needs.

Canada’s 2026 Budget commits more than $50-billion to doubling the country’s electricity grid capacity by 2050, but Mr. Chiang warns that meeting power demand in the near future will continue to be a challenge.

“Every neighborhood would actually require a $20-million upgrade, and we have thousands of neighborhoods in Canada,” he says. “We can power 190 homes with one battery that’s smaller than a parking stall for maybe a couple hundred thousand dollars.” That battery, which Mr. Chiang says will last up to 20 years, can store excess solar or wind energy, reduce the amount of power taken from the grid during peak times and provide a backup source in case of grid disruption. “I think that’s a pretty good deal.”

The company says that Bess can run a couple hours to several days without needing to recharge depending on the site and energy load.

Access to power is a significant challenge for the company, which ironically helps others solve their power needs. Building a battery repurposing plant requires access to a lot of energy, and while the company’s home province of B.C. produces some of the most affordable and sustainable energy on the continent, it’s not often available at the scale Moment Energy requires.

It’s one of the reasons the company has an EV battery repurposing “gigafactory” in Texas.

The Texas facility has 16,000 amps, compared to the 2,000 amps at the company’s Vancouver facility.

The lack of locations with sufficient power supply in Canada is a “massive hurdle for commercial manufacturers like us,” Mr. Chiang says.

The U.S. not only offered Moment Energy more energy, but also greater financial support. In 2024, the company was awarded more than US$20-million from the U.S. Department of Energy to fund its Texas gigafactory. On this side of the border, the Pacific Economic Development Agency of Canada has provided less than CAD$5-million in repayable loans.

Kaytlyn Barber, national lead for infrastructure, capital projects and sustainability at Kpmg Canada, says that access to affordable energy is becoming more of a challenge for companies in Canada “as we see the automation of many manufacturing businesses, growth in data centres and growth in how we’re using electricity.”

She adds, “The need for energy has never been greater, and we can’t get it online fast enough.”

According to a recent study conducted by Angus Reid on behalf of Kpmg, 41 per cent of Canadian manufacturers have already or are considering moving production to the U.S. When asked what would encourage them to remain, respondents cited access to cheaper energy alongside trade certainty and lower corporate taxes.

Despite those challenges, Ms. Barber says Canada still offers certain advantages, including a highly skilled workforce, a stable political environment, international trade partnerships, access to resources and expansive logistics capabilities.

“The autonomous and diversified energy grid that we have, the fact that we’re advancing significantly in nuclear, our access to abundant natural gas and hydro gives us a unique competitive advantage in terms of long-term affordability and sustainability,” she says.

For Mr. Chiang, keeping the company in Canada is a personal mission. He says his family hit the lottery twice; once when his single mother immigrated from China at the age of 25, and again when she was provided affordable housing in Vancouver.

Moment Energy has a strong desire to continue building the company on this side of the border but Mr. Chiang says the contrast in support and resources is hard to ignore.

“[The U.S.] had the building, the funding for us, and the friction has been essentially zero,” Mr. Chiang says. “The only reason why we’re doing this in Canada is because we’re just willing it to happen.”

stories.title: Judge gives break to highly violent Indigenous man, citing ‘colonialism’ and other factors
stories.summary: 'Criminality against vulnerable Indigenous women is a scourge on our society," whether by a stranger or someone known to them, says the B.C. Supreme Court
stories.author: Chris Lambie
stories.content:
A British Columbia judge has sentenced an Indigenous killer who attacked and threatened to kill his disabled female cousin to 20 months behind bars and two years’ probation, noting his “moral culpability is reduced” due to the systemic and background factors he’s faced.

Justin Arnet — who plead guilty to manslaughter in 2023 for beating his friend to death on the streets of Campbell River, B.C., in October 2000 — was found guilty in B.C. Supreme Court earlier this fall for assaulting his cousin, Tania Jack, threatening to kill her and obstructing a peace officer.

“Criminality against vulnerable Indigenous women is a scourge on our society, whether the person violating them is a stranger or someone known to them,” Justice Tina Dion, who is a member of the Kehewin Cree Nation, wrote in a Nov. 9 sentencing decision.

“In this case, Mr. Arnet knew his relative was street entrenched, drug addicted and disabled, yet he threatened her life and attacked her. His violence was gratuitous. It was shameful and cowardly.”

The attack on Jack was very serious, Dion said. But “the intergenerational trauma he experienced, combined with the impact of colonialism, influenced his upbringing such that he did not receive support, supervision or guidance,” said the decision, which notes “these experiences pushed him to alcohol and drug abuse and impacted his judgment.”

Arnet’s “moral culpability is reduced with his offending against Ms. Jack in the context of the systemic and background factors he has faced,” Dion said.

“Arnet has a criminal record of serious violence, which is alarming given his relatively youthful age of 35 years,” said the judge.

His moral blameworthiness is high, but it is also reduced on account of the systemic and background factors he has faced

Arnet and Jack “share in common their Indigenous community of Kyuquot located on northern Vancouver Island,” said the judge.

Arnet was on probation for attacking and robbing a different “sleeping vulnerable Indigenous woman,” in Campbell River in 2021 — punching her in the face, breaking her nose, and stealing her knapsack and phone — when he attacked Jack.

The court heard Arnet assaulted Jack in Campbell River’s downtown “in the early morning hours of April 14, 2025.”

The attack was captured on surveillance video.

“Mr. Arnet believed that Ms. Jack had taken some of his personal property earlier after he ‘went down’ from a suspected fentanyl overdose,” said the decision, which notes Arnet was revived with Narcan, which reverses life-threatening opioid overdoses.

Jack is “small in stature,” said the decision.

“She is drug addicted and is heavily street entrenched. She suffers from a significant disability on her neck, which causes her neck to hang; she walks with a hunch-like gait. She and others who are also vulnerable often stay and sleep in the downtown core of Campbell River, in part, because the services they utilize are located there.”

While standing over Jack, who was sitting on the ground, Arnet began shouting and threatening her, said the decision.

“He then attacked Ms. Jack using considerable force including twisting her arm behind her back. Although Ms. Jack tried to resist, she was no match for six-foot-tall Mr. Arnet, who flailed her about. While Ms. Jack was fearful Mr. Arnet would break her arm, it did not break, though it was sore and difficult for her to use for about a month.”

The judge “also found that Mr. Arnet kicked Ms. Jack at least once while she was down.”

Patrolling cops eventually arrested Arnet, who fled from them twice on foot.

The Crown argued he should get three and a half years in prison and two years of probation.

Arnet’s lawyer recommended a 120-day sentence and two years of probation.

Arnet is a member of the Kyuquot First Nation and his father is a member of the Michel First Nation, which is blended Iroquois, Cree and Métis.

His parents separated before he was born “due to substance misuse, his father’s criminality and his father’s violent behavior,” said the decision, which notes Arnet “stayed with his mother and their relationship was fractious and dysfunctional, with Mr. Arnet suffering mental and physical abuse.”

Arnet’s maternal grandparents “have experienced traumas,” said the decision, “they have struggled with alcohol and there has been violence in their relationship.”

His “grandmother went to Indian Day School and it is reported she spent a year tied to a bed at Nanaimo Indian hospital,” said the decision, without explaining further.

“Mr. Arnet’s grandfather was raised in the foster system and it is believed that he was an Indian Residential School Survivor.”

When he was 12 years old, Arnet “resisted house rules and he became increasingly oppositional and defiant,” said the decision. “Ultimately, Mr. Arnet’s mother sent him to live with his uncle and from there, he moved from family to family member.”

As he aged, Arnett “started working and abusing drugs and alcohol, which led to him a transient lifestyle.”

Gladue principles, set out in a Supreme Court of Canada decision, require sentencing judges to consider the unique circumstances of Indigenous offenders to address their over-representation in Canada’s prisons.

According to his Gladue report, Arnet “is an intergenerational survivor of the Indian residential school system.”

The author of Arnet’s Gladue report said he suffered from “family breakdown, emotional, verbal and physical abuse, unresolved trauma, maladaptive strategies impacting his sense of self-worth, interpersonal relationships and functional abilities. Additionally, low education, marginalized vocations, dislocation from paternal Aboriginal community and traditional supports. All of which has resulted in a loss of cultural identity, language, values, culture and ancestral knowledge.”

In 2023, Arnet pled guilty to manslaughter.

“He beat his male victim on the streets of Campbell River on October 15, 2020, after the men engaged in a verbal altercation started by the victim. The victim, who was intoxicated when he was beaten by Mr. Arnet, also hit his head after falling due to being struck, died a few days later.”

Arnet got a four-year jail sentence for the manslaughter conviction.

“He said that while he has been in custody, he has reflected on his use of violence in the past.”

It was an aggravating factor that Arnet “has an established pattern of committing offences against members of vulnerable or marginalized persons especially members of the Downtown Community,” said the judge.

“The only mitigating factor in this case is Mr. Arnet’s personal and intergenerational Gladue factors and the necessity to apply” a section of the Criminal Code that mandates all available sanctions other than imprisonment should be considered for Indigenous offenders, with a particular focus on restraint.

The Crown submitted that Arnet “has not been deterred even with the most recent sentence imposed in 2023, rather, he has continued his pattern of violence toward the most vulnerable of our society.”

The Crown was looking for “a strong message” to be sent to others “to dissuade them from similar conduct.”

According to the Crown, Arnet “must be separated from society. The community of Campbell River requires safety from him and his violent tendencies.”

The judge said that, in large part, she agrees with the Crown that Arnet “has demonstrated that he is not capable of restraining his violent impulses. However, I find Mr. Arnet has some insight into his offending, and he has taken some steps while in custody to address his reliance on violence as means of addressing problems he faces. His participation in at least one course to equip himself with coping mechanisms other than violence is commendable, but he clearly needs more.”

Three years behind bars is longer than needed, said the judge.

Dion agreed with Arnet’s lawyer that probation should be “just long enough” to re-integrate him back into the community and “give him some accountability and direction, for his own and the broader community’s benefit.”

Arnet didn’t have to serve any additional jail time because, after the judge applied the standard pre-trial custody credit, he’d already spent more than 20 months behind bars.

Chris Lambie is Atlantic bureau chief for National Post. He has worked for news organizations from Newfoundland to the Northwest Territories and is a three-time National Newspaper Award nominee, with a win for local reporting.

The judge said that, in large part, she agrees with the Crown that Arnet “has demonstrated that he is not capable of restraining his violent impulses. His participation in at least one course to equip himself with coping mechanisms other than violence is commendable, but he clearly needs more.”
Three years behind bars is longer than needed, said the judge.

Dion agreed with Arnet’s lawyer that probation should be “just long enough” to re-integrate him back into the community and “give him some accountability and direction, for his own and the broader community’s benefit.”
Arnet didn’t have to serve any additional jail time because, after the judge applied the standard pre-trial custody credit, he’d already spent more than 20 months behind bars.

stories.title: Francis vows fiscal restraint, housing growth in inaugural address as Windsor mayor
stories.summary: Across a speech of about 15 minutes, the new mayor outlined plans for the economy, housing, homelessness and transparency.
stories.author: Robert Lothian
stories.content:
Windsor Mayor Fred Francis plans to use his first term in the role to help see each part of the city flourish while ensuring all residents feel represented.

Francis shared the message as part of his inaugural address after being sworn in alongside members of council at the Capitol Theatre on Monday night.

Across a speech of about 15 minutes, the new mayor outlined plans for the economy, housing, homelessness and transparency.

“Let’s put politics aside, put people first and work together to deliver the future Windsor deserves. Our best days are still ahead of us,” Francis said.

A key point in the speech focused on fiscal responsibility without relying on large property tax increases and hikes to user fees.

Francis said the city will focus on spending and investing wisely, and seemingly took a shot at his predecessor, calling the “era of costly legacy projects” over.

“We must also build a city where people can afford to live, grow, and put down roots. That means making it easier to build housing, expanding affordable housing opportunities, and removing unnecessary barriers to development,” he said.

The development of the Fancsy Family Hospital and the Ojibway National Urban Park were specifically mentioned as projects Francis said they will look to support.

Francis takes the mayor’s office during a period of unease for Windsor amid ongoing trade disputes with the U.S., which have often centred on the manufacturing the city relies on.

Workers at the Windsor Assembly Plant have faced weeks of shutdowns, and owner Stellantis recently sold the Brampton Assembly Plant to a Canadian Defence Company.

“We will also recognize the economic uncertainty facing our community, particularly the challenges confronting our automotive sector. We will stand shoulder to shoulder with our autoworkers and use every tool available,” Francis said.

A key part of supporting the city’s economy has been through an emphasis on revitalizing Downtown Windsor.

The last term of city council adopted Strengthen the Core, a plan aimed at bringing new life to the downtown.

Francis believes the incoming council can help attract new businesses, fill empty storefronts and pursue a permanent downtown central library branch.

As part of efforts to draw more people downtown, Francis vowed increased neighbourhood policing, traffic enforcement, and safer streets.

He added council will also have to look to support those in need through accessible treatment, affordable housing, and support services.

“Compassion and public safety are not competing priorities, and we must deliver both,” Francis added.

On the campaign trail, Francis frequently said he would not use Strong Mayor Powers if elected. He delegated that authority to city council on Monday prior to the inauguration.

“I do not view members of council as competition. I view them as partners in leadership, each bringing different experiences, perspectives and ideas to the table in pursuit of a stronger Windsor,” he added.

The new term of Windsor City Council will hold its first regular meeting on Nov. 23.
