stories.title: ‘There is no easy solution’: A counter-drone system failed at this Canadian military base, reports show
stories.summary: Unidentified drones have been spotted over Canadian military bases, highlighting a potential defence gap that could be exploited to launch attacks or gather intelligence.
stories.author: Daniel Otis
stories.content:
When an unauthorized drone was spotted over one of Canada’s busiest air force bases, a new counter-drone system completely failed to detect it, according to a report obtained through an access to information request. With the drone operator remaining unidentified, experts say the September 2025 incident from CFB Trenton highlights a potential defence gap that could be exploited to attack or gather intelligence on the Canadian military.

“There’s no doubt that our adversaries have capabilities to cause us significant harm and we do not have the capabilities to deal with that,” retired Royal Canadian Air Force (Rcaf) lieutenant-general Christopher Coates told CTVNews.CA from Ottawa.

Rcaf reports obtained by CTVNews.CA through an access to information request detail seven similar cases from 2024 and 2025 at both CFB Trenton in Ontario and CFB Cold Lake in Alberta. Arguably two of the most important air bases in Canada, Trenton houses essential transport aircraft like the CC-177 Globemaster III while Cold Lake is home to a significant part of Canada’s CF-18 fighter jet fleet. In all seven cases, the reports show that there were no attempts to intercept the drones and their operators were never identified.

Coates previously served as the deputy commander and highest ranking Canadian at Norad, the joint Canada-U.S. continental defence group. He is now the director of foreign policy, national defence and national security at the Macdonald-Laurier Institute, a public policy think tank.

“To really affect Canada and our military, you don’t need to attack a base or the aircraft or the ships, you can attack dependent infrastructure,” Coates explained. “So electrical distribution and transmission networks, the transportation system, resupply systems – they’re all soft, none of them are protected.”

Some of the incidents identified by CTVNews.CA also roughly coincide with a wave of drone incursions across Europe , which have caused major disruptions at military facilities as well as airports and critical infrastructure sites like nuclear power plants.

While Coates is not aware of any evidence linking the Canadian cases to potentially hostile actors like Russia, he and others say Canada needs to be better prepared to deal with the potential threat even if adversaries are not currently showing intent.

“Drones are the ideal tools for sabotage operations because they can allow perpetrators to operate remotely and make attribution significantly more difficult,” Toronto-based Ukrainian defence analyst Olena Kryzhanivska told CTVNews.CA.

“I believe that the risk of hostile actors using drones to cause damage or gather intelligence in Canada is significant.”

Kryzhanivska is the author of Ukraine’s Arms Monitor , where she writes extensively about drone warfare and technology, which is evolving rapidly and redefining the battlefield in Russia’s war against Ukraine.

“These threats are not limited to military facilities,” Kryzhanivska added. “They could affect Canada’s broader security and defence infrastructure, as well as civilian sectors.”

The Cold Lake and Trenton cases

The four reports from CFB Cold Lake all detail military personnel spotting unauthorized drones in restricted airspace, including one that travelled at an estimated speed of 60 to 100 km/h that “was observed to be boxy in shape, approximately 60cm in width, emitting what appeared to be a yellowish light with no sound from it heard.”

Another – described as a small white drone carrying a “black tube” – apparently made two appearances at CFB Cold Lake within four days in September 2025. Those were the most recent Cold Lake reports uncovered by CTVNews.CA, and they plainly state that the base “does not currently have a means of tracking small UAS aircraft.” UAS is short for unmanned (or uncrewed) aircraft system.

At CFB Trenton, the first of the three reports reviewed by CTVNews.CA mention that the base was about to become one of the first military airfields in Canada to be equipped with counter-drone technology.

“The system will be a detection only system until the magnitude of the risk is realized,” the September 2024 report explains. “Numerous legal hurtles [sic] exist preventing the use of a counter-UAS system that could be used to destroy, neutralize or take control of a UAS.”

The reports say that system became operational in March 2025. But when a camera-equipped drone buzzed the base’s runway on Sept. 17, 2025, the system was offline due to a planned power outage.

The power, however, was on just days later during another drone sighting on Sept. 22, 2025, but according to a report, the “counter UAS system did not detect the drone.” On the same day across the Atlantic, unidentified drones led to serious disruptions at a military base in France and airports in Denmark and Norway, according to a drone incident tracker .

The Trenton reports note that signs around the base warn the public that “that operating drones in the vicinity of the airfield is prohibited.” They also mention that no civilian drone flights were authorized at the time of these incidents.

In a statement to CTVNews.CA, Canada’s Department of National Defence declined to comment on any of the cases mentioned in this article or any of its counter-drone measures.

“We can’t comment further for operational and security reasons,” a National Defence spokesperson said via email. “DND/CAF does not comment on current or planned security measures, operational capabilities, threat assessments, vulnerabilities, incidents, specific locations, or deployment plans.”

‘There is no silver-bullet solution’

Experts say creating and deploying an effective counter-drone system is easier said than done

“It’s not that somebody hasn’t done their job and gone out and bought what’s required,” former RCMP officer and counter-drone specialist Brian Fentiman told CTVNews.CA. “It’s this is a very complex problem and that there is no easy solution.”

Fentiman is the president and CEO of BlueForce UAV Consulting Inc., a Comox, B.C.-based company that specializes in drone and counter-drone training and consulting for clients like Canadian airports and law enforcement agencies.

“Let’s face it, no military in the world really thought drones were a big threat until the last couple of years and now everybody’s scrambling,” Fentiman said. “It really needs to be a multi-faceted approach because what you’re going to do domestically for installations in Canada is not going to be the same thing that you’re going to do in either the theatre of war or in a conflict zone, where you have more kinetic options.”

To be effective, counter-drone systems need to be able to detect, track, identify and engage potential threats. Detection, tracking and identification systems can include radar, radio frequency, optical and acoustic sensors, as well as AI tools.

Taking out or disabling a drone can utilize electronic warfare systems like radio frequency or GPS jammers, or kinetic methods such as nets, interceptor drones, projectiles like bullets or missiles, or even directed-energy weapons that use lasers or high-powered microwaves.

Simply put, it’s not as simple as aiming and pulling the trigger on a counter-drone jammer gun.

“If you just jam the control link, most drones are programmed so that they’ll just come back to where they took off from,” Fentiman explained. “People that have nefarious intent can also program their drone so that it flies to a target area if its control signal gets interrupted.”

In Ukraine, where drone warfare is rapidly evolving, Kryzhanivska notes that drones are now utilizing fibre-optic cables and autonomous capabilities that can allow them to operate despite attempts at electronic interference.

“Broadly speaking, it is a constant cat-and-mouse game,” Kryzhanivska said. “The main lesson is that there is no silver-bullet solution capable of countering every type of drone threat.”

While the Canadian military is authorized to use an array of tools to engage drones in operational settings like Canada’s mission in Latvia, doing so on Canadian soil is an entirely different matter. As one of the reports from CFB Trenton notes, there remain significant domestic legal and regulatory hurdles when it comes to downing a drone in domestic contexts, especially with kinetic options like live ammunition or interceptor drones.

But recent exemptions to the Radiocommunication Act now allow jammers to be used by the military as well as certain correctional services and law enforcement agencies in specific instances such as national security and protecting people and property from serious harm.

In addition to deploying a range of new technologies and making regulatory changes, Fentiman says creating effective counter-drone measures also requires new procedures and protocols that are aimed at minimizing collateral damage and defining acceptable risks when intercepting drones near civilian areas.

“If you do hit it, if all you do is damage it slightly, you’re sending it into a residential area,” Fentiman said. “So a lot of work has to be going into what is acceptable risk. … It’s a very complex problem to make that assessment.”

‘Improvements are still needed’

The Department of National Defence and the Canadian Armed Forces are actively looking to fill these gaps. This year, the department has issued counter-drone procurement notices and launched the Defence Drone Initiative , which in part will “explore affordable systems that could detect, track or defeat hostile drones” in order to “contribute to the protection of military personnel, installations and infrastructure.” Released on Nov. 7, the federal government’s latest budget proposes $2.3 billion over five years for advancing the Canadian military’s drone and counter-drone capabilities.

“C-UAS capabilities are a critical consideration in modern security and defence planning,” a National Defence spokesperson told CTVNews.CA. “DND has procurement activities planned to support the continued evolution and enhancement of its approach to countering UAS threats, building on existing measures and capabilities.”

While such systems are already being deployed in Latvia and at Canadian naval ports and air bases, the reports obtained by CTVNews.CA highlight that more work needs to be done.

Salt, whose research includes drone warfare, says potential adversaries could use commercially available and legally acquired drones to conduct surveillance and even sabotage at bases and critical infrastructure sites in Canada. Salt says “the threat is very real, and very urgent and requires immediate action.”

“There is no one technological solution, so Canada will have to invest and procure broadly to cover its bets in this area,” Salt added. “Essentially, the Canadian military, like many of its allies needs to work quickly to ‘harden’ its bases and infrastructure against potential future threats in this area.”

In a statement to CTVNews.CA, Canada’s Department of National Defence declined to comment on any of the cases mentioned in this article or any of its counter-drone measures.

“We can’t comment further for operational and security reasons,” a National Defence spokesperson said via email. “DND/CAF does not comment on current or planned security measures, operational capabilities, threat assessments, vulnerabilities, incidents, specific locations, or deployment plans.”
‘There is no silver-bullet solution’
Experts say creating and deploying an effective counter-drone system is easier said than done

“It’s not that somebody hasn’t done their job and gone out and bought what’s required,” former RCMP officer and counter-drone specialist Brian Fentiman told CTVNews.CA. “It’s this is a very complex problem and that there is no easy solution.”

Fentiman is the president and CEO of BlueForce UAV Consulting Inc., a Comox, B.C.-based company that specializes in drone and counter-drone training and consulting for clients like Canadian airports and law enforcement agencies.

“Let’s face it, no military in the world really thought drones were a big threat until the last couple of years and now everybody’s scrambling,” Fentiman said. “It really needs to be a multi-faceted approach because what you’re going to do domestically for installations in Canada is not going to be the same thing that you’re going to do in either the theatre of war or in a conflict zone, where you have more kinetic options.”

To be effective, counter-drone systems need to be able to detect, track, identify and engage potential threats. Detection, tracking and identification systems can include radar, radio frequency, optical and acoustic sensors, as well as AI tools.

Taking out or disabling a drone can utilize electronic warfare systems like radio frequency or GPS jammers, or kinetic methods such as nets, interceptor drones, projectiles like bullets or missiles, or even directed-energy weapons that use lasers or high-powered microwaves.
Simply put, it’s not as simple as aiming and pulling the trigger on a counter-drone jammer gun.

“If you just jam the control link, most drones are programmed so that they’ll just come back to where they took off from,” Fentiman explained. “People that have nefarious intent can also program their drone so that it flies to a target area if its control signal gets interrupted.”

In Ukraine, where drone warfare is rapidly evolving, Kryzhanivska notes that drones are now utilizing fibre-optic cables and autonomous capabilities that can allow them to operate despite attempts at electronic interference.
“Broadly speaking, it is a constant cat-and-mouse game,” Kryzhanivska said. “The main lesson is that there is no silver-bullet solution capable of countering every type of drone threat.”

While the Canadian military is authorized to use an array of tools to engage drones in operational settings like Canada’s mission in Latvia, doing so on Canadian soil is an entirely different matter. As one of the reports from CFB Trenton notes, there remain significant domestic legal and regulatory hurdles when it comes to downing a drone in domestic contexts, especially with kinetic options like live ammunition or interceptor drones.

But recent exemptions to the Radiocommunication Act now allow jammers to be used by the military as well as certain correctional services and law enforcement agencies in specific instances such as national security and protecting people and property from serious harm.

In addition to deploying a range of new technologies and making regulatory changes, Fentiman says creating effective counter-drone measures also requires new procedures and protocols that are aimed at minimizing collateral damage and defining acceptable risks when intercepting drones near civilian areas.

“If you do hit it, if all you do is damage it slightly, you’re sending it into a residential area,” Fentiman said. “So a lot of work has to be going into what is acceptable risk. … It’s a very complex problem to make that assessment.”
‘Improvements are still needed’

The Department of National Defence and the Canadian Armed Forces are actively looking to fill these gaps. This year, the department has issued counter-drone procurement notices and launched the Defence Drone Initiative , which in part will “explore affordable systems that could detect, track or defeat hostile drones” in order to “contribute to the protection of military personnel, installations and infrastructure.” Released on Nov. 7, the federal government’s latest budget proposes $2.3 billion over five years for advancing the Canadian military’s drone and counter-drone capabilities.

“C-UAS capabilities are a critical consideration in modern security and defence planning,” a National Defence spokesperson told CTVNews.CA. “DND has procurement activities planned to support the continued evolution and enhancement of its approach to countering UAS threats, building on existing measures and capabilities.”
While such systems are already being deployed in Latvia and at Canadian naval ports and air bases, the reports obtained by CTVNews.CA highlight that more work needs to be done.

Salt, whose research includes drone warfare, says potential adversaries could use commercially available and legally acquired drones to conduct surveillance and even sabotage at bases and critical infrastructure sites in Canada. Salt says “the threat is very real, and very urgent and requires immediate action.”

“There is no one technological solution, so Canada will have to invest and procure broadly to cover its bets in this area,” Salt added. “Essentially, the Canadian military, like many of its allies needs to work quickly to ‘harden’ its bases and infrastructure against potential future threats in this area.”

stories.title: Manitoba throne speech to include ban on AI images in real estate
stories.summary: Winnipeg - The Manitoba government is set to outline its plans for the upcoming election year in today's throne speech.
stories.author: Ian Bickis The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Winnipeg - The Manitoba government rolled out promises Tuesday focused on health care and seniors, and hinted at a middle-class tax cut, in what it said would be the last throne speech before next year’s provincial election.

Commitments include reopening the Victoria Hospital emergency room in Winnipeg’s south end by next summer and another in the Eriksdale hospital, north of the city, by next fall.

The province said it’s also taking next steps to rebuild ERs at Seven Oaks and Concordia hospitals in Winnipeg and to start construction on a new CancerCare headquarters.

The Manitoba government rolled out promises focused on health care and seniors, and hinted at a middle-class tax cut, in what it said would be the last throne speech before next year’s provincial election. Commitments include reopening Winnipeg’s Victoria General Hospital emergency room by summer and offering the shingles vaccine for free for seniors. (Nov. 17, 2026)

It said the shingles vaccine, which can cost at least $300 for the required two doses, would be free for seniors next summer. And it’s expanding home care with a pilot project.

However, one of the biggest commitments remained vague, with Premier Wab Kinew saying that a broad, middle-class tax cut is coming in the next budget.

“We’ve taken some steps since taking office, cutting the gas tax, freezing hydro rates to help, taking the tax off of our groceries. But we know we’ve got to do more,” he said at a press conference ahead of the throne speech.

While the premier promised a “mega deduction” for families, he said balancing the budget remains the top priority.

“The number 1 thing we can do to help with affordability is balancing the books. If you don’t balance the budget, the government’s always going to be coming back and asking for more, and that’s not fair.”

The government said it would also establish an independent provincial disability advocate and that it has already created a new legislative assistant role focused on seniors’ care.

There were also consumer protection promises, including a ban on the use of artificial intelligence in real estate and stores being required to display unit prices.

To boost the economy, the government said it would match a major tax deduction on capital investment rolled out by the federal government. It has also appointed Stacy Kennedy as the province’s chief mining officer to help speed up resource development.

The government said it would establish a white-collar crime unit and hire more Crown attorneys.

It’s also going to freeze Crown land leases for a fourth year.

The NDP government’s promises don’t amount to much, said Opposition Progressive Conservative Leader Konrad Narth.

“There’s a whole lot of nothing there. No substance of anything new.

“It’s basically the (2023) election campaign reiterated.”

Narth said the government hasn’t said how it will address affordability — compared with the PCs’ plan to raise the tax-exempt amount of income to $30,000 — and that wait times in health care continue to grow.

Dr. Alon Altman, president of Doctors Manitoba, said Kinew’s government is focused heavily on adding health-care staff to address wait times, touting a 4,700 increase in staff in the last three years.

But more needs to be done, he said.

“We’re still short on physicians. We’re about 25 per cent short of the national average for emergency physicians.”

Altman said he was glad to see the continued focus on health care but disappointed there wasn’t more mentioned about furthering retention and recruitment.

Darlene Jackson, president of the Manitoba Nurses Union, said it was especially concerning not to hear any mention of funding for nurse-to-patient ratios.

“It was very disappointing that there was no dedicated funding for that project to at least start being implemented.”

She said having staff managing an appropriate number of patients is a critical part of keeping nurses and recruiting more.

Adding more nurses will also be crucial for the province to move forward on its plans to open ERs, said Jackson.

“They’re talking about opening emergencies all over, and until they actually bolster the staffing, I don’t see how they’re going to open ERs. Because what they’re going do is rob Peter to pay Paul. It’s going to be a shell game. Nurses just moving from one facility to another.”

Kinew said the government has been working to build up health-care staffing after cuts from the previous Tory government, and that it’s only now reaching staffing levels to be able to follow through on its 2023 election campaign commitment to reopen the Victoria ER.

“It’s very meaningful for our team. It’s a signature promise,” he said.

“We need to continue hiring more staff to keep up with population growth, but we know that we’ve hit a point where we have the human resources in place where we can move ahead.”

To help pay for those investments in health care, the government is also working to boost business and the economy, said Kinew.

The throne speech didn’t provide much new on that front, said Loren Remillard, CEO of the Winnipeg Chamber of Commerce.

“It’s a pre-election throne speech, capturing more of what the government has done as opposed to what it will do moving forward.”

He said the tax incentive would put Manitoba more on the map for companies considering where to build big projects. But he hopes to see more in the spring budget to address the province’s low gross domestic product growth and overreliance on government spending.

“We’re really hoping the ensuing budget and campaign will bring that focus to our economy that’s so needed.”

The election is scheduled for Oct. 5, 2027, but Kinew has hinted that it could happen sooner.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 17, 2026.

stories.title: Sunshine returns as temperatures climb into double digits
stories.summary: Waking up to foggy patches Tuesday morning, but sunshine breaks through for the rest of the day.
stories.author: Fiona Robertson
stories.content:
Waking up to foggy patches Tuesday morning, but sunshine breaks through for the rest of the day.

“Beautiful mix of sun and cloud … 11 degrees this afternoon. We’re back into the double digits,” said CTV News London Meteorologist Julie Atchison. “A nice mix of sun and cloud to mainly sunny conditions by a sunset.”

Atchison says clear skies, dry air, and a high pressure system is taking hold.

“It’ll set up shop along the eastern seaboard and that means sunshine and days of it in the upper air pattern,” she added.

Temperatures stay above average with plenty of sunny days ahead in the seven-day forecast.

Here’s a look at the rest of the forecast

Tuesday: A mix of sun and cloud. Becoming sunny in the afternoon. Fog patches dissipating in the morning. Wind southwest 20 km/h becoming light early in the afternoon. High 10.

Tuesday night: Clear. Low zero.

Wednesday: Sunny. High 12.

Thursday: Sunny. High 13.

Friday: Sunny. High 14.

Saturday: Sunny. High 13.

Sunday: Cloudy with 30 per cent chance of showers. High 9.

stories.title: Manitoba names first chief mining officer as province looks to accelerate growth
stories.summary: Stacy Kennedy leaves director role at Vale for new position
stories.author: Temur Durrani
stories.content:
Industry stalwart Stacy Kennedy will become Manitoba’s first chief mining officer, as the provincial government aims to aggressively expand the pace of mineral-production projects and shipping corridors such as the northern Port of Churchill.

Ms. Kennedy will start in the new role for a five-year term on Tuesday, Premier Wab Kinew told The Globe and Mail ahead of a Throne Speech outlining Manitoba’s legislative agenda.

The 49-year-old brings nearly 20 years of experience at Vale Base Metals Ltd., the Toronto-headquartered subsidiary of global mining giant Vale S.A., where she became the first female director of their Manitoba operations. In addition, she was also the first female president of the provincial mining association. She’s leaving both roles for the new position.

Mr. Kinew said Ms. Kennedy will continue to be based in Thompson, a Manitoba hub nicknamed the Nickel City for its historic connection to the mining sector. She will report directly to the Premier, working tangentially albeit separately from Jamie Moses, Manitoba’s Minister of Business, Mining, Trade and Job Creation.

“I want her to be on the ground, running things from where the action is,” Mr. Kinew said. “We’ve got a big goal, a big ambition, and now we’ve got somebody with a big skill set to match.”

Ms. Kennedy’s appointment signifies a unique shift in nomenclature. No other province in Canada has a chief mining officer, a title that is typically only used in the private sector.

Since becoming Prime Minister last year, Mark Carney has introduced similar roles in Ottawa. His governance model has created a parallel network of arm’s-length offices with funds and agency styled in the fashion of corporate enterprises. That includes his new chief executive officers of the Major Projects Office, Build Canada Homes and the Defence Investment Agency.

In Manitoba, Mr. Kinew, who has maintained a particularly collaborative relationship with Mr. Carney, had thus far emphasized restoring morale within the province’s public service model rather than building another layer of operations.

But as he heads closer to next year’s provincial election, which will be held on or before Oct. 5, Mr. Kinew’s plans for “nation-building projects” through public-private partnerships are becoming a cornerstone of his campaign. Hiring Ms. Kennedy is part of that, Mr. Kinew acknowledged.

The Premier hinted last week at a New Democratic Party event that he may call a Manitoba election in the spring instead of next fall. He declined to confirm any election dates when asked about the matter on Monday.

“I’ll say this: If somebody with the calibre of Stacy Kennedy becomes available to you, you jump at the chance to hire her regardless of what’s going on with the electoral cycle,” Mr. Kinew said.

Ms. Kennedy has travelled alongside the provincial government’s delegations on several trade-related trips, including to the U.S., and for conferences such as the Canada Investment Summit this past fall.

She will be paid a $325,000-a-year salary, and Manitoba is allocating $5-million a year for her new department as part of its provincial budget “to help speed up the work around mining development,” Mr. Kinew said.

One of Ms. Kennedy’s priorities will be to identify bureaucratic hurdles, so that red tape on government regulations can be reduced, Mr. Kinew said. She will also be “instrumental” in Manitoba’s bid to construct a new pipeline to the Hudson Bay region, where Mr. Carney has given Manitoba a target of shipping liquefied natural gas from Churchill by 2030 , he added.

Ms. Kennedy told The Globe she was considering other positions in the private sector before Mr. Kinew took her for a walk recently and spoke to her about the role.

“I asked her: ‘Do you want to marginally increase value for some shareholders out there, or do you want to make Manitoba the best mining jurisdiction in the entire world?’” Mr. Kinew said.

Ms. Kennedy said it was a profound question and one she hopes to incorporate in her new mission – especially as the Premier has pledged to triple provincial mineral production within the next five years by expanding Manitoba’s potash, gold, silica and other mining facilities.

“I hope we do it much faster than that,” she said. “Manitoba has tremendous unrealized potential and we’re here to unlock it.”

stories.title: After 15 years of south-of-the-border success, designer Tanya Taylor is coming home
stories.summary: Since 2012, designer Tanya Taylor has built her optimistic fashion brand in New York. Now, she debuts her first Canadian boutique
stories.author: Randi Bergman
stories.content:
“Where are all the women designers?” It’s become one of fashion’s most persistent questions. Across the industry’s biggest brands, women are conspicuously absent from the top creative jobs. In last year’s vast reshuffling of creative directors across 15 major luxury houses, only two of the incoming designers were women.

That representation gap couldn’t feel further removed from Tanya Taylor’s world. At her headquarters near New York’s Union Square, the 40-year-old founder has created a veritable sanctuary for more than 40 employees, 90 per cent of whom identify as women. Part workplace, part sorority, the airy, loft-like office is where they map out the future of Taylor’s brand, including its first retail space in her hometown, Toronto.

I first speak with Taylor in late August, and she’s at her desk in full multi-tasking mode. It’s the crunch before New York Fashion Week, where she will present her spring 2027 collection, and just days before her two sons head back to school. “There are five people doing a fire drill outside my door right now,” she says. “It’s a grind.”

When this magazine first profiled her a decade ago, Taylor was riding a wave of wins for her colourful, patterned ready-to-wear. Michelle Obama, then the First Lady, had just worn a floral dress she designed to a White House holiday party. The year prior, Taylor was one of 10 finalists for the prestigious Cfda/Vogue Fashion Fund. Those milestones, which can feel momentous for a fledgling brand, seem miles away from what she’s been able to accomplish since. “I was so excited and grateful for that initial buzz. But what I’ve learned since then is that celebrities don’t make brands, and mentors in the industry don’t necessarily make brands,” she says. “An obsession with the customer makes brands.”

Taylor’s customers, who shop her line at 120 retailers across North America, are women that lead multifaceted lives. They connect with Taylor through bright, popping hues and silhouettes designed to work on a range of body types, and the confidence boost her clothes can create. “Over the last 10 years, I’ve added a real lens of reality to how we make clothes that are flattering,” she says. “I want women who’ve had babies and feel differently about their bodies to be able to wear our clothes and feel great.”

That practicality has come, in part, from maturity and motherhood changing her own preferences, but also from an obsession with the first-hand feedback and shopper data that influence what the brand offers. Taylor’s signature styles, often made from a forgiving stretch satin-crepe polyester blend, are sleek, joyful and, above all, easy to wear. “I live in the West Village, my kids go to school on the Upper East Side and I’m on the subway three times a day. I’m absorbing so much fun information,” she says.

That attention to how women actually dress leads Taylor to new endeavours. In 2024, she launched Delphine, an evening wear line that offers her clients options for big moments like weddings, cocktail parties and galas. In September, she expanded into handbags and shoes that capture the sense of colour and play at the heart of her main line’s clothing pieces.

To start the creative process for her spring 2027 foray into accessories, Taylor and her team looked to her personal archive of 200 handbags. “We laid them out on my living-room floor and obvious patterns started rising to the top,” she says. Bucket bags emerged as something of an obsession. “I always buy bucket bags. I’m a bucket-bag psychopath,” Taylor says. The fixation inspired a series of mini buckets that double as sculptural wristlets and come in an array of flower petal shades. One standout version, a yellow mini with an olive-green wrist strap, is embroidered with mother-of-pearl discs. A zebra-striped raffia shoulder bag transforms into an evening clutch when its strap is removed. Taylor’s signature silks and love of texture carry through the collection, which pairs supple Nappa leather with silk, raffia and linen.

The shoes are designed in similarly vibrant patterns – think a kitten-heel, brown-and-yellow polka-dot mule finished with a lavender bow. They’re made in collaboration with Montreal-based Black Suede Studio, a footwear label with its own devoted following.

Taylor has been based in the U.S. since studying at the Parsons School of Design in the mid-2000s, and her Canadian fan base has held strong despite fluctuating exchange rates and political temperatures. They find her online, through Canadian retailers like TNT and shopping south of the border at the brand’s boutiques on Madison Avenue on Manhattan’s Upper East Side, and in Greenwich, Connecticut. To navigate trade uncertainty, Taylor’s brand now ships to Canadian customers directly from its factories rather than routing orders through the U.S. The shift brings Canadian prices within about 10 per cent of what U.S. consumers pay, but a brick-and-mortar experience has been missing. “It has been a long time since Toronto customers have had access to the full expression of the brand,” she says.

Enter her Toronto boutique, which opened in Summerhill in October. “It was fun to find a store that felt a little off the beaten path,” she says of the residence-style space. She’s part of an influx of ambitious retail in the neighbourhood. Once best known for its strip of ritzy grocers and a sprinkling of fashion options including Smythe and the Roots Outpost store, the area is brimming with openings this season, including Absolutely Fabrics’ sprawling concept space and the first boutique from Body of Work, the design-forward athleisure brand. “I know many of the people who live in the neighbourhood, can see their patterns and want to be part of it,” she says.

Taylor’s strong Toronto ties also include a fashion program she co-created for students at her alma mater, Havergal College. And she co-founded Baby Love, an organization that manufactures and distributes diapers to Toronto families in need. What began with diapers collected in her friend’s basement during the pandemic has grown into an organization that has produced three million of its own, supporting 75,000 families and rallying fellow female-founded Canadian businesses, including Knix and Nutbar, around the cause.

It’s initiatives like these that keep her grounded through an unprecedented moment in cross-border relations. “I’m proud of the Americans who are standing up for Canadians,” she says. “I have friends in politics, and their general sentiment is that these are our neighbours, they deserve loyalty and North America only works through that partnership. Hearing that makes me happy.”

For Taylor, the Summerhill opening feels less like another step toward retail growth and more like a meaningful return to the city that shaped her – and perhaps the beginning of a more permanent homecoming. “I love Canada,” she says. “And definitely want to be back at some point in my life.”

They find her online, through Canadian retailers like TNT and shopping south of the border at the brand’s boutiques on Madison Avenue on Manhattan’s Upper East Side, and in Greenwich, Connecticut. To navigate trade uncertainty, Taylor’s brand now ships to Canadian customers directly from its factories rather than routing orders through the U.S. The shift brings Canadian prices within about 10 per cent of what U.S. consumers pay, but a brick-and-mortar experience has been missing. “It has been a long time since Toronto customers have had access to the full expression of the brand,” she says.

Enter her Toronto boutique, which opened in Summerhill in October. “It was fun to find a store that felt a little off the beaten path,” she says of the residence-style space. She’s part of an influx of ambitious retail in the neighbourhood. Once best known for its strip of ritzy grocers and a sprinkling of fashion options including Smythe and the Roots Outpost store, the area is brimming with openings this season, including Absolutely Fabrics’ sprawling concept space and the first boutique from Body of Work, the design-forward athleisure brand. “I know many of the people who live in the neighbourhood, can see their patterns and want to be part of it,” she says.

Taylor’s strong Toronto ties also include a fashion program she co-created for students at her alma mater, Havergal College. And she co-founded Baby Love, an organization that manufactures and distributes diapers to Toronto families in need. What began with diapers collected in her friend’s basement during the pandemic has grown into an organization that has produced three million of its own, supporting 75,000 families and rallying fellow female-founded Canadian businesses, including Knix and Nutbar, around the cause.

It’s initiatives like these that keep her grounded through an unprecedented moment in cross-border relations. “I’m proud of the Americans who are standing up for Canadians,” she says. “I have friends in politics, and their general sentiment is that these are our neighbours, they deserve loyalty and North America only works through that partnership. Hearing that makes me happy.”

For Taylor, the Summerhill opening feels less like another step toward retail growth and more like a meaningful return to the city that shaped her – and perhaps the beginning of a more permanent homecoming. “I love Canada,” she says. “And definitely want to be back at some point in my life.”

stories.title: Religious symbols ban for Quebec schoolchildren? Conservatives leave door open
stories.summary: Quebec Conservative Leader Eric Duhaime is leaving the door open to supporting the PQ government's plan to extend a religious symbols ban to elementary school students.
stories.author: Alessia Simona Maratta, Dan Spector
stories.content:
Conservative Leader Eric Duhaime is leaving the door open to supporting the Parti Québécois government’s proposal to extend a ban on religious symbols to elementary school students.

The minority PQ government will need support from opposition parties to advance its agenda, and Duhaime indicated his party could potentially support the proposed expansion while saying Conservatives first want more details about how it would work.

“Generally speaking, we’re in favour, you know, of living in a secular society,” Duhaime said.

The proposal would go further than the previous Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ) government’s ban on religious symbols for some public-sector workers, which sparked outrage from civil rights groups and a legal challenge that has reached the Supreme Court.

The new PQ government has promised to extend the ban to elementary school students.

Duhaime said his party sees a connection between restrictions on religious symbols for public-sector workers and the proposed rules for children in schools.

“The link is that we want to banish religious symbols in the public space, especially within public institutions,” he said.

Duhaime also pointed specifically to young girls wearing veils at school. “Like everyone else, we feel uneasy seeing a young girl arrive at school with a veil on her head,” he said Monday.

But Duhaime stopped short of committing his party’s support, saying Conservatives want to know how such a ban would be implemented.

“How are we gonna implement that? Who is going to be responsible? What’s the process?” he said. “We want the details before we have a clear stand.”

Both the Liberals and Québec solidaire (QS) have said they would vote against the proposal.

The possibility of extending the religious symbols ban to children is drawing criticism from the English Montreal School Board and civil rights groups.

Joe Ortona, chair of the English Montreal School Board, said legislating what children can wear would cross a line.

He argued the debate is also distracting from other issues facing the education system. “It’s just inappropriate and I think we’ve completely lost focus on the fact that there are real systemic ongoing problems in education.”

Civil rights groups are also calling on the Conservatives to reject the PQ proposal.

“This is really a new low and I think everyone should really be just as outraged as we are that the government would sink this low,” said Harini Sivalinga of the Canadian Civil Liberties Association.

Stephen Brown of the National Council of Canadian Muslims questioned what the proposed expansion could mean for children who wear religious symbols.

“Are we really, in Quebec, going to go down the road of watching kids being denied entry to math class because they’re wearing a turban or a kippah?” Brown said.

The debate comes as the Supreme Court’s decision on Bill 21 is expected in the coming weeks.

stories.title: After 7 years in Canada, young student faces deportation
stories.summary: A young student who has spent seven years in Canada is facing deportation as her classmates and teachers push the federal government to intervene.
stories.author: Alessia Simona Maratta, Phil Carpenter
stories.content:
Students and faculty at Dawson College in Montreal are rallying around a young student who has been ordered to leave Canada with her family by the end of December, arguing she should at least be allowed to finish her studies before being deported.

Luisa Juliana Chaves Munoz said her family received a deportation notice on Oct. 15, seven years after they arrived in Canada from Colombia seeking asylum.

The family’s asylum claim was denied. Munoz said they initially came to Canada because of violence and death threats against her mother.

Her teachers and fellow students are now calling on the federal government to intervene, arguing the way her deportation is being handled is inhumane and questioning why she cannot remain in Canada long enough to complete her studies.

Munoz said her family has already spent $28,000 on tuition fees and her courses are not transferable outside Quebec.

Katz said completing her Cegep studies would leave Munoz with a recognized credential, while leaving before graduation would mean the work she has already completed would not amount to a degree.

Munoz also said she no longer has ties to Colombia, where she left as a child. She said her only childhood friend was killed as an indirect result of the violence there.

“Now that she’s gone, I would have to relive the whole thing,” Munoz said about the prospect of returning to Colombia.

The family applied for permanent residency on humanitarian grounds two years ago.

Canada’s immigration department said that application does not cancel a deportation order and would still be reviewed, a process that could take several years.

On Monday, Dawson College students and faculty launched a letter-writing campaign directed at several members of Parliament, hoping political pressure could help Munoz and her family remain in Canada.

The office of Brossard-St-Lambert MP Alexandra Mendès said it is working with the family but declined to provide further details, citing privacy protocols.

“Now that she’s gone, I would have to relive the whole thing,” Munoz said about the prospect of returning to Colombia.
The family applied for permanent residency on humanitarian grounds two years ago.
Canada’s immigration department said that application does not cancel a deportation order and would still be reviewed, a process that could take several years.

On Monday, Dawson College students and faculty launched a letter-writing campaign directed at several members of Parliament, hoping political pressure could help Munoz and her family remain in Canada.
The office of Brossard-St-Lambert MP Alexandra Mendès said it is working with the family but declined to provide further details, citing privacy protocols.

stories.title: October home sales down 10.6% from a year ago, but edge up from September: Crea
stories.summary: Ottawa - The Canadian Real Estate Association says October home sales crept up slightly from September but were still down more than 10 per cent from a year ago.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
October home sales crept up slightly from the previous month but were still down more than 10 per cent from a year ago, the Canadian Real Estate Association said in its latest report Tuesday.

Home sales last month totalled 37,827, down 10.6 per cent from October 2025. But on a seasonally adjusted basis, activity edged up 0.3 per cent compared with September.

“Despite most forecasters sharpening their pencils and lowering their predictions, so far we’ve only seen a slight slowdown in housing activity from the summer to the fall, probably less than many would have predicted in an environment of rising interest rates,” Garry Bhaura, Crea’s chair, said in a news release.

“With the market moving into its traditionally quieter months, now is a great time to shift into planning mode for 2027.”

The Bank of Canada raised its policy interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point to 2.5 per cent last month — the first hike in more than three years — to reduce the risk that stubbornly high oil prices become persistent inflation.

The move prompted Canada’s big banks to raise their benchmark prime rates, pushing the amount charged on variable rate mortgages higher.

A summary of deliberations released earlier this month by the central bank also suggested its governing council thinks it might need to raise rates further, but will proceed carefully.

Michael Davenport, senior economist at Oxford Economics, wrote in a report Tuesday that Canada’s resale housing market had a quiet October and is heading into “hibernation” for the winter.

“Rising mortgage rates, a soft labour market and elevated job insecurity from the trade war with the United States will likely cause housing demand to weaken in the near term, pushing home sales and prices modestly lower before a tepid recovery gets underway next spring,” he wrote.

“We don’t expect the recent softness in the housing market to deter the (Bank of Canada) from hiking ... to 2.75 per cent in December.”

Meanwhile, Crea said the national average sale price in October ticked down 1.6 per cent from a year ago to $678,584.

New listings fell 5.5 per cent to 75,814, but on a seasonally adjusted basis, were up 0.8 per cent from the month before and outpaced sales activity.

Crea said there were about 197,000 properties listed for sale on all Canadian MLS systems at the end of October, up slightly from the long-term average of 190,000.

It said there were five months of inventory on a national basis at the end of October, up slightly from the summer.

Cailey Heaps, CEO at Heaps Estrin Real Estate Team in Toronto, said deals are coming together when sellers have realistic expectations about pricing and buyers are willing to act.

The segment that’s been the most challenging has been for properties that are “family homes” to be lived in long-term.

“Those people are currently housed, so they don’t feel any pressure to act. They want to take a bit of a wait-and-see approach,” she said.

“The first-time buyer market is very active — incredibly active.”

Heaps is expecting a “fairly flat” market through the winter as concern over job security and tariffs weigh on confidence.

“And then I do think that spring will start to see an uptick, not only in pricing but also in volume.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 17, 2026.

stories.title: No jail for Ontario drug trafficker because his son would end up in foster care, judge rules
stories.summary: The Crown was seeking four to five years in prison for 52-year-old Steven Armstrong, who trafficked cocaine to Newfoundland.
stories.author: Jacques Gallant
stories.content:
An Ontario man who exported cocaine to Newfoundland has avoided prison after the judge found it would cause “serious harm” to his high-needs son, who would end up in foster care.

The Crown was seeking four to five years in prison for 52-year-old Steven Armstrong, who drove a car with three kilograms of cocaine hidden in a secret compartment to Nova Scotia in 2020, leaving it near a ferry terminal for a co-accused to pick up and take to Newfoundland. Unbeknownst to them, they were under surveillance and their calls were being monitored.

Armstrong, who pleaded guilty to conspiracy to traffic cocaine, is his son’s sole caregiver. Court heard that the young boy, whose age is covered by a publication ban, has Adhd and is on the autism spectrum. If Armstrong was sent to prison, the boy would likely end up in foster care, and he would lose access to the specialized therapeutic services he’s been receiving.

In coming to his decision to instead impose a two-year conditional sentence — house arrest — followed by three years’ probation, Ontario Court Justice Louis Strezos drew a parallel between the boy’s life and that of his father: Armstrong’s mother died when he was very young, and his father was absent.

The judge expressed concern that separating Armstrong from his son and forcing the boy into the child welfare system would “result in serious harm” and expose him “to the same societal factors that contributed to Mr. Armstrong’s criminality at roughly the same age.”

Sex assault victim Susan Gilbreath was in disbelief — ‘Are we protecting the victim? Or are we protecting the perpetrator?’

Strezos also found that caring for his son “has had a significant rehabilitative impact”; while Armstrong has a lengthy criminal record going back to the 1990s, he has complied with his bail conditions and has not been convicted of any other offences in the last 15 years.

The judge turned to look at Armstrong in a Toronto courtroom last Thursday after reading his decision.

“Mr. Armstrong, I assure you that if you breach any term of this sentence, you will go to prison,” he said.

Federal Crown attorney Chris Kalantzis had acknowledged that a prison sentence would be “bad” for Armstrong’s son, but that it was necessary due to the seriousness of the crime. Armstrong’s two co-accused also received prison sentences following a trial in Newfoundland.

“Ordinarily, he would be correct,” Strezos said, but in the “extraordinary circumstances” of this case, the conditional sentence proposed by defence lawyer Adam Boni was appropriate.

“Many judges might say that for this offender, a downward sentence — much less a conditional sentence — is simply not proportionate or, as Mr. Kalantzis argues, is ‘demonstrably unfit,’” Strezos said.

But he concluded that the “social utility” of incarceration would not protect society in the long run, as Armstrong’s rehabilitation is “integrally intertwined” with his care of his son.

The boy’s pediatrician said in a letter to the court that they would be “very concerned” if the boy was placed in foster care and the strain it would put on his developmental functioning. Armstrong’s cousin, a special needs assistant in the public school system, said the boy had reached a “place of stability” with his father, and that no one else in the family would be able to take care of him.

“Meeting his daily needs is already a significant challenge,” she wrote.

A centre focused on therapy for children confirmed that if Armstrong went to prison, his son would lose access to their services as their model “requires the active involvement of a primary caregiver.”

If not for the “undisputed record” before him, the judge said he would have imposed a four-year prison sentence.

“We regard Justice Strezos’ judgment as speaking for itself and will not be providing any comment on this matter,” said defence lawyers Boni and Sherif Foda.

stories.title: Amazon workers near Vancouver secure historic first union contract
stories.summary: The 800-odd workers now have seat at the table to challenge company on safety issues, Unifor regional director says
stories.author: Vanmala Subramaniam
stories.content:
Hundreds of warehouse workers at an Amazon.com Inc. Amzn-Q facility near Vancouver have secured their first union contract with Unifor after a lengthy legal battle with the company that spanned almost 18 months.

The 800-odd workers – represented by Unifor, Canada’s largest private-sector union – are now the only group of Amazon workers in the world to be governed by a collective agreement. There are a handful of other Amazon warehouses globally that are unionized, but none have managed to reach a collective agreement with the company.

Unifor’s Western regional director Gavin McGarrigle said in an interview that the union now has a seat at the table to challenge the company on issues such as injuries and worker safety. “This has been a long time coming. We are pleased.”

Amazon, however, is disputing the process that led to the securing of a first contract. In a Nov. 13 statement, the company’s vice-president of global operations, Ofori Agboka, described the way in which Amazon workers obtained their first contract as “improper, unfair” and one that “defies common sense.” He said that some Amazon workers will effectively take home less money than they did before, despite wage increases, because they will have to pay union dues.

A copy of the three-year contract, viewed by The Globe and Mail, states that workers will receive wage increases of 3.25 per cent starting October 2027, and 3.5 per cent starting October 2028. By the end of the contract, ON Oct. 31, 2029, most workers will be paid at least $29 an hour. The contract also includes a clause that guarantees unionized workers will receive the same future pay increases that non-union workers receive, if greater than the percentages set out in the contract.

The sequence of events leading up to the agreement is long and complicated, with Unifor repeatedly accusing Amazon of employing stalling tactics to deter a first contract, and the BC Labour Relations Board issuing a series of rulings that penalized Amazon for its conduct during bargaining.

Warehouse workers at YVR2, the Amazon fulfilment centre in Delta, B.C., were first granted union certification by the board in July 2025. It ordered remedial certification (meaning that certification was granted without a vote) because it ruled that Amazon made a fair workplace vote impossible by rapidly boosting the number of new hires during the union drive.

For more than a year after the certification, Unifor and Amazon continued to disagree on terms of a new contract, with the union pushing for clauses that could address how fast workers are expected to work, and Amazon refusing to negotiate on worker productivity. Multiple unfair labour practice complaints were filed by the union against Amazon at the board. Then, in early August, the board again ruled against Amazon, saying that it had bargained in bad faith and was unwilling to negotiate on key items. The board ordered a first contract to be imposed on workers.

“The fact that this first contract had to come through arbitration is not great. It is a bit of a challenge for a union when the members themselves did not have direct input on the terms of the agreement,” said Adam King, assistant professor of labour studies at the University of Manitoba.

Bethany Hastie, director of the Centre for Law in the Contemporary Workplace at Queen’s University, said that ideally, the unionization process should not unfold with a labour board imposing arbitration but that these safeguards are in place for a reason.

“Labour boards exist to ensure fairness for workers who want to unionize. With this case, as it has proceeded, the labour board was attuned to the various ways in which the employer tried to undermine labour rights in the workplace.”

In January 2025, Amazon closed all seven of its warehouses and distribution facilities in Quebec, terminating 1,700 full-time employees. The company said it was a business decision. But the move came just months after its facility in Laval, Que., had voted to unionize and was on the verge of securing a first contract. At the time, labour experts and local politicians speculated that the closures were linked to the unionization and other union drives in Amazon facilities across the province.

Prof. King believes that Amazon is unlikely to shut down its Vancouver operations because they are too geographically important for the company. “In the case of Quebec, they had already shifted their network to rely on serving other geographic markets from the Greater Toronto Area,” he said.

Mr. McGarrigle, of Unifor, said it’s a big win for the workers the union represents, who can now enter a grievance process if they believe their working conditions have been violated. “This is particularly important at Amazon, where the worker injury rate is high,” he said.

Separately, a group of workers at the Delta fulfilment centre has been trying to decertify the union for months. Unifor believes Amazon is involved in the decertification drive, and has filed an unfair labour practice complaint at the provincial labour board. These workers have also filed a judicial review at the B.C. Supreme Court over an order by the labour board to seal the results of their decertification vote. No decision has been made on the issue.

stories.title: ‘The threat is very real’: Unidentified drones reported over Canadian military bases as recently as 2025
stories.summary: Unidentified drones have been spotted over Canadian military bases, highlighting a potential defence gap that could be exploited to launch attacks or gather intelligence.
stories.author: Daniel Otis
stories.content:
When an unauthorized drone was spotted over one of Canada’s busiest air force bases, a new counter-drone system completely failed to detect it, according to a report obtained through an access to information request. With the drone operator remaining unidentified, experts say the September 2025 incident from CFB Trenton highlights a potential defence gap that could be exploited to attack or gather intelligence on the Canadian military.

“There’s no doubt that our adversaries have capabilities to cause us significant harm and we do not have the capabilities to deal with that,” retired Royal Canadian Air Force (Rcaf) lieutenant-general Christopher Coates told CTVNews.CA from Ottawa.

Rcaf reports obtained by CTVNews.CA through an access to information request detail seven similar cases from 2024 and 2025 at both CFB Trenton in Ontario and CFB Cold Lake in Alberta. Arguably two of the most important air bases in Canada, Trenton houses essential transport aircraft like the CC-177 Globemaster III while Cold Lake is home to a significant part of Canada’s CF-18 fighter jet fleet. In all seven cases, the reports show that there were no attempts to intercept the drones and their operators were never identified.

Coates previously served as the deputy commander and highest ranking Canadian at Norad, the joint Canada-U.S. continental defence group. He is now the director of foreign policy, national defence and national security at the Macdonald-Laurier Institute, a public policy think tank.

“To really affect Canada and our military, you don’t need to attack a base or the aircraft or the ships, you can attack dependent infrastructure,” Coates explained. “So electrical distribution and transmission networks, the transportation system, resupply systems – they’re all soft, none of them are protected.”

Some of the incidents identified by CTVNews.CA also roughly coincide with a wave of drone incursions across Europe , which have caused major disruptions at military facilities as well as airports and critical infrastructure sites like nuclear power plants.

While Coates is not aware of any evidence linking the Canadian cases to potentially hostile actors like Russia, he and others say Canada needs to be better prepared to deal with the potential threat even if adversaries are not currently showing intent.

“Drones are the ideal tools for sabotage operations because they can allow perpetrators to operate remotely and make attribution significantly more difficult,” Toronto-based Ukrainian defence analyst Olena Kryzhanivska told CTVNews.CA.

“I believe that the risk of hostile actors using drones to cause damage or gather intelligence in Canada is significant.”

Kryzhanivska is the author of Ukraine’s Arms Monitor , where she writes extensively about drone warfare and technology, which is evolving rapidly and redefining the battlefield in Russia’s war against Ukraine.

“These threats are not limited to military facilities,” Kryzhanivska added. “They could affect Canada’s broader security and defence infrastructure, as well as civilian sectors.”

The Cold Lake and Trenton cases

The four reports from CFB Cold Lake all detail military personnel spotting unauthorized drones in restricted airspace, including one that travelled at an estimated speed of 60 to 100 km/h that “was observed to be boxy in shape, approximately 60cm in width, emitting what appeared to be a yellowish light with no sound from it heard.”

Another – described as a small white drone carrying a “black tube” – apparently made two appearances at CFB Cold Lake within four days in September 2025. Those were the most recent Cold Lake reports uncovered by CTVNews.CA, and they plainly state that the base “does not currently have a means of tracking small UAS aircraft.” UAS is short for unmanned (or uncrewed) aircraft system.

At CFB Trenton, the first of the three reports reviewed by CTVNews.CA mention that the base was about to become one of the first military airfields in Canada to be equipped with counter-drone technology.

“The system will be a detection only system until the magnitude of the risk is realized,” the September 2024 report explains. “Numerous legal hurtles [sic] exist preventing the use of a counter-UAS system that could be used to destroy, neutralize or take control of a UAS.”

The reports say that system became operational in March 2025. But when a camera-equipped drone buzzed the base’s runway on Sept. 17, 2025, the system was offline due to a planned power outage.

The power, however, was on just days later during another drone sighting on Sept. 22, 2025, but according to a report, the “counter UAS system did not detect the drone.” On the same day across the Atlantic, unidentified drones led to serious disruptions at a military base in France and airports in Denmark and Norway, according to a drone incident tracker .

The Trenton reports note that signs around the base warn the public that “that operating drones in the vicinity of the airfield is prohibited.” They also mention that no civilian drone flights were authorized at the time of these incidents.

In a statement to CTVNews.CA, Canada’s Department of National Defence declined to comment on any of the cases mentioned in this article or any of its counter-drone measures.

“We can’t comment further for operational and security reasons,” a National Defence spokesperson said via email. “DND/CAF does not comment on current or planned security measures, operational capabilities, threat assessments, vulnerabilities, incidents, specific locations, or deployment plans.”

‘There is no silver-bullet solution’

Experts say creating and deploying an effective counter-drone system is easier said than done

“It’s not that somebody hasn’t done their job and gone out and bought what’s required,” former RCMP officer and counter-drone specialist Brian Fentiman told CTVNews.CA. “It’s this is a very complex problem and that there is no easy solution.”

Fentiman is the president and CEO of BlueForce UAV Consulting Inc., a Comox, B.C.-based company that specializes in drone and counter-drone training and consulting for clients like Canadian airports and law enforcement agencies.

“Let’s face it, no military in the world really thought drones were a big threat until the last couple of years and now everybody’s scrambling,” Fentiman said. “It really needs to be a multi-faceted approach because what you’re going to do domestically for installations in Canada is not going to be the same thing that you’re going to do in either the theatre of war or in a conflict zone, where you have more kinetic options.”

To be effective, counter-drone systems need to be able to detect, track, identify and engage potential threats. Detection, tracking and identification systems can include radar, radio frequency, optical and acoustic sensors, as well as AI tools.

Taking out or disabling a drone can utilize electronic warfare systems like radio frequency or GPS jammers, or kinetic methods such as nets, interceptor drones, projectiles like bullets or missiles, or even directed-energy weapons that use lasers or high-powered microwaves.

Simply put, it’s not as simple as aiming and pulling the trigger on a counter-drone jammer gun.

“If you just jam the control link, most drones are programmed so that they’ll just come back to where they took off from,” Fentiman explained. “People that have nefarious intent can also program their drone so that it flies to a target area if its control signal gets interrupted.”

In Ukraine, where drone warfare is rapidly evolving, Kryzhanivska notes that drones are now utilizing fibre-optic cables and autonomous capabilities that can allow them to operate despite attempts at electronic interference.

“Broadly speaking, it is a constant cat-and-mouse game,” Kryzhanivska said. “The main lesson is that there is no silver-bullet solution capable of countering every type of drone threat.”

While the Canadian military is authorized to use an array of tools to engage drones in operational settings like Canada’s mission in Latvia, doing so on Canadian soil is an entirely different matter. As one of the reports from CFB Trenton notes, there remain significant domestic legal and regulatory hurdles when it comes to downing a drone in domestic contexts, especially with kinetic options like live ammunition or interceptor drones.

But recent exemptions to the Radiocommunication Act now allow jammers to be used by the military as well as certain correctional services and law enforcement agencies in specific instances such as national security and protecting people and property from serious harm.

In addition to deploying a range of new technologies and making regulatory changes, Fentiman says creating effective counter-drone measures also requires new procedures and protocols that are aimed at minimizing collateral damage and defining acceptable risks when intercepting drones near civilian areas.

“If you do hit it, if all you do is damage it slightly, you’re sending it into a residential area,” Fentiman said. “So a lot of work has to be going into what is acceptable risk. … It’s a very complex problem to make that assessment.”

‘Improvements are still needed’

The Department of National Defence and the Canadian Armed Forces are actively looking to fill these gaps. This year, the department has issued counter-drone procurement notices and launched the Defence Drone Initiative , which in part will “explore affordable systems that could detect, track or defeat hostile drones” in order to “contribute to the protection of military personnel, installations and infrastructure.” Released on Nov. 7, the federal government’s latest budget proposes $2.3 billion over five years for advancing the Canadian military’s drone and counter-drone capabilities.

“C-UAS capabilities are a critical consideration in modern security and defence planning,” a National Defence spokesperson told CTVNews.CA. “DND has procurement activities planned to support the continued evolution and enhancement of its approach to countering UAS threats, building on existing measures and capabilities.”

While such systems are already being deployed in Latvia and at Canadian naval ports and air bases, the reports obtained by CTVNews.CA highlight that more work needs to be done.

Salt, whose research includes drone warfare, says potential adversaries could use commercially available and legally acquired drones to conduct surveillance and even sabotage at bases and critical infrastructure sites in Canada. Salt says “the threat is very real, and very urgent and requires immediate action.”

“There is no one technological solution, so Canada will have to invest and procure broadly to cover its bets in this area,” Salt added. “Essentially, the Canadian military, like many of its allies needs to work quickly to ‘harden’ its bases and infrastructure against potential future threats in this area.”

The four reports from CFB Cold Lake all detail military personnel spotting unauthorized drones in restricted airspace, including one that travelled at an estimated speed of 60 to 100 km/h that “was observed to be boxy in shape, approximately 60cm in width, emitting what appeared to be a yellowish light with no sound from it heard.”

Another – described as a small white drone carrying a “black tube” – apparently made two appearances at CFB Cold Lake within four days in September 2025. Those were the most recent Cold Lake reports uncovered by CTVNews.CA, and they plainly state that the base “does not currently have a means of tracking small UAS aircraft.” UAS is short for unmanned (or uncrewed) aircraft system.

At CFB Trenton, the first of the three reports reviewed by CTVNews.CA mention that the base was about to become one of the first military airfields in Canada to be equipped with counter-drone technology.

“The system will be a detection only system until the magnitude of the risk is realized,” the September 2024 report explains. “Numerous legal hurtles [sic] exist preventing the use of a counter-UAS system that could be used to destroy, neutralize or take control of a UAS.”
The reports say that system became operational in March 2025. But when a camera-equipped drone buzzed the base’s runway on Sept. 17, 2025, the system was offline due to a planned power outage.

The power, however, was on just days later during another drone sighting on Sept. 22, 2025, but according to a report, the “counter UAS system did not detect the drone.” On the same day across the Atlantic, unidentified drones led to serious disruptions at a military base in France and airports in Denmark and Norway, according to a drone incident tracker .

The Trenton reports note that signs around the base warn the public that “that operating drones in the vicinity of the airfield is prohibited.” They also mention that no civilian drone flights were authorized at the time of these incidents.
In a statement to CTVNews.CA, Canada’s Department of National Defence declined to comment on any of the cases mentioned in this article or any of its counter-drone measures.

“We can’t comment further for operational and security reasons,” a National Defence spokesperson said via email. “DND/CAF does not comment on current or planned security measures, operational capabilities, threat assessments, vulnerabilities, incidents, specific locations, or deployment plans.”
‘There is no silver-bullet solution’
Experts say creating and deploying an effective counter-drone system is easier said than done

“It’s not that somebody hasn’t done their job and gone out and bought what’s required,” former RCMP officer and counter-drone specialist Brian Fentiman told CTVNews.CA. “It’s this is a very complex problem and that there is no easy solution.”

Fentiman is the president and CEO of BlueForce UAV Consulting Inc., a Comox, B.C.-based company that specializes in drone and counter-drone training and consulting for clients like Canadian airports and law enforcement agencies.

“Let’s face it, no military in the world really thought drones were a big threat until the last couple of years and now everybody’s scrambling,” Fentiman said. “It really needs to be a multi-faceted approach because what you’re going to do domestically for installations in Canada is not going to be the same thing that you’re going to do in either the theatre of war or in a conflict zone, where you have more kinetic options.”

To be effective, counter-drone systems need to be able to detect, track, identify and engage potential threats. Detection, tracking and identification systems can include radar, radio frequency, optical and acoustic sensors, as well as AI tools.

Taking out or disabling a drone can utilize electronic warfare systems like radio frequency or GPS jammers, or kinetic methods such as nets, interceptor drones, projectiles like bullets or missiles, or even directed-energy weapons that use lasers or high-powered microwaves.
Simply put, it’s not as simple as aiming and pulling the trigger on a counter-drone jammer gun.

“If you just jam the control link, most drones are programmed so that they’ll just come back to where they took off from,” Fentiman explained. “People that have nefarious intent can also program their drone so that it flies to a target area if its control signal gets interrupted.”

In Ukraine, where drone warfare is rapidly evolving, Kryzhanivska notes that drones are now utilizing fibre-optic cables and autonomous capabilities that can allow them to operate despite attempts at electronic interference.
“Broadly speaking, it is a constant cat-and-mouse game,” Kryzhanivska said. “The main lesson is that there is no silver-bullet solution capable of countering every type of drone threat.”

While the Canadian military is authorized to use an array of tools to engage drones in operational settings like Canada’s mission in Latvia, doing so on Canadian soil is an entirely different matter. As one of the reports from CFB Trenton notes, there remain significant domestic legal and regulatory hurdles when it comes to downing a drone in domestic contexts, especially with kinetic options like live ammunition or interceptor drones.

But recent exemptions to the Radiocommunication Act now allow jammers to be used by the military as well as certain correctional services and law enforcement agencies in specific instances such as national security and protecting people and property from serious harm.

In addition to deploying a range of new technologies and making regulatory changes, Fentiman says creating effective counter-drone measures also requires new procedures and protocols that are aimed at minimizing collateral damage and defining acceptable risks when intercepting drones near civilian areas.

“If you do hit it, if all you do is damage it slightly, you’re sending it into a residential area,” Fentiman said. “So a lot of work has to be going into what is acceptable risk. … It’s a very complex problem to make that assessment.”
‘Improvements are still needed’

The Department of National Defence and the Canadian Armed Forces are actively looking to fill these gaps. This year, the department has issued counter-drone procurement notices and launched the Defence Drone Initiative , which in part will “explore affordable systems that could detect, track or defeat hostile drones” in order to “contribute to the protection of military personnel, installations and infrastructure.” Released on Nov. 7, the federal government’s latest budget proposes $2.3 billion over five years for advancing the Canadian military’s drone and counter-drone capabilities.

“C-UAS capabilities are a critical consideration in modern security and defence planning,” a National Defence spokesperson told CTVNews.CA. “DND has procurement activities planned to support the continued evolution and enhancement of its approach to countering UAS threats, building on existing measures and capabilities.”
While such systems are already being deployed in Latvia and at Canadian naval ports and air bases, the reports obtained by CTVNews.CA highlight that more work needs to be done.

Salt, whose research includes drone warfare, says potential adversaries could use commercially available and legally acquired drones to conduct surveillance and even sabotage at bases and critical infrastructure sites in Canada. Salt says “the threat is very real, and very urgent and requires immediate action.”

“There is no one technological solution, so Canada will have to invest and procure broadly to cover its bets in this area,” Salt added. “Essentially, the Canadian military, like many of its allies needs to work quickly to ‘harden’ its bases and infrastructure against potential future threats in this area.”
