High propane and electricity prices are adding to the bill for buyers like Mary van den Broek-Grant. She co-owns and manages Cardigan Feed Services, which purchases and sells grain, cleans seed and supplies agricultural products.
“This is going to be an expensive corn harvest. And the price of corn will be expensive this year,” van den Broek-Grant said.

For her business, higher prices mean keeping more cash on hand. Her customers, including livestock producers raising cattle and hogs, will also feel the pressure. There’s only so much they can get for their animals in the marketplace, making it harder to turn a profit when feed prices rise.
There’s also a shortage of drying infrastructure. Van den Broek-Grant estimates there are about 20 dryers across P.E.I., some owned by farmers, while grain is also sent off-Island.

stories.title: Edmonton Elks want ‘City of Champions’ signs to return
stories.summary: The Edmonton Elks are champions again, and they want their city to show it.
stories.author: John Korobanik
stories.content:
The Edmonton Elks are champions again, and they want their city to show it.

Basking in the glory of Sunday’s Grey Cup victory — Edmonton’s first since 2015 — members of the Elks, from management to players, continued calling for a return of the City of Champions signs that once welcomed people to Alberta’s capital.

“The City of Champions is back,” proclaimed linebacker Nick Anderson, sustaining the call quarterback Cody Fajardo made after the Elks’ 37-30 win over the Montreal Alouettes in the CFL championship game.

Elks general manager Ed Hervey wondered why the signs were ever taken down as the team had arrived back at Commonwealth Stadium on Monday afternoon.

“See, here’s the reality for me. I always believe once you’re a champion, you’re always a champion,” he said.

“If you look at the Grey Cup and you look on there… Edmonton, those champions are still there … obviously the Oilers won their championships. I didn’t know it was the city of most recent champions. That’s not what the sign ever said, right?

“So, with that being said … put it back and let it be,” he said, pointing to the 15 Grey Cup championships the city now has, to go along with the five Stanley Cup wins by the Oilers.

The city first put up the signs in 1988 to honour championship victories by the then-named Eskimos, the Oilers, the Edmonton Grads basketball team, university championships and the city’s response to a devastating tornado in 1987.

The six signs marking the entrances to the city were removed in the spring of 2015.

Overnight, someone posted a temporary “City of Champions” sign on the southern entrance to the city on Monday, but mayor Andrew Knack told reporters the signs are still in the archives.

Head coach Mark Kilam, clutching the Grey Cup like he was never letting it go, said the Elks have taken one step towards bringing back the signs.

“There’s one more team that’s going to handle their business, and I know they will,” he said of the Oilers, who last won the Stanley Cup in 1990.

While it May take more than just one national championship to see the signs resurrected, Hervey said the Elks have the players and the program to be long-term Grey Cup contenders.

“Average age of this roster, we’re the youngest in the CFL,” Hervey said.

A mixture of youth and veterans, combined with the type of players on the roster now and in the future, and maintaining continuity will lead to continued success, Hervey said.

“We talked about continuity at the start of the year and continuing to build that,” he said. “And our goal is to do that. And as long as we have buy-in and there are people who see Edmonton as a destination we believe that we can be a force in this league for quite some time.”

Kilam said that while he would like to just enjoy the victory for a few more days, “you know we’re gonna continue to build. You know we’re just getting started here.”

Kilam said winning one championship is difficult to do, and it was a lot of hard work by a lot of people in the organization.

“And that’s why it’s so special, because this is representative of so many people on so many levels of this organization, putting in the time and buying into what we’re trying to do and what (president) Chris (Morris) is saying, what Ed is saying, you know, and representing the Thompson family. So that’s really what this is representative of.”

stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ontario’s police watchdog says it found no reasonable grounds to criminally charge Waterloo regional police officers in relation to a man’s broken collarbone during his arrest over the summer.

The Special Investigations Unit says officers observed a man committing an alleged traffic violation while riding a bike in the area of Duke Street West and Victoria Street North in Kitchener on July 24.

stories.title: Ford holds off on new cash for Stellantis plant, contradicting minister
stories.summary: Doug Ford's minister responsible for the tariffs response said the province is willing to offer Stellantis additional financial support to stay in Brampton.
stories.author: Colin D'Mello
stories.content:
Premier Doug Ford is tamping down suggestions that Ontario taxpayers might offer Stellantis even more funding to keep the Brampton auto assembly plant running, contradicting his own economic development minister, who said provincial funds are on the table.

Days after a face-to-face meeting with the auto maker, federal government and Unifor, Ford addressed the issue for the first time, ON Monday, and said the province is willing to entertain options that would keep the plant in operation.

“If they’re making sure that they’re going to employ three, four thousand people, then we’d sit down and have a discussion with them,” Ford told Global News. “We want to make sure that Stellantis hires back the people that they let go. Simple as that.”

In order to scuttle the sale, Ford’s minister responsible for the tariffs response said the province and federal governments are willing to offer the company additional financial support to stay in Brampton.

“We need Stellantis to keep the plant open, keep it warm and keep it ready for a new model,” Vic Fedeli told the Ontario legislature.

“Our plan is to meet with Stellantis’ global CEO in the coming weeks, where we will bring our message to him directly. We have the supports in place; we announced them weeks ago—$2.5 billion. Those supports are in place to keep these companies exactly where they are today.”

That $2.5 billion fund – a billion of which comes from Ontario taxpayers – offers automotive companies capital investments to prepare factories for “connected and electrified vehicles.”

While Fedeli didn’t say how much could be available to Stellantis, Ford suggested he’s not willing to put up any cash for now.

“I’m not confirming we’re going to offer money. The federal government will be sitting at the table with Stellantis like they have been the whole time,” Ford said.

The premier pointed out that while the province offered Stellantis $132 million in 2022 to help the automaker retool its facilities, the company received “absolutely nothing” from the province.

The company has received $55 million from provincial taxpayers to upgrade the Windsor plant, the government said.

NDP Leader Marit Stiles accused the government of allowing the situation to worsen.

“I don’t see any sense of urgency here,” Stiles said in the legislature. “The Premier loves a camera when he gets to pat himself on the back, but when it comes to standing up for workers, he is missing in action every single time.”

“Three thousand good union jobs are at stake here. At least 30,000 spin-off jobs all gone because this premier was asleep at the wheel.”

stories.title: Four more staff leave Pierre Poilievre's office, with two joining B.C. Conservatives
stories.summary: Departures comes at a tense moment for Pierre Poilievre, with much-watched byelection looming.
stories.author: Stephanie Taylor
stories.content:
Ottawa — At least four more staffers in Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre’s office are heading for the door, marking the largest exit from his staffing ranks since losing last year’s election.

Two of those leaving are Poilievre’s director of communications Micah Green along with Green’s wife Hayley Quipp, who also works in Poilievre’s office as his executive assistant and scheduler. Sam Lilly, Poilievre’s director of media relations, who has worked in that office under various leaders since 2021, is also departing.

Green and Lilly, who are both originally from British Columbia, will be moving to work for the newly elected B.C. Conservative government , led by incoming premier Lorne Doerkson. It comes as those inside Poilievre’s office are bracing for more potential departures to B.C., mainly among junior staff. In an email to the party’s caucus on Monday, the same day the current spate of exits were finalized, Steve Outhouse, his chief of staff and the party’s next campaign manager, pointed to that win to account for the departures.

“Last month’s election of a Conservative government in British Columbia was exciting for the conservative movement. As the BC Conservatives get ready to take the helm of the province, they are building a team, and that is obviously of particular interest to Conservatives across the country who hail from British Columbia, who are keen to bring about change in their home province,” he wrote in the email, obtained by the Star.

Outhouse also confirmed the exit of Poilievre’s senior policy adviser, Andrew Evans, who was leaving to work elsewhere in the private sector.

“More information about new team members will follow in due course,” he wrote.

The departures come after Aaron Wudrick, Poilievre’s deputy chief of staff who first entered his office as a policy director more than two years ago, announced earlier this month that he would be leaving to take a private-sector job.

In a statement at the time, Wudrick told MPs and fellow colleagues that “it had been an honour and a privilege to serve” Poilievre. He added that he was “fully confident” that the goal of making Poilievre Canada’s next prime minister “remains fully achievable in the next election.”

The spate of departures comes at a tense moment for Poilievre, as Conservatives watch to see whether he will be able to hold onto an Ontario seat the party has held for the past 18 years in an upcoming byelection on Dec. 7.

That race in Brantford-Brant South is expected to be a fight for the Conservatives, who have won it comfortably for years. Outhouse has been on the ground for that race, along with a flurry of Conservative MPs who have been out door-knocking.

With some on Poilievre’s team looking to work within B.C.‘s new Conservative government — a chance that came up earlier than expected, thanks to the snap election called by former NDP premier David Eby — McKenzie Kibler, who joined Poilievre’s office after last year’s election, left as his issues management director earlier this summer to return to working for Alberta’s United Conservative Party government.

Poilievre’s office has struggled to retain staff since last year’s election, with the first several months spent looking to replace those who left, including his former director of communications, Ben Woodfinden.

Katy Merrifield, who held that job until earlier this year, left and went on to steer the B.C. Conservatives to victory along with former members of Poilievre’s staff and leadership team, including Woodfinden and Anthony Koch.

Earlier this year Poilievre also saw the resignation of his longtime chief of staff Ian Todd, who had been in that job since shortly after Poilievre won the leadership in 2022.

Questions have swirled for months about Poilievre’s leadership within caucus and the wider party as successive public opinion polls show the Conservatives trailing Prime Minister Mark Carney’s Liberals. Poilievre has lost a total of eight MPs since the last election, four through defections to the Liberals, three to resignations and one who was appointed to the Senate.

Liberals' 'lawful access' bill vulnerable to constitutional challenge: professor

stories.title: Liberals’ ‘lawful access’ bill vulnerable to constitutional challenge: professor
stories.summary: Ottawa — A law professor says a Liberal government bill that would make it easier for police and spies to navigate the online world could be found unconstitutional due to a provision on retaining metadata.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — A law professor says a Liberal government bill that would make it easier for police and spies to navigate the online world could be found unconstitutional due to a provision on retaining metadata.

The “lawful access” bill would require service providers to keep metadata — digital traces of a communication, but not the email or text itself — for up to six months.

The government agreed to shorten the period, which was originally up to one year, after expressions of concern.

On Monday, University of Ottawa law professor Michael Geist told a Senate committee studying the bill the provision remains “constitutionally vulnerable with little evidence of its necessity.”

Geist said metadata May not include the content of a message, but it tells a story: who we contact, when, where and from what device.

The government says the bill will ensure law enforcement has the legal tools to prevent, investigate and respond to modern crime and protect Canadians in a manner consistent with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

Opponents argue the legislation unnecessarily expands the powers of police and intelligence agencies, endangering the privacy of Canadians, flouting the Charter and placing unreasonable demands on companies.

Geist said police seeking access to metadata can use existing Criminal Code provisions allowing targeted preservation and production orders tied to a specific investigation with judicial oversight.

He said the bill’s metadata regime should be removed. Failing that, requiring metadata retention for up to 30 days would address the concerns about meeting immediate investigative needs prior to obtaining a preservation order, Geist said.

Tamir Israel, director of the privacy, surveillance and technology program at the Canadian Civil Liberties Association, also called on Monday for removal of the data retention regime, or at least limiting it to apply only to data already under the control of telecommunication providers.

The bill would require electronic service providers to develop and maintain the technical capabilities necessary to enable police and the Canadian Security Intelligence Service to effectively obtain communications and information for investigations.

Critics of the legislation say it could allow the government to force companies to break encryption by inserting backdoors into their products.

Israel told the senators the bill “effectively grants the government a blank cheque to impose its evolving surveillance objectives onto electronic service providers in secret.”

Earlier this month, Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree told the Senate committee the bill “is not about weakening privacy protections. It is not about surveillance. It is not about creating backdoors to Canadians’ private communications.”

In addition to the shorter metadata retention period, a House of Commons committee adopted a safeguard clarifying that electronic service providers would not be required to comply with an order if it would introduce a systemic vulnerability in their services or prevent them from fixing one.

Robyn Greene, director of privacy and public policy at Meta Platforms, the company behind Facebook, told the senators Monday the company provides end-to-end encrypted services to help Canadians protect their most sensitive information.

“It is not technically feasible to give law enforcement backdoor access to encrypted data without introducing a vulnerability that malicious actors will exploit,” Greene said.

“Simply stated, forcing service providers like Meta to break, weaken, circumvent or undermine encryption would significantly harm Canadians’ privacy, cybersecurity, economic and national security.”

Greene said the government’s well-intentioned amendments do not achieve their goal.

“We also remain concerned the technical order authorities could force providers to install government or third-party spyware onto our systems.”

In addition, Greene said, the metadata retention obligations “treat all Canadians as potential criminal suspects.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 16, 2026.

Jim Bronskill, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Longtime Maritime broadcaster Todd Veinotte dies at 57
stories.summary: Long-time Maritime media personality and former Global News reporter, Todd Veinotte, has died at the age of 57.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau, Karen Bartko
stories.content:
Long-time Maritime media personality and former Global News reporter, Todd Veinotte , died Monday at the age of 57, following a battle with Parkinson’s disease.

His wife, Kelly Gillis Arsenault Veinotte, confirmed his passing in a social media post .

“Todd and I found each other later in life, and from the beginning, there was something so special about us,” she wrote in a tribute to her late husband.

“We May not have had decades together, but the love, laughter, adventures and memories we packed into our time together could have filled a lifetime.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "We May not have had decades together, but the love, laughter, adventures and memories we packed into our time together could have filled a lifetime."

Veinotte was a veteran journalist and broadcaster with more than 30 years of experience in television, radio, and podcasting.

He joined Global News in 2018 as a videojournalist and was based in Saint John, N.B.

Veinotte was a familiar voice to Maritimers as the host of The Todd Veinotte Show. He later hosted a twice-weekly podcast.

In recent years, he spoke about his Parkinson’s diagnosis and adjusting to the “new reality.”

Parkinson’s is a disorder of the central nervous system that mainly affects one’s motor functions. The condition causes gradual damage to parts of a person’s brain, resulting in numerous symptoms, including tremors, slow movement, and stiff and inflexible muscles.

More than 120,000 people in Canada live with Parkinson’s, according to Parkinson Canada.

While there is currently no cure, medications can help manage symptoms and treatments such as physiotherapy, speech therapy and exercise can play a vital role in improving quality of life, according to the organization.

Arsenault Veinotte said Parkinson’s disease is cruel and it slowly took so much from a man who had so much life left to live.

But, she added she was incredibly grateful for the time they had, saying it was a privilege to be his wife.

“Parkinson’s never took away the man I fell in love with,” she wrote in her post. “His humour, his intelligence, his love of music, his stubbornness, and that wonderful ability to make me laugh when I least expected it.

“I don’t want our story to be remembered for how it ended. I want it to be remembered for how beautifully we lived it.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "I don't want our story to be remembered for how it ended. I want it to be remembered for how beautifully we lived it."

Funeral details for Veinotte have not yet been released.

With a file from Katie Scott, Global News

Veinotte was a familiar voice to Maritimers as the host of The Todd Veinotte Show. He later hosted a twice-weekly podcast.
In recent years, he spoke about his Parkinson’s diagnosis and adjusting to the “new reality.”

Parkinson’s is a disorder of the central nervous system that mainly affects one’s motor functions. The condition causes gradual damage to parts of a person’s brain, resulting in numerous symptoms, including tremors, slow movement, and stiff and inflexible muscles.
More than 120,000 people in Canada live with Parkinson’s, according to Parkinson Canada.

While there is currently no cure, medications can help manage symptoms and treatments such as physiotherapy, speech therapy and exercise can play a vital role in improving quality of life, according to the organization.
Arsenault Veinotte said Parkinson’s disease is cruel and it slowly took so much from a man who had so much life left to live.
But, she added she was incredibly grateful for the time they had, saying it was a privilege to be his wife.

“Parkinson’s never took away the man I fell in love with,” she wrote in her post. “His humour, his intelligence, his love of music, his stubbornness, and that wonderful ability to make me laugh when I least expected it.

stories.title: Proposed Saint John data centre could generate tax windfall, critics unconvinced
stories.summary: The study on the proposed Spruce Lake data centre was commissioned by Beacon Data Centers, the company behind the proposal alongside U.S.-based VoltaGrid.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau, Reeti Rohilla
stories.content:
A proposed data centre in Saint John, N.B. could bring in tens of millions of dollars in property taxes annually, but while the potential windfall has the city’s mayor encouraged, it’s also begging the question of how realistic those projections are.

And there are concerns about what the city would have to give up in return if the controversial project goes ahead.

The study on the proposed Spruce Lake data centre was commissioned by Beacon Data Centers, the company behind the proposal alongside U.S.-based VoltaGrid.

The report estimates Saint John would receive $25 million annually in taxes and the province would receive $18 million each year.

“I was shocked to hear the number,” said Mayor Donna Reardon.

“And that’s just for the building, that’s without machinery and equipment, which is not taxable in the province of New Brunswick currently.”

Similar to some other jurisdictions, Reardon wants the province to consider taxing equipment at new industrial sites, while also letting cities keep all heavy-industry tax revenue.

She says the money could repair aging pipes and roads, improve transit and parks and potentially even lower taxes for citizens.

Consultant David Campbell, who prepared the report, estimates a $1 billion taxable value for the nearly $6 billion project.

For the property tax assessment, he counted land, buildings and power infrastructure.

“There could be a variance by a few million dollars either way. It could end up being considerably higher or it could be slightly lower,” said Campbell, president of Jupia Consultants Inc.

“If somebody were to look at other data centres across the country they would see similar amounts.”

Service New Brunswick, which officially assesses properties, tells Global News it considers land, building size, construction, age, condition, replacement costs and market values in its assessments.

Its methodology depends on the property, available evidence and information from the owner.

The mayor says property taxes are vital for a city.

“Every municipality in New Brunswick can only generate money through property tax,” she said.

But a group of citizens opposed to the data centre project says the environment and health implications attached to the project are too high a price to pay.

“Our community stance is that no dollar value can compensate for what our community is actually losing,” said Chris Watson, a member of Save Lorneville.

Watson questions the results of noise and air-quality testing for the development, which would use both NB Power and on-site natural gas generation.

The study also forecasts 210 permanent jobs, and up to 2,900 construction jobs at the peak of the project.

In an email to Global News, Beacon Data Centers says the projected benefits depend on regulatory approvals and construction and adds that the final property assessment and tax bill will be determined by authorities.

stories.title: Guilty pleas entered in fatal beating of London man
stories.summary: Four people appeared in court Monday, charged in the death of a man from an incident in July 2024.
stories.author: Fiona Robertson, Nick Paparella
stories.content:
Four people appeared in court Monday, charged in the death of a man from an incident in July 2024.

In an agreed statement of facts, the court heard that 48-year-old Darko Lukic was beaten to death when confronted over a drug overdose at an apartment on Base Line Road.

The court also heard that Lukic had severe head trauma and a severe brain bleed caused by blunt force trauma after being beaten with a bat.

A victim impact statement from the victim’s family read, in part, “It (Lukic’s death) altered the lives of everyone who were close to him. We fear we May never fully recover from what happened.”

Dauntae Johnson and Joseph Mark Mercer Veneau were initially charged with first-degree murder, but pleaded guilty to manslaughter.

Both the Crown and the defence agreed on a five-year sentence for Johnson.

Mercer Veneau also pleaded guilty to assault with a weapon. His sentence is still to be determined on April 1, 2027.

Kerry Ann Bailey and Jamile-Lynn Bailey were charged with accessory after the fact to murder, and those charges were withdrawn.

stories.title: Western student entrepreneur builds promising tech startup to support founders
stories.summary: Western student entrepreneur Vinesh Nathan founded Formbase, a platform to help companies keep corporate records and be ready for fundraising
stories.author: Colleen MacDonald
stories.content:
“If your ambition isn’t scaring you, it’s not big enough.”

Western student entrepreneur Vinesh Nathan lives by these words. Over the last year, the fifth-year software engineering student founded Formbase, an online platform that helps businesses automate the administrative and regulatory work of running a company.

“I want Canadian founders to be able to easily run their business, focus on their product and customers, and leave the housekeeping to us,” he said.

Rather than looking for a job after graduation this spring, Nathan plans to devote his full-time efforts to growing his company.

Vinesh Nathan

“If not now, then when am I ever going to do this? It’s the best time to be a student taking business risks,” he said. “We have access to some of the greatest tools at Western, nearly for free, and so much opportunity.”

Nathan will be able to build momentum before he graduates, with his recent acceptance into the Western Accelerator, a 13-week program run by the Morrissette Institute for Entrepreneurship. The Accelerator offers funding, mentorship, workspaces and resources for scaling up a business. He starts in January, joining other Western students, alumni, faculty and staff who have founded high-potential ventures. Nathan says two startups, and even one long-established company, have already signed on as Formbase customers.

“I’m not building this to stay small. In five years, I want thousands of Canadian companies running on Formbase, and a team of 30 to 50 people behind it,” he said.

The ambition that turned Nathan into a Western student entrepreneur was first forged at home. He grew up in a family where “convertible notes” and “fully diluted shares” were part of ordinary talk around the dinner table. Both his parents and his grandfather ran businesses in India. Their conversations about strategy, financing and business development influenced him early.

Western student entrepreneur Vinesh Nathan credits his parents (L to R) Venkat Nathan and Aarti Venkat, for nurturing his interest in business from an early age. (Submitted)

“For my entire childhood, I watched my parents build an amazing software services company, and I saw the struggle and the sacrifice that goes on behind the scenes,” he said.

Nathan developed his own company when he saw the needs of other founders who struggled to keep up with corporate compliance obligations while juggling product development, customers, employees and fundraising. As companies raise money and issue shares or stock options, keeping track of who owns what – and managing the growing volume of corporate records – becomes increasingly complex. Formbase simplifies the process and even manages the documentation founders need when seeking investment. He says the stakes go well beyond administrative inconvenience.

“I’ve talked to founders who lost deals because of messy data rooms, and that’s millions of dollars,” he said. “Making sure all your compliance and documents are clean, on record and fundraise-ready can save your company.”

Nathan says spreadsheets aren’t built for this kind of record-keeping, and U.S. software may not suit Canadian corporations. With Canadian tech founders leaving the country in growing numbers, he hopes Formbase will help more companies stay and grow in Canada. He plans to be one of them.

Formbase isn’t Nathan’s only business venture. In his first year, he tutored his fellow Saugeen-Maitland residents in calculus. As more students approached him for help, he and his roommate, Sneh Patel, began matching students with peers interested in tutoring for extra income.

Western students (L to R) Vinesh Nathan and Sneh Patel, went from roommates to business partners, founding TutorMatch. (Submitted)

Demand grew so quickly that the pair built an online platform called TutorMatch to line up qualified tutors with students, and manage the payments. Nathan says the platform led to more than 600 tutoring sessions, with another 400 likely by the end of the year, though the co-founders have no plans for expansion.

“We’ve scaled to about 14 universities and we’re keeping it that way for now. It pays both our rents,” he said.

That experience actually sparked his main venture. The difficulties of incorporating TutorMatch and running its compliance requirements motivated Nathan to build Formbase. He developed his business and his entrepreneurial mindset by taking advantage of opportunities both within and beyond Western.

He took a year off his studies to complete an eight-month co-op placement, supported by Student Experience, at a fintech startup company in New York. Last year, he spent two months in an incubator program affiliated with Toronto Metropolitan University. While in Toronto, he also connected with staff from Morrissette Entrepreneurship and later pitched his idea to its advisory board. He also attended the speaker series events among Morrissette’s offerings for founders or students exploring business ideas.

“The Morrissette team was very supportive in connecting me with founders who could use my product, even before I’d been accepted into the Accelerator,” he said.

Those connections are particularly valuable as Nathan works to overcome one of his biggest challenges – earning respect as a 22-year-old founder pitching his product to leaders who have spent decades building their companies.

“It’s been a challenge to convince larger companies to rate my product on its merit, instead of my age, but I’m building their trust by showing them what it’s capable of,” he said.

For Nathan, the confidence to embrace risk comes from knowing he has done everything possible to make his business succeed. Now, with a working product, paying customers and resources at Morrissette, he’s eager to find out just how far that ambition can take him.

“I’m ready to take the big swing, trust the process and do the work.”

Those connections are particularly valuable as Nathan works to overcome one of his biggest challenges – earning respect as a 22-year-old founder pitching his product to leaders who have spent decades building their companies.
“It’s been a challenge to convince larger companies to rate my product on its merit, instead of my age, but I’m building their trust by showing them what it’s capable of,” he said.

For Nathan, the confidence to embrace risk comes from knowing he has done everything possible to make his business succeed. Now, with a working product, paying customers and resources at Morrissette, he’s eager to find out just how far that ambition can take him.
“I’m ready to take the big swing, trust the process and do the work.”

stories.title: Undefeated Western lacrosse team wins national championship
stories.summary: Western University's men's lacrosse team went undefeated in the 2026 season before winning the national championship.
stories.author: Special to Western News
stories.content:
| Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... |

The Mustangs have earned the national lacrosse title for the 10th time, finishing a perfect season with an 8-6 win over Guelph on Nov. 14.

The victory at the 2026 Baggataway Cup Finals, the national championships for the Canadian University Field Lacrosse Association, marked the 13th consecutive victory for the Western team this season.

“This win is incredibly special. Last season, our team failed to qualify for the Baggataway Cup weekend, which was heartbreaking. Going into this year, we returned most of our team and used that feeling of failure from the prior year as motivation,” said Christopher da Silva, who was named game MVP, with three goals and two assists in the finals.

“Since the beginning of training camp, we had one goal in mind, and that was to win a national championship. Every practice, game and every sacrifice we made throughout the season was driven by that shared goal.” – Christopher da Silva, Western Mustangs men’s lacrosse team

The Mustangs undefeated season marked a significant comeback.

“I think what makes this championship so meaningful is knowing how far we’ve come as a group,” da Silva said. “To go from not even qualifying for the tournament last year to winning it all this year is something we’re incredibly proud of.”

After Guelph opened the scoring, Western answered with a pair of goals from Cyrus Sinopole and Zach Abu-Ali to give the Mustangs a 2-1 lead. In the second quarter, Western would bookend a Guelph goal, the first coming from Mason Williams and the second from Christopher da Silva, giving Western a 4-2 lead at the midway break. The Gryphons cut the Mustangs lead early in the third quarter, but once again Western had the answer. A minute later, da Silva scored and John Collins-Williams added another goal shortly after.

At the 11:45 mark, da Silva would net the eventual game-winner to push the Western advantage to 7-4. The Gryphons put on a late push with two goals, but the Mustangs held on for the win and the national banner.

stories.title: Quebec union executive resigns after posting altered image of Conservative politician
stories.summary: MONTRÉAL - An executive of a major Quebec labour union resigned on Monday, days after posting an artificial intelligence-generated image on social media of a provincial Conservative politician with a black eye.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
MONTRÉAL - An executive of a major Quebec labour union resigned on Monday, days after posting an artificial intelligence-generated image on social media of a provincial Conservative politician with a black eye.

In a news release, the union known as the Fédération des travailleurs et travailleuses du Québec (FTQ) distanced itself from its former executive, adding that “this type of publication has no place in the public debate.”

In the generated image, Éloïse Coulombe, a Conservative member of the national assembly, was depicted wearing a unicorn costume and sporting a black eye.

The image was shared on a social media account of Vincent Leclair, who served as president of the Ftq’s Montreal regional council.

The post on Leclair’s account was critical of the Conservative representative’s initiative to meet with striking students at Université de Laval last week.

The union said in its statement that it denounced the image as soon as it was made aware of it being posted on social media. The statement identified Leclair by his former position, but didn’t mention him by name.

“In a context where violence against women, especially online, remains a major concern, we all have a responsibility to be vigilant and respectful in our words and publications,” says the union’s statement.

Coulombe told reporters at the Quebec City legislature that she had arranged to meet with the striking students to understand their demands and frustrations. The 23-year-old said she herself is a student at the university and serves as her party’s youth critic.

She is the youngest representative to sit at the national assembly.

She explained that she had received the green light to meet with the students from the student association’s general coordinator. But once on campus, she said she was confronted by other members of the student association who told her she was not welcome.

“And so, we had to leave, unfortunately, and I have not had an opportunity to discuss the concerns of the student community,” Coulombe said at the news conference, alongside Quebec Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime.

During the news conference, Duhaime took aim at labour unions and called for “calm” ahead of the parliamentary session set to begin on Dec. 1.

Duhaime also rejected the premise of the message posted on Leclair’s account that suggested Coulombe arranged the meeting to provoke the students.

The Conservative leader said that though the original post was deleted, screenshots of the “violent” and “unacceptable” image are still circulating online.

“We will not tolerate intimidation or the Ftq’s strongmen in any way whatsoever. Those days are over,” said Duhaime.

The Conservative leader also repeated parts of the message posted on the former union executive’s account and held up a copy of the altered picture at the news conference.

“I will quote only the beginning and the end of his message, because it’s a long message: ‘Éloïse Coulombe is meeting student associations in the middle of a strike and, surprise, she is poorly received,’” Duhaime read out at the news conference.

“‘Hello, Éloïse, you represent the Conservative Party of Quebec.’ He ends his message by saying: ‘What do you find in this party that responds to the demands of the young people you went to meet?’”

Premier Paul St-Pierre-Plamondon had promised during the provincial election campaign to amend laws passed by the previous government restricting the right to strike. The amendments led to major union protests, including a demonstration in which an effigy of Quebec’s former labour minister was beheaded.

Union leaders distanced themselves from the action at the time, which was organized by an independent collective known as the workers’ alliance.

Duhaime, who has authored a book criticizing Quebec’s labour unions, reiterated that his party is “totally opposed” to loosening strike laws. He stressed that he wants government crackdowns on strikes to “go even further.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 16, 2026.

stories.title: Explainer: Understanding what’s in Canada’s Immigration Levels Plan
stories.summary: The new targets continue to be lower than the peak of the Trudeau years, but a collection of "one-time" measures has pushed expected permanent resident admissions in 2027 to 662,000 people.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By David Baxter, The Canadian Press

Posted November 16, 2026 4:20 pm.

Last Updated November 16, 2026 4:28 pm.

Ottawa — The federal government’s updated immigration levels plan was published in the federal budget on Nov. 5, setting out Canada’s targets for admitting new residents — both permanent and temporary — for the next three years.

The new targets continue to be lower than the peak of the Trudeau years, but a collection of “one-time” measures has pushed expected permanent resident admissions in 2027 to 662,000 people.

However, that doesn’t mean 662,000 newcomers will be entering Canada for the first time.

Conservative MPs are critical of the one-time measures, saying Canada can’t accommodate that many newcomers with unemployment north of six per cent, while the government says many of the expected permanent residents are already here and won’t strain services or create new housing demand.

Here is a look at the key figures in the levels plan and what they mean:

The annual permanent resident target

A permanent resident is someone who has the right to live and work anywhere in Canada, with access to most benefits afforded to citizens, including health care coverage. Permanent residency is a prerequisite to make a citizenship application.

They aren’t able to vote, hold public office or certain jobs that require a high-level security clearance.

The levels plan broadly targets 380,000 new annual permanent resident admissions in each of 2027, 2028 and 2029. It is the same target in place in 2026.

The plan shows a range of between 352,000 people on the low end, and 422,000 on the high end, with the broad target close to the midpoint between the two.

Immigration department officials said in a technical briefing earlier this month about half of the 380,000 new permanent residents are expected be people already living and working in Canada.

In 2025, Canada admitted 393,770 permanent residents — including 20,790 who were in Canada already on student visas and 145,735 on work permits.

Who is eligible to apply within the permanent residency target?

The permanent residency target is divided into subcategories, including economic immigrants and family reunification.

Almost 245,000 of the 380,000 permanent residents from the main target are economic immigrants. About 100,000 of these will be people applying through skilled worker programs.

Another 95,000 will come through the Provincial Nominee Program — these are people nominated by their respective provincial or territorial government based on their economic needs.

The remainder of the economic category are selected through programs specific to certain industries or regions.

There are around 81,000 permanent residency spaces earmarked for family members, with 66,000 set aside for the spouses, domestic partners and children of people already living in Canada. Another 15,000 spaces are for parents and grandparents.

Just over 49,000 permanent residency spaces are set aside for refugees and protected persons, and 5,000 for those who are applying under humanitarian and compassionate grounds.

What are “one-time” measures for permanent residency?

With an aim to cut program wait times — some of which are years long — the government has introduced some one-time programs targeting some specific types of permanent resident applications.

This year’s levels plan includes a one-time program to admit up to 200,000 permanent residents across two main categories: workers and humanitarian and compassionate cases.

The worker stream is for people and their families who are already living and working in the country on visas. Who is selected will be decided in collaboration between Ottawa and the provinces and territories based on regional labour market needs. This is similar to how the Provincial Nominee Program works.

The other 100,000 is for people who have been stuck in a more than decade-long wait for humanitarian and compassionate permanent residency slots.

This includes about 32,000 former Hong Kong residents who came to Canada on a special program for those fleeing government persecution and nearly 19,000 Ukrainians who came after Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. All of those people are already here.

Another 45,000 will be for spouses, common-law partners and children of Canadians or existing permanent residents. That number is expected to include people not already in Canada.

A similar one-time initiative was started in 2025 to grant permanent residency to about 115,000 protected persons in Canada and 33,000 workers, both over a two-year period.

About 77,000 of those are expected to be admitted in 2027 — 69,000 protected persons and 8,000 workers.

Temporary residents, new arrivals and renewals

A temporary resident is someone who holds a special permit to be in Canada, most commonly a work or study permit. This category also includes asylum claimants, who apply for status upon arriving in Canada because they fear persecution at home.

The levels plan for 2027-2029 includes a target of 370,000 temporary resident admissions each year, a number solely made up of people who are not already in Canada. It does not include any temporary residents already in Canada who are renewing their permits to stay.

The number includes 220,000 temporary foreign workers, including 170,000 for the international Mobility Program and 50,000 in the Temporary Foreign Worker Program.

These targets do not include seasonal agricultural workers who enter and exit Canada within the same calendar year.

What programs exist within the temporary resident target?

The International Mobility Program covers jobs that don’t require a Labour Market Impact Assessment, commonly referred to as a Lmia. This is the document an employer needs to hire someone through the Temporary Foreign Worker Program showing they couldn’t find a Canadian applicant.

The program includes, but is not limited to, highly skilled workers and researchers, performers, full-time international students and those with open work permits.

The target for new arrivals through the International Mobility Program is 170,000 people for each of the next three years.

The Temporary Foreign Worker Program is for jobs where an employer needs to prove they are not able to find a Canadian applicant to fill a job and apply for a Lmia. These tend to include a closed work permit that ties the holder to the specific job they were hired to do.

The target for this program is 50,000 people annually through 2029.

This program has been the subject of much debate with high youth unemployment in many parts of the country, and rules have been brought in to restrict the program’s use in cities with more than six per cent unemployment.

Reforms to the program were announced earlier this month that include extending the maximum work permit period from one to two years.

In 2025, the target was to admit 674,000 temporary residents, but the most recent report to Parliament says 324,000 actually arrived.

How many non-permanent residents are in Canada?

The number of non-permanent residents in Canada includes temporary foreign workers, international students, refugees and asylum claimants.

In 2024, that number peaked at around three million people, or 7.2 per cent of the total population.

The government wants to cut that to five per cent by the end of 2027.

Statistics Canada estimates as of July 1, 2026, there were about 2.8 million non-permanent residents in Canada, about 6.7 per cent of the population.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. XX, 2026.

David Baxter, The Canadian Press

In 2025, Canada admitted 393,770 permanent residents — including 20,790 who were in Canada already on student visas and 145,735 on work permits.
Who is eligible to apply within the permanent residency target?
The permanent residency target is divided into subcategories, including economic immigrants and family reunification.
Almost 245,000 of the 380,000 permanent residents from the main target are economic immigrants. About 100,000 of these will be people applying through skilled worker programs.
Another 95,000 will come through the Provincial Nominee Program — these are people nominated by their respective provincial or territorial government based on their economic needs.
The remainder of the economic category are selected through programs specific to certain industries or regions.

There are around 81,000 permanent residency spaces earmarked for family members, with 66,000 set aside for the spouses, domestic partners and children of people already living in Canada. Another 15,000 spaces are for parents and grandparents.
Just over 49,000 permanent residency spaces are set aside for refugees and protected persons, and 5,000 for those who are applying under humanitarian and compassionate grounds.
What are “one-time” measures for permanent residency?
With an aim to cut program wait times — some of which are years long — the government has introduced some one-time programs targeting some specific types of permanent resident applications.
This year’s levels plan includes a one-time program to admit up to 200,000 permanent residents across two main categories: workers and humanitarian and compassionate cases.

The worker stream is for people and their families who are already living and working in the country on visas. Who is selected will be decided in collaboration between Ottawa and the provinces and territories based on regional labour market needs. This is similar to how the Provincial Nominee Program works.
The other 100,000 is for people who have been stuck in a more than decade-long wait for humanitarian and compassionate permanent residency slots.

This includes about 32,000 former Hong Kong residents who came to Canada on a special program for those fleeing government persecution and nearly 19,000 Ukrainians who came after Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. All of those people are already here.
Another 45,000 will be for spouses, common-law partners and children of Canadians or existing permanent residents. That number is expected to include people not already in Canada.
A similar one-time initiative was started in 2025 to grant permanent residency to about 115,000 protected persons in Canada and 33,000 workers, both over a two-year period.
About 77,000 of those are expected to be admitted in 2027 — 69,000 protected persons and 8,000 workers.
Temporary residents, new arrivals and renewals

A temporary resident is someone who holds a special permit to be in Canada, most commonly a work or study permit. This category also includes asylum claimants, who apply for status upon arriving in Canada because they fear persecution at home.

The levels plan for 2027-2029 includes a target of 370,000 temporary resident admissions each year, a number solely made up of people who are not already in Canada. It does not include any temporary residents already in Canada who are renewing their permits to stay.
The number includes 220,000 temporary foreign workers, including 170,000 for the international Mobility Program and 50,000 in the Temporary Foreign Worker Program.
These targets do not include seasonal agricultural workers who enter and exit Canada within the same calendar year.
What programs exist within the temporary resident target?

The International Mobility Program covers jobs that don’t require a Labour Market Impact Assessment, commonly referred to as a Lmia. This is the document an employer needs to hire someone through the Temporary Foreign Worker Program showing they couldn’t find a Canadian applicant.
The program includes, but is not limited to, highly skilled workers and researchers, performers, full-time international students and those with open work permits.
The target for new arrivals through the International Mobility Program is 170,000 people for each of the next three years.

The Temporary Foreign Worker Program is for jobs where an employer needs to prove they are not able to find a Canadian applicant to fill a job and apply for a Lmia. These tend to include a closed work permit that ties the holder to the specific job they were hired to do.
The target for this program is 50,000 people annually through 2029.

This program has been the subject of much debate with high youth unemployment in many parts of the country, and rules have been brought in to restrict the program’s use in cities with more than six per cent unemployment.
Reforms to the program were announced earlier this month that include extending the maximum work permit period from one to two years.
In 2025, the target was to admit 674,000 temporary residents, but the most recent report to Parliament says 324,000 actually arrived.
How many non-permanent residents are in Canada?
The number of non-permanent residents in Canada includes temporary foreign workers, international students, refugees and asylum claimants.
In 2024, that number peaked at around three million people, or 7.2 per cent of the total population.
The government wants to cut that to five per cent by the end of 2027.
Statistics Canada estimates as of July 1, 2026, there were about 2.8 million non-permanent residents in Canada, about 6.7 per cent of the population.

stories.content: A video of a pro-Palestinian March on Parliament Hill has attracted significant online attention, with many users sharing it and claiming it took place this year on Remembrance Day. The video shows a group of people holding a massive Palestinian flag in front of the Parliament Buildings. However, both the user who originally posted the video at the centre of these claims and a reverse image search of the video reveal it was shot in April 2025.

stories.title: Historic hearing begins as B.C. company wants to sell electricity exclusively to U.S.
stories.summary: For many years, the hydroelectric facilities provided power to a local pulp and paper mill and exported extra electricity to the United States.
stories.author: Amy Judd
stories.content:
A historic five-day hearing began in Powell River on Monday regarding electricity exports.

The Canada Energy Regulator (CER) is hearing the electricity export application from Powell River Energy Inc. (Prei).

The corporation has applied to the CER for a 30-year, contract-specific electricity export authorization.

Prei operates hydroelectric facilities at Powell Lake and Lois Lake in Powell River.

For many years, the hydroelectric facilities provided power to a local pulp and paper mill and exported extra electricity to the U.S.

However, the mill closed in 2021 and all the electricity generated began being exported to the U.S.

Now, Prei wants to obtain from the CER a 30-year electricity export authorization to sell all its electricity to the U.S., which has resulted in a first-of-its-kind licensing procedure.

“Prei is seeking an export electricity licence to support the ongoing financing and ongoing renewal of its power facilities,” Steve Eckert, vice president of Brookfield, told the hearing on Monday.

“This will, in turn, help Prei continue to contribute to the local and provincial economy. Prei continues to contribute to the local economy through employment, economic opportunities for local suppliers and contractors, local community contributions, taxes and other government fees.”

The CER regulates exports of electricity from Canada.

John Keller, media spokesperson for Energy Democracy For BC, told Global News that initially, the Prei had applied to the B.C. Utilities Commission for exemptions from certain regulations, which they challenged through legal assistance and were successful.

However, the situation is now before the B.C. Court of Appeal.

“When they applied earlier this year for an export licence, which would cover 30 years of exporting of this clean, renewable power, we, the community here in Power River, that’s including multiple First Nations, local governments, the chamber of commerce and over 2,600 individuals, all submitted objections to this application on the grounds that 30 years was too long and that there was not a sufficient amount of local benefit for control,” Keller said.

“Thirty years seems like a long time when the norm is only five years. In addition to that, as a result of the mill closing, Power River is now in a situation where we would like to expand our economic base and having that power available locally would be a big factor in doing so.

“So if all that power is being exported out of our community, that leaves nothing again for redevelopment of local economic activity.”

Powell River Energy Inc. is a subsidiary of Brookfield Renewable, where now-Prime Minister Mark Carney was the board chair from 2020 to 2025.

Over the next five days, all parties will get a chance to make their presentations in front of the CER panel.

“We are asking the Canadian Energy Regulator to reject this application, absolutely, and at minimum only allow a five-year renewal of the current permit, which runs until 2031,” Keller said.

content_blocks.text: The corporation has applied to the CER for a 30-year, contract-specific electricity export authorization.
Prei operates hydroelectric facilities at Powell Lake and Lois Lake in Powell River.
For many years, the hydroelectric facilities provided power to a local pulp and paper mill and exported extra electricity to the U.S.
However, the mill closed in 2021 and all the electricity generated began being exported to the U.S.
Now, Prei wants to obtain from the CER a 30-year electricity export authorization to sell all its electricity to the U.S., which has resulted in a first-of-its-kind licensing procedure.
“Prei is seeking an export electricity licence to support the ongoing financing and ongoing renewal of its power facilities,” Steve Eckert, vice president of Brookfield, told the hearing on Monday.

“This will, in turn, help Prei continue to contribute to the local and provincial economy. Prei continues to contribute to the local economy through employment, economic opportunities for local suppliers and contractors, local community contributions, taxes and other government fees.”
The CER regulates exports of electricity from Canada.

John Keller, media spokesperson for Energy Democracy For BC, told Global News that initially, the Prei had applied to the B.C. Utilities Commission for exemptions from certain regulations, which they challenged through legal assistance and were successful.
However, the situation is now before the B.C. Court of Appeal.

“When they applied earlier this year for an export licence, which would cover 30 years of exporting of this clean, renewable power, we, the community here in Power River, that’s including multiple First Nations, local governments, the chamber of commerce and over 2,600 individuals, all submitted objections to this application on the grounds that 30 years was too long and that there was not a sufficient amount of local benefit for control,” Keller said.

“Thirty years seems like a long time when the norm is only five years. In addition to that, as a result of the mill closing, Power River is now in a situation where we would like to expand our economic base and having that power available locally would be a big factor in doing so.
“So if all that power is being exported out of our community, that leaves nothing again for redevelopment of local economic activity.”

stories.title: Health Canada urges Canadians to check radon detectors
stories.summary: Health Canada is warning that inaccurate radon detectors sold online could leave Canadians unaware of dangerous gas levels in their homes.
stories.author: Archie Niari
stories.content:
Health Canada is warning Canadians that inaccurate radon detectors sold online could leave households unknowingly exposed to a radioactive gas linked to lung cancer.

In a public advisory issued Monday, the agency urged homeowners to use approved testing devices, following several warnings and recalls involving electronic monitors that provided misleading readings.

Faulty readings raise health concerns

Radon is a naturally occurring radioactive gas released from the breakdown of uranium in soil and rock. It is invisible, odourless and tasteless, and can accumulate inside homes.

Long-term exposure to elevated radon levels is the second-leading cause of lung cancer in Canada after smoking.

Health Canada said inaccurate detectors can provide readings that are either higher or lower than actual radon concentrations. The biggest concern is that homeowners could receive falsely reassuring results and remain unaware of dangerous exposure.

Previously flagged products include InkBird ⁠, Life Basis ⁠, Hanchen ⁠ and Spolehli ⁠ detectors, along with other devices sold on Amazon.CA.

How to test your home

Health Canada recommends testing during winter, when homes are more tightly sealed and radon levels are often higher.

A long-term test lasting at least three months provides the most accurate assessment of a home’s average radon levels.

Consumers should purchase electronic monitors that have passed performance testing by the Canadian National Radon Proficiency Program ⁠.

Anyone with a recalled detector should stop using it and dispose of it according to municipal electronic waste requirements.

More information is available in Health Canada’s radon testing guide ⁠.

stories.title: How Carney’s China visit highlights the stakes—and risks—of closer ties
stories.summary: It’s not a question of 'if' but 'how' Canada wants to deepen economic cooperation with China, experts say, as Carney continues push for trade diversification.
stories.author: Alex Boutilier
stories.content:
It’s not a question of “if” but “how” Prime Minister Mark Carney will seek to deepen economic ties with China amidst a global reordering provoked by U.S. President Donald Trump, experts say.

Carney is set to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping on Tuesday, the two leaders’ second meetings since Carney was elected in part on a promise to diversify Canadian trade away from the U.S.

China is a significant part of that strategy. After years of diplomatic hostilities — including China’s arrest and detention of Michael Kovrig and Michael Spavor — the Carney government signed a “strategic partnership” with Beijing to collaborate on energy and clean technology.

Deanna Horton, Canada’s former ambassador to Vietnam and a fellow at the Munk School of Global Affairs, said there’s a “great deal at stake” in the Canada-China relationship given the trade tensions with Trump’s administration.

Horton said despite the Democrats dramatic victory in this month’s midterm elections, she thinks it’s unlikely that Canada and the U.S. will return to the kind of tariff-free trade the two countries enjoyed in the past.

“We’re evolving into G2 world, the U.S. and China, and Canada needs to not have all its eggs in the U.S. basket,” Horton, who was also involved in the negotiations of the original North American Free Trade Agreement (Nafta), said in an interview Monday.

“I don’t think we’re in a position now where we’re going to not want to deepen relations in China. I don’t think that is really an option for Canada. The question is: where do we place the emphasis in terms of improving relationships?”

Much of the attention around the meeting has been focused on Canada’s auto sector, already hurting from Trump’s trade war and bracing for higher tariffs in the new year.

In a January 2026 deal, Canada reduced its 100 per cent tariff on Chinese electric vehicles to 6.1 per cent and allowed up to 49,000 of the vehicles to be sold annually, with the cap increasing over time.

China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural goods as a result.

Speaking to reporters in Cambodia Monday, Carney said that depending on what happens with U.S. trade talks, Canada could look elsewhere — including to China — to bolster its automotive industry.

“(Canada has) great autoworkers; important market, real assets in Canada. If they’re not fully utilized in a North American context, that provides other opportunities,” Carney said.

“Canada is going to move forward either way.”

Margaret McCuaig-Johnston, a senior fellow at the University of Ottawa and a leading expert on Canada-China relations, said Carney’s talk of greater Chinese involvement in the Canadian auto industry May be a bargaining move as talks with the U.S. stretch on.

“That, in my view, would be encouraging. If it’s a bargaining chip, it can be dropped,” McCuaig-Johnston said in an interview Monday.

“If it’s an offer to China to open up our manufacturing to them, that’s got a lot of concerns. They don’t want to use Canadian parts, they don’t want to follow Canadian labour standards … and they don’t want technology transfer (to Canadian companies).”

McCuaig-Johnston said those factors were the “guardrails” the federal government often talks about when it comes to protecting Canada’s auto sector while allowing greater Chinese investment.

And while Carney and the government talk about “guardrails” in other sectors — such as critical minerals and defence — McCuaig-Johnston said what those protections are is not exactly clear.

Beyond the economic relationship, Carney also said he would raise the issue of Chinese foreign interference in Canadian political affairs with Xi.

The Canadian intelligence community has repeatedly warned that China, among other countries, has attempted to covertly interfere in Canadian politics, as well as engage in transnational repression against Chinese diaspora groups living Canada.

Carney himself said just last year that China was one of the greatest threat to Canadian national security.

“The advantage of these meetings is you can raise these issues directly and frankly. And I will be raising the importance with which we attach to the non-interference in our affairs by China and other countries,” Carney told reporters earlier this month.

Another meeting at this week’s Apec summit could be of keen interest to Canada and its foreign policy — the planned trilateral meeting between Xi, Trump, and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

The meeting, which was proposed by Trump and accepted by Xi, is reportedly to discuss nuclear disarmament. The U.S. and Russia have the world’s largest stockpiles of nuclear weapons, and China has balked at talks of nuclear de-escalation.

China’s foreign ministry said on Monday that the meeting will be of “groundbreaking significance” and will promote peace and stability.

With files from the Associated Press and Reuters.

stories.title: Nova Scotia officials warn toxic drugs increasingly mixed with veterinary sedative
stories.summary: Officials in Nova Scotia are warning that the unregulated drug supply is becoming more toxic as it's commonly laced with unknown ingredients, including strong veterinary sedatives.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau
stories.content:
Officials in Nova Scotia are warning that the unregulated drug supply is becoming more toxic as it’s commonly laced with unknown ingredients, including strong veterinary sedatives.

Halifax Regional Police confirmed that as recently as Sept. 4, a search at a home in Dartmouth included a sample of fentanyl that tested positive for medetomidine — a potent sedative used primarily by veterinarians.

As part of that investigation, police seized 6.2 kg of fentanyl, an additional 1,400 fentanyl pills and 10.5 litres of GHB — commonly known as the date rape drug. The case is believed to be the largest ever seizure of fentanyl and GHB in Atlantic Canada.

As well, Nova Scotia Health said last week that a drug sample that was seized by police in Pictou County and sent to Health Canada’s drug analysis lab tested positive for a variety of substances including medetomidine or its salts, fluorofentanyl, ketamine, methylfentanyl, phenacetin, caffeine, diphenhydramine and nefopam.

According to Nova Scotia Health, the drug was described as being a “sticky brownish soft resinous substance.”

Officials in British Columbia, Ontario and New Brunswick have raised growing concerns about the detection of medetomidine in the drug supply, which can be mixed with opioids like fentanyl.

Nova Scotia RCMP confirmed to Global News that medetomidine has been found in the province but the force could not say how many times the drug has been identified in their jurisdiction.

“There is always a risk that unregulated drugs May contain unexpected, stronger than expected, or potentially harmful ingredients,” said spokesperson Cpl. Carlie McCann in a statement.

“An overdose is a medical emergency. Under the Good Samaritan Drug Overdose Act , people who experience or witness an overdose and call 911 are protected from being charged with possession of a controlled substance and breach of conditions regarding simple possession of controlled substances.”

Dr. Ryan Sommers, senior regional medical officer of health and senior medical director population and public health, said the unregulated drug supply is “becoming more dangerous” because it can contain not only strong opioids, but veterinary sedatives as well.

“These substances are often mixed with other opioids and benzodiazepines, which can cause deep sedation, slow or stopped breathing, low blood pressure, and a very slow heart rate,” he said in a statement.

“Naloxone reverses the effects of opioids and helps restore breathing, but it does not work on tranquillizers or benzodiazepines. As a result, a person May stay unconscious even after receiving naloxone.”

He said naloxone should be given in a suspected overdose because it can restore breathing when opioids are involved, “and they almost always are.”

Users should also assume that any unregulated drug taken May contain fentanyl and medetomidine.

Anyone who sees a suspected overdose should call 911 immediately.

“Naloxone May not wake someone up when drugs like medetomidine are involved, but it can restore breathing. Call 911, prioritize breathing, and do not leave them alone,” he added.

“There is always a risk that unregulated drugs May contain unexpected, stronger than expected, or potentially harmful ingredients,” said spokesperson Cpl. Carlie McCann in a statement.

“An overdose is a medical emergency. Under the Good Samaritan Drug Overdose Act , people who experience or witness an overdose and call 911 are protected from being charged with possession of a controlled substance and breach of conditions regarding simple possession of controlled substances.”
content_blocks.html: “An overdose is a medical emergency. Under the Good Samaritan Drug Overdose Act, people who experience or witness an overdose and call 911 are protected from being charged with possession of a controlled substance and breach of conditions regarding simple possession of controlled substances.”

content_blocks.text: Dr. Ryan Sommers, senior regional medical officer of health and senior medical director population and public health, said the unregulated drug supply is “becoming more dangerous” because it can contain not only strong opioids, but veterinary sedatives as well.

“These substances are often mixed with other opioids and benzodiazepines, which can cause deep sedation, slow or stopped breathing, low blood pressure, and a very slow heart rate,” he said in a statement.

“Naloxone reverses the effects of opioids and helps restore breathing, but it does not work on tranquillizers or benzodiazepines. As a result, a person May stay unconscious even after receiving naloxone.”
He said naloxone should be given in a suspected overdose because it can restore breathing when opioids are involved, “and they almost always are.”
Users should also assume that any unregulated drug taken May contain fentanyl and medetomidine.
Anyone who sees a suspected overdose should call 911 immediately.
“Naloxone May not wake someone up when drugs like medetomidine are involved, but it can restore breathing. Call 911, prioritize breathing, and do not leave them alone,” he added.

stories.title: Settlement approved in N.S. First Nation class action over non-consensual MRI scans
stories.summary: A $400,000 settlement has been approved in a class action that alleged members of a Nova Scotia First Nation were subjected to MRI scans without their consent.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A $400,000 settlement has been approved in a class action that alleged members of a Nova Scotia First Nation were subjected to MRI scans without their consent.

A statement from McKiggan Hebert Lawyers says the settlement was approved in Nova Scotia Supreme Court on Friday.

The lawsuit alleged that two Halifax doctors performed some magnetic resonance (MRI) scans of about 60 people from Pictou Landing First Nation without the participants’ knowledge or consent.

A statement of claim says band members agreed to undergo scans as part of a research project in 2017 but were subjected to additional “secret” scans of their livers for a separate study that they weren’t told about.

None of the allegations in the lawsuit have been tested in court.

Brian Hebert, who represented the plaintiffs in the class action, says the settlement ends a long journey for these members of the Pictou Landing First Nation.

The lawsuit alleged the defendants, both radiologists, were liable for invasion of privacy, acting recklessly and causing distress and anguish.

The lawsuit also accused them of failing to advise participants of serious health issues that were discovered on the scans.

A lawyer representing the two doctors declined to comment.

stories.title: Ex-CRA employee sentenced after pleading guilty to fraud, breach of trust
stories.summary: Mounties say Yoan Zola pleaded guilty to three of the charges — breach of trust, fraud and trafficking in identity information — last July
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Police say a former Canada Revenue Agency employee who pleaded guilty to three breach of trust and fraud-related charges will be serving his sentence in the community.

A statement from the RCMP says federal Mounties in the Pacific region conducted an “exhaustive” investigation into Yoan Zola starting in 2022 after the agency reported that an employee had compromised taxpayer information.

Zola was arrested in Vancouver in January 2026 and charged with breach of trust, trafficking in identity information, identity theft, fraud under $5,000, fraudulent personation, and use of a credit card obtained by crime.

Mounties say Zola pleaded guilty to three of the charges — breach of trust, fraud and trafficking in identity information — last July, while the other charges against him were stayed.

Zola was given a conditional sentence on Nov. 10 to serve two years less a day for the beach of trust and identity trafficking charges, and a concurrent two-month conditional sentence for the fraud charge, to be served in the community as long as he follows the supervision orders of the court.

Staff Sgt. David Grey with the Federal Policing Pacific Region’s cyber and financial investigation team says Zola’s actions undermined Canadians’ trust in public institutions and their employees who have access to sensitive personal information.
