stories.title: Is it too early for Christmas lights? Even the pro installers say yes
stories.summary: Wanda Garrett’s house in the Kilbride neighbourhood of St. John’s, N.L., is set to become the envy of the neighbourhood.
stories.author: Garrett Barry
stories.content:
Wanda Garrett’s house in the Kilbride neighbourhood of St. John’s, N.L., is set to become the envy of the neighbourhood.

Perched at the very end of a residential street, she’s in the perfect position to display her brand-new permanent holiday lights, hung up and fastened in place on Friday.

“I’m at the top of the hill, so everybody will see it!,” she said Friday morning, as installers circled her home.

There’s only one thing left to do: Flip those lights on.

“It’s a little too soon for me,” she said. “My daughter, who — this is her Christmas gift by the way — she would want to turn them on right away. But I usually wait till December 1st.”

“It’s just a date that I’ve always done.”

With the calendar flipped past Remembrance Day commemorations, there’s little to stop homeowners like Garrett from putting up their Christmas decorations and turning up the holiday cheer. But even some of the pros — like the installers working on her house Friday — say it’s too early to start decking the halls just yet.

“There’s definitely a stage where it’s too early,” said Charles Bell. “If you’re celebrating Christmas before Halloween, I think there might — there could be some questioning going on there.”

Bell’s taking on permanent light installation as a side-hustle, away from his normal 9-5 job working at a bank.

He agrees with Garrett — Dec. 1 just seems like the right time to flip the switch.

“That’s when you kind of see everybody around the city and retail outlets start to pick up their celebrations for the holiday season,” he said “In my mind, that’s a good time.”

But the bookings for his new business — he’s two years in — start to fill up around Nov. 1. He’s happy to accommodate those wanting to install early.

“If people want to get it done now, more than happy to do it,” he said with a smile.

Bell installs so-called permanent holiday lights — LEDs on a strip with fixtures that can be screwed into siding or soffits underneath a roof.

It’s the latest trend in holiday decorating.

“Usually it picks up when Costco brings in the Govee lights,” he said. “It started about two weeks ago.”

Those lights can be controlled by an phone app to change colours and brightness — making them perfect, Bell said, for all-year-round use.

“We want to grow and expand our service beyond just this time of year. We want to get into installs in the spring and summer, because these lights can be used to celebrate St. Patrick’s day, Canada Day, anything like that.”

While both Bell and Garrett are happy to wait for now, there’s some evidence that others in St. John’s are anxious for holiday cheer to come.

This winter, the City of St. John’s has moved it’s annual park lighting ceremony in Bowring Park ahead to Nov. 28. Weather delays forced the celebration to Dec. 13 last year.

“I think we’re just looking for some joy,” said Councillor Jill Bruce. “I just think that these lights in the park bring people so much joy.”

Bruce said the city moved up their timeline due to resident feedback, and there’s been plenty more requests to keep the lights on longer into the winter too.

“We have a long winter season that starts sometimes in November and doesn’t end until, like, April,” she said. “So it’s just encouraging people to get out over the Christmas season. And if that brings people joy, we are all for it.”

The lights in Bowring Park have already been installed — with some just final touches to go — but Bruce said the city’s not looking to just turn them on suddenly. She says the festival atmosphere of the lighting ceremony is worth waiting for.

“I think that I think we found a good balance here,” she said. “I wouldn’t want to do it before Remembrance Day.

“I think we found the sweet spot. I think like the end of November is a nice time.”

With the calendar flipped past Remembrance Day commemorations, there’s little to stop homeowners like Garrett from putting up their Christmas decorations and turning up the holiday cheer. But even some of the pros — like the installers working on her house Friday — say it’s too early to start decking the halls just yet.
“There’s definitely a stage where it’s too early,” said Charles Bell. “If you’re celebrating Christmas before Halloween, I think there might — there could be some questioning going on there.”

content_blocks.alt: Wanda Garrett
content_blocks.caption: With the calendar flipped past Remembrance Day commemorations, there’s little to stop homeowners like Wanda from putting up their Christmas decorations and turning up the holiday cheer. (CTV News)

content_blocks.text: Bell’s taking on permanent light installation as a side-hustle, away from his normal 9-5 job working at a bank.
He agrees with Garrett — Dec. 1 just seems like the right time to flip the switch.
“That’s when you kind of see everybody around the city and retail outlets start to pick up their celebrations for the holiday season,” he said “In my mind, that’s a good time.”
But the bookings for his new business — he’s two years in — start to fill up around Nov. 1. He’s happy to accommodate those wanting to install early.
“If people want to get it done now, more than happy to do it,” he said with a smile.
Bell installs so-called permanent holiday lights — LEDs on a strip with fixtures that can be screwed into siding or soffits underneath a roof.
It’s the latest trend in holiday decorating.
“Usually it picks up when Costco brings in the Govee lights,” he said. “It started about two weeks ago.”
Those lights can be controlled by an phone app to change colours and brightness — making them perfect, Bell said, for all-year-round use.

“We want to grow and expand our service beyond just this time of year. We want to get into installs in the spring and summer, because these lights can be used to celebrate St. Patrick’s day, Canada Day, anything like that.”

content_blocks.alt: Coun. Jill Bruce
content_blocks.caption: Coun. Jill Bruce speaks to the city's annual park lighting ceremony for the Christmas season. (CTV News).

content_blocks.text: While both Bell and Garrett are happy to wait for now, there’s some evidence that others in St. John’s are anxious for holiday cheer to come.
This winter, the City of St. John’s has moved it’s annual park lighting ceremony in Bowring Park ahead to Nov. 28. Weather delays forced the celebration to Dec. 13 last year.
“I think we’re just looking for some joy,” said Councillor Jill Bruce. “I just think that these lights in the park bring people so much joy.”
Bruce said the city moved up their timeline due to resident feedback, and there’s been plenty more requests to keep the lights on longer into the winter too.

“We have a long winter season that starts sometimes in November and doesn’t end until, like, April,” she said. “So it’s just encouraging people to get out over the Christmas season. And if that brings people joy, we are all for it.”

The lights in Bowring Park have already been installed — with some just final touches to go — but Bruce said the city’s not looking to just turn them on suddenly. She says the festival atmosphere of the lighting ceremony is worth waiting for.
“I think that I think we found a good balance here,” she said. “I wouldn’t want to do it before Remembrance Day.
“I think we found the sweet spot. I think like the end of November is a nice time.”

stories.title: North Atlantic right whale population declines as U.S. weakens protections
stories.summary: Latest estimate puts number at about 382 animals at the end of 2025, seven fewer than a year earlier and 20% below peak of 483 in 2011
stories.author: Jenn Thornhill Verma
stories.content:
The North Atlantic right whale population has slipped back into decline, ending four years of fragile growth just as the United States weakens its protections for the critically endangered species.

The latest estimate , released Monday by the North Atlantic Right Whale Consortium at its annual meeting in Halifax, puts the population at about 382 animals at the end of 2025. That’s seven fewer than a year earlier and 20-per-cent below its most recent peak of 483 in 2011.

The species lost about a quarter of its population in less than a decade after that peak. “This population cannot afford another slide like that,” said Heather Pettis of the New England Aquarium, who chairs the consortium.

Entanglements in fishing gear and vessel strikes remain the leading threats to the animals, which migrate between Canadian and U.S. waters to feed and give birth. Climate change, which has pushed the whales into new feeding grounds, and ocean noise add to the pressure.

Scientists say recovery depends on both countries – at a time when their approaches are diverging. In the U.S., “we’re seeing movements to deregulate and backslide on protective measures,” Dr. Pettis said.

Congress has barred new rules for U.S. lobster and crab fisheries to prevent entanglement through 2028, and the House of Representatives has passed a bill , still awaiting Senate approval, to extend that pause to 2035. That could stall talks on the next round of rules, Dr. Pettis said, and “the last thing we need is a delay.”

The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration is also considering “ deregulatory action ” on its rule requiring large vessels to slow in seasonal right whale zones along the U.S. East Coast, including swapping speed limits for acoustic or other forms of technology that detects whales and alerts ships in real time. The 2008 rule remains in effect while the agency reviews public comments, said Noaa Fisheries spokesperson John Chu in an e-mail.

Dr. Pettis said the new technology, while promising, isn’t ready to replace the vessel speed rule. “They’re an ‘and,’ not an ‘or.’”

Another federal rule , which came into effect Sept. 14, narrows the definition of “harm” under the Endangered Species Act. Since right whale deaths are incidental, Dr. Pettis called the change “cause for alarm,” though the whales are still covered by the Marine Mammal Protection Act.

Mr. Chu said the change targets “unnecessary or duplicative permitting requirements” for projects and industries, not protections.

Canada, by contrast, has been “much more nimble,” Dr. Pettis said. And with the U.S. pulling back, Ottawa needs to “hold or step up our efforts,” said Sean Brillant, senior conservation biologist at the Canadian Wildlife Federation.

Mr. Chu said risk reduction “must be a shared responsibility.”

Canada first brought in fishing closures and vessel speed limits for right whales after a wave of deaths in the Gulf of St. Lawrence in 2017. “All we’ve done at best was end the nosedive,” said Dr. Brillant. “This species is still on a knife’s edge.”

Two of the three whales found entangled with fishing gear this year were in the gulf, the most recent on Oct. 21, said Lindsey Jones, who manages the North Atlantic Right Whale Catalog at the New England Aquarium.

In February, Fisheries and Oceans Canada rolled out its Whalesafe Fishing Gear Strategy, which aims to keep fishing areas open when right whales are present. It allows harvesters to use on-demand, or “ropeless,” gear that keeps buoy lines on the sea floor until traps are hauled in.

“Canadian harvesters and industry have been the real leaders in testing it,” said Alexis Van Bemmel, acting manager of the whales team in Dfo’s national programs branch.

After closures near North Lake, PEI, and Chéticamp, N.S., this year, the Canadian Wildlife Federation’s gear-lending program, CanFISH , trained about 85 harvesters and deckhands, nearly as many as in all the years since 2022. It was also the first year lobster was landed commercially from a right whale closure in Canada.

But new gear can’t solve an older problem: fishing gear already lost at sea. Division ( #5217 in the right whale catalogue), a four-year-old male found dead off North Carolina in January, was entangled in rope from a snow crab fishing area in the southern Gulf of St. Lawrence that had not been fished in five years, officials determined . Canada’s gear-marking rules allowed the department to trace it, said Marina Petrovic, Dfo’s acting director of national programs.

Since 2019, Dfo’s ghost gear program has removed more than 2,620 tonnes of lost fishing gear and more than 1,040 kilometres of rope. A national ghost gear action plan is expected next spring.

The 2025-26 season brought some good news: 24 calves, the fourth-highest on record. The last went undetected until September, when it was spotted with its mother, Silt ( #1817 ), off Anticosti Island, Que. The calves will count toward next year’s estimate.

But the number of reproductive females held at 73, when it should be climbing, Dr. Pettis said. “These whales are biologically programmed to eat and reproduce, and so they are going to do that if we give them the space.”

Last week, the first calf of the 2026-27 season was spotted off St. Augustine, Fla., with Curlew ( #4190 ), a first-time mother.

“Clearly this species is doing everything it can to survive,” Dr. Brillant said. “And we need to match its efforts.”

stories.title: Is a cougar prowling the Dundas Valley? Two men set out to prove it
stories.summary: A Facebook group has logged more than 10 reported sightings near Cootes Paradise and the RBG in five months. Now its administrators have set up a trail camera, hoping for the first verified cougar footage in Hamilton.
stories.author: Annaliese Gumboc
stories.content:
After trekking through shrubbery and scat-littered game trails, Scott March and James Piruha arrive at an undisclosed location south of Waterdown and set up a motion-activated camera.

They believe a cougar is on its way, following hydro lines, railway tracks and white-tailed deer cutting through the grasses. If the camera catches a clear shot of the presumed feline, it could be the first officially verified footage of a cougar in Hamilton.

Non-believers “consider cougars to be similar, in Ontario, to Bigfoot,” said March. He hopes to prove them wrong.

As administrators for Big Cats Urban Ontario, a Facebook group for those interested in large wild cats in the province, March and Piruha are chasing an “alarming amount” of cougar sightings reported in the area.

“Most cases we get are misidentifications,” said March. “I’d say about 80 per cent. But then there’s still that 20 per cent hope.”

Ontario’s Ministry of Natural Resources says there is no known breeding population of cougars in the province.

In the past five months, they’ve heard of more than 10 reported cougar sightings in the vicinity of Cootes Paradise, Dundas Valley and the Royal Botanical Gardens, according to March. Submitted evidence includes photos of a deer carcass in a tree, taken last year, and apparent animal tracks in Dundas Valley, sent to March a few days ago.

Based on reports, he believes a cougar has been prowling the area for roughly a year, and hopes the camera will prove it. But the presence of cougars in southern Ontario is a messy, much-debated subject.

The provincial government recognizes the existence of wild cougars in Ontario, but does not have a concrete answer when it comes to the origins of these animals or their population distribution.

Cougars are known to be elusive and shy, complicating efforts to track the population.

The felines are believed to live primarily in northwestern Ontario, where “remote wilderness areas border existing populations in Manitoba,” stated an email from the Ministry of Natural Resources, which tracks sightings.

The government acknowledges “many reports” from the south, but only a few have been officially verified.

In 2014, for example, a cougar was caught in the town of Cobourg after it was spotted repeatedly in the area, including on a resident’s deck. The animal’s origins were never proven. At the time, a Ministry of Natural Resources official said the cougar showed some behaviour suggesting it May once have been in captivity.

Ten years earlier, Anne Yagi, then a biologist for the MNR, confirmed the presence of cougar DNA in scat in the southern Niagara region.

Yagi, now the president of an environmental consulting firm, suggested the recent Hamilton-area sightings could be caused by “natural expansions through the escarpment zone.”

“Given it’s Dundas Valley, that’s a huge tract of suitable habitat for a large predatory animal to move through,” Yagi added.

She noted the valley supports an abundance of deer, an important food source for cougars.

The biologist said it’s “natural behaviour for an animal to move along a corridor like that and move into areas where it’s a suitable habitat.”

March’s deer carcass photos aligned with cougar predation behaviour, according to Yagi, though she cautioned something else could explain what they show.

The remains of a deer in a tree, photographed last year and sent to Scott March. A biologist says it fits how cougars prey on deer, but something else could explain it.

She confirmed the Dundas Valley photos showed animal tracks that were “certainly a large cat,” though she could not determine the type of feline.

Yagi said the sightings and evidence could originate from an escaped or released exotic pet, cougar or otherwise.

“Cougars are extremely shy and rarely seen by humans,” the MNR told The Spectator. “Although occurrence of cougars has also been confirmed in southern Ontario, evidence suggests that most of these animals are of domestic/captive origin. Most reported sightings in southern Ontario turn out to be other animals, such as bobcats, large dogs, coyotes or wolves.”

Cougars in Ontario could consist of native felines, released and escaped exotic pets, cougars dispersing from the West’s more established populations or some combination of the three, according to the province. DNA evidence from cougar carcasses in northwestern Ontario suggests some of the animals May originate from populations in the United States, including the Dakotas, said the MNR.

The MNR told The Spectator there is no known breeding population of cougars in Ontario.

March dreams of a breakthrough that would prove otherwise.

Adopted from Peru, March grew up in the Hamilton area surrounded by animals — including rats, rescued racing dogs and bearded dragons — but said he’s always gravitated to cats.

After watching a YouTube video about big cats in Ontario, March was hooked and founded the Big Cats Facebook group in early 2025. The group has grown to include more than 12,000 members, including MNR research scientist Brent Patterson, who helps evaluate sightings.

March said concrete evidence, like a photo of a mother cougar with cubs, would be enough to establish a breeding population.

“If we figure this out and we can change their conservation status to established population, that means that the government acknowledges that they’re back in the region and they’re here to stay,” said March.

From left, James Piruha and Scott March set up a motion-activated camera south of Waterdown, hoping to capture the first verified footage of a cougar in Hamilton.

“The (conservation authorities) do nothing for these cats in the way of protection, in the way of tracking, in the way of everything,” said March. “They don’t even focus on them because they don’t believe that they’re around.”

In Ontario, cougars are currently classified as a “special concern” species which “means they’re vulnerable to being threatened or endangered if they start getting killed off,” said Yagi, noting that this designation is “probably correct.”

Nonetheless, March holds out hope the camera, or the expansion of his group, will lead to new evidence. His posts are flooded with comments from residents of Hamilton and surrounding communities relating stories of apparent cougar sightings — but no verified pictures.

“Maybe someone has a picture of a mother and a cub walking that doesn’t know about our project,” said March. “And that would be our breakthrough.”

They believe a cougar is on its way, following hydro lines, railway tracks and white-tailed deer cutting through the grasses. If the camera catches a clear shot of the presumed feline, it could be the first officially verified footage of a cougar in Hamilton.
Non-believers “consider cougars to be similar, in Ontario, to Bigfoot,” said March. He hopes to prove them wrong.

As administrators for Big Cats Urban Ontario, a Facebook group for those interested in large wild cats in the province, March and Piruha are chasing an “alarming amount” of cougar sightings reported in the area.
“Most cases we get are misidentifications,” said March. “I’d say about 80 per cent. But then there’s still that 20 per cent hope.”
Ontario’s Ministry of Natural Resources says there is no known breeding population of cougars in the province.

In the past five months, they’ve heard of more than 10 reported cougar sightings in the vicinity of Cootes Paradise, Dundas Valley and the Royal Botanical Gardens, according to March. Submitted evidence includes photos of a deer carcass in a tree, taken last year, and apparent animal tracks in Dundas Valley, sent to March a few days ago.

Based on reports, he believes a cougar has been prowling the area for roughly a year, and hopes the camera will prove it. But the presence of cougars in southern Ontario is a messy, much-debated subject.
The provincial government recognizes the existence of wild cougars in Ontario, but does not have a concrete answer when it comes to the origins of these animals or their population distribution.
Cougars are known to be elusive and shy, complicating efforts to track the population.

The felines are believed to live primarily in northwestern Ontario, where “remote wilderness areas border existing populations in Manitoba,” stated an email from the Ministry of Natural Resources, which tracks sightings.
The government acknowledges “many reports” from the south, but only a few have been officially verified.

In 2014, for example, a cougar was caught in the town of Cobourg after it was spotted repeatedly in the area, including on a resident’s deck. The animal’s origins were never proven. At the time, a Ministry of Natural Resources official said the cougar showed some behaviour suggesting it May once have been in captivity.
Ten years earlier, Anne Yagi, then a biologist for the MNR, confirmed the presence of cougar DNA in scat in the southern Niagara region.
Yagi, now the president of an environmental consulting firm, suggested the recent Hamilton-area sightings could be caused by “natural expansions through the escarpment zone.”
“Given it’s Dundas Valley, that’s a huge tract of suitable habitat for a large predatory animal to move through,” Yagi added.
She noted the valley supports an abundance of deer, an important food source for cougars.
The biologist said it’s “natural behaviour for an animal to move along a corridor like that and move into areas where it’s a suitable habitat.”
March’s deer carcass photos aligned with cougar predation behaviour, according to Yagi, though she cautioned something else could explain what they show.

She confirmed the Dundas Valley photos showed animal tracks that were “certainly a large cat,” though she could not determine the type of feline.

stories.title: Carney heads to China to meet with President Xi, leaders from across Pacific Rim
stories.summary: Phnom Penh — Prime Minister Mark Carney is travelling to China today, where he is set to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and leaders from across the Pacific Rim.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Shenzhen — Prime Minister Mark Carney arrived in China Monday, where he is set to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and leaders from across the Pacific Rim.

On his fourth and final stop of a nine-day overseas trip, Carney is in the city of Shenzhen, a tech hub in southeastern China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation summit.

His first official task, however, will be a bilateral meeting with Xi on Tuesday morning in China. Ahead of the trip, Carney said Canada could do more with China in terms of agriculture, clean and conventional energy, and financial services.

“We’ve established pretty clear guardrails on the areas that we’re going to focus on … I’m using our words, not theirs,” he told reporters in Phnom Penh on Sunday, where he was attending the Francophonie summit.

Earlier on this trip he was in Manila for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, and Dublin for a European Political Community meeting.

Carney said he expects to speak with Xi about “the evolution of the international system, China’s role in that and Canadian priorities.”

An overarching topic will be Chinese investments into Canada’s auto sector. Both countries agreed earlier this year to allow a limited amount of Chinese electric vehicles into Canada.

Carney has said he wants Chinese carmakers to set up shop, but only if they provide decent jobs, saying he is wary of plants where workers assemble cars using components mostly made in China.

He said trade talks with Washington will shape how Canada approaches Chinese investment.

“It’s part of the trade negotiations,” he said. “Depending (on) where that settles, there’ll be other options — European options, Asian options.”

“This is not leverage, but you know, action-reaction. It depends.”

This is the second time this year Carney has met with Xi in China — he travelled to Beijing in January for the first meeting between a Canadian prime minister and Chinese president in eight years. The relationship between Canada and China had soured during the tenure of former prime minister Justin Trudeau, largely over accusations from Canada about foreign interference from China.

Before leaving Canada, Carney said he would raise foreign interference with XI, prompting a Chinese government spokesperson to deny any such activities take place.

Carney will also meet with various leaders from the Apec forum, a group of 21 economies on both sides of the Pacific that work together to break down trade barriers. The grouping includes members as varied as Taiwan, Australia and Peru.

Carney’s office says he will stick with his focus of drumming up more investment and diversifying Canadian trade.

Vina Nadjibulla, co-founder of the Centre for Strategic Statecraft, said she’ll be watching to see whether Carney allows more Chinese investments into Canada “in critical sectors, in energy and technology, particularly related to renewables and batteries” in addition to auto manufacturing.

“We have to constantly triangulate our relationship with China with our discussions with the U.S. — and also watch then what happens between the U.S. and China bilaterally,” she said.

In 2022, Canada ordered three Chinese firms to divest their interests in critical minerals operations in Canada, citing national security concerns.

Nadjibulla also said the summit should help craft the foreign policy review that Carney aims to table in the House of Commons in the coming weeks, as well as next year’s planned renewal of the 2022 Indo-Pacific strategy launched by his predecessor Justin Trudeau.

“We now have a really solid foundation,” Nadjibulla said, noting that leaders from Asia have visited Canada or are planning to, notably Vietnam and India.

“Canada is finally on their radar and has relevance to their own diversification agendas and their own economic security and resilience agendas.”

She said any update to Ottawa’s regional strategy must include a look at relations with Taiwan, a self-governing island which China claims. The federal cabinet has left a trade arrangement sitting unsigned for more than a year, despite the House foreign-affairs committee urging the government to proceed with more economic relations.

U.S. President Donald Trump will also be in attendance, and a meeting with him, Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin is planned for Thursday.

That has raised alarm among European officials, as some suggest U.S.-brokered peace talks between Russia and Ukraine have included proposals they say would leave both Ukraine and Europe vulnerable.

Carney said Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva recently told him he encouraged the talks in order to end the war. Carney said Canada wants a just peace for Ukraine and a ceasefire is needed.

Nadjibulla said it’s incredible the trilateral meeting might happen, adding it reinforces Carney’s warnings about “unconstrained great-power politics” in his January speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos.

“It’s a reminder that other countries need to double down on their efforts to build resilience and agency, so that they don’t become collateral — so they don’t end up on the menu of great-power competition, but rather have a seat at the table,” she said.

China has indicated great enthusiasm for Carney’s visit. The state-controlled English-language newspaper Global Times has framed it as a mutually beneficial partnership in a turbulent world.

“The ability of China and Canada to address previous trade frictions through calm and equal-footed dialogue not only helps strengthen bilateral strategic mutual trust, but also injects confidence into global economic and trade co-operation,” said Zhao Xingshu of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, according to the newspaper.

“Nearly eight years of limited high-level exchanges mean rebuilding mutual understanding between officials and institutions will require time. At this stage, maintaining the momentum of stabilization in bilateral relations is itself an important and realistic objective.”

The Apec summit takes place in Shenzhen, which borders Hong Kong. Canada has repeatedly expressed concern about growing repression in Hong Kong as the territory transitions from semi-autonomy to full Chinese rule.

Earlier this month, Canada joined Western peers in condemning 10-year sentences for politicians and democracy activists under national-security laws, particularly Joshua Wong.

“We call for an immediate end to all unjust prosecutions of individuals charged under the (national security law),” the joint statement says.

It urges Chinese leaders to “uphold their international commitments and honour the rights and freedoms guaranteed to the people of Hong Kong” when the British government ceded sovereignty.

Carney has said he raises human rights issues privately with China but avoids public criticism.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 16, 2026.

Dylan Robertson, The Canadian Press

stories.title: GTA fever: Sick leaves, absences expected on ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ release day
stories.summary: Edmonton — PB Berge expects several students to skip classes and their jobs on Thursday so they can be immersed in a virtual world of car thefts, police chases and heists.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
EDMONTON — PB Berge expects several students to skip classes and their jobs on Thursday so they can be immersed in a virtual world of car thefts, police chases and heists.

It’s the day the long-awaited “Grand Theft Auto VI” drops.

Classrooms and offices will likely be quieter than usual, said Berge.

“I had one student who was like, ‘Oh, by the way, I’m going to be sick on the 19th.’ And a handful of other students (agreed),” said Berge, a gaming professor at the University of Alberta in Edmonton.

“A number of them also have jobs. So if they’re skipping class, they might just as well be skipping work.

“I just hope they learn something interesting in the process.”

Berge, who uses pronouns they and them, said many people of many ages, in generations X through Z, are excited about the latest release in the iconic GTA series.

“(It) is one of the most successful and best selling game franchises of all time,” Berge said.

It was created by video game developer Rockstar Games.

Take-Two Interactive, the developer’s parent company, has said more than 470 million GTA games have been sold worldwide.

The franchise is set in fictional cities inspired by real locations in the United States. One of the most popular spots is the neon-soaked Vice City, which is akin to Miami.

The first instalment in the series was released in 1997. Back then it was a simple, two-dimensional game.

Players select a protagonist with a complex backstory and go on missions for a mob family in exchange for money the character desperately needs.

“Grand Theft Auto III” in 2001, and ensuing games in the series, redefined video games.

Though the concept and theme stayed relatively the same, players were given greater freedom to explore sprawling three-dimensional cities.

Berge said the details in the 3D games are immaculate.

“The franchise has poured a ton of attention into creating an incredibly realistic, interactive, rich and dynamic world,” they said.

“There’s something very pulpy and fun about blowing up a yacht and hopping on a Jet Ski, and making a daring escape from police helicopters.”

Sexual components of the games have been criticized, and Berge acknowledges the game is raunchy and violent.

“But the game is also highly satirical and it makes fun of American culture. And every character is in some ways an exaggeration of different political or corporate figures.”

The last instalment, “Grand Theft Auto V,” was released in 2013.

The Canadian Taxpayers Federation filed a freedom of information request with the Saskatchewan government that showed more than 500 provincial workers called in sick on that release day.

In its first three days, the game reached US$1 billion in sales.

This year, Charlie Herrera Vacaflor said it’s anticipated thousands of workers across Canada will also call in sick on the release day, as well as some of the following days.

Herrera Vacaflor works for Peninsula Canada, a human resources and occupational health consulting firm.

“Businesses, particularly in the big urban areas, like Vancouver, Toronto, Calgary, have reached out (to us) because they obviously want to be prepared for the time-off requests.”

He advises employees to be sincere and request a vacation day instead of calling in sick if they want to play the game.

“If this is something that you really value and it’s something that is fulfilling, then why not take a vacation day?”

Employers should also consult with their workers in advance, he said.

Louis-Etienne Dubois, a creative studies management professor at Toronto Metropolitan University, said he’s also expecting empty chairs in his classroom this week.

“There’s a lot of hype around the game,” he said.

“It’s not just students skipping class, it’s also people not showing up to work.”

He said what’s interesting about GTA is that it’s a multi-generational “phenomenon,” as well as highly critical of societal issues.

Dubois said he, too, will be downloading it but will wait until the winter holidays when he gets some time to play.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 16, 2026.

Fakiha Baig, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Montreal Opposition wants city to appoint executive responsible for systemic racism
stories.summary: Montreal - The Opposition at Montreal’s City Hall will ask Soraya Martinez Ferrada’s administration at its council meeting to name a point person on its executive committee to address systemic racism.
stories.author: Erika Morris The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada is dismissing calls for her to appoint someone to address the issue of systemic racism in her administration, noting that her team already has an executive overseeing diversity and inclusion.

Martinez Ferrada made the comments on Monday in response to calls from the Opposition, pressing her to go further.

The mayor said the issue of racism and discrimination is a personal priority, which she also tackles in her capacity as mayor.

“You have a mayor that actually thinks that it is something we need to do across the city. That’s the commitment that I took as a mayor and that’s what I’m going to continue to do,” Martinez Ferrada said.

But Opposition Leader Ericka Alneus says it’s crucial for the public to know who is keeping tabs on the issue of systemic racism and can be held accountable. In an interview, the Projet Montréal leader said the mayor cannot do it all.

Councillor Josué Corvil oversees diversity and inclusion issues on the mayor’s executive committee. He told council that he has been working with the city’s commissioner for the fight against racism and discrimination to produce a 2026-2030 action plan.

The executive committee serves as the decision-making body on the city’s operations.

Projet Montréal’s request comes two weeks after Montreal Police Chief Fady Dagher announced that seven officers were fired following various allegations of racism and misconduct.

The union representing police officers has said it planned to challenge the dismissals.

Last June, Dagher said a 16-member night patrol unit in a multicultural neighbourhood was dismantled and three officers were suspended after alleged criminal and racist misconduct. Some officers at the station allegedly tore racialized people’s hair and kept them as “trophies.”

Following the announcement, Black public servants working for the City of Montreal drafted a letter calling for major reforms to crack down on systemic racism.

The city employees wrote that racism wasn’t limited to the police force, noting that blue-collar workers already took steps to raise concerns, including meeting with human resources and government officials. Some also drafted memos to recommend solutions.

“This is a question of accountability,” said Alneus. “In light of what happened with the (police), there are issues that need to be addressed and discussed.”

The Opposition has also requested that the police chief answer questions at council following reports of troubling interactions between officers and unhoused people.

The request was denied in council, with the mayor saying her administration does not want to interfere with ongoing investigations.

Dagher and Martinez Ferrada have repeatedly said the city wants to rebuild public trust following the allegations of police misconduct. Alneus believes naming someone responsible for the implementation of solutions at the executive committee would send a strong message to the population.

Alneus stresses she believes the mayor is taking the issue seriously.

“Some people want change drastically and rapidly, but those kinds of changes are difficult to implement,” said Alneus. “This is what we want to propose; that someone, as it used to be for many years, someone is there to take the lead on this and make sure things are implemented.”

Following petitions and recommendations by Montreal’s public consultation office, the city appointed Cathy Wong to the file at the executive committee in 2020 under former Projet Montréal mayor Valérie Plante. The file was later taken over by Dominique Olivier followed by Gracia Kasoki Katahwa.

In an interview, Wong, who is mayor of the Plateau-Mont-Royal borough of the city, said the position allowed her to create the bureau of the commissioner for the fight against racism and discrimination within the city administration and police force. She also worked with the police and provincial government to implement reforms to police training, hiring practices, and protocols for officers who stop civilians on the street.

Through her position, Wong said she also addressed the underrepresentation of diverse populations in the public service, particularly in leadership positions, and created a plan for diversity, equity and inclusion.

The city then amended its charter of rights and responsibilities to officially recognize the issue of systemic racism and institutionalize its commitment against discrimination.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 16, 2026.

stories.title: The Giller Prize, Canada's richest fiction award, to be handed out tonight
stories.summary: Toronto - Five Canadian authors will vie for one of the country's top literary awards tonight.
stories.author: Nicole Thompson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Nicholas Herring accepted his Giller Prize with an expletive.

The flustered author, who also works as a carpenter and fisherman, almost swore a second time, but managed to cut himself off. He won the $100,000 prize Monday night for his second novel, “Your Breath in Charcoal.”

“When I sat down to write this book, I figured, well, shoot, I should probably kind of swing for the fences and I should try to write something that would change the life of my wife, my beautiful wife, Norma Jean, and my daughter, Gwen,” he said, vibrating onstage.

“So I wrote this book for them, to change their lives, and I guess change my life too.”

Prince Edward Island author-fisherman-carpenter Nicholas Herring has won the Giller Prize for his second novel, “Your Breath in Charcoal.” The book follows a directionless young Islander who finds himself on a road trip to Toronto. Herring says he wasn’t expecting to win the prize, so he didn’t write a speech. (Nov. 16, 2026)

Jurors praised the novel as “a deeply philosophical narrative filled with pop culture references, literary allusions, and mordant, quotable witticisms.”

It follows Knickle, a directionless young Islander who finds himself on a road trip to Toronto after picking up an acquaintance’s brother from a mental health hospital in New Brunswick.

Herring, who’s based in Murray Harbour, P.E.I., previously won the Atwood Gibson Writers’ Trust Fiction Prize for his debut, “Some Hellish.”

He said that award, which carries a $60,000 purse, allowed him to take 10 months off work to focus on writing.

“And I wrote the book in six months,” he said. “And I haven’t found any time to do any writing since because I’ve just been busy working and raising my daughter.”

After the ceremony, Herring said he plans to set some of the money aside for his three-year-old daughter’s university tuition, and hopefully write another book.

Comedian Rick Mercer hosted the event for the sixth time on Monday night at the Ritz-Carlton in Toronto.

Last month, Mercer told The Canadian Press that he considers the Giller the “most important award in Canadian fiction.”

“And not just because of the money,” he said. “The money is nice and really important, but (the prize) cements a writer’s reputation, and it brings eyeballs to the page and that’s harder and harder to do all the time.”

Canada-U.S. relations took centre stage in Mercer’s remarks as host.

He made what seems at this point to be the requisite joke about Lake Ontario’s name, after U.S. President Donald Trump’s executive order renaming it Lake America earlier this year.

Mercer added: “It’s a wonderful place to be this time of year. The shore is teeming with Canada geese, and way on the other side, one lame duck.”

He also quipped that the trophy was made with “pure Canadian steel. That’s right: hand forged by 175 returning Stelco workers.”

(In fact, the statuette is made of tempered glass.)

The Giller Prize changed its jury makeup this year. Previously, the three- to five-member jury that selects the long list, short list and winner was made predominantly of authors. But for the first time, the Giller enlisted booksellers to sit on the jury — and upped the number to nine.

They include Rupert and Danielle McNally of Ben McNally Books in Toronto, Dan MacDonald of Bookmark Books in Prince Edward Island and Jenn Baerg Steyn of Yellowknife Books in the Northwest Territories.

Baerg Steyn said she took the responsibility of holding a “career-altering moment” in her hands very seriously.

“There was definitely a mind to: what is Canadian publishing? What is the voice we’re looking for?” she said ahead of the ceremony Monday.

Chris Hall, co-owner of McNally Robinson Booksellers, which has locations in Winnipeg and Saskatoon, also sat on the jury.

“Independent booksellers like to sell interesting books, so we are looking for different things. We’re looking for unique things. We’re looking for somebody who’s telling us something about the world we didn’t already know,” he said.

The winner was selected from 140 submissions from across Canada.

The other Giller finalists included Michelle Good for “Eliza Sunshine,” which follows three generations of Cree women whose family history is forever altered by colonialism; and Nazanine Hozar for “The Small Ones,” about children caught up in a military insurgency along the Iran-Iraq border in the early 1980s.

Rounding out the short list were Tara Gereaux for “Wild People Quiet,” about what happens when a woman hides her Métis identity from the Prairie town where she lives in the 1940s; and Patmeena Sabit for “Good People,” which uses the testimony of friends and acquaintances to show how a wealthy Afghan-American family is picked apart in the wake of tragedy.

The four runners-up each receive $10,000.

Last year’s winner was Souvankham Thammavongsa for “Pick a Colour,” a novel about a quiet nail technician’s rich inner life.

The Giller was established by Jack Rabinovitch in 1994 in memory of his late wife, literary journalist Doris Giller.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 16, 2026.

stories.title: Canada's exports to China up almost 40 per cent since last year
stories.summary: Ottawa - Canadian exports to China surged by roughly 40 per cent in the first nine months of this year — an increase the federal government says far outpaces growth in exports to anywhere else.
stories.author: Catherine Morrison The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - Canadian exports to China surged by roughly 40 per cent in the first nine months of this year — an increase the federal government says far outpaces growth in exports to anywhere else.

Much of that increase has happened since January, when Prime Minister Mark Carney made his first visit to China. The trip was part of the prime minister’s campaign to overcome political tensions with Beijing and tear down trade barriers that had been erected between the two countries.

Carney arrived in China on Monday, where he is set to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and leaders from across the Pacific Rim. On his fourth and final stop of a nine-day overseas trip, Carney is in the city of Shenzhen, a tech hub in southeastern China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation summit.

His first official task, however, will be a bilateral meeting with Xi on Tuesday morning in China. Ahead of that trip, Carney said Canada could do more with China in terms of agriculture, clean and conventional energy, and financial services.

Statistics Canada data shows Canada’s exports to China reached $33.5 billion in the first three quarters of this year, an increase of $9.5 billion or almost 40 per cent over the same time period last year.

The data represents merchandise exports and does not include services.

China’s exports to Canada remained relatively flat by comparison. Between January and September of this year, Canada imported $68.8 billion in Chinese goods, compared with $68.1 billion in the same period a year earlier.

Canada’s goods exports to China reached $35 billion in 2025, while imports totalled around $90 billion.

Bilateral services trade reached $13.8 billion in 2025.

Mujtaba Hussain, a spokesperson for International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu, said that figure represents a rate of growth roughly four times faster than growth rates for exports to all other countries.

“That growth reflects the work Minister Sidhu and our government have done to create a stable, predictable trading relationship with China,” said Hussain.

Beijing and Ottawa announced earlier this month they’re extending a January agreement to provide Chinese market access to Canadian imports in exchange for Canadian market access for Chinese steel and aluminum.

In March, China dropped tariffs on Canadian canola meal, peas, lobster and crab. Canada agreed in return to allow in certain Chinese steel and aluminum products.

The deal was negotiated in January by Carney and Xi in Beijing but initially had been set to expire at the end of this year.

Sidhu said last week the deal is being extended by two years, to the end of 2028.

Hussain said exports of canola seed and meal, beef and peas to China have reached nearly $3.5 billion this year, an increase of nearly $1.6 billion, or 82 per cent.

Canadian beef exports have reached $377 million, he said — nearly double what Canada exported in all of 2021.

Hussain also said Canadian crude oil exports to China have more than doubled to $9.5 billion, and exports of minerals and fertilizer continue to grow.

“Minister Sidhu is focused on increasing our exports to China by 50 per cent by 2030,” said Hussain. “That is how we will support Canadian businesses and workers.

“We will keep pushing for greater and more predictable access to the Chinese market so that more Canadian businesses can grow and create good-paying jobs here at home.”

Vina Nadjibulla, co-founder and CEO of the Centre for Strategic Statecraft, said the increase in energy exports is related to the Trans Mountain pipeline expansion being fully operational.

“We’re seeing Canada exporting a lot more of our energy resources to Asia, and China is a huge market,” said Nadjibulla.

Nadjibulla said that while the increase in exports as imports remain steady is positive news, it’s important for Canada not to become overly dependent on China for any particular export.

“This is particularly relevant for canola,” she said. “We are already exporting about two-thirds of our canola seed exports to China. That kind of strategic concentration opens us up to leverage and potential coercion from China.

“While we deepen economic engagement with China, we have to avoid strategic dependence and we have to make sure that we strengthen economic security too here at home.”

Nadjibulla said she will be watching for news on Chinese investments, including in manufacturing and the auto sector.

Carney’s is visiting China’s tech hub of Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation summit, set for Nov. 18 and 19. Leaders from across the Pacific Rim will gather in the city bordering Hong Kong to take stock of an increasingly disordered trading system.

Xi and Carney are set to meet Tuesday morning in Shenzhen and Carney will address business leaders the next day.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 16, 2026.

— With files from Dylan Robertson

stories.title: Stabbing investigation
stories.summary: London, ON (November 16, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service (LPS) Patrol Operations Investigative Section are seeking the public’s assistance in identifying a suspect in relation to a stabbing earlier this month.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (November 16, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service (LPS) Patrol Operations Investigative Section are seeking the public’s assistance in identifying a suspect in relation to a stabbing earlier this month.

On Saturday, November 7, 2026, at approximately 9 p.m., officers responded to the area of Dundas and Elizabeth streets after receiving a report of a stabbing.

A male victim was located and transported to hospital by paramedic services with serious, non-life-threatening injuries.

The suspect fled northbound from the area on an e-bike prior to police arrival. Officers searched the area but were unable to locate him.

The suspect is described as male, White, approximately 5’8”, 25 – 40 years old, wearing a black jacket, black jogging pants with a white logo on the left pant leg, and white and blue running shoes.

Photographs of the suspect are being released in hopes that members of the public can assist investigators in identifying him.

Investigators are asking anyone who was in the area at the time, knows the identity of the suspect, or May have dashcam, residential or business video surveillance from the area of Dundas and Elizabeth streets on November 7, 2026, between 8:40 and 9:10 p.m. to contact police.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670.

stories.title: Overnight road closures begin November 16 for final paving on Fanshawe Park Road
stories.summary: Final paving on
stories.content:
Final paving on Fanshawe Park Road , between North Centre Road and Adelaide Street North, begins Monday, November 16 at 7 p.m.

Fanshawe Park Road will be closed in both directions overnight while crews complete paving. The work is expected to take four nights, with a fifth night if needed, weather permitting.

Crews will start at Adelaide Street North and move west toward North Centre Road, completing approximately one section each night. Work will take place nightly from 7 p.m. to 7 a.m.

Drivers should follow posted detours using Adelaide Street North, Windermere Road or Sunningdale Road, and Richmond Street.

Stoneybrook residents living south of Fanshawe Park Road will have limited access from Adelaide Street during paving. Daleview Crescent residents can still access their homes from Adelaide Street.

On Monday night, all other residents in this area should use the west leg of Hastings Drive to get home. As paving moves west, the east leg of Stoneybrook Crescent will become another neighbourhood entrance.

Special Constables will be on site to help direct traffic and maintain access.

Sidewalks will generally remain open, although some sections May be temporarily closed with signed detours.

Local businesses will remain open during regular hours, with access maintained wherever possible.

LTC buses will need to detour around the work area. Visit the London Transit Commission website for the latest bus schedules and detour information.

After paving, crews will complete road markings and other finishing work, including boulevard restoration, sidewalk placement where needed and electrical work.

This work is expected to take two to three weeks, beginning the week of November 23. Some temporary lane or sidewalk restrictions May be needed while crews finish the work.

To learn more about construction projects across London, visit the Renew London map .

stories.title: Bullying Awareness & Prevention Week: Kindness Starts With Us. See It. Choose It. Do It.
stories.summary: General News
stories.author: Thames Valley District School Board
stories.content:
General News

All Notices and Updates

November 16-20, 2026, is Bullying Awareness and Prevention Week in Ontario. This week is an opportunity for Thames Valley students, families and staff to learn more about bullying, its effects on student learning, and how we can work together to create safe and inclusive learning environments.

This year’s theme, Kindness Starts With Us. See It. Choose It. Do It. , encourages students to recognize what bullying is, make intentional choices and take safe, meaningful action to support others.

Students are also invited to participate in our annual Art Contest by creating original artwork that reflects this year’s theme. Winning artwork will be displayed and printed on TVDSB notecards!

More tips, strategies and resources:

stories.title: Rising safety incidents, growing deficits inside Ontario children’s aid societies, long-awaited report reveals
stories.summary: Nearly two-thirds of Ontario children’s aid societies are in some kind of financial distress as the cost of caring for kids with complex needs has skyrocketed, with agencies spending millions more on care even when they’re helping fewer children. The alarming portrait of the province’s child welfare system is included in a long-awaited report released Monda…
stories.author: Megan Ogilvie; Amy Dempsey Raven
stories.content:
An audit of Ontario children’s aid societies has not uncovered the “nightmare stories” of agencies misusing taxpayer dollars that Premier Doug Ford vowed to expose when he announced the review two years ago.

Instead, it has found that the cost of caring for children and youth with complex needs has skyrocketed as child welfare agencies — forced to become “providers of last resort” for desperate families — lean on high-cost emergency placements.

The audit says nearly two-thirds of children’s aid societies are in some kind of financial distress and the number of serious safety incidents for kids in care has nearly doubled from 2020 to 2025.

The alarming portrait of the province’s child welfare system is included in the long-awaited report, released Monday as the provincial government announced new legislation and regulatory changes it says will strengthen the sector.

But while the changes tighten financial oversight and impose new safety measures, experts and critics say they do not address the underlying issues that are sending kids with complex health needs to the doorsteps of children’s aid.

“We have a child welfare system that is ill-equipped to deal with the demands presenting themselves,” said Kiaras Gharabaghi, professor at Toronto Metropolitan University’s school of child and youth care, after reviewing the audit’s findings.

“Ontario governments continue to respond to these issues with a mixture of indignation that it costs money to ensure the well-being of children and an absurd confidence that tinkering with technical aspects of the system is somehow going to produce transformative change,” Gharabaghi said. “It will not.”

When asked Monday why the legislation does not address long-standing systemic issues, Michael Parsa, minister of children, community and social services, pointed to the government’s “record funding” in the sector — some $2 billion — even as the number of children and youth in care has decreased by 20 per cent. He said placement decisions are made by societies, not the government.

“We have an expectation to make sure that those placements are safe, so every child and youth in the province is supported, protected, and their outcomes improved,” he said.

Alexa Gilmour, NDP critic for children, community and social services and MPP for Parkdale—High Park, said on Monday that she is “livid” the legislation meant to address the audit findings are “tucked in” to an omnibus bill, along with health-care issues, long-term-care home requirements and sweeping new changes to Osap .

“There is nothing that really tackles the seriousness of (the issues) these families are facing,” Gilmour said, adding that children who are in crisis now cannot wait months for change.

The release of the report, which examined 37 non-Indigenous societies, comes in the wake of Star reporting that revealed the findings have been in the government’s hands for almost a year — despite repeated promises from the province it would make the results public.

The delay drew sharp criticism from advocates and critics who say the child welfare system has continued to deteriorate in the two years since the premier announced the audit.

Despite raising the alarm since 2020, child welfare agencies are still struggling to find appropriate treatment and housing for kids with complex mental health and other developmental needs. The lack of options has forced agencies to rely on unlicensed settings, including budget motels, and other emergency placements.

The Star recently reported on a teen boy in southwestern Ontario who lived in his family’s shed for months while under the watch of children’s aid.

Previous Star reporting has shown these emergency placements are driving up agency costs and harming vulnerable children and youth.

The audit found the same. Spending across the child welfare sector is heavily concentrated in high-cost, reactive protection ($437 million) and care ($642 million), while prevention and early intervention accounts for only $53 million — under four per cent — of spending.

Three quarters of all placement spending went to outside purchased resources, or OPRs, which can include private foster or group care providers that children’s aid societies purchase services from.

The increasing reliance on OPRs stems from a provincewide decline in foster families and the increasing complexity of needs among children in care, the audit said.

The number of serious safety incidents for kids in care nearly doubled over the five years reviewed by auditors, with incidents of exploitation such as sex trafficking increasing by 33 per cent and assaults up 18 per cent. Most of these incidents occurred in OPRs, the audit noted.

Ford ordered the third-party audit of the sector in October 2024, alleging he’d heard “nightmare stories” of agencies misusing taxpayer dollars instead of properly funding care.

At the time, union leaders representing thousands of child protection workers called the audit a “smokescreen” and stated the government needed to adequately fund the social services system to ensure children got the help they need.

The audit was conducted by an outside contractor and looked at the quality of child protection services and examined operational costs, including executive compensation and staffing. The review did not include Indigenous child and family well-being agencies.

While the Kpmg audit did not make formal recommendations, noting that it wasn’t in the scope of its contract with the provincial government, it offered “considerations” for future policy and decision-making. Among them, auditors warned that sector-wide structural changes May be needed to address high-cost placements that are out of agencies’ control.

Parsa said the proposed legislation includes new oversight for social workers that would see their licenses suspended or revoked if they are found to have committed sexual misconduct involving a client. That ban would remain in place for a minimum of 10 years.

stories.title: Canada exploring ‘other options’ with Europe, Asia to grow auto sector: Carney
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney says the auto sector remains part of trade talks with the U.S., but Canada is also looking at "other options" in Europe and Asia.
stories.author: Aaron Sousa
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney says the auto sector remains part of trade talks with the U.S., but Canada is also looking at “other options” in Europe and Asia.

Carney made the remarks while taking questions from reporters at the Francophonie summit in Phnom Penh, Cambodia.

The prime minister says Ottawa wants Canadian auto workers to have the best opportunities possible in an integrated North American market.

He says that market has become less integrated as Washington has threatened hefty tariffs of up to 50 per cent on Canadian autos by January.

“It’s an ongoing discussion that we’re having with the U.S. administration, myself with the president,” Carney told reporters.

“It’s part of the trade negotiations, as you know, depending (on) where that settles, there’ll be other options — European options, Asian options.”

Carney has said Canada would not ink a U.S. trade deal that failed to support a viable Canadian auto sector.

Amid trade tensions, Carney signed a deal with China earlier this year to import up to 49,000 Chinese electric vehicles at a tariff rate of 6.1 per cent.

Carney is expected to meet this week with President Xi Jinping, where more discussions around the two nations’ trading relationships are likely.

By Ryan Baynton Nov 15, 2026 | 10:03 PM

Around lunch Thursday many people reported that Microsoft’s Outlook, alongside other services were not working. The network stayed down for nearly a full day, the longest shutdown in Microsoft history.

Microsoft has not come out with what happened but said it was not a cyber attack.

“It’s like removing a lane from a highway, the remaining servers had to handle all the traffic,” said London technology analyst Carmi Levy, when describing why the servers went down in quick succession and why some people may still have been receiving emails.

The mass network failure had many businesses in a panic, as they were not able to work without the networks provided from Microsoft.

Many companies have been advised to re-evaluate their emergency plans not just for when they are facing internal problems, but also when the client they use goes down.

stories.title: Carney says Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if Trump trade talks fail
stories.summary: Phnom Penh, Cambodia (AP) — Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said that Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump fail to preserve an integrated North American auto industry.
stories.author: The Associated Press
stories.content:
Phnom Penh, Cambodia (AP) — Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Monday that Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump fail to preserve an integrated North American auto industry.

Carney’s comments in Cambodia came ahead of a planned meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping this week in Shenzhen, China, where Chinese auto manufacturing is expected to be discussed. The two leaders reached an agreement in January allowing tens of thousands of Chinese electric vehicles into Canada at reduced tariffs.

“We have the best auto workers in the world, and we want them fully deployed, full opportunity, in an integrated North American market,” Carney told reporters in Cambodia. “That market has become less integrated because of U.S. trade actions.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney says auto sector remains part of trade talks with U.S. but that Canada is looking at ‘other options’ in Europe and Asia. Carney was taking questions from reporters at the Francophonie summit in Phnom Penh, Cambodia. (Nov. 16, 2026)

Carney said Saturday in Manila, Philippines, that any trade agreement with Washington must leave Canada with a viable auto industry. He said Monday that negotiations with the United States remain his priority, but their outcome could determine whether Canada pursues alternatives involving European, Chinese or Japanese automakers.

Asked whether potential Chinese investment was leverage in the U.S. negotiations, Carney replied: “It’s not leverage. But action, reaction” on behalf of Canada’s auto workers and manufacturing assets.

“If they’re not fully utilized in a North American context, that provides other opportunities,” Carney said. “Canada is going to move forward either way.”

White House trade adviser Peter Navarro lashed out on social media Monday in response to Carney’s suggestion that Canada could turn to Chinese automakers.

“Are u really threatening to play China off the U.S.? This is offensive in the extreme,” Navarro wrote on X. “You should be far more worried China is going to eat Canada alive.”

The Detroit Three — Ford, General Motors and Stellantis — operate factories across Canada, the United States and Mexico, with parts sometimes crossing borders multiple times before a vehicle is completed. Trump has repeatedly pushed automakers to move production to the United States from Canada.

Carney said any Chinese investment would have to involve substantial manufacturing in Canada rather than simply assembling imported parts. He said it would require proper labor standards, manufacturing facilities and domestic supply chains that expand over time, including the use of Canadian critical minerals in electric vehicles.

“It’s not just about kit cars,” he said. “There has to be a manufacturing aspect involved.”

Under the January agreement, Canada reduced its 100% tariff on Chinese electric vehicles to 6.1%, initially allowing up to 49,000 vehicles annually, with the cap increasing over time. In exchange, China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola.

Carney said at the time that he expected the agreement to attract Chinese investment in Canada’s auto industry and create jobs.

The deal drew criticism from Ontario Premier Doug Ford, whose province is the center of Canada’s auto industry. Ford warned that allowing Chinese electric vehicles into Canada could threaten Canadian jobs and jeopardize access to the U.S. market.

“The federal government’s focus needs to be on protecting Canadian auto workers, not undermining them by importing even more state-subsidized cheap Chinese cars,” Ford said on social media on Monday.

Trump’s tariffs have battered Canada’s auto industry, potentially unraveling decades of cross-border integration. Canada recently threatened to sue Stellantis after the company moved its plans for Jeep Compass production from Ontario to Illinois and agreed to sell its idled Canadian assembly plant.

Carney said Saturday that he had spoken at length with Trump and senior U.S. officials and that the two countries were making progress toward a possible trade agreement, although differences remained.

Associated Press writer Rob Gillies in Toronto reported from Toronto.

stories.title: Death of fifth soldier highlights vulnerable state of CFB Wainwright fire victims
stories.summary: Severely burnt soldiers have suffered devastating trauma to their faces, heads and torsos, according to sources
stories.author: Mercedes Stephenson, Alanna Smith, Tu Thanh Ha
stories.content:
The death of a fifth soldier from injuries sustained in last month’s massive fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright has underlined the vulnerable condition of the more seriously hurt victims of the Oct. 17 blaze.

Three sources with direct knowledge of some of the military personnel who remain in hospital described a number of soldiers’ injuries as profound, severe and life-altering. The sources described cases of devastating facial, head and neck trauma from the burns, as well as severe damage to hands, arms and upper torsos.

For some, the sources said, the injuries to the upper-body area were so significant the victims could not be easily identified after being pulled from the grass fire that erupted near the CAF base in central Alberta during a training exercise, or later in hospital.

The Globe and Mail is not identifying the sources because they were not authorized to discuss the soldiers’ conditions publicly.

The latest fatality, Private William Douglas Dal Bianco of the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry, died Friday, nearly four weeks after he was hospitalized. He was receiving medical care in Ontario, the Department of National Defence said in a statement Saturday.

Of the 38 remaining injured soldiers, 24 are still in hospital, the statement said. Four members of the battalion – Sergeant Morgan Wong, Private Shaun Farrell, Private Aidan Goulding and Private Hayden Lykkemark – were pronounced dead in the immediate aftermath of the fire.

In an e-mail response to The Globe, the department said it cannot provide more information on the hospitalized soldiers because “patient status falls within the clinical purview of provincial health authorities and attending clinicians.”

The department has refused to answer broad questions about how many soldiers remain in critical condition or remain intubated, citing privacy.

Acute Care Alberta said 21 of the military victims remain hospitalized in that province, with nine of them in critical condition as of Nov. 10.

Patients who suffer severe burns can die from complications weeks or months after the original injury, because they are in such a medically vulnerable state, Alan Rogers, a surgeon at the Ross Tilley Burn Centre, said in an interview.

“This is a recognized feature of severe burn injury. Surviving the first few days is an important milestone, but it does not necessarily mean that the danger has passed,” Dr. Rogers said. “This is particularly relevant when burns involve more than half the body’s surface, although burn depth, age, smoke inhalation and underlying health also influence the outlook.”

Part of Toronto’s Sunnybrook Health Sciences Centre, the Ross Tilley facility is Canada’s highest-volume adult burn unit, and it is among the hospital departments that have dispatched specialists to help treat the victims of the Wainwright fire.

Many of the soldiers injured at CFB Wainwright sustained extreme burns that will require multiple surgeries and extensive rehabilitation. Those with skin so scorched that it cannot heal on its own have required skin grafts, a surgical procedure where donated skin or a patch of healthy skin from another part of the patient’s body is removed and transplanted to the area needing repair.

In the first few hours and days after a serious burn, the immediate priorities involve maintaining the patient’s blood circulation and breathing, Dr. Rogers said. Following that initial phase, he said the threat becomes complications, such as infections, sepsis, blood clots, organ failure and lung issues.

“One reason for the prolonged vulnerability is that the skin is a vital protective organ,” he said. “Extensive, deep burns remove a large part of that barrier, and restoring durable wound coverage can require multiple operations. At the same time, a major burn profoundly disrupts the immune system.”

For those reasons, Dr. Rogers said, a patient can improve for a period of time, but then deteriorate rapidly should a complication develop.

“There is no particular day or week after which every patient is safely out of danger,” he said. “Many people survive very extensive burns, but achieving that recovery can require weeks or months of co-ordinated surgery, intensive care, specialist nursing, nutritional support and rehabilitation.”

The CFB Wainwright incident is one of Canada’s worst peacetime training tragedies on home soil, with dozens more affected than the Slesse Range disaster in 1988 that killed six military engineer trainees and seriously injured three others during a demolition exercise at CFB Chilliwack.

Prime Minister Mark Carney, in a statement posted to social media on Saturday, said Canadians are holding all those who are grieving in the wake of last month’s tragedy in their hearts.

“Private Dal Bianco and his fellow soldiers were training to defend Canada. With their bright futures still before them, they chose to safeguard ours,” he said. “That is service. Now, we serve them.”

General Jennie Carignan, Chief of the Defence Staff, offered her condolences to Pte. Dal Bianco’s family, friends and those who served alongside him.

“We will honour his dedicated service and continue to stand with all those affected by this tragedy along the difficult road ahead. My thoughts are also with our injured members and their families, and I am deeply grateful to everyone involved in providing care and support during this time of tremendous sadness,” Gen. Carignan said in a statement.

Canadian Forces Provost Marshal Vanessa Hanrahan, who heads the military police, has said that the fire had started on CFB Wainwright’s automatic grenade launcher range and was monitored continuously throughout the day. “A subsequent change in wind direction and velocity significantly increased the fire’s intensity and rate of speed which led to these tragic events,” Brigadier-General Hanrahan said.

Military police have launched an investigation into the circumstances of the fire. The CAF has promised a separate investigation by its board of inquiry. Alberta’s chief medical examiner is also investigating.
