stories.title: Sunday Sports: Mustangs win Yates Cup, Knights lose in Saginaw, local stars win NSL Championship
stories.summary: The Western Mustangs are Yates Cup Champions for the 36th time in program history. The Mustangs beat rival Queen’s 36-27 at Richardson Stadium in Kingston, Ont. Saturday to win the Ontario University Athletics (OUA) title.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
The Western Mustangs are Yates Cup Champions for the 36th time in program history. The Mustangs beat rival Queen’s 36-27 at Richardson Stadium in Kingston, Ont. Saturday to win the Ontario University Athletics (OUA) title.

Western dominated both the second and third quarter taking a 3-0 deficit and turning it into a 36-3 lead before surrendering 24 points in the final quarter.

It was a game full of big plays for Western who had a 105-yard interception return for a touchdown by game MVP Thomson Silcox, an 80-yard touchdown reception by Emmett Charles added a 77-yard punt return score by Brenna Keba. The win gives head coach Michael Faulds five career Yates Cup titles, two as a Western player and now his first as a Mustangs head coach.

“It feels incredible. I told our guys, I’ve been to many Yates Cups as a player and as a coach,” Faulds told media after the game.

“Although we’re going to play a bigger game next week and we hope to play a bigger game in 2 weeks, Yates Cup Day is my favourite day of the year.”

Western will move on to host the Mitchell Bowl against St. Mary’s University, who won the Loney Bowl, next Saturday at 12 p.m. at Alumni Field.

”Just a huge credit to our defence, Coach (Paul) Gleason, Coach (Craig) Butler, really putting our guys in a good position. You can see we got pressure on their quarterback and didn’t make it easy for them in the first half," said Head Coach Michael Faulds. ”Offensively, we did pretty well in the first half, mainly the one explosive play by Emmett Charles, which everyone’s getting used to. Coming out in the 3rd quarter, we knew we wanted to take the wind and show our dominance. You’ve got the big touchdown there by Emmett, followed by Keba’s big return touchdown, and that kind of opened the floodgates.

Western’s offence finished with 228 passing yards (QB Ben Casselman) and 144 on the ground with Ethan Dolby accounting for 106 rushing yards on 12 carries. Keba’s big punt return gave Western a 26-3 lead. “I just trust in my blocks all the time and I know the guys are always great and at any moment we can score on them,” said Keba.

“I’ve had a couple that have landed inside the 10 and been tackled. It’s finally great to get the monkey off my back and finally get in.”

Western had a 29-3 lead in the fourth quarter when Queen’s looked to be headed into the endzone for the first time. That’s when Silcox intercepted Gaels’ quarterback Alex Vreeken and took it back the other way for the score which iced the game.

“The guys up front putting pressure on their quarterback, making him air the throw out, and I just wanted to capitalize on it,” Silcox said after the game.

“Towards the end, I was starting to get tired; our guys were doing a great job blocking because I think their receiver was catching up to me.”

Knights drop fourth straight game in loss to Saginaw

The London Knights lost a third period lead in Saginaw Saturday to drop their fourth straight game overall.

In a wild third period that saw eight goals scored, the Spirit beat London 6-5.

Trailing 2-1 going into the final 20 minutes, Thomas Zocco scored two goals within 27 seconds to give the Knights a 3-2 lead. Just 20 seconds later, the Spirit tied the game at three.

That’s when things started to get a bit crazy.

Knights forward Jaxon Cover cut the deficit to just one but when London pulled the goalie for an extra attacker, the Spirit scored again.

Marcus Nordmark would cut it to just one again but with less than six seconds on the clock, the comeback came up short.

London has fallen behind Kitchner in the Midwest standings during this losing skid and now sit sixth place in a very tight Western Conference.

AFC Toronto wins national super league title with local talent

Olivia Chisholm’s goal in the first half gave AFC Toronto their first Diana B. Matheson Cup with a 1-0 victory over the Montreal Roses Saturday afternoon at TD Place.

Former FC London star Lauren Rowe beat her defender in the box and sent a pass from near the endline to Chisholm, who had some space near the top of the box, and she side-footed a shot past the outstretched arms of the keeper.

London native Shelina Zadorsky, who joined AFC Toronto this year, had a great chance to add to the lead but Montreal keeper Gabrielle Lambert got her fingertips on the shot.

St. Thomas native Kaila Novak is also bringing home hardware as a member of AFC Toronto.

With files from Canadian Press

stories.title: Five things to watch for in the Canadian business world in the coming week
stories.summary: Canada
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - Five things to watch for in the Canadian business world in the coming week:

Statistics Canada is set to release its latest inflation figures on Monday when it publishes its consumer price index for October. The annual inflation rate rose to 3.1 per cent in September, boosted by gasoline prices.

The Canadian Real Estate Association is scheduled to release its October home sales figures on Tuesday. The association downgraded its forecast for home sales activity in 2026 for the third straight quarter last month. CREA now expects a total of 444,530 homes to be sold by the end of this year, representing a 5.2 per cent decrease from 2025.

Prime Minister Mark Carney is expected to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation leaders meeting set for Wednesday and Thursday in Shenzhen, China. The conference comes at the end of a marathon trip by Carney that includes the summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations in the Philippines, the Francophonie summit in Cambodia and the European Political Community summit in Ireland.

Loblaw earnings

Loblaw Cos. Ltd. will report its third-quarter results on Thursday before markets open. The grocery and drugstore retailer has been expanding with more small-format grocery stores under its discount banners in a bid to attract shoppers.

Retail sales

Statistics Canada will release its retail sales figures for September on Friday. The agency’s preliminary estimate for the month suggested a gain of 0.7 per cent, but it cautioned the figure would be revised. Retail sales in August were up 1.2 per cent at $74.6 billion, helped by strength at motor vehicle and parts dealers.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 15, 2026.

stories.title: Canada’s security, prosperity at risk from freshwater supply challenges
stories.summary: The document, prepared for Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin, stresses a need to assess how Canada protects and sustainably manages freshwater resources.
stories.author: Jim Bronskill
stories.content:
Pressures on the supply of fresh water pose challenges that will affect Canada’s “long-term security and prosperity” if left unaddressed, an internal government memo warns.

The document, prepared for Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin, stresses a need to assess how Canada protects and sustainably manages freshwater resources — including waters shared with the United States — and how it responds to global water risks.

“Canadians will need more water to grow our cities and our economy, but it is unclear whether Canada is water secure for the long term,” the memo says.

The Canadian Press used the Access to Information Act to obtain the memo, written for Dabrusin by the Canada Water Agency, a federal organization that works to improve freshwater management.

Portions of the 12-page document were withheld under a provision of the law that allows the government to shield advice or recommendations from release.

The memo was intended to update the minister on the development of a national water security strategy. It says Dabrusin identified such a strategy as “a mission critical priority” in her reply to a call from Prime Minister Mark Carney for key portfolio objectives for cabinet members and secretaries of state.

A public consultation on developing the water security strategy took place from Sept. 9 through Oct. 25. Water stewardship is a shared responsibility in Canada and the water agency also engaged directly with provincial, territorial and Indigenous partners.

The memo to Dabrusin underscores the urgency of the exercise.

It says although Canada has 20 per cent of the world’s surface fresh water, only one-third is salt-free and replaced annually through precipitation.

Most of Canada’s renewable surface fresh water drains northward, away from the most populated regions and economic centres located within 300 kilometres of the Canada-United States border, the document adds.

It says groundwater aquifers — Canada’s largest freshwater resource — are unmapped in some parts of the country, even though almost one in three Canadians rely on groundwater for their supply of clean water.

Climate change is affecting where and when fresh water is available, the memo says. It warns some parts of Canada are facing, or could soon face, restricted or depleting water supplies, even in the Great Lakes-St. Lawrence River basin.

It says in many of Canada’s settled areas, water is polluted and is either unsuitable for human, animal or industrial use or is usable only after treatment at a high cost.

For the 2021 to 2023 period, for example, water quality at 49 per cent of 165 monitoring sites in southern Canadian rivers was rated as excellent or good, while water at 51 per cent of the sites was rated as fair to poor, the memo says.

While progress is being made to restore the quality of large lake systems, protecting them from major stressors is challenging. Complex freshwater ecosystems like the lower Great Lakes and Lake Winnipeg remain in fair or poor condition, the document adds.

It says water quality data for northern rivers and lakes and groundwater aquifers is limited, making it difficult to assess the health of these resources.

“Overall, freshwater ecosystems across southern Canada are under stress, which poses risks to water security, due to factors including a rapidly changing climate, shifts in land-use, population growth, pollution, overconsumption, and aging and inadequate water infrastructure,” the memo says.

“The Arctic and the North also face critical issues from increased development and climate change impacts on already overwhelmed infrastructure. Furthermore, First Nations, Métis, and Inuit communities are among the most water insecure in Canada.”

More than 40 per cent of the border between Canada and the United States crosses water, the document notes. It says these transboundary waters provide drinking water, hydro power, navigation, recreation, irrigation and support for biodiversity in both countries. Tens of millions of people live and work along these shared waters.

While the two nations are parties to over a dozen bilateral freshwater agreements, “new water-related disputes could emerge and become more frequent” as freshwater supplies in North America shrink and demands rise, the memo warns.

It says the pressures on Canada’s water emerge against a global backdrop of declining water security due to climate change, population growth and industrial pollution.

“For decades, Canadians have been raising concerns about the possibility of fresh water being exported in bulk to the U.S. and beyond,” the memo says. “Some Canadians strongly oppose diverting lakes and rivers, and this opposition has extended to any form of bulk export of water.”

On a positive note, actions to strengthen water security in Canada can create “significant development opportunities,” as long-term access to sufficient supplies of water will become a strategic advantage in a water-stressed world, the document says.

It points out that more than half of Canada’s electricity comes from hydro power, which supports the shift to cleaner energy and a low-carbon economy.

“Water storage and irrigation is critical to high-value crop production, particularly in the Prairies and interior British Columbia, as well as the greenhouse sector,” the memo adds.

“Major manufacturing industries are among the largest users of water in Canada and growing Canada’s digital economy will depend on a secure and sustainably managed water supply.”

It says in many of Canada’s settled areas, water is polluted and is either unsuitable for human, animal or industrial use or is usable only after treatment at a high cost.

For the 2021 to 2023 period, for example, water quality at 49 per cent of 165 monitoring sites in southern Canadian rivers was rated as excellent or good, while water at 51 per cent of the sites was rated as fair to poor, the memo says.

While progress is being made to restore the quality of large lake systems, protecting them from major stressors is challenging. Complex freshwater ecosystems like the lower Great Lakes and Lake Winnipeg remain in fair or poor condition, the document adds.
It says water quality data for northern rivers and lakes and groundwater aquifers is limited, making it difficult to assess the health of these resources.

“Overall, freshwater ecosystems across southern Canada are under stress, which poses risks to water security, due to factors including a rapidly changing climate, shifts in land-use, population growth, pollution, overconsumption, and aging and inadequate water infrastructure,” the memo says.

“The Arctic and the North also face critical issues from increased development and climate change impacts on already overwhelmed infrastructure. Furthermore, First Nations, Métis, and Inuit communities are among the most water insecure in Canada.”

More than 40 per cent of the border between Canada and the United States crosses water, the document notes. It says these transboundary waters provide drinking water, hydro power, navigation, recreation, irrigation and support for biodiversity in both countries. Tens of millions of people live and work along these shared waters.

While the two nations are parties to over a dozen bilateral freshwater agreements, “new water-related disputes could emerge and become more frequent” as freshwater supplies in North America shrink and demands rise, the memo warns.
It says the pressures on Canada’s water emerge against a global backdrop of declining water security due to climate change, population growth and industrial pollution.

“For decades, Canadians have been raising concerns about the possibility of fresh water being exported in bulk to the U.S. and beyond,” the memo says. “Some Canadians strongly oppose diverting lakes and rivers, and this opposition has extended to any form of bulk export of water.”

On a positive note, actions to strengthen water security in Canada can create “significant development opportunities,” as long-term access to sufficient supplies of water will become a strategic advantage in a water-stressed world, the document says.
It points out that more than half of Canada’s electricity comes from hydro power, which supports the shift to cleaner energy and a low-carbon economy.
“Water storage and irrigation is critical to high-value crop production, particularly in the Prairies and interior British Columbia, as well as the greenhouse sector,” the memo adds.
“Major manufacturing industries are among the largest users of water in Canada and growing Canada’s digital economy will depend on a secure and sustainably managed water supply.”

The memo to Dabrusin underscores the urgency of the exercise.

stories.title: Canada, Brazil announce $540M for rainforest protection project
stories.summary: Ottawa is continuing talks for a trade deal with Asean, while Canada also has deeper agreements with Indonesia and the Philippines.
stories.author: Dylan Robertson
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney has wrapped up a brief visit to the Philippines and is heading to Cambodia, as the government pushes for more trade access in the region.

On his one-night visit to Manila, Carney attended a summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, announced the conclusion of free-trade negotiations with the Philippines and unveiled funding for protecting tropical rainforests.

“What Canada presents is certainty to the world,” Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu told reporters in Manila on Sunday, which was late Saturday in Canada.

Carney was among foreign leaders including U.S. President Donald Trump who were invited to the summit by the Philippine chair, who is holding the rotating presidency of Asean, a bloc of 11 countries.

Ottawa is continuing talks for a trade deal with Asean, which Sidhu said would give Canada access to smaller countries, while Canada also has deeper agreements with Indonesia and the Philippines.

“You can get more into the weeds. You can upgrade later on, when you’re dealing with (one deal that is) bilateral, as opposed to an agreement with 11 partners,” he said in Manila on Sunday, which was late Saturday in Canada.

“It’s the fastest growing region in the world, 700 million consumers, an economy valued at $6 trillion.”

Sidhu also expressed confidence for Canadian pork producers, as the Philippines moves toward restricting pork imports from a wide array of countries, including Canada.

“They’ve got a global safeguards investigation … for 60 days. Canada is not the culprit, and you’ll find out once the investigation is done,” he said.

Carney also met meet with Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva on the sidelines of the summit, where he announced $540 million for an initiative to protect rainforests, as part of a project co-led by Brazil and Norway.

The money is part of a $6 billion fund promised by Ottawa this spring in support for international climate finance. It is meant to attract public and private investment for preserving biodiversity and supporting communities that rely on these ecosystems.

Through an interpreter, Lula described the money as investments that will yield a profit and not “donations, money for free.”

Carney suggested he would have further talks with Brazil, which is part of the Mercosur trade bloc with whom Canada is negotiating a trade deal. Lula’s office has previously said Carney would visit the country.

“By May, we will also have an opportunity to discuss our economic co-operation, our largest training partner in Latin America by far, (with) $15 billion dollars in trade,” Carney said.

Carney is now en route to Cambodia for a summit of the Francophonie, including a side event on technology trade in Phnom Penh.

While there, Carney will meet with Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon who is pushing for more autonomy in Quebec’s international relations, though Sidhu says Ottawa is working constructively with the province.

“Quebec has many of their own trade officers in our embassies around the world, and we’ll continue working collaboratively,” Sidhu said, noting that Quebec’s aerospace sector has recently achieved large sales in Asia.

Later this week, Carney will attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation summit in China, months after Carney and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed to have a limited number of Chinese electrical vehicles sold in Canada.

Sidhu also said Chinese automaker Chery is among those seeking Transport Canada certification to sell lower-cost vehicles into Canada. He said some Chinese manufacturers will likely clear that process by the end of the year.

He said he is also hopeful Chinese companies will create automotive jobs for Canadians.

“There is an interest from Chinese manufacturers to utilize our workforce in Canada, but before you invest billions of dollars you need to understand the market,” he said.

“Every time I sit down with them I look at what they’re doing in Europe and I ask them how they can replicate that in Canada with Canadian supply chains, with Canadian workers.”

The minister said Canada is still navigating trade issues with China, despite some recent progress on extending access to beef, canola meal, crab and peas.

“We’re still continuing to engage on pork, ON pet food and others. We’re not relenting,” he said.

Sidhu also said Canada is working with Beijing to have more opportunities for Canadian small and medium businesses to sell consumer goods to China on online platforms like Alibaba.

stories.title: How Danielle Smith’s risky bet on data centres could backfire
stories.summary: Premier could face same fate as Republicans ousted in sweeping fashion during U.S. midterms, rebuked in part for data-centre friendly policies
stories.author: Emma Graney, Kate Helmore, Matthew Scace
stories.content:
During the August long weekend, Connie Challice and several of her neighbours cornered Alberta Premier Danielle Smith in the back of a horse-drawn wagon during the stampede parade in Strathmore, Alta.

Ms. Challice owns a horse-carriage business, and she was at the reins, her four black Clydesdales pulling the Premier’s wagon. She was determined to get 20 minutes with Ms. Smith.

Ms. Challlice lives in Indus, a rural community just outside Calgary. The community is facing what Ms. Challice considers an existential threat: a massive data centre project with a 1,494-megawatt gas-fired power plant on site. That’s enough electricity to power a city the size of Edmonton, and it would be located just over a mile away from her home. The project is currently awaiting approval from the provincial utilities regulator.

She thought she was aligned with the Premier on their vision for the province. Ms. Challice is a long-time United Conservative Party member, she sits on her local UCP constituency board. She’d proudly pulled the Premier in the Calgary Stampede three years in a row.

But her faith in the Premier’s leadership has since wavered. Ms. Smith listened to her concerns while she was in the back of the wagon, but has ignored Albertans’ worries about data centres ever since, said Ms. Challice.

The sprawling facilities are bad for rural communities, cause pollution that affects livestock, crops and people, she said, adding that there has also been a “complete lack of transparency and a lack of communication to the landowners” regarding their development.

“It’s ridiculous what’s going on.”

Ms. Challice is not alone in her disdain for data centres, and her growing distrust for the Premier who has backed their development.

And backed them she has: Ms. Smith has drawn the interest of the world’s largest tech companies to the province, promising an abundance of natural gas for power generation, land, cool temperatures and a business-friendly environment that are perfect for multibillion-dollar investments.

And more opportunity could be coming. As U.S. states that were also bidding for these investments turn against them, tech giants are looking for jurisdictions that are still welcoming.

“As long as Alberta gets out of its own way we could see significant investment,” said Matt Solberg, a former adviser to the Premier and partner at New West Public Affairs, a Calgary-based lobbying firm.

But Albertans are getting in the way.

There is currently one data centre moratorium in the province, and a group of city councillors in Calgary are pushing for another one. The province’s technology and innovation minister, Nate Glubish, has faced boos and jeers from hundreds of constituents packed into town halls to oppose data centres, and far-right factions of Ms. Smith’s party could be eyeing the cause as their next crusade after a resounding defeat of a separation referendum last month.

In this way, the Premier could face the same fate as the Republican governors and congressmen and women who were ousted in sweeping fashion during the U.S. midterms, rebuked in part for their data-centre friendly policies.

It is a threat Ms. Smith will soon have to confront. The issue is bound to come up when thousands of UCP members descend on Calgary for the party’s annual general meeting on Nov. 27, and Ms. Smith is preparing to face voters in a provincial election next October.

“Our government is not listening,” Ms. Challice said.

On the night of the U.S. midterm elections, tech trillionaire Elon Musk summarized the AI backlash in a single post: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.”

He was referencing the blue wave washing over the country. Public fear over data centre development was a factor in many of the races.

In Texas, voters elected a Democrat governor for the first time in decades, after months of public fury over Republican Governor Greg Abbott’s welcoming approach to the AI industry . His successor, Gina Hinojosa, has promised to tighten regulations on data centres but not stop them entirely. In Ohio and Kansas, voters in more than a dozen municipalities passed bans or restrictions on data centre development. In total, 26 gubernatorial candidates across 21 states backed some form of moratorium on data centre development in the run-up to election day.

Ms. Smith would be wise to pay close attention to this “cautionary tale,” Mr. Solberg said.

Much like the U.S. states of Texas and Georgia, Alberta launched itself into the race to attract a piece of the estimated global total of US$2-trillion of data centre investment.

The province rolled out its data centre strategy in late 2024. It promised a “concierge service” to streamline project proposals in a bid to capture $100-billion of investment within five years – a cash injection that would also be a boon to the natural gas sector and independent power providers that use the fuel to generate electricity to feed the power-hungry facilities.

The strategy got off to a promising start.

In July, during the Calgary Stampede, Ms. Smith announced that Meta Platforms Inc. META-Q , the parent of Facebook, would build a $13-billion data centre campus north of Edmonton. The “historic win” was one of the largest private-sector investments in Canadian history, Ms. Smith declared.

There are now more than 145 data centre projects proposed for the province.

Data centres announced, under construction or operating, in ridings coloured by party that won them in 2023 provincial election

Data centre: under construction or operating

Map shows individual data centre buildings, which can be organized into campuses containing several buildings.

Project information is reviewed and updated by Aterio at least once a month. Announced projects with only an estimated location are not mapped.

mahima singh/the globe and mail, source: Aterio; Elections Alberta

mahima singh/the globe and mail, source: Aterio; Elections Alberta

But the sentiments that drove opposition in the U.S. are crossing the 49th parallel.

On the surface, the pushback is about water usage, rising electricity rates, environmental impacts and a lack of adequate community consultation, said Dan Balaban, chief executive officer of Calgary-based renewables developer Greengate Power and an investor in AI infrastructure.

But the true motives for this distrust go deeper, he said.

“We’re having a debate broadly about whether or not AI is something that’s positive for society,” he said. “It’s a technology that has the potential to be highly disruptive.”

The province has tried to get ahead of this pushback by being more cautious in its data centre rollout than some U.S. states, said Janet Brown, a prominent Alberta pollster.

It has prioritized projects whereby developers bring their own power in a bid to minimize demands on the grid and the prospect of higher rates for consumers. And the Premier has been careful to recognize the downsides associated with these projects. For example, in her Meta deal announcement, she addressed concerns about water, energy infrastructure and energy bills. Why? The Premier realizes that data centres are not “the slam dunk pipelines would be,” Ms. Brown said.

Data centres proposed for sites close to homes have also been rejected by the utilities regulator . One was a project located a kilometre from roughly 800 homes proposed by Synapse Real Estate Corp. (Ms. Smith initially backed this project.)

In recent months, the Premier has also started referring to data centres as “digital refineries,” wrapping them in language used by the energy sector, the province’s dominant industry.

But arguments in favour of data centres have not been convincing, and the province doesn’t yet have a major data centre to point to as an example of a project “done the right way,” said Mr. Solberg, the former adviser.

The Globe and Mail has reported that rural communities in Alberta are struggling to stay ahead of the rush on data centre development. Staff and consultation directors at municipalities and First Nations are being inundated with proposals before they’ve had a chance to develop a policy framework, and while the province is still developing its own.

Mr. Glubish, Alberta’s technology minister, was not made available for an interview, but said in a statement that the government will introduce legislation before year’s end “to establish consistent, province-wide siting standards to ensure large data centres are located in the right places, away from residential neighbourhoods. We will also introduce measures to further address water use and expand environmental oversight.”

Developers are also offering First Nations money to drop their objections to projects, and proponents are visiting farmers with land close to proposed sites and offering to buy it for many times above market price, The Globe reported.

These local communities are out of their depth, said Quinn Nicholson, CEO of Reverb, an Edmonton-based communications firm that works on behalf of data centre developers and municipalities weighing projects. They have found themselves in the middle of a fast-moving, global “gold rush.”

“Some of Canada’s smallest communities are now being asked to make its biggest decisions, and they’re largely doing it in a void or a vacuum.”

Analysis: Ottawa and Silicon Valley are both after Canadian AI processing power. Who will win?

And for politicians in those communities, rising data centre dissent has political consequences.

Anthony Heinrich saw this play out in his 7,000-resident county located in Alberta’s conservative heartland. In 2023, nearly three-quarters of residents in the rural riding that covers the county voted for the UCP and about 45 per cent endorsed holding a separation referendum in last month’s provincewide vote. Earlier this month, Mr. Heinrich won a by-election to serve as reeve.

Rumours have been flying about AI companies eyeing land in the area, Mr. Heinrich said. And while he doesn’t believe his stand against data centres contributed to his by-election win, he said when the topic came up during a campaign debate in Buck Creek, Alta., the roughly 60 to 70 attendees voiced a deep skepticism about the developments.

One of his opponents, Jason Lavigne, disagrees with Mr. Heinrich on data centres.

The crowd packed into the community hall groaned when Mr. Lavigne stated his support for data centres, which he pitched as a new tax base for the county struggling with what he described as “crippling and deteriorating infrastructure.”

“Even just bringing it to the table as a conversation frustrated them,” said Mr. Lavigne, an independent journalist who spent the past year urging Albertans to vote for holding a separation referendum.

While Mr. Lavigne doesn’t believe his position tanked his campaign, he said one opponent later used his support for data centres “to play into the fear and misinformation.”

“They treat them like prisons. Everybody agrees we need them, but not in our backyard,” Mr. Lavigne said of the public sentiment he witnessed as a candidate.

The data centre debate also has the potential to become a major issue for the right flank of Ms. Smith’s party, said Ms. Brown.

Ms. Smith seems to recognize that data centres are not “the slam dunk pipelines would be,” but it may not be enough to satisfy the right side of her party who are searching for a new crusade.

“Will that group of people who are anti-vax, pro-trucker, pro-blockade, pro-separation add anti-AI on to that?” she asked.

The subject has become a cultural issue “prone to conspiratorial thinking,” said Feodor Snagovsky, an associate professor of political science at the University of Alberta.

And that’s bad news for Ms. Smith, whose ascent to Premier and hold on the role has relied on that group’s support.

In two weeks, she will hear from them at her party’s AGM.

This year’s proposed resolutions include discontinuing land acknowledgments, gun rights and making public washrooms and change rooms exclusive to biological men and women. Data centres, however, are not on the agenda.

That is the reason why Ms. Challice is making the trip to the AGM.

It will cost her thousands of dollars to attend; the end of November is a busy time of year for her business. It is the start of Christmas wagon ride season. She should be driving across the province with her wagons and horses. But she says she can’t miss the opportunity to make her voice and those of her neighbours heard.

“This is not okay. Why are we not addressing this? Why can’t we talk about it? Why does it just get shut down?”

paragraphs: During the August long weekend, Connie Challice and several of her neighbours cornered Alberta Premier Danielle Smith in the back of a horse-drawn wagon during the stampede parade in Strathmore, Alta.
Ms. Challice owns a horse-carriage business, and she was at the reins, her four black Clydesdales pulling the Premier’s wagon. She was determined to get 20 minutes with Ms. Smith.

Ms. Challlice lives in Indus, a rural community just outside Calgary. The community is facing what Ms. Challice considers an existential threat: a massive data centre project with a 1,494-megawatt gas-fired power plant on site. That’s enough electricity to power a city the size of Edmonton, and it would be located just over a mile away from her home. The project is currently awaiting approval from the provincial utilities regulator.

She thought she was aligned with the Premier on their vision for the province. Ms. Challice is a long-time United Conservative Party member, she sits on her local UCP constituency board. She’d proudly pulled the Premier in the Calgary Stampede three years in a row.

But her faith in the Premier’s leadership has since wavered. Ms. Smith listened to her concerns while she was in the back of the wagon, but has ignored Albertans’ worries about data centres ever since, said Ms. Challice.

The sprawling facilities are bad for rural communities, cause pollution that affects livestock, crops and people, she said, adding that there has also been a “complete lack of transparency and a lack of communication to the landowners” regarding their development.
“It’s ridiculous what’s going on.”
Ms. Challice is not alone in her disdain for data centres, and her growing distrust for the Premier who has backed their development.

And backed them she has: Ms. Smith has drawn the interest of the world’s largest tech companies to the province, promising an abundance of natural gas for power generation, land, cool temperatures and a business-friendly environment that are perfect for multibillion-dollar investments.
And more opportunity could be coming. As U.S. states that were also bidding for these investments turn against them, tech giants are looking for jurisdictions that are still welcoming.

“As long as Alberta gets out of its own way we could see significant investment,” said Matt Solberg, a former adviser to the Premier and partner at New West Public Affairs, a Calgary-based lobbying firm.
But Albertans are getting in the way.

There is currently one data centre moratorium in the province, and a group of city councillors in Calgary are pushing for another one. The province’s technology and innovation minister, Nate Glubish, has faced boos and jeers from hundreds of constituents packed into town halls to oppose data centres, and far-right factions of Ms. Smith’s party could be eyeing the cause as their next crusade after a resounding defeat of a separation referendum last month.

In this way, the Premier could face the same fate as the Republican governors and congressmen and women who were ousted in sweeping fashion during the U.S. midterms, rebuked in part for their data-centre friendly policies.

It is a threat Ms. Smith will soon have to confront. The issue is bound to come up when thousands of UCP members descend on Calgary for the party’s annual general meeting on Nov. 27, and Ms. Smith is preparing to face voters in a provincial election next October.
“Our government is not listening,” Ms. Challice said.
On the night of the U.S. midterm elections, tech trillionaire Elon Musk summarized the AI backlash in a single post: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.”
He was referencing the blue wave washing over the country. Public fear over data centre development was a factor in many of the races.

In Texas, voters elected a Democrat governor for the first time in decades, after months of public fury over Republican Governor Greg Abbott’s welcoming approach to the AI industry . His successor, Gina Hinojosa, has promised to tighten regulations on data centres but not stop them entirely. In Ohio and Kansas, voters in more than a dozen municipalities passed bans or restrictions on data centre development. In total, 26 gubernatorial candidates across 21 states backed some form of moratorium on data centre development in the run-up to election day.
Ms. Smith would be wise to pay close attention to this “cautionary tale,” Mr. Solberg said.
Much like the U.S. states of Texas and Georgia, Alberta launched itself into the race to attract a piece of the estimated global total of US$2-trillion of data centre investment.

The province rolled out its data centre strategy in late 2024. It promised a “concierge service” to streamline project proposals in a bid to capture $100-billion of investment within five years – a cash injection that would also be a boon to the natural gas sector and independent power providers that use the fuel to generate electricity to feed the power-hungry facilities.
The strategy got off to a promising start.

In July, during the Calgary Stampede, Ms. Smith announced that Meta Platforms Inc. META-Q , the parent of Facebook, would build a $13-billion data centre campus north of Edmonton. The “historic win” was one of the largest private-sector investments in Canadian history, Ms. Smith declared.
There are now more than 145 data centre projects proposed for the province.

But the sentiments that drove opposition in the U.S. are crossing the 49th parallel.

On the surface, the pushback is about water usage, rising electricity rates, environmental impacts and a lack of adequate community consultation, said Dan Balaban, chief executive officer of Calgary-based renewables developer Greengate Power and an investor in AI infrastructure.
But the true motives for this distrust go deeper, he said.
“We’re having a debate broadly about whether or not AI is something that’s positive for society,” he said. “It’s a technology that has the potential to be highly disruptive.”
The province has tried to get ahead of this pushback by being more cautious in its data centre rollout than some U.S. states, said Janet Brown, a prominent Alberta pollster.

It has prioritized projects whereby developers bring their own power in a bid to minimize demands on the grid and the prospect of higher rates for consumers. And the Premier has been careful to recognize the downsides associated with these projects. For example, in her Meta deal announcement, she addressed concerns about water, energy infrastructure and energy bills. Why? The Premier realizes that data centres are not “the slam dunk pipelines would be,” Ms. Brown said.

Data centres proposed for sites close to homes have also been rejected by the utilities regulator . One was a project located a kilometre from roughly 800 homes proposed by Synapse Real Estate Corp. (Ms. Smith initially backed this project.)
In recent months, the Premier has also started referring to data centres as “digital refineries,” wrapping them in language used by the energy sector, the province’s dominant industry.

But arguments in favour of data centres have not been convincing, and the province doesn’t yet have a major data centre to point to as an example of a project “done the right way,” said Mr. Solberg, the former adviser.

The Globe and Mail has reported that rural communities in Alberta are struggling to stay ahead of the rush on data centre development. Staff and consultation directors at municipalities and First Nations are being inundated with proposals before they’ve had a chance to develop a policy framework, and while the province is still developing its own.

Mr. Glubish, Alberta’s technology minister, was not made available for an interview, but said in a statement that the government will introduce legislation before year’s end “to establish consistent, province-wide siting standards to ensure large data centres are located in the right places, away from residential neighbourhoods. We will also introduce measures to further address water use and expand environmental oversight.”

Developers are also offering First Nations money to drop their objections to projects, and proponents are visiting farmers with land close to proposed sites and offering to buy it for many times above market price, The Globe reported.

These local communities are out of their depth, said Quinn Nicholson, CEO of Reverb, an Edmonton-based communications firm that works on behalf of data centre developers and municipalities weighing projects. They have found themselves in the middle of a fast-moving, global “gold rush.”
“Some of Canada’s smallest communities are now being asked to make its biggest decisions, and they’re largely doing it in a void or a vacuum.”
Analysis: Ottawa and Silicon Valley are both after Canadian AI processing power. Who will win?
And for politicians in those communities, rising data centre dissent has political consequences.

Anthony Heinrich saw this play out in his 7,000-resident county located in Alberta’s conservative heartland. In 2023, nearly three-quarters of residents in the rural riding that covers the county voted for the UCP and about 45 per cent endorsed holding a separation referendum in last month’s provincewide vote. Earlier this month, Mr. Heinrich won a by-election to serve as reeve.

Rumours have been flying about AI companies eyeing land in the area, Mr. Heinrich said. And while he doesn’t believe his stand against data centres contributed to his by-election win, he said when the topic came up during a campaign debate in Buck Creek, Alta., the roughly 60 to 70 attendees voiced a deep skepticism about the developments.
One of his opponents, Jason Lavigne, disagrees with Mr. Heinrich on data centres.

The crowd packed into the community hall groaned when Mr. Lavigne stated his support for data centres, which he pitched as a new tax base for the county struggling with what he described as “crippling and deteriorating infrastructure.”

“Even just bringing it to the table as a conversation frustrated them,” said Mr. Lavigne, an independent journalist who spent the past year urging Albertans to vote for holding a separation referendum.
While Mr. Lavigne doesn’t believe his position tanked his campaign, he said one opponent later used his support for data centres “to play into the fear and misinformation.”
“They treat them like prisons. Everybody agrees we need them, but not in our backyard,” Mr. Lavigne said of the public sentiment he witnessed as a candidate.
The data centre debate also has the potential to become a major issue for the right flank of Ms. Smith’s party, said Ms. Brown.
Ms. Smith seems to recognize that data centres are not “the slam dunk pipelines would be,” but it may not be enough to satisfy the right side of her party who are searching for a new crusade.
“Will that group of people who are anti-vax, pro-trucker, pro-blockade, pro-separation add anti-AI on to that?” she asked.
The subject has become a cultural issue “prone to conspiratorial thinking,” said Feodor Snagovsky, an associate professor of political science at the University of Alberta.
And that’s bad news for Ms. Smith, whose ascent to Premier and hold on the role has relied on that group’s support.
In two weeks, she will hear from them at her party’s AGM.

This year’s proposed resolutions include discontinuing land acknowledgments, gun rights and making public washrooms and change rooms exclusive to biological men and women. Data centres, however, are not on the agenda.
That is the reason why Ms. Challice is making the trip to the AGM.

It will cost her thousands of dollars to attend; the end of November is a busy time of year for her business. It is the start of Christmas wagon ride season. She should be driving across the province with her wagons and horses. But she says she can’t miss the opportunity to make her voice and those of her neighbours heard.
“This is not okay. Why are we not addressing this? Why can’t we talk about it? Why does it just get shut down?”

Should the province continue along this trajectory and approve the data centre proposed for Ms. Challice’s community, the Premier may also have to find a new horse for her wagon, Ms. Challice said. She will not be inclined to carry the Premier through the streets of any Albertan city.
“If she doesn’t have the backs of the people who are coming and talking to her, I’ll have to put my energy into other things.”

stories.title: What Michael Chong wants you to understand about ‘big-borrowing, big-spending’ Mark Carney
stories.summary: The Conservative critic says Justin Trudeau spent a lot of money, but his replacement is spending far more -- and the cost to Canada will be high
stories.author: Donna Kennedy-Glans
stories.content:
Michael Chong is the fiscal conservative that he says Mark Carney is pretending to be.

“The prime minister is not a fiscal conservative,” Chong says calmly. The Conservative shadow minister of finance has represented Wellington-Halton Hills North since 2004. In question period he is the rare politician who finishes his sentences. On the phone this week, he was the same: calm, precise and thoroughly unimpressed with Budget 2026.

“Carney is borrowing and spending way more money than Mr. Trudeau did,” he says. “That’s a quantifiable fact. The numbers tell the story.” Deficits under Carney are roughly double those in Justin Trudeau’s final budget, and a growing share of the spending is being shoved off the main balance sheet into new Crown corporations and funds. Government debt is rising more than twice as fast as the annual deficit.

Budget 2026, tabled Nov. 5, has been called “more of the same.” Chong’s verdict is sharper: Carney has doubled down. This is his second budget; it’s not a minority Parliament anymore, he’s got a solid majority. And he’s still borrowing and spending ever-increasing amounts of money.

The clearest warning light is the interest bill. A few years ago debt service ate five or six cents of every federal tax dollar. Today it is about 11 cents — roughly $60 billion a year, already more than the entire Canada Health Transfer. By 2030 it is projected to hit 14 cents, or $86 billion. “The fastest-growing expense in the federal government is interest on the national debt,” Chong warns.

Many still buy the image of Carney as the steady CEO who will right the Liberal ship. Chong doesn’t buy it. What he sees is “a big-borrowing, big-spending prime minister. That’s the reality of the government he’s running.”

Skyrocketing debt does more than raise interest costs; it shrinks the fiscal room Ottawa needs when the next crisis hits. In 2008 the federal government borrowed the equivalent of about five per cent of GDP to get us through the financial crisis. In the 2020 pandemic, it borrowed closer to 15 per cent. Today the debt-to-GDP ratio sits near 40 per cent and is climbing toward 50.

“We are reducing the capacity of the federal government to respond to a future crisis — the very thing the prime minister himself says we must be prepared for,” Chong suggests, pointing to Carney’s own national security statement, which warns of the need to be ready for an actual disaster, or actual war. “This budget does not put us on a track to be prepared for it.”

The borrowing also crowds out everyone else. Governments are competing with households and businesses for the same pool of savings, pushing up interest rates for families who need mortgages, car loans, or credit to expand. Massive expansion of federal borrowing is increasing the cost of interest for ordinary Canadians.

Affordability is the daily concern for most people. “Subsidizing, providing more assistance to individuals, to families, to companies, hasn’t worked in the past, and it isn’t going to work going forward,” Chong says. He says there is one statistic that pops out for him: “We’re now on the third increase to the groceries and essentials benefit, and yet food bank usage this year is at record high levels. Some 2.35 million Canadians, this month, will visit a food bank.”

“We’re seeing the biggest expansion of the federal government in decades under Mr. Carney,” says Conservative MP Michael Chong. Blair Gable/Postmedia

The solution, he offers, is to create the conditions for incomes and paycheques to grow faster than the cost of living.

That means supply-side reforms: major tax changes, a serious overhaul of competition rules, regulatory cleanup that covers not just big resource projects but small and medium-sized businesses, and the removal of interprovincial barriers.

“We’re seeing the biggest expansion of the federal government in decades under Mr. Carney,” Chong asserts, “the government is now starting to get involved in areas of our lives that it never previously was involved with … crowding out private initiatives and private investment.”

He posits: If some companies are getting massive subsidies, how can companies that don’t get those subsidies compete? “The short answer is they can’t.”

The government’s planned equity stake of up to $1.6 billion in Cohere, the Canadian AI company, is a case in point. “More money has been raised for AI in the last couple of years in the private sector than for almost anything else in recent decades,” he says, arguing the government is inserting itself into a space the private sector has been perfectly capable of funding.

Crown corporations are not new, but “they’ve never been so massively expanded and so filled with public money as we’ve seen in the last 18 months,” Chong suggests. Tens of billions — and potentially hundreds of billions over the next several years — are being borrowed outside the normal budget process. That is not only a fiscal problem, it is a democratic one, he says. “Parliament’s responsibility is to hold the government democratically accountable for the public purse, for taxation, for spending. It’s sacrosanct. It’s one of the reasons Parliament came into existence.”

Arm’s-length entities such as the Defence Investment Agency, Build Canada Homes, and the Canada Strong Fund move large sums outside the ordinary scrutiny of the House of Commons. Defence spending itself is a legitimate federal role, Chong notes, but “they are doing it off-budget.” Build Canada Homes is already drifting into territory once left to the private sector, including proposals to subsidize condo developers. The Canada Strong Fund is presented as a commercially driven sovereign wealth fund. Chong is skeptical: “Sovereign wealth funds around the world are built on the solid foundation of surpluses,” this one is built on government debt.

All this spending, all this debt that Carney is taking on isn’t showing up in the numbers and we’re now into year two of the Carney government. “None of this is changing the trajectory of the Canadian economy,” Chong concludes, “despite all the announcements.”

There is a cost to what Chong sees as Carney’s false fiscal conservatism. “Ultimately,” Chong says, “it’s going to lead to the government increasing taxes or cutting social programs. That’s the path this budget sets us on.” I fear he’s right.

stories.title: Legion pushes back against white poppy campaign
stories.summary: The Legion upholds the red poppy as something worn by millions of Canadians as 'a visual pledge ... to never forget those who served and sacrificed.'
stories.author: Stewart Lewis
stories.content:
For the Royal Canadian Legion, the traditional red poppy is “a visual pledge … to never forget those who served and sacrificed.”

However, Canadians were confronted before this year’s Remembrance Day with a campaign advocating white pacifist poppies. An anti-war organization known as World Beyond War proposed on Nov. 6, what it called “an alternative to traditional, militaristic Remembrance Day education, centred around the White Poppy — a symbol meant to recognize all victims of war.”

The Legion is pushing back.

“The red Poppy is Canada’s longstanding and traditional symbol of Remembrance,” says Legion spokesperson Nujma Bond. “It encompasses all conflicts, races, genders, and backgrounds, and was always meant to be all-inclusive.”

Bond adds that the “Legion believes that ‘a Veteran is a Veteran is a Veteran.’ All are equally deserving of recognition and that recognition is reflected in the red Poppy.”

She insists that the red Poppy “has one meaning only – to remember all those who died in service to Canada. It is absolutely not a political symbol, and we do respectfully request that any groups or organizations wishing to represent any other cause or personal belief, choose other symbols.”

World Beyond War’s website messaging is that though Remembrance Day “was founded to abolish war, the way it is marked increasingly serves to glorify war, militarism, and violence. Most concerningly, school curricula across Canada still make the glorification of war and notions of bravery and sacrifice through military violence central to Remembrance Day.”

The group promoted its new handbook entitled Reframing Remembrance Day in Canada: A Handbook for Educators. There is no indication on its website whether the campaign was picked up by Canadian teachers. National Post has not received a response to a request for comment from the organization.

The red poppy was trademarked by an Act of Parliament in 1948, says the Legion. Guidelines for the use of the poppy are set out in the Legion Poppy Manual.

The Legion says on its website that “the Remembrance Poppy was imagined by Madame Anna Guérin of France … Later, Anna presented her concept to France’s allies, including the precursor to The Royal Canadian Legion, The Great War Veterans Association. The idea was considered at a meeting in Port Arthur, Ontario (now Thunder Bay) and was adopted on July 6, 1921.”

In 2021, the late Tim Cook, who was then director of research at the Canadian War Museum, told National Post that the creation of the poppy as a symbol can be credited to Lieutenant-Colonel John McCrae, a Guelph, Ont. doctor who wrote the poem “In Flanders Fields” while serving as a medical officer in the First World War.

“It’s deeply entrenched with John McCrae and In Flanders Fields,” Cook said.

He added that the Western world has since regularly recited the poem, with many Canadian schoolchildren reciting it over the decades. “In Flanders fields the poppies blow, between the crosses, row on row,” it begins.

Meanwhile, World Beyond War cites several organizations in Canada and abroad that support its cause. That includes the white poppy campaign promoted by Canadian Voice of W o men for Peace.

VOW says it hosts annual “peace poppy-making parties” and distributes them in “trying to raise awareness of the horrors of war (aiming) to make war unimaginable and to invest in peaceful institutions, processes and diplomacy to abolish war, forever.”

In the U.K. residents can buy white poppies online from the Peace Pledge Union. The organization has a Canadian branch in Vancouver.

A U.S. organization linked to the World Beyond War website, known as Veterans for Peace, seeks to “reclaim Armistice Day,” citing the Middle East war and “850 foreign bases in over 80 countries, and threatens nuclear war against its perceived ‘enemies.’”

These efforts are just the most recent in a lengthy history of white poppy promotions.

Back in 2011, National Post reported on a white poppy campaign in Quebec. It marked the first time such a campaign has been organized in Quebec. It was driven by the Collectif Échec à la guerre, an anti-war organization. Approximately 5,000 white poppy pins were shipped to Quebec, the organizer told the Post.

However, the Post report stated that the effort generated backlash from Quebeckers who said the traditional poppy is an important symbol of remembrance that should be honoured.

According to commentary published in National Post, in 2013, a group of University of Ottawa students embraced an initiative to wear white poppies and distribute them ahead of Remembrance Day. Ottawa’s Rideau Institute had encouraged Canadians to wear the white poppy as a symbol of peace, through its website, ceasefire.CA.

The commentary writers, Jonathan Weier and Christopher Schultz, then Ph.D. Candidates at Western University, wrote the red poppy was first promoted by an American, Moina Michael, and French woman, Anna Guerin, both volunteers with the Ymca during the First World War. Inspired by John McCrae’s In Flanders Fields, during a 1918 Ymca conference they decided to encourage wearing red poppies as a symbol of remembrance and promoted it among veteran associations.

Afterwards, Weir and Schultz wrote, the sale of “artificial poppies, often hand-made by disabled veterans, became an important fundraising tool to pay for training and rehabilitation services offered by veterans’ organizations.”

A sense of optimism arose after the First World War during the early 1920s, in part due to the founding of the League of Nations 1919, and the 1925 Treaty of Locarno, aimed at normalizing relations with Germany, and seemed to offer the possibility of enduring peace. But then, the authors note, the 1929 stock market crash with effects that rippled around the world, unsettled world politics.

Increasingly hardened political lines sprouted new seeds of conflict. It was then that the “white poppy became a symbol of the total renunciation of war, to be worn alongside the red poppy as a reminder of the desire for enduring peace and using peaceful means to resolve disputes. “

The original idea for a pacifist poppy came in 1926. It was a product of the No More War Movement in England and involved placing a pin at the centre of the red poppy stating: ‘No More War.’

Weir and Schultz recount that the U.K’s Women’s Co-operative Guild created the white poppy in 1933. The Pledge Peace Union (PPU), still active today, took over its production and distribution. “The white poppy became a symbol of the pacifist left and has been distributed for Remembrance Day…in the United Kingdom every year since.”

However, Canada took a different course than the U.K. Pacifist groups cropped up here in the 1930s, too, the most prominent associated with the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, the Ndp’s predecessor, but within the Canadian left, “disputes arose about whether or not they should condemn all military actions, or just some. Given the schism in the political left, it’s equally unsurprising that the white poppy never caught on in this country.”

paragraphs: For the Royal Canadian Legion, the traditional red poppy is “a visual pledge … to never forget those who served and sacrificed.”

However, Canadians were confronted before this year’s Remembrance Day with a campaign advocating white pacifist poppies. An anti-war organization known as World Beyond War proposed on Nov. 6, what it called “an alternative to traditional, militaristic Remembrance Day education, centred around the White Poppy — a symbol meant to recognize all victims of war.”
The Legion is pushing back.

“The red Poppy is Canada’s longstanding and traditional symbol of Remembrance,” says Legion spokesperson Nujma Bond. “It encompasses all conflicts, races, genders, and backgrounds, and was always meant to be all-inclusive.”
Bond adds that the “Legion believes that ‘a Veteran is a Veteran is a Veteran.’ All are equally deserving of recognition and that recognition is reflected in the red Poppy.”

She insists that the red Poppy “has one meaning only – to remember all those who died in service to Canada. It is absolutely not a political symbol, and we do respectfully request that any groups or organizations wishing to represent any other cause or personal belief, choose other symbols.”

World Beyond War’s website messaging is that though Remembrance Day “was founded to abolish war, the way it is marked increasingly serves to glorify war, militarism, and violence. Most concerningly, school curricula across Canada still make the glorification of war and notions of bravery and sacrifice through military violence central to Remembrance Day.”

The group promoted its new handbook entitled Reframing Remembrance Day in Canada: A Handbook for Educators. There is no indication on its website whether the campaign was picked up by Canadian teachers. National Post has not received a response to a request for comment from the organization.
The red poppy was trademarked by an Act of Parliament in 1948, says the Legion. Guidelines for the use of the poppy are set out in the Legion Poppy Manual.

The Legion says on its website that “the Remembrance Poppy was imagined by Madame Anna Guérin of France … Later, Anna presented her concept to France’s allies, including the precursor to The Royal Canadian Legion, The Great War Veterans Association. The idea was considered at a meeting in Port Arthur, Ontario (now Thunder Bay) and was adopted on July 6, 1921.”

In 2021, the late Tim Cook, who was then director of research at the Canadian War Museum, told National Post that the creation of the poppy as a symbol can be credited to Lieutenant-Colonel John McCrae, a Guelph, Ont. doctor who wrote the poem “In Flanders Fields” while serving as a medical officer in the First World War.
“It’s deeply entrenched with John McCrae and In Flanders Fields,” Cook said.

He added that the Western world has since regularly recited the poem, with many Canadian schoolchildren reciting it over the decades. “In Flanders fields the poppies blow, between the crosses, row on row,” it begins.
Meanwhile, World Beyond War cites several organizations in Canada and abroad that support its cause. That includes the white poppy campaign promoted by Canadian Voice of W o men for Peace.

VOW says it hosts annual “peace poppy-making parties” and distributes them in “trying to raise awareness of the horrors of war (aiming) to make war unimaginable and to invest in peaceful institutions, processes and diplomacy to abolish war, forever.”
In the U.K. residents can buy white poppies online from the Peace Pledge Union. The organization has a Canadian branch in Vancouver.

A U.S. organization linked to the World Beyond War website, known as Veterans for Peace, seeks to “reclaim Armistice Day,” citing the Middle East war and “850 foreign bases in over 80 countries, and threatens nuclear war against its perceived ‘enemies.’”
These efforts are just the most recent in a lengthy history of white poppy promotions.

Back in 2011, National Post reported on a white poppy campaign in Quebec. It marked the first time such a campaign has been organized in Quebec. It was driven by the Collectif Échec à la guerre, an anti-war organization. Approximately 5,000 white poppy pins were shipped to Quebec, the organizer told the Post.
However, the Post report stated that the effort generated backlash from Quebeckers who said the traditional poppy is an important symbol of remembrance that should be honoured.

According to commentary published in National Post, in 2013, a group of University of Ottawa students embraced an initiative to wear white poppies and distribute them ahead of Remembrance Day. Ottawa’s Rideau Institute had encouraged Canadians to wear the white poppy as a symbol of peace, through its website, ceasefire.CA.

The commentary writers, Jonathan Weier and Christopher Schultz, then Ph.D. Candidates at Western University, wrote the red poppy was first promoted by an American, Moina Michael, and French woman, Anna Guerin, both volunteers with the Ymca during the First World War. Inspired by John McCrae’s In Flanders Fields, during a 1918 Ymca conference they decided to encourage wearing red poppies as a symbol of remembrance and promoted it among veteran associations.

Afterwards, Weir and Schultz wrote, the sale of “artificial poppies, often hand-made by disabled veterans, became an important fundraising tool to pay for training and rehabilitation services offered by veterans’ organizations.”

A sense of optimism arose after the First World War during the early 1920s, in part due to the founding of the League of Nations 1919, and the 1925 Treaty of Locarno, aimed at normalizing relations with Germany, and seemed to offer the possibility of enduring peace. But then, the authors note, the 1929 stock market crash with effects that rippled around the world, unsettled world politics.

Increasingly hardened political lines sprouted new seeds of conflict. It was then that the “white poppy became a symbol of the total renunciation of war, to be worn alongside the red poppy as a reminder of the desire for enduring peace and using peaceful means to resolve disputes. “
The original idea for a pacifist poppy came in 1926. It was a product of the No More War Movement in England and involved placing a pin at the centre of the red poppy stating: ‘No More War.’

Weir and Schultz recount that the U.K’s Women’s Co-operative Guild created the white poppy in 1933. The Pledge Peace Union (PPU), still active today, took over its production and distribution. “The white poppy became a symbol of the pacifist left and has been distributed for Remembrance Day…in the United Kingdom every year since.”

However, Canada took a different course than the U.K. Pacifist groups cropped up here in the 1930s, too, the most prominent associated with the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, the Ndp’s predecessor, but within the Canadian left, “disputes arose about whether or not they should condemn all military actions, or just some. Given the schism in the political left, it’s equally unsurprising that the white poppy never caught on in this country.”
During the Cold War, nuclear disarmament groups resurrected the white poppy. “Then, as now,” write Weir and Shultz, “the official response was mostly one of disdain.

“If anything is clear in the great poppy debate, though, it’s this: the white poppy symbol, like the flower itself, is not native to Flanders as is its red cousin. Accordingly, it has never caught on as a symbol of remembrance. Perhaps major Canadian involvement in recent wars has caused it to blossom anew.”

Stewart Lewis is a writer and editor with National Post. A journalist and lawyer, he has worked in newspapers, radio and TV, and served a legal stint with Global Affairs Canada at the United Nations in New York City.

stories.title: Growing freshwater challenges threaten Canada’s long-term security, federal memo warns
stories.summary: Climate change, pollution and growing demand are putting pressure on water resources, raising concerns about supply
stories.author: Jim Bronskill
stories.content:
Pressures on the supply of fresh water pose challenges that will affect Canada’s “long-term security and prosperity” if left unaddressed, an internal government memo warns.

The document, prepared for Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin, stresses a need to assess how Canada protects and sustainably manages freshwater resources – including waters shared with the United States – and how it responds to global water risks.

“Canadians will need more water to grow our cities and our economy, but it is unclear whether Canada is water secure for the long term,” the memo says.

The Canadian Press used the Access to Information Act to obtain the memo, written for Dabrusin by the Canada Water Agency, a federal organization that works to improve freshwater management.

Portions of the 12-page document were withheld under a provision of the law that allows the government to shield advice or recommendations from release.

The memo was intended to update the minister on the development of a national water security strategy. It says Dabrusin identified such a strategy as “a mission critical priority” in her reply to a call from Prime Minister Mark Carney for key portfolio objectives for cabinet members and secretaries of state.

A public consultation on developing the water security strategy took place from Sept. 9 through Oct. 25. Water stewardship is a shared responsibility in Canada and the water agency also engaged directly with provincial, territorial and Indigenous partners.

The memo to Dabrusin underscores the urgency of the exercise.

It says although Canada has 20 per cent of the world’s surface fresh water, only one-third is salt-free and replaced annually through precipitation.

Most of Canada’s renewable surface fresh water drains northward, away from the most populated regions and economic centres located within 300 kilometres of the Canada-United States border, the document adds.

It says groundwater aquifers – Canada’s largest freshwater resource – are unmapped in some parts of the country, even though almost one in three Canadians rely on groundwater for their supply of clean water.

Climate change is affecting where and when fresh water is available, the memo says. It warns some parts of Canada are facing, or could soon face, restricted or depleting water supplies, even in the Great Lakes-St. Lawrence River basin.

It says in many of Canada’s settled areas, water is polluted and is either unsuitable for human, animal or industrial use or is usable only after treatment at a high cost.

For the 2021 to 2023 period, for example, water quality at 49 per cent of 165 monitoring sites in southern Canadian rivers was rated as excellent or good, while water at 51 per cent of the sites was rated as fair to poor, the memo says.

While progress is being made to restore the quality of large lake systems, protecting them from major stressors is challenging. Complex freshwater ecosystems like the lower Great Lakes and Lake Winnipeg remain in fair or poor condition, the document adds.

It says water quality data for northern rivers and lakes and groundwater aquifers is limited, making it difficult to assess the health of these resources.

“Overall, freshwater ecosystems across southern Canada are under stress, which poses risks to water security, due to factors including a rapidly changing climate, shifts in land-use, population growth, pollution, overconsumption, and aging and inadequate water infrastructure,” the memo says.

“The Arctic and the North also face critical issues from increased development and climate change impacts on already overwhelmed infrastructure. Furthermore, First Nations, Métis, and Inuit communities are among the most water insecure in Canada.”

More than 40 per cent of the border between Canada and the United States crosses water, the document notes. It says these transboundary waters provide drinking water, hydro power, navigation, recreation, irrigation and support for biodiversity in both countries. Tens of millions of people live and work along these shared waters.

While the two nations are parties to over a dozen bilateral freshwater agreements, “new water-related disputes could emerge and become more frequent” as freshwater supplies in North America shrink and demands rise, the memo warns.

It says the pressures on Canada’s water emerge against a global backdrop of declining water security due to climate change, population growth and industrial pollution.

“For decades, Canadians have been raising concerns about the possibility of fresh water being exported in bulk to the U.S. and beyond,” the memo says. “Some Canadians strongly oppose diverting lakes and rivers, and this opposition has extended to any form of bulk export of water.”

On a positive note, actions to strengthen water security in Canada can create “significant development opportunities,” as long-term access to sufficient supplies of water will become a strategic advantage in a water-stressed world, the document says.

It points out that more than half of Canada’s electricity comes from hydro power, which supports the shift to cleaner energy and a low-carbon economy.

“Water storage and irrigation is critical to high-value crop production, particularly in the Prairies and interior British Columbia, as well as the greenhouse sector,” the memo adds.

“Major manufacturing industries are among the largest users of water in Canada and growing Canada’s digital economy will depend on a secure and sustainably managed water supply.”

stories.title: Freshwater supply challenges threaten Canada's security, internal federal memo says
stories.summary: Pressures on the supply of fresh water pose challenges that will affect Canada’s “long-term security and prosperity” if left unaddressed, an internal government memo warns.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — Pressures on the supply of fresh water pose challenges that will affect Canada’s “long-term security and prosperity” if left unaddressed, an internal government memo warns.

The document, prepared for Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin, stresses a need to assess how Canada protects and sustainably manages freshwater resources — including waters shared with the United States — and how it responds to global water risks.

“Canadians will need more water to grow our cities and our economy, but it is unclear whether Canada is water secure for the long term,” the memo says.

The Canadian Press used the Access to Information Act to obtain the memo, written for Dabrusin by the Canada Water Agency, a federal organization that works to improve freshwater management.

Portions of the 12-page document were withheld under a provision of the law that allows the government to shield advice or recommendations from release.

The memo was intended to update the minister on the development of a national water security strategy. It says Dabrusin identified such a strategy as “a mission critical priority” in her reply to a call from Prime Minister Mark Carney for key portfolio objectives for cabinet members and secretaries of state.

A public consultation on developing the water security strategy took place from Sept. 9 through Oct. 25. Water stewardship is a shared responsibility in Canada and the water agency also engaged directly with provincial, territorial and Indigenous partners.

The memo to Dabrusin underscores the urgency of the exercise.

It says although Canada has 20 per cent of the world’s surface fresh water, only one-third is salt-free and replaced annually through precipitation.

Most of Canada’s renewable surface fresh water drains northward, away from the most populated regions and economic centres located within 300 kilometres of the Canada-United States border, the document adds.

It says groundwater aquifers — Canada’s largest freshwater resource — are unmapped in some parts of the country, even though almost one in three Canadians rely on groundwater for their supply of clean water.

Climate change is affecting where and when fresh water is available, the memo says. It warns some parts of Canada are facing, or could soon face, restricted or depleting water supplies, even in the Great Lakes-St. Lawrence River basin.

It says in many of Canada’s settled areas, water is polluted and is either unsuitable for human, animal or industrial use or is usable only after treatment at a high cost.

For the 2021 to 2023 period, for example, water quality at 49 per cent of 165 monitoring sites in southern Canadian rivers was rated as excellent or good, while water at 51 per cent of the sites was rated as fair to poor, the memo says.

While progress is being made to restore the quality of large lake systems, protecting them from major stressors is challenging. Complex freshwater ecosystems like the lower Great Lakes and Lake Winnipeg remain in fair or poor condition, the document adds.

It says water quality data for northern rivers and lakes and groundwater aquifers is limited, making it difficult to assess the health of these resources.

“Overall, freshwater ecosystems across southern Canada are under stress, which poses risks to water security, due to factors including a rapidly changing climate, shifts in land-use, population growth, pollution, overconsumption, and aging and inadequate water infrastructure,” the memo says.

“The Arctic and the North also face critical issues from increased development and climate change impacts on already overwhelmed infrastructure. Furthermore, First Nations, Métis, and Inuit communities are among the most water insecure in Canada.”

More than 40 per cent of the border between Canada and the United States crosses water, the document notes. It says these transboundary waters provide drinking water, hydro power, navigation, recreation, irrigation and support for biodiversity in both countries. Tens of millions of people live and work along these shared waters.

While the two nations are parties to over a dozen bilateral freshwater agreements, “new water-related disputes could emerge and become more frequent” as freshwater supplies in North America shrink and demands rise, the memo warns.

It says the pressures on Canada’s water emerge against a global backdrop of declining water security due to climate change, population growth and industrial pollution.

“For decades, Canadians have been raising concerns about the possibility of fresh water being exported in bulk to the U.S. and beyond,” the memo says. “Some Canadians strongly oppose diverting lakes and rivers, and this opposition has extended to any form of bulk export of water.”

On a positive note, actions to strengthen water security in Canada can create “significant development opportunities,” as long-term access to sufficient supplies of water will become a strategic advantage in a water-stressed world, the document says.

It points out that more than half of Canada’s electricity comes from hydro power, which supports the shift to cleaner energy and a low-carbon economy.

“Water storage and irrigation is critical to high-value crop production, particularly in the Prairies and interior British Columbia, as well as the greenhouse sector,” the memo adds.

“Major manufacturing industries are among the largest users of water in Canada and growing Canada’s digital economy will depend on a secure and sustainably managed water supply.”

Jim Bronskill, The Canadian Press
