stories.title: Alouettes, Elks clash in a battle of divisional powers at 113th Grey Cup game
stories.summary: The 113th Grey Cup game today at McMahon Stadium will be a battle of divisional leaders and winners. The Montreal Alouettes topped the CFL’s East Division with a league-best 14-4 record, then won the East final with a 33-23 win over the visiting Winnipeg Blue Bombers. The Edmonton Elks finished first in the West Division […]
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
From the football heartland of Alberta to the passionate gridiron culture of Quebec, the Edmonton Elks and Montreal Alouettes will go head-to-head in the 113th Grey Cup on Sunday, bringing together two franchises with plenty to prove and a championship to chase.

For Edmonton, this is a return to familiar territory. One of the league’s most storied franchises, the Elks are back on the Grey Cup stage, reclaiming a place in the championship conversation that the organization and its fans have long been accustomed to.

For Montreal, it’s another opportunity to showcase the consistency that has made the Alouettes one of the CFL’s most reliable contenders in recent years.

It’s the first Grey Cup between the two squads since Edmonton beat Montreal 38-35 in overtime in 2005. Sunday also marks the two teams’ 12th Grey Cup clash, breaking a tie to become the most frequent title-game matchup in CFL history.

The Alouettes (14-4 in the regular season) have been the class of the league most of the year behind Most Outstanding Player Davis Alexander, while the Elks (13-5) surged back into contention under Cody Fajardo to reach their first Grey Cup since 2015.

Here’s a capsule look at this year’s game:

The schedule

Sunday, Nov. 15, 6 p.m. ET / 5 p.m. ABT at McMahon Stadium in Calgary.

Montreal opened as a 3.5-point favourite, according to BetMGM , as of Sunday. The underdogs have covered the spread in eight of the past 10 Grey Cups.

The forecast calls for cloudy conditions in Calgary, with a daytime high of 11 degrees C and overnight temperatures around 3 C. For a mid-November Grey Cup game, those are pretty ideal conditions.

The Alouettes are looking to capture their ninth Grey Cup championship and their second title in four seasons. Montreal won the 110th Grey Cup in 2023 before falling to Saskatchewan in last year’s championship.

Edmonton is looking to end an 11-year championship drought. The Elks last lifted the Grey Cup in 2015 and are seeking their 15th championship in franchise history. They have won their last three appearances in the championship game.

Pre-game and halftime

Blue Rodeo’s Jim Cuddy and Greg Keelor will perform ahead of the game, while Canadian singer-songwriter Sarah McLachlan will sing the national anthem.

Country artist Riley Green headlines the halftime show, while the James Barker Band will perform during the kickoff show.

The season series

The teams split their two regular-season meetings, with each winning on home field.

Edmonton took the first matchup 32-29 in Week 3, while Montreal responded with a convincing 48-30 victory in Week 10.

Alexander threw for 708 yards and accounted for six touchdowns across the two games, including five passing touchdowns. Tyson Philpot caught 18 passes for 251 yards and three touchdowns.

Fajardo threw for 462 yards and five total touchdowns in the two meetings. Running back Justin Rankin also made his presence felt, recording 292 yards from scrimmage on 30 touches.

Playoff history

The Alouettes are making their sixth consecutive playoff appearance and their third Grey Cup appearance in four seasons. Montreal has advanced to the championship game in back-to-back years under head coach Jason Maas. The Alouettes defeated Winnipeg 33-23 in the East Final to book their return to the championship.

The Elks are returning to the playoffs for the first time since 2019, snapping a six-year post-season drought. Edmonton captured the West Division title for the first time since 2015 before defeating the B.C. Lions 28-16 in the West Final.

Edmonton holds an 8-3 advantage over Montreal in their previous Grey Cup meetings. The Elks have won their last three Grey Cup appearances, while Montreal is looking to capture its ninth championship.

The quarterbacks

Davis Alexander (Montreal) vs. Cody Fajardo (Edmonton)

This is one of the more intriguing quarterback matchups in recent Grey Cup history because of the relationship between the two players.

Alexander and Fajardo were teammates in Montreal before the Alouettes moved forward with Alexander as their starting quarterback following the 2024 season and traded Fajardo to Edmonton.

Alexander is coming off a remarkable season that earned him the Most Outstanding Player award. He led the CFL with a 72.9 per cent completion rate, a 120.2 passer efficiency rating and 39 passing touchdowns.

Fajardo brings a different dimension to Edmonton’s offence. The veteran quarterback was one of the league’s most effective running threats at his position, finishing with 517 rushing yards during the regular season. He added another 84 yards and a touchdown in the Western Final.

Fajardo has previous Grey Cup success, winning with Montreal in 2023 and serving as a backup with Toronto in 2017. Alexander, meanwhile, is looking to capture his first championship as a starting quarterback after losing last year’s Grey Cup.

Jason Maas (Montreal) vs. Mark Kilam (Edmonton)

Maas has become one of the CFL’s most successful head coaches since taking over the Alouettes. He’s making his third Grey Cup appearance in four seasons and secured a title in 2023.

The former quarterback has also experienced championship success as a player, winning two Grey Cups with Edmonton in 2003 and 2005, along with another as Toronto’s quarterbacks coach in 2012.

Kilam is making his Grey Cup head coaching debut after taking over the Elks in November 2024.

The turnaround has been impressive. Edmonton finished last in the West Division in 2025 before climbing to the top of the division this season with a 13-5 record.

While he might not bring as much experience as a head coach, Kilam has three Grey Cups as a member of the Calgary Stampeders staff, with his last coming in 2018.

McMahon Stadium in Calgary hosts its sixth Grey Cup, having last welcomed the championship in 2019.

The stadium previously hosted the 1975, 1993, 2000, 2009 and 2019 Grey Cups.

2026 at a glance

Montreal was remarkably consistent throughout the regular season, finishing 14-4 without ever losing consecutive games.

The Alouettes had one of the CFL’s most explosive offences, averaging 34.7 points per game and leading the league in completion percentage. Alexander’s connection with Philpot and Tyler Snead was particularly effective, with both receivers finishing with 13 touchdown catches.

Montreal also finished first in total offensive touchdowns with 65, while its defence was particularly effective at preventing big plays.

Edmonton’s turnaround was one of the biggest stories of the CFL season.

The Elks finished first in the West Division with a 13-5 record, establishing themselves as one of the league’s most balanced teams.

Their running game was particularly effective, averaging a league-best 127.6 yards per game. Rankin and ShunDerrick Powell provided a strong one-two punch, while Fajardo’s ability to create plays with his legs gave the offence another dimension.

Defensively, Edmonton finished first in points allowed and led the league with a plus-23 turnover ratio. The Elks also recorded a league-high 27 interceptions, making their secondary a major factor in their success.

stories.title: UN mission goes after Haitian gangs with backing from Canada
stories.summary: What's been cast as a last-ditch effort by the United Nations to stabilize Haiti is being bankrolled in large part by Canada.
stories.author: Allan Woods
stories.content:
Four Salvadoran soldiers disappeared last month after a firefight in an area of the Haitian capital controlled by powerful gangs, gone without a trace but for the charred hull of their armoured vehicle.

A planned recovery mission has turned to one of retribution. A massive troop surge has been followed by missile strikes on the headquarters of a prominent gang leader, with the devastation captured in videos and posted to social media channels of Nayib Bukele, El Salvador’s charismatic president.

“We are not invaders. We are people with the same courage as you,” Bukele wrote in a message addressed to the Haitian people . “We will help you take back your country … and finally, Haiti will be free.”

It has all the daring and drama of a blockbuster action film. But it’s the backdrop to what’s been cast as a last-ditch effort to stabilize Haiti — one being bankrolled in large part by Canada.

This week, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio singled out Canada for praise at a G7 foreign minister’s meeting in Paris, where Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand led a session focused on Haiti .

“The Canadians deserve a lot of credit,” he said. “They’ve really stepped up. They’ve been a big catalyst in the work that’s been done.”

Canada has been the largest financial backer of the United Nations-backed mission to deploy a gang suppression force, tasked with beating back the gangs in Haiti and creating space for its government to assert control over the country, according to UN figures.

Ottawa has contributed about $85 million of the $225 million pledged so far for the force and the multinational security support mission that preceded it — nearly double that of the second-largest contributor, Germany.

Anand said in Paris that the American praise comes from her fundraising work as well as her efforts getting countries to commit troops for the gang suppression force, which is authorized to deploy up to 5,500 troops in Haiti.

This was high on her agenda during an August trip to Ivory Coast and Benin, where she said “part of my work … was to speak with some of those countries to ensure that there will be that support for the gang suppression force going forward.”

Success is vital.

National elections are planned in Haiti for next summer, but risk being pushed back or cancelled if the dire security situation does not improve.

The UN mission in Haiti said this week that at least 1,167 people had died in the country between July 1 and Sept. 30, with gang members responsible for an estimated 45 per cent of the killings.

The most shocking acts of violence occurred in Kenscoff, on the southern outskirts of the capital, Port-au-Prince, and left more than 100 dead, including 19 children.

An August report by Armed Conflict Location and Event Data , an organization that monitors global conflicts, said the attacks in July and August were part of ongoing attempt by the sanctioned gang coalition known as Viv Ansanm (“Live Together”) to exert control and expand its reach in the neighbourhood.

The August attack, in which 47 were killed and nine were taken hostage, targeted displaced people sheltering in a church, and prompted appeals for peace from Pope Leo XIV .

Another half or more of the reported killings have been attributed to attacks by security forces targeting gangs. A number of those victims have been civilians and children caught in the crossfire. The UN has also documented 44 cases in which Haitian National Police members have attempted or carried out “extrajudicial executions.”

It’s against this desolate backdrop that Bukele’s brazen attack on the headquarters of Haiti’s largest active gang, 400 Mawozo, was so enthusiastically welcomed.

“In the streets of Port-au-Prince and in provincial towns, his name is being sung,” Frantz Duval, editor-in-chief of Le Nouvelliste, a Haitian daily newspaper, wrote this week . “Crowds dance while recalling his actions.”

“Haiti, El Salvador, GSF: same fight, same determination!” Haitian Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé wrote on X . “The gangs will get no sleep!”

The reaction is understandable, said Haitian-Canadian journalist Harold Isaac.

“The problem is we’ve been in such a dire situation that people will essentially take hope from wherever it comes,” said Isaac, who is based in Port-au-Prince.

But he referred to Bukele and the 2,000 additional Salvadoran troops who surged into Haiti as “a wild card” because they are acting not as part of the UN-mandated anti-gang force but at the invitation of the Haitian government. The length of their stay and their rules of engagement aren’t known.

Human rights group Amnesty International called this week on Haiti and El Salvador to ensure that security operations respect human rights law and protect the public from forced displacement while ensuring access to food and medical care.

Bukele’s actions in Haiti could also highlight the limitations of the UN’s gang suppression force of about 2,400 troops from Chad, Sri Lanka, Jamaica, Guatemala and Mongolia.

Many Haitians are doubtful about its chances of improving security, seeing the force as just another international plan that follows on the failures of the previous Kenyan-led multinational security support mission.

“I think the international community is hopeful” about the gang suppression force,” said Wolf Pamphile, chief executive officer of Haiti Policy House, a Washington-based think tank. “Haitians on the ground, they haven’t seen the results that would show why they should be confident or hopeful.”

Rubio told reporters this week that failure was not an option.

“If the gang suppression force effort doesn’t work, then we’re out of ideas, so we have to make it work,” he said in Paris. “There really is no other option. There’s no plan B here anymore.”

But human rights lawyer Brian Concannon, executive director of the U.S.-based Institute for Justice & Democracy in Haiti, said it’s not enough to simply eliminate gang members and seize control of their territory with military force.

“Part of the problem with killing enough people is that it’s been tried before,” he said, referring to UN-backed missions stretching back more than two decades.

“That did in fact reduce the violence, but it just all springboarded back because nobody dealt with the underlying conditions that are probably going to irrevocably lead to gang violence when you have a whole bunch of young men with nothing else to do, no prospects in life and a very weak government.”

There is a three-stage plan that the gang suppression force hopes to complete before its mandate expires in September 2028.

The first two stages have it dismantling gang control across the territory alongside Haitian police and military and securing critical infrastructure like airports, marine terminals and highways, which gangs use to traffic goods and raise funds .

The third stage is to have “established the minimum security conditions” to gradually rebuild the capacity of Haiti’s own security forces.

If it works, it will admittedly be a just small step in the right direction.

“On the real issues that have kept the gangs alive for decades, the gang suppression force, El Salvador — none of them can fix that. They are issues that the Haitians have to fix themselves,” said Pamphile.

“The issue of corruption, the issue of commingling between politicians and gangs — these are issues where Haitians have to vote on and decide.”

stories.title: PM Carney in Cambodia for Francophonie summit, will meet Quebec premier Plamondon
stories.summary: Phnom Penh - Prime Minister Mark Carney will meet shortly with Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon at a summit in Cambodia, after the province elected a sovereigntist government.
stories.author: Dylan Robertson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Phnom Penh - Prime Minister Mark Carney defended the French language in the digital age to the leaders of countries gathered in Cambodia as he urged them to band together against the forces of big tech.

Carney also brought his pitch for Canada as an investment destination to the Francophonie summit, where he arrived Sunday.

“Canada will always defend the French language and francophone cultures, including in the face of pressure from tech giants and our closest neighbour,” he said in French at a closing session Monday in Phnom Penh.

He said Canada wants to mobilize other countries to make sure American tech giants allow for French-language content to have a prominent place on online platforms.

Carney said French-language content should be easily retrievable, like in a library catalogue — rather than an old warehouse of books with the lights turned off.

He also said artificial intelligence risks leaving behind French speakers and flattening linguistic diversity. He said French-speaking Canadians were proud of their unique expressions and updating masculine words to create feminine forms.

He also said French-speaking countries should partner with Canada in seeking economic gains through responsible use of AI.

The Francophonie summit takes place every few years, and Canada is set to host the next summit in 2028 in the Ottawa region.

The group includes Canada, Quebec and New Brunswick as full members, as well as numerous African countries and many in Asia — including those with a historical affinity for the French language without a large francophone population.

Earlier, Carney attended an innovation event called FrancoTech, where the Cambodian host’s introductory remarks were delivered solely in English.

Carney said Canada’s hosting of the 2028 summit is to focus on protecting the French language in the digital age, as well as issues of youth and the economy.

“Canada is now one of the best places in the world to invest,” Carney said in French remarks that drew loud applause.

The prime minister also spoke at the summit with multiple leaders. He told Senegalese President Bassirou Diomaye Faye that Canada wanted to partner in business as the West African country reforms its economy.

The summit faced multiple logistical hurdles, with the Cambodian hosts rescheduling events multiple times, which led to some bilateral meetings being postponed.

The prime minister also met Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon for the first time since the province elected a sovereigntist government last month.

St-Pierre Plamondon has repeatedly raised his aspiration to have Quebec become an independent country.

The two were cordial and focused on shared objectives, with Carney mentioning homelessness and St-Pierre Plamondon speaking about the use of the Francophonie for business investment. They agreed to have regular talks.

Carney said the meeting touched on many subjects given it was their first chat, including health care, transport infrastructure and the Churchill Falls agreement with Newfoundland and Labrador.

“We will continue in a professional way — friendly but not necessarily a bromance. I have a wife,” Carney quipped in French.

He added that Quebec could engage with American counterparts on trade as a stakeholder but not as a sovereign country.

“I understand stakeholders making their views known to those in the United States, and it’s important to get those views across,” Carney said in English. “International agreements are negotiated between federal governments.”

During their meeting, St-Pierre Plamondon joked about being a better Oxford hockey goalie, while Carney said the Quebec premier was in good shape.

St-Pierre Plamondon played goaltender for Oxford University’s hockey team while studying in England, telling Sucré givré — a program on Quebec’s French-language television network TVA in March 2026 — that he made the team despite not being a particularly skilled goalie.

Carney, meanwhile, was a third-string goaltender at Harvard and was co-captain of the Oxford University Blues hockey team.

At the summit, Carney also announced $24 million in development projects such as for sustainable transportation and women’s economic empowerment.

The funding includes $2 million to prevent and reduce the spread of Ebola in affected African countries.

The Public Health Agency of Canada has also launched talks with the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention on health surveillance and research.

With Cambodia, Canada launched talks for a possible investment-protection treaty. That would operate on top of a trade deal between Canada and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, of which Cambodia is a member.

That deal is set to be finalized next year.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 15, 2026.

stories.title: Inside a Canada Post mail carrier's last day of home delivery in Toronto
stories.summary: Toronto - Like clockwork, Anita McCulloch moves from house to house with a stack of flyers and letters tucked under her arm.
stories.author: Sadeen Mohsen The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Like clockwork, Anita McCulloch moves from house to house with a stack of flyers and letters tucked under her arm.

The dogs know when the Canada Post mail carrier is coming up the driveway. They perch on the windowsill at the sight of McCulloch’s bright green vest, their tails wagging as they rush to meet her at the front door before their owners know she’s there.

It’s one of her favourite parts of the job — and on Friday, she said goodbye to all of it.

Rexdale resident Steve Kay talks about Canada Post mail carrier Anita McCulloch’s last day doing home delivery. On Friday, she said goodbye to the community as Canada Post begins phasing out home delivery services in favour of community mailboxes. (Nov. 15, 2026)

It was 60-year-old McCulloch’s last day of door-to-door delivery in Rexdale, her beloved northwest Toronto neighbourhood, filled with people she’s grown to care for over the last 2 1/2 years.

“Even a smile or a ‘hello’ makes a difference in a person’s life, it makes a difference in mine,” McCulloch said, tearing up just before her shift began. “That is now all changing.”

Hundreds of homes and businesses in that part of the city had their last day of door-to-door delivery as Canada Post phases in community mailboxes for roughly four million addresses over several years. It’s a key pillar of the beleaguered Crown corporation’s plans to overhaul its business model amid the decline of letter mail and huge financial losses.

The neighbourhood, decorated with old trees and crunchy autumn leaves, is on the list of Canada Post’s earliest home delivery conversions, starting on Monday, despite concerns over accommodation for those with accessibility issues.

Several other neighbourhoods in the Greater Toronto Area set to lose door-to-door mail delivery in 2027 include those in Pickering, Ajax, Mississauga and Brampton.

In an April news release, Canada Post said the change will “strengthen the post service” and meet its mandate without being a “recurring burden on taxpayers.” It added that nearly three out of every four Canadian addresses already receive their mail through “some form of centralized delivery.”

For McCulloch and other mail carriers, the change has been devastating. After the COVID-19 pandemic years, she said human contact has never been more important. She has countless stories of the connections she’s made over the years, including elderly residents who know her by name and dogs that follow her from home to home with their tails wagging.

“Whether you’re a part of it for two years or 25 years, you are part of that community. You know your people,” McCulloch said. “It is a very sad, sad moment in our history.”

A thank-you message awaited McCulloch on Carol and Steve Kay’s driveway, written in brightly coloured chalk by the couple’s grandchildren. As soon as the mail carrier saw it, she immediately teared up as the couple and their seven-year-old dog, Red, rushed down the steps to give her a hug goodbye.

Steve Kay said McCulloch has been almost a part of the family and has always looked out for the couple and their neighbours.

“She cares about what she does,” Steve said. “It’s just wrong to see her taken away.”

The couple watched as Red followed McCulloch the rest of her route down the block. It’s their normal routine every time the mail carrier comes by.

“I can’t take the dog for a walk ‘till after she delivers (the mail),” Steve said.

For the Kays and their neighbours, including Martin Murchie, the switch to community mailboxes has been an unwelcome change.

“We’re not fond of the idea. We still prefer that door-to-door access,” Murchie said.

“There’s a human element to this that I think everybody’s missing out on.”

Rain or shine, Katherine Petrie said she knew she’d be seeing McCulloch at her doorstep with a smile on her face. Petrie, who has lived in her home for 59 years, said the mail carrier still stops by in any case to say hello.

Beyond not being able to see her favourite mail carrier every day, Petrie said she has concerns about possible community mailbox vandalism and having her mail stolen.

“I know I’m going to get my cheque and (McCulloch) will put it in the mailbox,” she said. But with community mailboxes, “you can never tell.”

McCulloch’s role goes beyond slotting pieces of paper into people’s mailboxes; she also keeps an eye on residents that May need help. She recalled how a two-year-old girl wandered into the street one day as she was delivering mail in the neighbourhood and elderly residents who needed help after suffering an injury inside their home.

“I can’t tell you the number of times 911 has been called because we’ve noticed something that’s not supposed to be in the community or something’s happened to somebody,” she said. “We’re there every day.”

Zach Avdelopoulos, president of the Canadian Union of Postal Workers Toronto local, said the change will be difficult for mail carriers and they are urging communities to voice their concerns over the switch to community mailboxes.

The union has been advocating to keep home delivery, especially for residents with a disability or accommodation needs.

“You see how much connection she has with the public,” he said of McCulloch. “Now, you’re just going to be subjected to going to a box and the box has a lot of issues.”

McCulloch, who has been with Canada Post for a decade, will still be coming around the neighbourhood but spending most of her time staring inside the community mailbox slots, shuffling mail to empty trays. Throughout her Friday morning route, she promised several residents she would swing by to say hello once in a while.

Later down the route, 85-year-old Gail Buntin is out on the front lawn. Her leaf collection machine has been jammed for a few minutes when McCulloch stops by.

McCulloch gets down on the cold grass and fixes Buntin’s machine. It runs smoothly in a few minutes. The pair share a hug and say their goodbyes before McCulloch takes the short walk up Buntin’s driveway to slot in a few envelopes.

She then briskly makes her way over to the next house, repeating the process over and over again, for the last time.

stories.title: Less than half of Crown-owned heritage buildings in fair or better condition
stories.summary: Ottawa - Forty-five per cent of Crown-owned heritage buildings are in fair or better condition, says a federal government report.
stories.author: Catherine Morrison The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - Forty-five per cent of Crown-owned heritage buildings are in fair or better condition, says a federal government report.

Public Services and Procurement Canada’s departmental results report for 2025-26 says its target for the share of heritage buildings hitting those standards is at least 35 per cent.

The target was 53 per cent a year before. The department says the target changed to align with “funding reallocation and evolving priorities.”

The government’s directory of federal heritage designations shows there are almost 1,260 federal heritage buildings across the country, from northern Nunavut to Newfoundland.

Last year, the department said it worked on the rehabilitation of the Lester B. Pearson and the West Memorial buildings in Ottawa.

Public Services and Procurement Canada said in its report that it will continue to “rehabilitate and reinvigorate” heritage assets in the parliamentary precinct.

Public Works and Procurement Minister Joël Lightbound said in the report that investments in the rehabilitation of heritage and national buildings help to keep those assets safe, accessible, sustainable and valuable for Canadians.

The report says the overall percentage of Crown-owned buildings that are in fair or better condition is higher — almost 55 per cent.

Chris Wiebe, manager of heritage policy at the National Trust for Canada, said he’d like to see heritage buildings maintained at a level more comparable with the rest of the federal portfolio.

“These are iconic buildings,” he said. “They’ve very important assets that are public facing and have a lot of public recognition. It’s important to keep them in good condition.

“The worry is that if you allow them to go too long with deferred maintenance, which they’ve indicated is also something that’s happening … it puts these buildings in a position where they May be further gone in terms of the deterioration and it May be more difficult to justify their upkeep and refurbishment down the road.”

Wiebe said the maintenance of heritage buildings is a “perennial problem” in Canada.

Canada’s auditor general found in 2018 that the federal agencies that owned most of Canada’s heritage buildings were not doing enough to preserve them.

It found National Defence, Fisheries and Oceans and Parks Canada didn’t have a handle on which buildings they owned, or on resources and strategies for conserving heritage sites.

The prime minister’s former residence at 24 Sussex in Ottawa has served as an example of the government’s neglect of heritage sites. It has been vacant since 2015 due to significant structural problems, including a rodent infestation, decrepit plumbing, faulty electrical wiring and a leaky roof.

Taxpayers have been shelling out tens of thousands of dollars per year to maintain the vacant property.

In June, Prime Minister Mark Carney laid out a plan to have a public fundraiser and design competition to restore 24 Sussex.

Carney said the winning design proposal will be announced by Canada Day of next year.

Wiebe said Canada is the only G7 country without legislation protecting its federal heritage buildings. He said a bill was tabled in Parliament in 2022 to lock in protections for federal heritage buildings but it did not pass second reading.

“It’s up to policy to protect and manage these buildings and ensure their kind of longevity for Canadians. In other countries, it’s codified, there’s particular restrictions put around things,” Wiebe said.

Wiebe said he’s also concerned about the government’s plan to sell off or lease surplus office space. April 2024’s federal budget said reducing the federal office footprint would generate “substantial” savings of $3.9 billion over the next 10 years, and $900 million per year after that.

“It’s indicative of a lot of things in the private sector where you run down these buildings with deferred maintenance and then you pass them off to another owner who May or May not demolish them for their land value,” he said.

Wiebe said the government has a responsibility to Canadians to manage “important, iconic” heritage sites, including those outside of the Ottawa area.

“I think some of the ones here in Ottawa they’re focused on quite a bit, but there’s others around the country that have equal importance that should be focused on as well.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 15, 2026.

“It’s indicative of a lot of things in the private sector where you run down these buildings with deferred maintenance and then you pass them off to another owner who May or May not demolish them for their land value,” he said.
Wiebe said the government has a responsibility to Canadians to manage “important, iconic” heritage sites, including those outside of the Ottawa area.
“I think some of the ones here in Ottawa they’re focused on quite a bit, but there’s others around the country that have equal importance that should be focused on as well.”

stories.title: What can Canadians do to protect themselves from bag tag switching?
stories.summary: You might think the worst thing an airport employee could do to your luggage is lose it. You’d be wrong.
stories.author: Jack Hauen, Avery Haines
stories.content:
What happens when a simple trip turns into a nightmare? Part five of W5’s five-part investigation on CTVNews.CA follows travellers who say they went from passenger to prisoner, caught in a scheme that crossed borders and changed lives forever.

You might think the worst thing an airport employee could do to your luggage is lose it.

W5 has identified more than two dozen cases of so-called bag tag switching — where a corrupt worker takes the tag off a checked bag and attaches it to a suitcase filled with drugs, allowing the dirty luggage to speed across continents under an unsuspecting traveller’s name.

In some cases, Canadians victimized by the scheme have served jail time in countries where police aren’t interested in hearing, “That’s not my bag.”

It’s an issue the federal transport minister said he’s trying to fix, after going “back to the drawing board” in the wake of W5’s original investigation into the issue earlier this year.

However, one Canadian says he has a solution that’s cheaper and easier than legislation: an un-switchable baggage tag.

The invention that could stop tampering

Bill Drori created a prototype 10 years ago and demonstrated it for W5.

While a normal tag can be stuck and re-stuck dozens of times without losing its adhesive, Drori’s reveals a “Void” message the first time it’s taken off. The glue also disappears, making it impossible to re-attach.

Drori runs Tamperguard, a Montreal company that makes the tamper-evident tape for police evidence and the bags that hold airport duty-free purchases.

He created tamper-evident tags in 2016 for the Colombian airline Avianca, which ultimately lost interest. That same year, Drori said he pitched the idea to aviation industry leaders at the Avsec (aviation security) World Conference in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia.

“Everybody thought it was a great idea,” including Canadian and American officials, Drori said.

But no one, he said, wanted to take the lead.

“Everybody said it was somebody else’s decision,” he said. “So it ended up going nowhere.”

If you have any information regarding tag switching or corruption at Canadian airports, please reach out to avery.haines@bellmedia.CA and jack.hauen@bellmedia.CA.

After W5’s documentary aired in May, Drori said he emailed the office of federal Transportation Minister Steven MacKinnon right away.

“I know he - I’m sure - receives … many, many emails, but I sent one out to him saying that there is a solution that exists,” he said.

He didn’t hear back.

But despite multiple follow-ups from Drori, that conversation also fizzled, he said.

Drori said there was virtually no difference in price between his product and the standard baggage tags when he priced it out for Avianca in 2016. He said he could have the tamper-evident material ready for a label-maker in four weeks.

W5 raised Drori’s technology with MacKinnon during an interview. The minister said he would be open to learning more about it.

“We are open to all manner of measures that can ward off criminal behavior,” he said.

Tamper-proof stickers are already in use

Drori noted the irony that his products are already in airports, but only to secure duty-free booze — a necessity to allow secure alcohol purchases after passengers were banned from travelling with more than 100 millilitres of liquid.

“The product that we made for the baggage tags is the same type of thing, but there was no loss of revenue. So I guess there was no impetus to put it through,” he said.

“Until there’s a fire lit, until there is a mandate, a specific request saying, ‘Let’s do something,’ be it from the public or from the government, that nothing’s going to happen.”

Watch the one-hour special presentation of W5’s Avery Haines Investigates Sunday at 10 p.m. ET live on W5’s official YouTube channel and on CTV and Crave following the Grey Cup.

stories.title: There's a catch: Investigation shows it’s hard to keep clean hands in the global fish trade
stories.summary: The reporting for this story was part of a larger investigation conducted by an international team of journalists based at The Outlaw Ocean Project.
stories.author: Ian Urbina
stories.content:
Much of the fish meal and fish oil that support farmed salmon and imported seafood consumed in Canada come from global supply chains linked to pollution, labour abuses, overfishing, and food insecurity in poorer countries.

In November 2024, the Canadian Aquaculture Industry Alliance gathered in Ottawa to unveil what it called its first national sustainability report for salmon farming. The industry’s message was blunt: Wild fisheries had reached their limits, and farmed salmon was the responsible way forward. “Farm-raised salmon have a key role in helping to feed Canada and the world as capture fisheries reach their limits,” the group said. Its president, Timothy Kennedy, was even more sweeping: “Our goal is to be nothing less than the most sustainable animal protein product in the world.”

This ocean-sustainability argument for fish farming — “grow more, so we can catch less” — is one of the reasons that the $313-billion (U.S.) global aquaculture industry is currently the fastest-growing food sector, and why half of the seafood eaten around the world is now farm-raised rather than caught at sea.

There’s a problem, though, one which is not limited to Canada. “The aquaculture industry’s sales pitch is flat wrong,” said Daniel Pauly, project director of the Sea Around Us initiative at the University of British Columbia. The most popular types of farmed seafood in the U.S. and elsewhere — salmon, shrimp, trout, sea bass, sea bream — are fed the kinds of wild fish that aquaculture claims to be saving, thereby accelerating ocean depletion, not slowing it, he explained. Two-thirds of global aquaculture grows species that are fed fish meal and fish oil, ingredients made by cooking and pulverizing wild-caught fish. Before it reaches market, a farmed salmon, for instance, eats at some farms more than six times its weight in wild-caught fish.

An extensive five-year investigation by The Outlaw Ocean Project, a news organization in Washington, DC, uncovered a variety of the hidden costs involved in producing this feed, including the loss of artisanal fishing jobs, chronic chemical exposure, avoidable worker deaths, and violent protests spurred by the horrid stench from fish meal factories. The investigation found that these social and environmental impacts exact a price primarily paid by the poorer countries where the feed ingredient is harvested and processed, far from where the resulting luxury seafood is eaten.

In Gambia and Mauritania , the investigation documented how the industry drives food insecurity as fish that once sustained local communities are diverted into fish meal factories for export. In remote islands in Russia’s far east and in China’s Xinjiang region, the reporting detailed the use of forced labour on ships, farms, and in factories. In other countries, including India and Peru , this industry was tied to at least 80 incidents of civil unrest, some of them violent, usually in the form of labour strikes and community protests sparked by the water pollution or the stench from factories cooking thousands of tons of decomposing fish.

The Outlaw Ocean Project mapped roughly the entire global fish meal industry, including more than 1,400 fish meal factories across 64 countries, tracing supply chains from fishing vessels to processing plants, feed mills, fish farms, and seafood retailers. The reporting effort involved dozens of journalists from as many countries, visiting factories and farms and boarding fish meal ships at sea.

The investigation revealed that the fish meal industry also contributes to geopolitical tensions. For example, in 2021, a dozen Turkish bottom trawlers fishing illegally in the Aegean Sea tried to ram a Greek research vessel when the scientists began filming their activity. In 2018, riots broke out in Saint-Louis, Senegal , after a fisherman was shot and killed by Mauritanian coast guards, during what the Mauritanians said was a cross-border raid by a fish meal boat. Since the mid-1970s, Morocco has militarily occupied Western Sahara , a presence that more than 10 EU Court of Justice rulings and various UN resolutions have deemed illegal. Still, Moroccan ships routinely fish in Western Saharan waters, turning their illegal catch into fish meal in Western Saharan plants, then exporting it with Moroccan labels to farms globally. A violent clash over trucks, many of them carrying this fish and fish meal out of Western Sahara, led to the collapse of a 29-year ceasefire between the countries in 2020.

The unsustainability of this feed protein is a global challenge. Unlike growing bivalves, like oysters, clams, and mussels, which do not typically require external feed, the toughest challenge to raising carnivorous seafood, such as salmon and shrimp, is feeding them. Canada prohibits boats targeting fish for the sole purpose of making fish meal or fish oil. Therefore, the fish meal produced in Canada is typically made by processing offcuts, or inedible parts of fish that would otherwise be thrown away, which is widely viewed as a more sustainable way to produce feed protein than using whole fish suitable for human consumption.

Canada has more than 200 fish farms, most of them depending on fish meal or fish oil that, when made domestically, comes primarily from Pacific anchoveta, chub mackerel, herring, haddock, pollock, sardines, and frigate tuna. However, much of the fish meal Canadian fish farms use — roughly 55,000 tons in 2024 — is sourced from abroad, tying Canadian consumers to these hidden and overseas social costs. Canada also imports more than $4 billion of seafood annually, of which a third is primarily farmed salmon and shrimp that rely heavily on fish meal and fish oil, making the country further complicit.

The investigation assessed more than 2,400 ships tied to fish meal production in at least 30 countries. It found that most of these ships do not fully comply with the Global Charter for Fisheries Transparency, a guide created by ocean-focused civil-society groups detailing accountability standards for industrial fishing fleets. For example, less than 30 per cent of the fleet had publicly available location information, and less than 25 per cent had a unique vessel identification number, or ship licence plate. Such opacity makes the fleet difficult to police.

Scientific studies classified at least half of the species landed by the assessed fish meal vessels as “overexploited” or worse. Most of the ships in this fleet are purse seiners or trawlers, which deploy vast nets to capture dense schools of fish, often indiscriminately sweeping in large volumes of bycatch and nontarget species. At least 165 of the ships in the global fish meal fleet were bottom trawlers, conducting a destructive form of fishing that uses weighted nets that scrape the ocean floor, destroying virtually everything in their paths.

“Any accounting of the true impact of aquaculture has to start not with the farm, but with the feed,” said Pauly. “And that kind of accounting offers a very different picture than the industry offers.”

The feed industry has emphasized that it is decreasing its reliance on fish meal and fish oil. However, as aquaculture overall grows, so too does the demand for fish meal. Asked about sustainability concerns tied to her industry, Véronique Jamin, a spokesperson from the IFFO , the international fish meal association, said that fish farming is “the most efficient animal protein system.” She added that “sustainability frameworks won’t work if they ignore real-world economics,” and seafood companies have to respond to “what people actually want to buy and eat.”

Researchers have explored alternative protein sources — seaweed, cassava waste, black soldier-fly larvae, even single-cell proteins derived from fungi or bacteria — but none are yet affordable at scale. For now, the pattern persists: Wild fish are caught and rendered into feed, while the costs of this production are left elsewhere.

In 2025, there were at least seven fish meal and fish oil plants in Canada : four on the Atlantic Coast, two on the Pacific coast, and one on Hudson Bay. Two of the Atlantic plants export fish oil.

These facilities are not without problems. Between 2021 and 2024, at least two Canadian fish meal plants were reportedly tied to pollution or unsustainable fishing practices, according to Bait to Plate , an online tool that tracks the fishing and seafood industries. In one case, local news coverage described a plant’s stench as “rancid, fishy, bloody, sour, and chemical.” Another plant reportedly processed fish species that Fisheries and Oceans Canada described as being in the “critical zone,” a designation for heavily depleted stocks.

The far greater burden of food insecurity, collapsed fish stocks, social unrest, and air and water pollution is borne by the poorer countries that produce the fish meal or fishmeal-fed seafood Canada imports. Stumberg, professor at Georgetown Law and supply-chain expert, said this is partly because grocers typically buy from wholesalers and rarely track their suppliers. Instead, the programs frequently alert companies before inspectors show up, which gives them a chance to clean up the scene so there are no violations. Often, these claims fail to reckon with crimes or social concerns further up their supply chains, including on the ships or plants that produce the feed for the fish farms. This disconnect is creating growing legal risk for seafood companies and grocers. Since 2020, at least nine lawsuits alleging false advertising have been brought against six seafood companies across five U.S. jurisdictions.

Plaintiffs challenged language such as “sustainable,” “eco-friendly,” “all-natural,” “wild-caught,” and “from the coast of Maine,” as well as claims of superior worker-safety standards.

In at least four cases, the use of fish meal or fish oil and their link to industrial fishing and ecosystem depletion were central to arguments that the products were not environmentally sustainable. Additional allegations included forced labour on fishing vessels and reliance on harmful pesticides and antibiotics. That’s likely to happen when more countries impose import controls on seafood tainted with illegalities or unsustainable practices. “That’s when investors will begin to see material — not just reputational — risk, and companies will have to adjust.”

In November 2024, the Canadian Aquaculture Industry Alliance gathered in Ottawa to unveil what it called its first national sustainability report for salmon farming. The industry’s message was blunt: Wild fisheries had reached their limits, and farmed salmon was the responsible way forward. “Farm-raised salmon have a key role in helping to feed Canada and the world as capture fisheries reach their limits,” the group said. Its president, Timothy Kennedy, was even more sweeping: “Our goal is to be nothing less than the most sustainable animal protein product in the world.”

This ocean-sustainability argument for fish farming — “grow more, so we can catch less” — is one of the reasons that the $313-billion (U.S.) global aquaculture industry is currently the fastest-growing food sector, and why half of the seafood eaten around the world is now farm-raised rather than caught at sea.

There’s a problem, though, one which is not limited to Canada. “The aquaculture industry’s sales pitch is flat wrong,” said Daniel Pauly, project director of the Sea Around Us initiative at the University of British Columbia. The most popular types of farmed seafood in the U.S. and elsewhere — salmon, shrimp, trout, sea bass, sea bream — are fed the kinds of wild fish that aquaculture claims to be saving, thereby accelerating ocean depletion, not slowing it, he explained. Two-thirds of global aquaculture grows species that are fed fish meal and fish oil, ingredients made by cooking and pulverizing wild-caught fish. Before it reaches market, a farmed salmon, for instance, eats at some farms more than six times its weight in wild-caught fish.

An extensive five-year investigation by The Outlaw Ocean Project, a news organization in Washington, DC, uncovered a variety of the hidden costs involved in producing this feed, including the loss of artisanal fishing jobs, chronic chemical exposure, avoidable worker deaths, and violent protests spurred by the horrid stench from fish meal factories. The investigation found that these social and environmental impacts exact a price primarily paid by the poorer countries where the feed ingredient is harvested and processed, far from where the resulting luxury seafood is eaten.

content_blocks.text: The investigation assessed more than 2,400 ships tied to fish meal production in at least 30 countries. For example, less than 30 per cent of the fleet had publicly available location information, and less than 25 per cent had a unique vessel identification number, or ship licence plate. Such opacity makes the fleet difficult to police.

content_blocks.text: The programs generally focus on environmental crimes, mostly overlooking labour abuses on ships. Allie Brudney, a senior staff attorney at the strategic litigation non-profit group Corporate Accountability Lab, said that on land — at processing plants or on farms — certification programs rarely conduct true spot checks to authenticate the reassurances given by managers at the factories. At sea, these programs also often rely on self-reported information from ship captains rather than having auditors directly visit and check conditions offshore on vessels, where crimes are most common.

stories.title: Is it legal to mount a phone on the windshield?
stories.summary: In British Columbia, a mounted phone can’t block your view of the road – practically, that means it shouldn’t be on your windshield at all, experts said
stories.author: Jason Tchir
stories.content:
I see people driving around with phones mounted on the windshield that look like they might block the view of the road. Is that legal? I even saw a guy talking to his mounted phone in what looked like a video call. I got a ticket a few years ago for just having my phone sitting in my centre console so it seems surprising that people can have phones mounted and visible. – Sarah, Vancouver

In British Columbia, a mounted phone can’t block your view of the road – practically, that means it shouldn’t be on your windshield at all, experts said.

“Realistically, if you’re going to stick it on the windshield, it is going to obstruct your view in some fashion,” said Kyla Lee, a Vancouver-based criminal defence lawyer. “So they’re not supposed to be mounted there – but, of course, I see people with [phones mounted on their windshields] all the time.”

In B.C., there’s not a law that specifically addresses distracted driving. Instead, the law covers electronic devices , including cellphones.

Generally, that law doesn’t specify where your phone can or can’t be mounted, just that it can’t obstruct your view or interfere with your car’s controls, Lee said.

“The wording is broad, so it allows for leeway,” she said.

Lee said she’s never had anyone ask her to fight a ticket for having a phone mounted on a windshield. But proving that a mounted phone obstructed the driver’s view could be tough because what a driver can see depends on their height and how seats are adjusted, she said.

RCMP Sergeant Michael McLaughlin, a spokesman for B.C. Highway Patrol, pointed to a separate B.C. law against driving with an obstructed view and said it bans driving with a cellphone mounted on the windshield.

While the rules vary by province, most, including Alberta , Ontario and Quebec , ban anything that can block your view.

Sean Shapiro, a traffic safety consultant and former Toronto traffic cop, said it’s generally up to an officer to decide if your mounted phone is a problem.

“If [it’s] in the driver’s view and blocks their vision in any way, [you could be charged],” he said. “I use a cupholder mount.“

The rules vary by province , but most ban holding or touching a hand-held electronic device while driving – even when you’re stopped at a red light.

In B.C., ”you’re only allowed one touch for the purposes of ending, accepting, or declining a [hands-free] call,” Lee said. “So if you were to touch it to shuffle to a different song or to accept a change to your GPS directions, that would be using it even if it was mounted.”

Also, whether it’s mounted or not, you generally can’t physically “interact with the features of the device,” Lee said, or watch anything other than GPS directions on the screen.

That means no TikTok, YouTube or Zoom calls. You also can’t scroll through contacts or playlists, or read texts or anything else off the screen.

In most provinces, including B.C. and Ontario , you can generally only look at a GPS map on your phone or tap it to answer or end a call if it’s securely mounted – and not, for instance, if it’s sitting loose in a cupholder, open centre console or on the seat.

In B.C., there were cases of police charging drivers just for having phones loose in the cupholders or in the centre console – even when they weren’t touching or looking at them. But courts there have ruled that just having a phone sitting in your cupholder or otherwise loose in your vehicle isn’t illegal if you’re not using it, Lee said.

That includes a 2021 B.C. Supreme Court ruling that a driver didn’t break the law just because his phone was playing a podcast through the car’s audio system while loose in the cupholder – because he wasn’t holding it, touching it or watching the screen.

“Just sitting there [isn’t an] offence,” Lee said, adding that the message isn’t out to all police officers. “Every once in a while we get clients who’ve been ticketed for it, and usually it’s a pretty easy win in court.”

But BCHP’s McLaughlin said you could get a ticket – which comes with a $368 fine and four demerits – if your screen is lit.

That’s why it’s a good idea to keep your phone out of sight, for instance, in a bag or the glove compartment, Lee said.

“You can’t touch it, [so] you won’t fall prey to the temptation of your phone just sitting there,” she said. “But also, if the police can’t see a phone, they can’t charge you.”

We couldn’t find any province that specifically bans keeping your phone loose in the vehicle.

“You’re perfectly entitled to keep your phone [in the cupholder],” Shapiro said. “However, if it rings, you generally can’t reach down and start interacting with it.”

Screen time?

In B.C., the electronic device law has been in place since 2010 and doesn’t specifically ban using your phone – and apps on it – through your car’s infotainment system.

“You can be playing [around] on your Apple CarPlay on the [infotainment] screen, and that’s perfectly legal because it’s part of the vehicle, even though it’s just as distracting,” Lee said. “The law is out of step with technology these days.”

But if fiddling with your infotainment screen causes you to make a dangerous move on the road or get into a crash, you could face charges including careless driving , McLaughlin said.

Distracted driving is a serious problem on B.C. roads and “may be getting worse,” he said.

In B.C. last year, police issued more than 27,000 tickets for using an electronic device while driving.

And in a month-long campaign against driving while using devices this year, BCHP issued 1,587 tickets and warnings – more than twice as many as last year’s campaign.

“[Using cellphones] is still by far the biggest issue,” McLaughlin said. ”Infotainment screens, eating while driving and distractions with other vehicle occupants are also concerning.”

Have a driving question? Send it to globedrive@globeandmail.com and put ‘Driving Concerns’ in your subject line. E-mails without the correct subject line may not be answered. Canada’s a big place, so let us know where you are so we can find the answer for your city and province.

stories.title: Toronto-born artist Lotus L. Kang wins $100,000 2026 Sobey Art Award
stories.summary: A Toronto-born artist known for combining photography, sculpture and installation work has received one of Canada's most prestigious contemporary art honours.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
A Toronto-born artist known for combining photography, sculpture and installation work has received one of Canada’s most prestigious contemporary art honours.

Lotus L. Kang was named the winner of the 2026 Sobey Art Award during a ceremony at the National Gallery of Canada in Ottawa, receiving the $100,000 grand prize.

The jury praised Kang’s decade-long commitment to her craft and the growing international recognition of her work, which often incorporates photographic film, found objects and everyday materials.

Five other shortlisted artists, Melaw Nakehk’o, Samuel Roy-Bois, Audie Murray, Caroline Monnet and Shane Perley-Dutcher, will each receive $25,000. Another 24 longlisted artists will receive $10,000 apiece, bringing the award’s total value to $465,000.

Now in its 23rd year, the award recognizes Canadian contemporary artists at pivotal stages in their careers.

Works by all six finalists are on display at the National Gallery until Jan. 3, 2027.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published November 15th, 2026.

David Augustine, The Canadian Press

stories.title: A dementia diagnosis is devastating. What happens when you're only 48?
stories.summary: Toronto - Mark Breslaw sat in his car at a four-way stop just minutes from home, but suddenly didn't know which way to turn.
stories.author: Nicole Ireland The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - Mark Breslaw sat in his car at a four-way stop just minutes from home, but suddenly didn’t know which way to turn.

“It was like I blinked and I opened my eyes and I didn’t know where I was. I had no recollection of how I got to this particular position and the worst feeling was I didn’t know what to do and there’s people lining up behind me,” recalled the 50-year-old former human resources executive.

“I just thought the safest thing is just to go straight, which wasn’t actually what I was supposed to (do),” said Breslaw, who had been driving the same route from work to his home in Surrey, B.C., for 18 years.

“I didn’t get far before I went, ‘OK, there’s the elementary school. I know I’m close ... and then I was back.”

Although he was scared, Breslaw didn’t tell his wife what had happened when he got home that day three years ago, because he didn’t want to alarm her. He also didn’t connect the memory lapse to some problems that he — normally a very high performer in a fast-paced job — had been having at work.

Sometimes he would forget the names of people he worked with every day. Other times he couldn’t remember what floor he was taking the elevator to. Usually an excellent planner, he was finding tasks like scheduling his week took far longer than they used to. Once he missed three back-to-back meetings.

“None of this was constant and so, you know, it would happen and you’d be like ‘that was weird.’ But then it would happen again, maybe a week later, two weeks later,” Breslaw said.

He was worried, but chalked it up to stress, lack of sleep and a busy life balancing work with raising a young son. He also has two grown children who live on their own.

But when he found himself lost at that four-way stop two more times, he made an appointment to see his family doctor in January 2024.

What he thought would be a quick discussion turned into a long process that resulted in a diagnosis neither he nor his doctor expected: young-onset Alzheimer’s disease.

Alzheimer’s disease is the most common type of dementia, which is the umbrella term for a group of diseases that damage brain cells. Although it most often affects older adults, dementia is not a normal part of aging.

An estimated 772,000 people live with dementia in Canada and could grow to a million by 2030, the Alzheimer Society of Canada says.

Dementia is defined as “young-onset” when it is diagnosed in someone under 65 years old. It’s relatively rare — a 2024 report by the society estimates there were about 28,000 people living with young-onset dementia in Canada in 2020. It projects that number will reach more than 40,000 by 2050.

“Gathering accurate statistics on young onset dementia in Canada is ... complicated by the fact that currently there is no national system for tracking all cases of dementia more broadly, let alone for people who develop dementia under the age of 65,” the report says.

A dementia diagnosis is devastating for anyone, but younger people face specific issues and services often don’t meet their needs, said Cathy Barrick, CEO of the Alzheimer Society of Ontario.

“These are people who are often in the prime of their life. They’re still working. They may have children still at home. They may have children in university,” she said.

“The very first service that is the biggest challenge is actually (getting) a diagnosis. So, I mean, diagnosis is challenging for dementia at any age, but even more so at a younger age because it is so not assumed that that is the problem.”

That was Breslaw’s experience during visits with both his family doctor and a neurologist.

“You’re too young to have dementia, essentially, was the message,” he said.

He went through a series of tests and scans looking for brain tumours, evidence of stroke, depression, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder — anything that could explain his symptoms.

Even when he scored lower than expected for his age on a cognitive test, his neurologist still didn’t think dementia was likely.

Finally, about a year after he first went to his doctor, a cerebrospinal fluid test revealed the amyloid beta protein that is a hallmark of Alzheimer’s disease.

Breslaw was 48 years old.

Immediately, Breslaw had to give up his driver’s licence because he now had spatial impairment. He also had to leave the career he loved, because his doctor explained the work would quickly become too complex to manage as his disease progressed.

He and his wife pushed through their shock and grief to take control of anything they could, from seeing a financial planner to picking out a cemetery plot.

People with Alzheimer’s disease can live for 10 years or more and have a good quality of life with the right supports, said Saskia Sivananthan, CEO and co-founder of the Brainwell Institute, a dementia think-tank.

Although there is no cure, there are a few medications approved by Health Canada that can help manage symptoms or slow the rate of progression — but each individual case is different and patients need to discuss the risks and benefits with their doctor.

The disease is ultimately fatal as it progresses through different parts of the brain and eventually affects control over breathing, swallowing and other bodily functions, said Sivananthan, who is a neuroscientist.

Developing dementia while they are still young often forces patients and their families to figure out how to deal with the unexpected loss of income, she said.

Breslaw’s wife, now 46, has a senior job she loves at a local hospital foundation. He said he wants her to continue working full-time rather than taking time off to be his caregiver — not only because of the financial need, but because she has an identity that extends beyond his illness.

They worry about what they’ll have to spend as Breslaw needs more and more care, as they want to make sure their eight-year-old son has money for post-secondary education in the future.

“These are the things that we have to think about. You get diagnosed at 48, you immediately go into all the what-if scenarios,” he said.

LONG-TERM CARE VS HOME CARE

Breslaw’s family also figures prominently into where he wants to receive round-the-clock care when he needs it.

“I hear ... people who are younger want to stay at home longer and I believe that to be very true for many people. It’s not true for me because I have an eight-year-old son,” he said.

“I don’t want it to look like a hospital and kind of see dad in that sort of very vulnerable way.”

Breslaw would rather move into a long-term care home to spare his family.

“I’m going to be largely surrounded by people who are, you know, two and a half decades older than me, if not older than that.”

His ideal living situation would be a transition house that could keep younger people who can no longer function on their own safely, but also allow them to have a better quality of life than in long-term care.

That’s an area where young-onset dementia support is definitely lacking, Sivananthan said.

“Most long-term care or assisted living places are not really set up for him. They are set up for older adults.”

Almost two years after his diagnosis, Breslaw can still walk his son to school and stay home while his wife is at work.

But he can no longer use the stove or microwave after doing so “almost led to a very catastrophic fire in our house.”

He was warming up some food for what he thought was 30 seconds but was actually 30 minutes and then walked away to fold laundry.

Breslaw forgot about the microwave altogether until the kitchen was full of smoke.

He knows as his Alzheimer’s disease progresses, he may need to go to a day program. They are available in many communities, but mostly designed for older people in their 70s, 80s and 90s, Breslaw said.

Barrick, of the Alzheimer’s Society, said someone with young-onset dementia may actually find that experience confusing if they are in later stages of the disease.

“He may be like, ‘why am I here with all these old people? Like, this is weird, I should be at work. Where is my wife?’” she said.

“As his brain changes, he may not be able to put those pieces together. And so it can actually create some behaviours that get exhibited in programs like that, because they can become quite distressed.”

Breslaw, who volunteers for the Alzheimer Society of British Columbia and Yukon, is part of a “small and mighty group” of people with young-onset dementia that advocates for more resources, such as transition houses, age-appropriate day programs and guidance on how to talk to children about what lies ahead.

The federal government recently announced it planned to amend the Criminal Code to allow people with dementia to make advance requests for medically assisted dying (MAID) before they lose their mental capacity to do so.

Those requests would lay out specific conditions when they would reach the point of intolerable suffering and want MAID to be administered, such as deterioration to the point where they don’t recognize their family.

But it’s up to the provinces to decide if their health-care systems will honour advance requests.

B.C. has not announced a position yet.

Breslaw doesn’t know whether or not he would make an advance request if it’s allowed, but said knowing it’s an option would give him peace of mind.

“It literally is something that keeps me up at night and it would be a weight lifted off my family just to have the choice,” he said.

A dementia diagnosis is devastating for anyone, but younger people face specific issues and services often don’t meet their needs, said Cathy Barrick, CEO of the Alzheimer Society of Ontario.
“These are people who are often in the prime of their life. They’re still working. They may have children still at home. They may have children in university,” she said.

“The very first service that is the biggest challenge is actually (getting) a diagnosis. So, I mean, diagnosis is challenging for dementia at any age, but even more so at a younger age because it is so not assumed that that is the problem.”
That was Breslaw’s experience during visits with both his family doctor and a neurologist.
“You’re too young to have dementia, essentially, was the message,” he said.
He went through a series of tests and scans looking for brain tumours, evidence of stroke, depression, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder — anything that could explain his symptoms.
Even when he scored lower than expected for his age on a cognitive test, his neurologist still didn’t think dementia was likely.
Finally, about a year after he first went to his doctor, a cerebrospinal fluid test revealed the amyloid beta protein that is a hallmark of Alzheimer’s disease.
Breslaw was 48 years old.

Immediately, Breslaw had to give up his driver’s licence because he now had spatial impairment. He also had to leave the career he loved, because his doctor explained the work would quickly become too complex to manage as his disease progressed.
He and his wife pushed through their shock and grief to take control of anything they could, from seeing a financial planner to picking out a cemetery plot.

People with Alzheimer’s disease can live for 10 years or more and have a good quality of life with the right supports, said Saskia Sivananthan, CEO and co-founder of the Brainwell Institute, a dementia think-tank.

Although there is no cure, there are a few medications approved by Health Canada that can help manage symptoms or slow the rate of progression — but each individual case is different and patients need to discuss the risks and benefits with their doctor.

The disease is ultimately fatal as it progresses through different parts of the brain and eventually affects control over breathing, swallowing and other bodily functions, said Sivananthan, who is a neuroscientist.
Developing dementia while they are still young often forces patients and their families to figure out how to deal with the unexpected loss of income, she said.

Breslaw’s wife, now 46, has a senior job she loves at a local hospital foundation. He said he wants her to continue working full-time rather than taking time off to be his caregiver — not only because of the financial need, but because she has an identity that extends beyond his illness.
They worry about what they’ll have to spend as Breslaw needs more and more care, as they want to make sure their eight-year-old son has money for post-secondary education in the future.
“These are the things that we have to think about. You get diagnosed at 48, you immediately go into all the what-if scenarios,” he said.
LONG-TERM CARE VS HOME CARE
Breslaw’s family also figures prominently into where he wants to receive round-the-clock care when he needs it.
“I hear ... people who are younger want to stay at home longer and I believe that to be very true for many people. It’s not true for me because I have an eight-year-old son,” he said.
“I don’t want it to look like a hospital and kind of see dad in that sort of very vulnerable way.”
Breslaw would rather move into a long-term care home to spare his family.
“I’m going to be largely surrounded by people who are, you know, two and a half decades older than me, if not older than that.”

His ideal living situation would be a transition house that could keep younger people who can no longer function on their own safely, but also allow them to have a better quality of life than in long-term care.
That’s an area where young-onset dementia support is definitely lacking, Sivananthan said.
“Most long-term care or assisted living places are not really set up for him. They are set up for older adults.”
Almost two years after his diagnosis, Breslaw can still walk his son to school and stay home while his wife is at work.
But he can no longer use the stove or microwave after doing so “almost led to a very catastrophic fire in our house.”
He was warming up some food for what he thought was 30 seconds but was actually 30 minutes and then walked away to fold laundry.
Breslaw forgot about the microwave altogether until the kitchen was full of smoke.

He knows as his Alzheimer’s disease progresses, he may need to go to a day program. They are available in many communities, but mostly designed for older people in their 70s, 80s and 90s, Breslaw said.
Barrick, of the Alzheimer’s Society, said someone with young-onset dementia may actually find that experience confusing if they are in later stages of the disease.
“He may be like, ‘why am I here with all these old people? Like, this is weird, I should be at work. Where is my wife?’” she said.

“As his brain changes, he may not be able to put those pieces together. And so it can actually create some behaviours that get exhibited in programs like that, because they can become quite distressed.”

Breslaw, who volunteers for the Alzheimer Society of British Columbia and Yukon, is part of a “small and mighty group” of people with young-onset dementia that advocates for more resources, such as transition houses, age-appropriate day programs and guidance on how to talk to children about what lies ahead.

The federal government recently announced it planned to amend the Criminal Code to allow people with dementia to make advance requests for medically assisted dying (MAID) before they lose their mental capacity to do so.

Those requests would lay out specific conditions when they would reach the point of intolerable suffering and want MAID to be administered, such as deterioration to the point where they don’t recognize their family.
But it’s up to the provinces to decide if their health-care systems will honour advance requests.
B.C. has not announced a position yet.
Breslaw doesn’t know whether or not he would make an advance request if it’s allowed, but said knowing it’s an option would give him peace of mind.
“It literally is something that keeps me up at night and it would be a weight lifted off my family just to have the choice,” he said.
