stories.title: Amid climate pessimism, a surprise: Global emissions are down for 2026
stories.summary: A new report finds the drop is driven more by the Iran crisis than by a durable change.
stories.author: Marco Chown Oved
stories.content:
Despite widespread sentiment that the world is failing in its effort to limit the most pernicious effects of global warming, with deadly climate-fuelled natural disasters like wildfires , heat waves and flash floods proliferating, a surprising study has found fossil fuel emissions are actually falling.

As delegates from around the world met in Turkey this week for the annual climate talks known as COP, the carbon emissions caused by burning fossil fuels unexpectedly dropped in 2026, according to projections published in Nature .

The authors, researchers at the Cicero Center for International Climate Research in Oslo, Norway, said the slight reduction of 0.4 per cent (the equivalent of 22 per cent of Canada’s national emissions) was more due to the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz than a real, durable transition away from them.

The cost of fuel has soared after the U.S.-Iran conflict choked off the strait to shipping earlier this year. In Canada, diesel hit a peak national average of more than $2.70 a litre in September.

“The only times in history when emissions have gone down is when there is a global crisis — and this is just another one,” said Robbie Andrew, a senior researcher at Cicero and one of the report’s authors. “Instead of hoping that we’ll have more and more crises to get emissions down, which is of course a ridiculous idea, we actually need to turn this around.”

The last two times global emissions dropped — in 2008, after the financial crisis and 2020, after the COVID-19 pandemic — carbon emissions quickly rebounded and continued to grow.

The UN has warned that the global goal set in Paris a decade ago, to keep global warming to 1.5 degrees, is effectively impossible to meet . The federal government’s climate report found that Canada has already warmed 2 degrees and can expect one more by 2040. While these results mean climate disasters are now inevitable, they also underline the importance of limiting future warming by cutting fossil fuel use as quickly as possible, experts say.

Fortunately, there are quiet signs that beyond the oil shock, there are economic forces accelerating the adoption of clean energy and electrification, which have been causing emissions growth to slow down.

“Under that global number, there are lots and lots of things that add up. And lots of those have turned. They are on the way down,” Andrew said.

Every EV and heat pump sold around the world reduces demand for fossil fuels, and every solar panel, battery and wind turbine installed creates the clean energy to power those electric technologies. And while adoption and deployment of these non-emitting alternatives is currently insufficient to start bringing down global emissions on their own, they’re growing at a phenomenal rate.

Ships anchored near the Strait of Hormuz. Middle East oil exports have rebounded significantly since the early days of the crisis.

For the past several years, China’s production of renewable power and clean technology were greater than the rest of the world combined , allowing it to slow down and stop the rise in its national emissions (which are by far the largest of any country in the world). This year, with the domestic economy stalling, Chinese clean tech is being exported, flooding markets around the world, which are in turn seeing dramatic effects on their own emissions.

In 2026, Chinese clean tech exports grew at a rapid pace, increasing by 61 per cent for EVs, 45 per cent for wind turbines, 39 per cent for batteries and 22 per cent for solar panels. According to an analysis by the Finland-based Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air, these exports allowed the world to avoid emitting 450 megatonnes of carbon — the equivalent of Brazil’s national emissions — this year alone.

Unlike fossil fuels, which are burned once and then need to be extracted again, clean tech continues to operate, emissions-free, for 20 years or more. Over the course of the lifetime of these pieces of equipment, they will replace enough fossil fuels to prevent the emission of 8.4 gigatonnes of carbon — the same as the U.S. and India combined emit in a year, Crea found. The solar panels and wind turbines alone will generate the same amount of power as 100 coal plants.

“China is the world’s largest manufacturer of clean energy technologies … It can enable other countries to reduce their reliance on fossil fuels,” said Qi Qin, a China policy analyst at Crea.

Of course, it’s not just solar panels and wind turbines, Chinese EVs are also selling rapidly in countries around the world, and every kilometre driven without burning gas provides immediate climate benefits. According to Mobility Global, which tracks auto sales, electric and hybrid vehicles are increasing their market share worldwide.

Cars that run on gasoline made up less than half of global passenger vehicle sales for the first time in 2026, down from 73 per cent five years ago. While American policies hostile to EVs have slowed sales in North America, the transition to electric driving is accelerating nearly everywhere else, with 49 of the 56 countries tracked by clean energy think tank Ember setting EV sales records this year .

People walk past a showroom for Chinese EV maker BYD in Seoul, South Korea.

Many of these leading indicators are tracked closely on the international level, but granular information on the trends that contribute to Canada’s emissions have, until recently, been harder to come by. This week, however, the Canadian Climate Institute published its Climate Progress Tracker that provides up-to-date data on 40 indicators of the country’s transition to a carbon-free economy.

Ontario’s Home Renovation Savings Program requires homeowners to choose between $10,000 and the ability to sell power back to the grid.

While researchers, policymakers and the public used to have to wait almost two years to get official government emissions numbers, now the climate tracker updates a myriad of statistics ranging from electricity generation to carbon pricing on a monthly basis with a three-month lag.

“The transition to cleaner energy is multi-faceted and to see it, you need to put a lot of indicators together,” said Ross Linden-Fraser, Acting Director of Cci’s 440 Megatonnes data project. ”We’ve organized the data into these signals that reflect our understanding of the most important things that need to happen to bring our emissions down and build a cleaner economy.”

Canada’s picture is decidedly mixed, he said, with individual indicators performing well, “but if you zoom out to the overall context, we’re not moving fast enough.”

Renewable energy generation, for example, has grown by 40 per cent since 2020, but its share of overall generation is actually dropping as drought reduced hydro production and nuclear refurbishments led to increased reliance on gas plants .

While the Hormuz crisis is the largest factor in 2026’s global emission drop, crises don’t always produce lasting change, says Cicero’s Andrew. A lot of industries and consumers will attempt to soften the blow of increased prices by reducing their use of fossil fuels, but the cost of buying new equipment to permanently switch to electricity is a big deterrent to lasting change.

Historically, oil shocks have started long-term trends that far outlasted the crisis — toward smaller, more economical cars after the 70s oil embargo, for example. Researchers at Cicero say fuel-switching could be enough to reduce emissions growth, but is not yet sufficient to “lock in a peak and decline.”

Increasing emissions from AI data centres are also a big question mark over the next decade. Already responsible for approximately 0.5 per cent of the world’s emissions, the UN has projected they could nearly double in size by 2030 — though the emissions produced would vary depending on whether they’re powered by fossil fuels or renewables.

One market intelligence firm projects that the current crisis in the Persian Gulf could push countries to electrify in order to bolster energy sovereignty, lowering their emissions along the way.

“Energy security and decarbonization do not always pull in opposite directions,” said Wood Mackenzie in a statement accompanying their Energy Transition Outlook this week. “As countries seek to reduce dependence on imported fuels, greater electrification, renewables, nuclear, storage and domestic infrastructure can strengthen energy security while lowering emissions as a by-product.”

paragraphs: Despite widespread sentiment that the world is failing in its effort to limit the most pernicious effects of global warming, with deadly climate-fuelled natural disasters like wildfires , heat waves and flash floods proliferating, a surprising study has found fossil fuel emissions are actually falling.

As delegates from around the world met in Turkey this week for the annual climate talks known as COP, the carbon emissions caused by burning fossil fuels unexpectedly dropped in 2026, according to projections published in Nature .

The authors, researchers at the Cicero Center for International Climate Research in Oslo, Norway, said the slight reduction of 0.4 per cent (the equivalent of 22 per cent of Canada’s national emissions) was more due to the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz than a real, durable transition away from them.
The cost of fuel has soared after the U.S.-Iran conflict choked off the strait to shipping earlier this year. In Canada, diesel hit a peak national average of more than $2.70 a litre in September.

“The only times in history when emissions have gone down is when there is a global crisis — and this is just another one,” said Robbie Andrew, a senior researcher at Cicero and one of the report’s authors. “Instead of hoping that we’ll have more and more crises to get emissions down, which is of course a ridiculous idea, we actually need to turn this around.”
The last two times global emissions dropped — in 2008, after the financial crisis and 2020, after the COVID-19 pandemic — carbon emissions quickly rebounded and continued to grow.

The UN has warned that the global goal set in Paris a decade ago, to keep global warming to 1.5 degrees, is effectively impossible to meet . The federal government’s climate report found that Canada has already warmed 2 degrees and can expect one more by 2040. While these results mean climate disasters are now inevitable, they also underline the importance of limiting future warming by cutting fossil fuel use as quickly as possible, experts say.

Fortunately, there are quiet signs that beyond the oil shock, there are economic forces accelerating the adoption of clean energy and electrification, which have been causing emissions growth to slow down.
“Under that global number, there are lots and lots of things that add up. And lots of those have turned. They are on the way down,” Andrew said.

Every EV and heat pump sold around the world reduces demand for fossil fuels, and every solar panel, battery and wind turbine installed creates the clean energy to power those electric technologies. And while adoption and deployment of these non-emitting alternatives is currently insufficient to start bringing down global emissions on their own, they’re growing at a phenomenal rate.

For the past several years, China’s production of renewable power and clean technology were greater than the rest of the world combined , allowing it to slow down and stop the rise in its national emissions (which are by far the largest of any country in the world). stories.title: Mark Carney defuses tensions with Quebec premier before facing Xi, Putin and Trump at Apec
stories.summary: The prime minister described his conversation with Paul St-Pierre Plamondon as 'fun,' constructive and respectful.
stories.author: Tonda MacCharles
stories.content:
Phnom Penh, Cambodia—Prime Minister Mark Carney says the level of Chinese investment he’ll allow in Canada’s auto sector depends on the outcome of U.S. trade talks and whether any deal protects a North American auto supply chain.

Ahead of his meetings in China , where he will sit down with Asia-Pacific summit host President Xi Jinping, Carney told reporters that Canada is working on options other than the U.S., and is open to more Chinese investment as long as it meets certain conditions, including the use of critical minerals from Canada, labour standards for Canadian workers and the exclusion of knock-down or ready-to-assemble kits. He said there must be a “strong value-add” in what is manufactured in Canada, not just the addition of final or finished components.

“There have to be real factories, real processes with supply chains that increase with time in Canada.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney says auto sector remains part of trade talks with U.S. but that Canada is looking at ‘other options’ in Europe and Asia. Carney was taking questions from reporters at the Francophonie summit in Phnom Penh, Cambodia. (Nov. 16, 2026)

However, Carney suggested his first option is to retain the fully integrated North American automotive industry.

“We have the best autoworkers in the world, and we want them fully deployed, full opportunity, in an integrated North American market. That market has become less integrated because of U.S. trade actions. It’s an ongoing discussion that we’re having with U.S. administration — myself with the president. And it depends; that’s the first issue.”

“It’s not leverage, but, you know, action: reaction. It depends what — great autoworkers, important market, real assets in Canada — if they’re not fully utilized in a North American context that provides other opportunities, Canada’s gonna move forward either way.”

If international summits are all about showing up for valuable face time with other leaders, this year’s Francophonie and Asia-Pacific summits show the upsides, and the potential downsides, for the prime minister.

On the sidelines, the prime minister appeared to score a significant win when he met with the newly elected premier of Quebec.

The separatist Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon emerged Sunday from his first face-to-face meeting with Carney declaring that, despite their public sparring in recent weeks, he was delighted with a conversation he described as “fun,” constructive and respectful.

Quebec reporters asked Carney if it was a new “bromance,” and Carney laughed, replying “bromance? Why not?” before soon saying, “Non. I have a wife.”

Plamondon had enthused over the meeting, mentioning six times that he and Carney exchanged phone numbers, calling it “a good sign,” and toned down some of his sharpest rhetoric against Ottawa. This is from a premier who has antagonized Carney since taking office in early October.

Plamondon was unapologetic about his demands for a greater say in Canada-U.S. trade negotiations and more power to set temporary immigration levels, saying not all of his disputes with Carney could be resolved in an initial meeting that ran past its allotted half-hour and lasted 47 minutes.

But he claimed victories, saying Carney agreed to provide more transparency and to consult with Quebec in the Canada-U.S. trade talks .

“What we agreed upon is that we needed immediate and enhanced communication among our staff and between each other.”

However, Carney made clear Monday morning before leaving Cambodia that it is the federal government that will negotiate trade treaties.

Plamondon touted as victories the fact that Carney supported his proposed 2027 francophone business leaders’ summit in Quebec, and agreed Quebec will decide how homelessness and housing funding will be spent. Plamondon said he “regretted nothing” about his advocacy for Quebec’s interests.

Yet from the perspective of the prime minister, those were easy concessions.

So, what seemed like a charm offensive from the get-go appears to have worked.

In the same way Carney has deflated tensions with other ornery or Ottawa-skeptical premiers, whether over energy in Alberta, environmental policy in British Columbia or auto-sector jobs in Ontario, he appears to have deflated Quebec-Ottawa tensions, at least for now.

And it was clear which of the two was more at ease when Carney and he shook hands and smiled for the cameras before their meeting. They joked about who was in shape and who was the better goalie when each played hockey at Oxford University, but their body language signalled this was the start of an uneasy friendship.

Carney was looser, more relaxed and complimentary toward the Quebec leader. Plamondon stood in an awkward, legs-akimbo posture throughout the photo opportunity. Earlier, cameras also captured images of a more serious exchange between the duo.

Carney speaks at an event at Francotech in Phnom Penh Sunday.

Plamondon had skipped the Canada-EU summit in Montreal , calling Carney’s invitation, which did not include a prominent speaking role, tantamount to making him a “waiter” at the table. He declared Quebec would negotiate trade terms directly with U.S. lawmakers. Most importantly, Plamondon has vowed to hold another referendum on Quebec sovereignty once U.S. President Donald Trump is out of the White House.

On Sunday, Plamondon dodged questions about whether he raised his sovereigntist project at the francophone summit.

Next stop Monday on Carney’s whirlwind Asia tour is the Asia-Pacific summit in China, where there will be more dragons from a political perspective.

Xi will welcome Russian President Vladimir Putin and Trump alongside the other leaders of the 21-member Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum.

Carney said on Monday that Brazil President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva told him he had encouraged Xi, Trump and Putin to meet in order to try to find a way forward to resolve the war in Ukraine. But Carney has already made clear he will not be equally welcoming to Putin. “Out of respect for the host,” Carney said in Manila that he will stand onstage with Putin for the Apec leaders’ so-called family photo.

But he emphasized Canada’s repudiation of Putin’s invasion of Ukraine.

Carney will meet separately with Xi to advance the Canada-China relationship reset that began in January after a deep freeze triggered by the Meng Wanzhou affair, trade reprisals and the nearly three-year detention of the Two Michaels.

And although he said he would welcome a trilateral meeting on the sidelines with Trump and Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum, he isn’t holding his breath, given the “current trajectory” of trade talks between them with the U.S.

Even before Carney set foot on Chinese soil, Canada’s Conservatives dismissed his approach to trade and international relations, which he describes as “values-based realism” — tailoring relations to areas where Canada can find common ground even amid disagreements.

“From China to Qatar, Turkey and the UAE, Prime Minister Carney has made the deliberate choice to build not only deeper trading relationships but also ‘strategic partnerships’ with nations that, in many cases, do not share our fundamental values and freedoms,” said Conservative international trade critic Stephanie Kusie.

stories.title: Carney to cap off Asean summit with focus on trade deals, ahead of Francophonie
stories.summary: Manila - Prime Minister Mark Carney is wrapping up a brief visit to the Philippines and heading to Cambodia, as the government pushes for more trade access in the region.
stories.author: Dylan Robertson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Manila - Prime Minister Mark Carney has wrapped up a brief visit to the Philippines and is heading to Cambodia, as the government pushes for more trade access in the region.

On his one-night visit to Manila, Carney attended a summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, announced the conclusion of free-trade negotiations with the Philippines and unveiled funding for protecting tropical rainforests.

“What Canada presents is certainty to the world,” Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu told reporters in Manila on Sunday, which was late Saturday in Canada.

Carney was among foreign leaders including U.S. President Donald Trump who were invited to the summit by the Philippine chair, who is holding the rotating presidency of Asean, a bloc of 11 countries.

Ottawa is continuing talks for a trade deal with Asean, which Sidhu said would give Canada access to smaller countries, while Canada also has deeper agreements with Indonesia and the Philippines.

“You can get more into the weeds. You can upgrade later on, when you’re dealing with (one deal that is) bilateral, as opposed to an agreement with 11 partners,” he said in Manila on Sunday, which was late Saturday in Canada.

“It’s the fastest growing region in the world, 700 million consumers, an economy valued at $6 trillion.”

Sidhu also expressed confidence for Canadian pork producers, as the Philippines moves toward restricting pork imports from a wide array of countries, including Canada.

“They’ve got a global safeguards investigation ... for 60 days. Canada is not the culprit, and you’ll find out once the investigation is done,” he said.

Carney also met meet with Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva on the sidelines of the summit, where he announced $540 million for an initiative to protect rainforests, as part of a project co-led by Brazil and Norway.

The money is part of a $6 billion fund promised by Ottawa this spring in support for international climate finance. It is meant to attract public and private investment for preserving biodiversity and supporting communities that rely on these ecosystems.

Through an interpreter, Lula described the money as investments that will yield a profit and not “donations, money for free.”

Carney suggested he would have further talks with Brazil, which is part of the Mercosur trade bloc with whom Canada is negotiating a trade deal. Lula’s office has previously said Carney would visit the country.

“By May, we will also have an opportunity to discuss our economic co-operation, our largest training partner in Latin America by far, (with) $15 billion dollars in trade,” Carney said.

Carney is now en route to Cambodia for a summit of the Francophonie, including a side event on technology trade in Phnom Penh.

While there, Carney will meet with Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon who is pushing for more autonomy in Quebec’s international relations, though Sidhu says Ottawa is working constructively with the province.

“Quebec has many of their own trade officers in our embassies around the world, and we’ll continue working collaboratively,” Sidhu said, noting that Quebec’s aerospace sector has recently achieved large sales in Asia.

Later this week, Carney will attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation summit in China, months after Carney and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed to have a limited number of Chinese electrical vehicles sold in Canada.

Sidhu also said Chinese automaker Chery is among those seeking Transport Canada certification to sell lower-cost vehicles into Canada. He said some Chinese manufacturers will likely clear that process by the end of the year.

He said he is also hopeful Chinese companies will create automotive jobs for Canadians.

“There is an interest from Chinese manufacturers to utilize our workforce in Canada, but before you invest billions of dollars you need to understand the market,” he said.

“Every time I sit down with them I look at what they’re doing in Europe and I ask them how they can replicate that in Canada with Canadian supply chains, with Canadian workers.”

The minister said Canada is still navigating trade issues with China, despite some recent progress on extending access to beef, canola meal, crab and peas.

“We’re still continuing to engage on pork, ON pet food and others. We’re not relenting,” he said.

Sidhu also said Canada is working with Beijing to have more opportunities for Canadian small and medium businesses to sell consumer goods to China on online platforms like Alibaba.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 14, 2026.

Carney suggested he would have further talks with Brazil, which is part of the Mercosur trade bloc with whom Canada is negotiating a trade deal. Lula’s office has previously said Carney would visit the country.
“By May, we will also have an opportunity to discuss our economic co-operation, our largest training partner in Latin America by far, (with) $15 billion dollars in trade,” Carney said.
Carney is now en route to Cambodia for a summit of the Francophonie, including a side event on technology trade in Phnom Penh.

While there, Carney will meet with Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon who is pushing for more autonomy in Quebec’s international relations, though Sidhu says Ottawa is working constructively with the province.

“Quebec has many of their own trade officers in our embassies around the world, and we’ll continue working collaboratively,” Sidhu said, noting that Quebec’s aerospace sector has recently achieved large sales in Asia.

Later this week, Carney will attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation summit in China, months after Carney and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed to have a limited number of Chinese electrical vehicles sold in Canada.

Sidhu also said Chinese automaker Chery is among those seeking Transport Canada certification to sell lower-cost vehicles into Canada. He said some Chinese manufacturers will likely clear that process by the end of the year.
He said he is also hopeful Chinese companies will create automotive jobs for Canadians.
“There is an interest from Chinese manufacturers to utilize our workforce in Canada, but before you invest billions of dollars you need to understand the market,” he said.
“Every time I sit down with them I look at what they’re doing in Europe and I ask them how they can replicate that in Canada with Canadian supply chains, with Canadian workers.”
The minister said Canada is still navigating trade issues with China, despite some recent progress on extending access to beef, canola meal, crab and peas.
“We’re still continuing to engage on pork, ON pet food and others. We’re not relenting,” he said.
Sidhu also said Canada is working with Beijing to have more opportunities for Canadian small and medium businesses to sell consumer goods to China on online platforms like Alibaba.

stories.title: Latest travel disruption could cost Canadian airlines millions, expert says
stories.summary: Carriers are expected to take until Tuesday to resume normal operations after the U.S. ordered a nationwide ground stop
stories.author: Eric Atkins
stories.content:
Canadian airlines could face millions of dollars in costs and days before operations return to normal after the United States halted all flights on Friday night when its air traffic control system went down.

The carriers are expected to take until Tuesday to resume normal operations after cancelling 720 flights on Friday, when the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop for all civilian flights.

Traffic resumed on Friday night but at least 260 Canadian flights are cancelled on Saturday and Sunday, according to Cirium, an aviation analytics company. This includes flights from the U.S., Mexico and the Caribbean.

Airlines are now grappling with the challenge of getting fresh crews to destinations where their planes were grounded and pilots and flight attendants burned through their available flight duty hours on the ground, said John Gradek, an aviation lecturer at McGill University. This can lead to crew shortages elsewhere in the network.

“The knock-on effect can be significant,” he said.

The U.S. ground stop brings expenses that include the costs of moving fresh crews and planes around to help stranded customers, in addition to hotel and food claims made by passengers whose journeys were delayed during rebooking.

Airlines are rebooking customers on the next available flight or offering refunds. Given the backlog, the next available flight might not be until the next day or later, which could leave the airline open to claims for hotel and meal expenses under Canada’s Air Passenger Protection Regulations, Mr. Gradek said. The initial delay or cancellation is outside the control of the airlines and therefore not covered.

Canadian airlines have responded to reduced demand for travel to the U.S. under President Donald Trump by trimming cross-border schedules beginning last year. This lessened the impact of the outage. However, flights to and from Mexico and the Caribbean were also affected, given they must pass through U.S. airspace and use U.S. air traffic control.

It is impossible to place a price tag on the impact of the ground stoppage, but Canada’s airlines could face millions of dollars in new costs. “It’s significant,” Mr. Gradek said.

The toll of the stoppage comes as airlines are grappling with soaring jet fuel prices caused by the U.S. war on Iran.

Christophe Hennebelle, a spokesman for Air Canada, said the U.S. ground stoppage affected 23,000 customers on Friday. It is hard to say when normal operations will resume, he said, or how quickly stranded passengers can resume their trips.

“It’s really case by case,” he said by phone.

“We are rebooking people, so we will contact people directly, and of course they’ve got the option either to accept the rebooking that we’re proposing or get a refund if they don’t want to travel any more,” Mr. Hennebelle said.

Almost a third of Friday’s 26,200 flights departing in the U.S. were cancelled, Cirium said. On Saturday, more than 4,100 flights are cancelled. This includes flights operated by Canadian airlines.

In a statement, Porter Airlines said it will likely take the weekend for normal scheduling to resume. For customers with flexibility, the airline is waiving fees for rebooking a different flight or selecting a nearby airport.

WestJet Airlines said on Saturday it is preparing for a return to normal operations over the next 48 hours.

stories.title: What Canadians should know about their air passenger rights amid U.S. travel chaos
stories.summary: As Canadian airlines and airports continue to deal with the aftershocks of the Friday grounding of U.S. air traffic, some travellers are facing cancellations and delays to their plans.
stories.author: Kathryn Mannie The Canadian Press
stories.content:
As Canadian airlines and airports continue to deal with the aftershocks of the Friday grounding of U.S. air traffic, some travellers are facing cancellations and delays to their plans.

Under Canada’s Air Passenger Protection Regulations, passengers have the right to be rebooked if their flight is cancelled or subject to a lengthy delay.

Airlines must rebook travellers on the next available flight operated by them or a partner airline that departs within 48 hours of the passenger’s original departure time.

Some Canadian airports and airlines spent Saturday issuing travel notices and catching up on a backlog left behind by a freeze on U.S. air traffic. (Nov. 14, 2026)

Gabor Lukacs, an air passenger rights advocate, says for international travel, like to and from the U.S., if airlines can’t find a flight within that 48-hour period, they are required to rebook passengers on a competing airline.

When disruptions are within an airline’s control, passengers are guaranteed more protections and can claim compensation, but Lukacs says that isn’t the case here.

The nationwide grounding of U.S. air traffic is an “extraordinary circumstance” that is out of the airline’s control, Lukacs says.

Air Canada says it cancelled about 250 flights, affecting some 27,000 passengers after the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration issued the ground stop order on Friday, halting all U.S. flights for more than four hours.

Meanwhile, Porter Airlines and WestJet say it will likely take the whole weekend for flights to return to normal schedules.

Lukacs notes that travellers flying between Canada and the U.S. are protected under both countries’ air passenger regulations, but Canada’s protections are stronger.

For Canadians stuck in the U.S. who May have had to book hotels and cover the cost of additional meals because of travel delays, Lukacs says airlines are not required to pay travellers back.

“In Europe, passengers would still be getting meals and accommodation,” Lukacs says, even for disruptions outside the airline’s control. “In Canada, that’s not an obligation.”

Lukacs says if Canadians feel airlines have not met their obligations under the law, they should document their communications with the airline and take them to small claims court.

The U.S. government says the ground stop order was issued on Friday after new technology was added to the nation’s air traffic control system, overloading antiquated equipment and causing intermittent communications and radar gaps.

The matter is under investigation.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 14, 2026.

stories.title: Canadian travellers face delays, cancellations as airlines recover from U.S. ground stop
stories.summary: More than 100 flights were cancelled Saturday, leaving some travellers stranded
stories.author: Matthew Scace, Kate Helmore
stories.content:
Canadian air travellers continued to face disruptions Saturday as more than 100 flights were cancelled and airlines scrambled to deal with the fallout from Friday’s U.S. nationwide ground stop that brought air travel to a grinding halt.

While Canadian air traffic systems continued to operate normally, the grounding of all flights departing from the U.S., which lasted about five hours, triggered a major knock-on effect in Canada and around the world.

Air Canada said Saturday it was adding extra flights to help stranded travellers get to their destinations, and several other airlines including WestJet and Porter said they were offering flight changes free of charge.

Spokesperson Yasmine Mehdi said Air Canada cancelled roughly 250 flights on Friday, affecting about 27,000 passengers.

“This was a significant disruption, and its effects have carried over into today, with additional cancellations as aircraft and crews are out of position across our network,” Ms. Mehdi wrote in an e-mail statement.

In Toronto, 143 U.S.-bound flights were cancelled on Friday, a spokesperson for Pearson International Airport said. Another 63 were cancelled on Saturday.

Dozens of flights were also cancelled on Saturday in Montreal, Ottawa, Vancouver and Calgary.

The U.S. air travel schedule should be back to normal by the end of Sunday, Bryan Bedford, administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration, said on Saturday.

Some Canadians stranded away from home said they were anxious to resume their journeys after spending hours stuck in airports or onboard parked planes.

John Jacques had just walked up to his gate in Brisbane, Australia when news of the ground stoppage broke. The Toronto resident was returning home on a flight connecting through Dallas, Texas.

“When you’re on the opposite side of the world it’s just about the last thing you would expect,” he told The Globe and Mail.

His flight to Dallas still boarded but had to await takeoff clearance on the tarmac. Including the journey time, Mr. Jacques spent 16 hours inside the plane. He arrived in Dallas in time to make a connection to Toronto, which was also delayed. For the time being, he is making the most of being off a plane.

“I’m quite happy to just be out of that and stretching my legs before the second hop,” he said.

“I’m used to the long hauls from Brizzy to Toronto but today is really feeling long,” he said, adding that the total journey is now stretching more than 24 hours.

But Mr. Jacques feels he got lucky compared to other passengers on his flight. He has a seat on the plane back home to Toronto. Others had to scramble to find other options, he said.

Maggie Sepulveda is a long-haul truck driver who drove from Dallas to Ontario this week. She had hoped to fly home to Dallas on Friday but said she’s still stuck in Toronto Pearson airport.

Her flight has changed three times. She had to pay to stay in an airport hotel last night and is late for her next job. On top of that, her phone is acting up and she’s had to sit in the airport Starbucks to get wireless internet.

In total, the delay has cost her more than $250 in accommodation and food, and she’s not expecting to be reimbursed. It’s the last thing she needs right now. Life is already expensive enough, she said. But she’s keeping things in perspective.

“I’m hopeful that I’ll be able to get out tonight, and I’m thankful that I’m safe,” she said. “Everything happens for a reason.”

South of the border, meanwhile, officials are still searching for answers around what caused the longest nationwide flight shutdown since the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.

U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on Saturday that FAA contractor L3Harris’ installation of at least one new router at a remote facility triggered the disruption.

Mr. Duffy said that the router being replaced started “flooding” other routers in the country’s air traffic control system, disrupting communication lines to airplanes and scrambling radar feeds.

But it’s unclear whether the problems were the result of “incompetence” or a faulty router, Mr. Duffy said.

stories.title: Airport in Gander, N.L., was ready to receive diverted passengers in U.S. flight stop
stories.summary: An airport in a Newfoundland town known for its care of stranded plane passengers was on the ready Friday evening as flights were grounded for several hours in the United States.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Gander -- An airport in a Newfoundland town known for its care of stranded plane passengers was on the ready Friday evening as flights were grounded for several hours in the United States.

Officials called around to hotels to get a sense of how many rooms might be available, and they made sure there were staff on hand who could keep the restaurant open, said Reg White, chief executive of the international airport authority, in Gander, N.L.

Though the airport was ready to welcome anyone who needed a hand, White said there was some relief when the so-called ground stop was lifted Friday night without any diversions to Gander -- it meant the community Christmas craft fair could go ahead as planned in the airport lounge on Saturday.

“The Christmas craft fair was at stake!” White said in an interview Saturday. “Airport operations clearly comes first, but there would have been a lot of vendors and Christmas shoppers who would have been unhappy if it hadn’t gone our way.”

The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration had a so-called ground stop order in place for more than four hours beginning Friday afternoon, citing communications issues affecting air-traffic-control centres. It was called off on Friday night.

Because of its key position in the airspace between Europe and North America, Gander’s airport has long, sprawling runways that could accommodate planes needing to refuel on transatlantic journeys, particularly in the Second World War.

When the United States shut down its airspace after terrorists hijacked planes and crashed them into the World Trade Center on Sept. 11, 2001, dozens of planes were diverted to Gander. The town was home to about 9,600 people at the time, and many came together to feed, house and comfort thousands of passengers, who were stranded there for days.

The story of their hospitality was turned into the hit Broadway musical, “Come From Away.”

American officials emphasized on Friday that the situation that forced the ground stop was nothing like 9/11.

U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters at the White House that nobody was ever in danger during the communications failure.

“There was never any lives at risk,” Mullin said. “There was no flights at risk. FAA was able to handle it.”

White said he didn’t brace for a huge onslaught of planes on Friday because there were no flights between Gander and the United States, nor was it a peak time for flights between the U.S. and Europe. But there was still a possibility Gander would be needed.

Percy Farwell, the town’s mayor, said he had “informal communications” with airport officials and Nav Canada to be ready. Nav Canada is the privately run non-profit corporation that operates Canada’s civil air navigation system.

“Everybody (was) putting out feelers and starting to quasi-prepare in the event that we were going to be impacted,” Farwell said Saturday, speaking to The Canadian Press from the packed craft fair inside the airport’s lounge.

There were almost 100 tables set up with goods for sale, and the event was going well, he said.

Farwell said that for him, the incident Friday was a reminder that Canada’s air-traffic-control technology is excellent, and deployed around the world. Flight-grounding communications breakdowns aren’t impossible in Canada, but they’re less likely, he said.

“It’s sort of something we should be proud of in Canada, that the air-traffic-control system is very much state of the art,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 14, 2026.

stories.title: Fifth Canadian soldier has died after fire in Wainwright, CAF says
stories.summary: A fifth Canadian soldier has died from injuries sustained during a training exercise last month at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
A fifth Canadian soldier has died from injuries sustained during a training exercise at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta last month.

Pte. William Douglas Dal Bianco of the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry died on Friday, the Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) said in a news release.

Dal Bianco was receiving medical treatment in Ontario following the incident.

“I extend my deepest condolences to the family, friends and fellow service members mourning the loss of Private William Douglas Dal Bianco. stories.title: CP NewsAlert: CAF says fifth Canadian soldier has died after fire in Wainwright
stories.summary: Wainwright - A fifth Canadian soldier has died from injuries sustained during a training exercise last month at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Wainwright - Nearly a month after a deadly fire tore through a military base in Alberta, the Canadian Armed Forces announced Saturday that the tragedy has claimed a fifth life.

The military said in a statement that Pte. William Douglas Dal Bianco died on Friday in Ontario, where he was receiving care after the Oct. 17 blaze at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, southeast of Edmonton.

A fifth Canadian soldier has died from injuries he sustained in a fire last month at a military base in Alberta, the Canadian Armed Forces said Saturday. (Nov. 14, 2026)

Prime Minister Mark Carney, who has called the fire one of the worst tragedies for the Armed Forces on home soil during peacetime, said he is thinking about the Dal Bianco’s loved ones.

Yesterday, Private William Douglas Dal Bianco passed away from injuries sustained in the fire last month at CFB Wainwright. Private Dal Bianco and his fellow soldiers were training to defend Canada. With their bright futures still before them, they chose to safeguard ours. That is service. Now, we serve them. Canadians are holding Private Dal Bianco's loved ones, and all those still grieving in the wake of this terrible tragedy, in our hearts. — Mark Carney (@MarkJCarney) November 14, 2026

“Private Dal Bianco and his fellow soldiers were training to defend Canada,” Carney said in a social media post.

“With their bright futures still before them, they chose to safeguard ours. That is service.

“Canadians are holding Private Dal Bianco’s loved ones, and all those still grieving in the wake of this terrible tragedy, in our hearts.”

Defence Minister David McGuinty said he extends his deepest condolences to the Dal Bianco’s family and friends for their profound loss.

“No words can ease the pain of this loss, but their service and sacrifice will never be forgotten,” he said in a statement.

Federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said he was heartbroken

“He is the fifth soldier to have lost his life in this tragedy,” he said in a social media post. “He wore the uniform to serve Canada, and Canada will never forget him.”

About 84 soldiers with the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry were taking part in attack training when wind pushed flames from a grass fire onto the troops.

Pte. Shaun Farrell, 23, of Prince Albert, Sask.; Pte. Aidan Goulding, 23, of North Vancouver; Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, 19, of Langley, B.C.; and Sgt. Morgan Wong, 26, of Edmonton also died in the blaze.

Dozens of others were injured, with some in critical condition.

The Canadian Armed Forces said Saturday that 24 soldiers remain in various hospitals.

Three investigations are looking into what happened.

Dal Bianco’s death comes days after he and the others were honoured during Remembrance Day ceremonies across the country.

Poilievre, after the ceremony in Wainwright, described the injuries some of the soldiers were dealing with as “horrendous.”

“These young people literally ran into balls of fire to save their brothers and sisters in arms,” he said.

“Third-degree burns on 80 to 90 per cent of their bodies. We reflect on the courage of the people on that day.”

Poilievre represents the riding of Battle River-Crowfoot, which includes the base.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 14, 2026

—- By Fakiha Baig in Edmonton

stories.title: Festive season underway with Christmas events, parades and markets
stories.summary: Hundreds of people packed Talbot Street in St. Thomas, Ont. Friday night for an annual event geared at driving people downtown to shop.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
Hundreds of people packed Talbot Street in St. Thomas, Ont. Friday night for an annual event geared at driving people downtown to shop.

“Tonight is ‘Light Up Talbot’’ said Grayden Laing, president of the St. Thomas Downtown Development Board (DDB).

“It’s an event that was started by Suzanne Faris (St. Thomas business owner), and then she graciously said, ‘Hey Downtown Development Board, it is getting a little bit big, do you guys want to work on that?’. We said, ‘absolutely.’”

The evening featured the lightning of the tree at City Hall, elementary school choirs, photos with Santa Claus, horse drawn wagon rides, live music and entertainment, a warming station and contests for the best decorated storefront.

“Tonight is kind of our kickoff to Christmas in downtown St. Thomas,” said Sarah Lynch, downtown and development engagement officer with the St. Thomas Economic Development Corporation (EDC).

“It’s always to celebrate our downtown and the businesses that make our community so special. Giving back to them a little gift for what they give to us all the time.”

The EDC has been working with the DDB for a couple of years now on this annual event.

“It’s just been amazing to see how much this event has grown under Sarah’s leadership, just to really make sure that these people who are shopping for Christmas know that downtown St. Thomas has what they’re looking for,” said Sean Dyke, CEO of the EDC.

“We all can shop online, but it’s really great to keep it local if we can and now we have that opportunity with events like this.”

Outside City Hall, mayor Joe Preston along with city councillors were greeting visitors and handing out goodies.

“We’ve really been pushing the safety of being downtown,” said Preston.

“The downtown is fuller than we’ve had in a long time. Take a look, when you put a lot of people in it, it sure does look good. Here comes Santa on the fire truck, and we are making sure Santa is safe too.”

Local businesses have been thriving during events like this one and the recent Pumpkin Prowl which brought thousands downtown on Halloween.

“It is one of the biggest things that happens around the year and we look forward to it,” said Aurora Alcocer, owner of Taco House on Talbot St.

“We welcome new customers and we welcome the community. It’s a great idea to have this type of events, especially when it’s the holiday season. It just gives opportunity to a lot of people to get to know our business, to actually try our food and be here for the first time.”

The DDB has heard from a lot of businesses downtown that it is difficult to make ends meet.

“We need to be able to get people downtown to support the businesses,” said Laing.

“If they can come in here and they can see how amazing some of our shops are, hopefully they’ll come down tonight and they’ll come back again throughout the holiday season looking for that special gift to buy for someone they love.”

With six weeks to go until Christmas many festive events including holiday markets are getting underway. London held its Santa Claus Parade Saturday, and the Hyde Park and Argyle Santa Claus Parades are still to come.

Over the next couple of weeks there are more than a dozen Christmas parades in Elgin and Middlesex County.

stories.title: Fifth soldier dies from injuries after October fire at CFB Wainwright
stories.summary: Private William Douglas Dal Bianco, of the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry, died on Friday in Ontario
stories.author: Mercedes Stephenson, Alanna Smith, Greg Mercer
stories.content:
A fifth member of the Canadian Forces has died as a result of injuries sustained from the deadly fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta, the Department of National Defence confirmed to The Globe and Mail.

Private William Douglas Dal Bianco, of the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry, who was among those seriously injured in the fire, died on Friday in Ontario, according to the Canadian Armed Forces.

General Jennie Carignan, Chief of the Defence Staff, offered her condolences to Pte. Dal Bianco’s family, friends and those who served alongside him in a statement on Saturday.

“We will honour his dedicated service and continue to stand with all those affected by this tragedy along the difficult road ahead. My thoughts are also with our injured members and their families, and I am deeply grateful to everyone involved in providing care and support during this time of tremendous sadness,” she said.

The death toll from the Oct. 17 fire at CFB Wainwright has risen to five, up from four deaths reported in the immediate aftermath of the disaster. Twenty-four of the 38 injured soldiers remain in hospital.

Most of the Wainwright patients are being cared for in Alberta hospitals, which are overseen by Acute Care Alberta.

ACA, in a statement on Saturday, said there were 21 soldiers being treated in the province, nine of whom were in critical condition, as of Nov. 10. The provincial agency is expected to give another update on Tuesday.

The CFB Wainwright incident is one of Canada’s worst peacetime training tragedies on home soil, with dozens more injured than the Slesse Range disaster in 1988 that killed six military engineer trainees and seriously injured three others during a demolition exercise at CFB Chilliwack.

Prime Minister Mark Carney , in a statement posted to social media on Saturday, said Canadians are holding all those who are grieving in the wake of last month’s tragedy in their hearts.

“Private Dal Bianco and his fellow soldiers were training to defend Canada. With their bright futures still before them, they chose to safeguard ours,” he said. “That is service. Now, we serve them.”

The majority of the injured suffered extreme burns that require multiple surgeries and extensive rehabilitation. Some of the individuals receiving care in hospital have had more than 50 per cent of their body scorched by the flames.

David McGuinty, Canada’s Minister of National Defence, also offered his sympathies in a statement on Saturday to the loved ones of Pte. Dal Bianco. “No words can ease the pain of losing a loved one, and my thoughts remain with all those affected by this tragedy,” he said.

Mr. McGuinty said the federal government will honour Pte. Dal Bianco’s “service, dedication and sacrifice to Canada” and remains committed to supporting the families affected by the fatal fire.

Before Saturday, the military provided its last update on the casualties on Nov. 4, saying 14 soldiers had been released from hospital, and four others were transferred from Alberta to health care facilities closer to their home communities, including in British Columbia and Ontario where they will continue receiving care.

Three funerals have been held and one is planned for the other soldiers who died in the fire: Sergeant Morgan Wong, 26, of Edmonton; Private Shaun Farrell, 23, of Prince Albert, Saskatchewan; Private Aidan Goulding, 23, of North Vancouver, B.C.; and Private Hayden Lykkemark 19, of Langley, B.C. All four were Edmonton-based members serving with the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.

CFB Wainwright, located 200 kilometres southeast of Edmonton, is used as a combat and live-fire training ground for troops about to go overseas. Officials said the soldiers who died were among those training for deployment to Latvia, as part of the Nato presence to deter Russian aggression in the Baltics.

The deadly blaze began as a smouldering grass fire that was whipped into a “wall of flame” by high winds, according to military officials.

There are multiple investigations under way into the fire, including by Alberta’s chief medical examiner and the Canadian Forces National Investigation Service, a military police unit.

The military promised a board of inquiry to examine the circumstances of the fire and adequacy of safety protocols, but the board has not yet been convened.

At a news conference last month, Brigadier-General Vanessa Hanrahan, the military’s top police officer, said the fire had started hours earlier on CFB Wainwright’s automatic grenade launcher range and was monitored continuously for hours. She did not say whether the firing of live ammunition or explosive rounds ignited the fire.

Editor’s note: An earlier version of this story stated that funerals had been held for four of the soldiers killed in the fire at CFB Wainwright in Alberta.

stories.title: Quebec ready to vote independently from Canada for Francophonie leadership: premier
stories.summary: Phnom Penh - Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon is further distancing himself from the Canadian government in his first international outing since winning last month's provincial election.
stories.author: Caroline Plante The Canadian Press
stories.content:
PHNOM PENH - Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon is further distancing himself from the Canadian government in his first international outing since winning last month’s provincial election.

He suggested today that he was prepared to vote differently from Canada in the election for secretary-general of the Francophonie.

St-Pierre Plamondon is in Phnom Penh, the capital of Cambodia, to attend a summit of the international body of French-speaking states and governments.

Quebec, Canada and New Brunswick all have the right to vote in Monday’s election to choose a new secretary-general.

Louise Mushikiwabo of Rwanda is seeking a third term as head of the organization, and is running against Juliana Amato Lumumba of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Dacian Ciolos of Romania, and Coumba Bâ of Mauritania.

St-Pierre Plamondon hasn’t said who he’ll support, but said he won’t necessarily align with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and New Brunswick Premier Susan Holt.

“We’re not bound by another candidate’s vote,” he said, adding that discussions are ongoing among member states.

Mushikiwabo has expressed her desire for support from Quebec, saying she maintains “very good relations” with the province.

“I would very much like to have Quebec’s support,” she said alongside her deputy, Quebec native Caroline St-Hilaire, whose position is also at stake.

The topic may be on the agenda as St-Pierre Plamondon and Carney have their first in-person meeting on Sunday.

St-Pierre Plamondon said Saturday that he’s optimistic about the discussions, despite his outspoken criticism of Ottawa.

“We’re preparing an (economic) update, so there will be important discussions on that,” he said.

Speaking in the Philippines, Carney also expressed confidence that he and St-Pierre Plamondon will be able to work together.

“I work with all the other premiers in Canada and leaders from countries around the world, so I’m sure we’ll find common priorities,” he said.

St-Pierre Plamondon began his day in Cambodia by addressing a roundtable of Quebec entrepreneurs, and encouraging them to use the Francophonie to pursue trade opportunities.

He then gave a speech at another entrepreneurs’ gathering, where he reminded the attendees that Quebec has been a full member of the Francophonie for over 50 years.

“The (organization) is an example of how we can exercise our sovereignty at the international level,” he said.

While Quebec’s international relations minister has said the province wouldn’t be raising the issue of independence in Cambodia, the premier said his sovereigntist government is sparking interest from other states.

“I won’t hide the fact that we’ve had ... several hallway conversations in which people are curious because we are the Parti Québécois,” he said.

“So, we discuss the topic of independence, but informally.”

St-Pierre Plamondon has promised his government will hold a referendum on sovereignty towards the end of his term, once U.S. President Donald Trump leaves the White House.

On Saturday, however, the Quebec premier’s appearance on stage drew laughs as he was mistakenly introduced as the prime minister of Canada.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 14, 2026.

stories.title: ‘It’s crazy’: Travellers, airlines report busy day at airports after U.S. flight stop
stories.summary: The ripple effects of a four-hour freeze on U.S. air traffic continued across Canadian airports on Saturday, as airlines issued flight notices and travellers spent hours tethered to their phones waiting for updates.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The ripple effects of a four-hour freeze on U.S. air traffic continued across Canadian airports on Saturday, as airlines issued flight notices and travellers spent hours tethered to their phones waiting for updates. Airports from Vancouver to Halifax posted on social media that they were facing delays, and the one in Toronto said it even called in more staff to help out.

“A busy day of travel is underway,” said Toronto Pearson International Airport. Traveller Edward Langer, who is in New York with his 15-year-old daughter, said his Saturday flight back home to Edmonton was postponed by about four days due to the freeze.

He said he and his daughter are facing several missed days of school and work, as well as thousands of dollars in extra hotel costs. He had not been able to reach Porter Airlines as of Saturday afternoon despite spending hours on hold.

“When you go on some of the travel sites to book hotels, (the price) is just doubling and tripling,” he said. “It’s crazy.” Global travel chaos began after the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration issued a so-called ground stop order on Friday that brought air traffic in that country to a halt for more than four hours.

The U.S. government said new technology being added to the nation’s air traffic control system overloaded antiquated equipment and caused intermittent communications and radar gaps. The matter was under investigation. Air Canada said Saturday it cancelled approximately 250 flights after the order, which affected some 27,000 passengers.

“This was a significant disruption, and its effects have carried over into today, with additional cancellations as aircraft and crews are out of position across our network,” said Yasmine Mehdi, an Air Canada spokesperson.

“Returning to normal operations will take some time.” Porter Airlines and WestJet said it would likely take the whole weekend for its flights to return to normal schedules. Porter said it would refund its customers who can’t accommodate rescheduled flights while Calgary-based WestJet said its policy allowing flexible rescheduling was activated.

Isabelle Rochefort said she had been standing in line at Montreal’s Trudeau International Airport to board her Air Canada flight to Cancun, Mexico, around 5 p.m. Friday when she received word that it was cancelled. She said the situation was initially confusing because her plane wasn’t touching down in the United States.

“We didn’t know what to do, of course,” she said in a series of Facebook messages. “The Air Canada staff had no information on what was next except that we had to wait for news.” She was able to retrieve her bag after leaving the line and call someone to drive her home to Sorel-Tracy, more than an hour-and-a-half away.

She’s since been rebooked on a new flight leaving Sunday, though she’ll have to pay for yet another expensive ride to the airport. Rochefort believes that both the airport and airline are managing as best as they can. “The real question now is, will it be possible to be compensated?” she asked.

“That remains to be seen.” By Morgan Lowrie in Montreal, Sarah Smellie in St. John’s, and Fakiha Baig in Edmonton, with files from The Associated Press

stories.title: Busy day at Canadian airports as airlines scramble to recover from U.S. flight stop
stories.summary: Some Canadian airports and airlines spent Saturday issuing travel notices and catching up on a backlog left behind by a freeze on U.S. air traffic.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto — Some Canadian airports and airlines spent Saturday issuing travel notices and catching up on a backlog left behind by a freeze on U.S. air traffic.

One of Canada’s largest airports, Toronto Pearson International Airport, said it called in more staff to help out with the day.

“A busy day of travel is underway at Toronto Pearson,” it said in a social media post early Saturday.

Calgary-based WestJet said in a separate post that it was responding to a significant travel disruption, while Porter Airlines said it would likely take the whole weekend for its flights to return to normal schedules.

“We appreciate everyone’s patience and understanding,” a Porter spokesperson said in an email Saturday.

Chaos at airports across Canada began after the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration issued a so-called ground stop order on Friday that brought air traffic in that country to a halt for roughly four hours.

The U.S. government said new technology being added to the nation’s air traffic control system overloaded antiquated equipment and caused intermittent communications and radar gaps.

Air Canada said Saturday it cancelled approximately 250 flights after the order, which affected some 27,000 passengers.

“This was a significant disruption, and its effects have carried over into today, with additional cancellations as aircraft and crews are out of position across our network,” said Yasmine Mehdi, an Air Canada spokesperson.

“Returning to normal operations will take some time.”

It said it was working as quickly as possible to add new flights to its schedule and help people catch flights.

A Porter Airlines spokesperson said in an email that it would refund its customers who can’t accommodate rescheduled flights.

Airports in Vancouver, Edmonton, Calgary and Halifax issued travel notices and asked travellers to double-check their flight statuses before leaving their homes.

“We appreciate travellers’ patience as schedules begin to normalize,” the airport in Calgary said.

With files from The Associated Press

stories.title: Joly says Stellantis could get more government money if it promised to keep Brampton plant open
stories.summary: Industry Minister Melanie Joly says the automaker Stellantis could be eligible for more taxpayer funds to support workers, if it agrees not to sell its Brantford, Ont. plant.
stories.author: Spencer Van Dyk
stories.content:
Industry Minister Melanie Joly says the automaker Stellantis could be eligible for more taxpayer funds to support workers, if it agrees not to sell its Brampton, Ont. plant.

“If it’s to save the plant, we would be actually doing what we’ve done with Ford, what we’ve done with Honda, and what we’ve done with Toyota, and what we’re willing to do with all automakers and auto suppliers that are affected by the tariffs,” Joly said in an interview with CTV Question Period airing Sunday, after referencing federal government funding for the auto industry impacted by the U.S. trade war on Canada.

After months of speculation, Stellantis announced this week its plan to sell its Brampton plant — which has been idled since 2023 — to Roshel, a Canadian armoured vehicle manufacturer.

The federal government expressed outrage at the announcement of the sale, and has pledged to hold the company accountable, with Prime Minister Mark Carney calling the move a “betrayal,” and Joly threatening to sue Stellantis if it sells the plant. Carney later called the sale a “partial solution.”

Multiple sources, meanwhile, told CTV News this week that senior officials within both the Prime Minister’s Office and Joly’s office were aware of the proposed sale for months, and behind the scenes , did not stand in the way of it advancing.

During the interview, host Vassy Kapelos pressed Joly on her assertion that the federal government would still give Stellantis taxpayer funds despite having spent so much time this week decrying the character of the company.

“We can’t give money to a company that is actually going against its contractual obligations, and that’s my point,” Joly said. “They need to make sure that they don’t sell the plant, and then we can have a conversation.”

She insisted that Canadian auto workers are “very happy” the government is “putting money on the table” for industries affected by U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs.

When pressed again by Kapelos on whether that means her government is comfortable with more taxpayer dollars going toward companies that it ultimately can’t trust, Joly said: “No, the bottom line is actually protecting the jobs.”

She added, “I think it’s important that we all frame this in the context of a trade war that is affecting so many workers.”

Speaking to reporters in Manila, Philippines on Saturday, Carney was asked to define what an “aggressive package” offered to Stellantis would involve.

“The details of that and the implications of that will come out in due course as part of this,” Carney said. “But make no mistake, the expectation is that Stellantis fully respects its engagements to the workers and to Canada.”

Also in an interview on CTV Question Period airing Sunday, Kapelos asked Conservative labour critic Kyle Seeback whether his party would support Stellantis receiving government funds if it kept the Brampton plant open. He did not rule the prospect out.

“I think you’d have to have a really good contract, first of all, if you’re even going to consider it,” Seeback said. “But I don’t think we can ever be there.”

“(Joly) is saying if Stellantis keeps the plant, we have some extra money for Stellantis, but if that’d be news to the CEO of Roshel, who says ‘we’ve got a signed agreement of purchase and sale,’” he added.

The MP for Dufferin–Caledon said he doesn’t think the minister’s comments “track.”

When asked again by Kapelos whether his party would support Stellantis accessing more government funding if it kept the plant open, Seeback didn’t directly answer, but said there would need to be “better guarantees” that the company would keep its promises.

You can watch Industry Minister Melanie Joly and Conservative labour critic Kyle Seeback’s full interviews on CTV Question Period Sunday at 11 a.m. ET.

stories.title: Air travel schedule should recover by Sunday, FAA says
stories.summary: Passengers can expect some delays and cancellations to continue throughout the day Saturday as air travel returns to normal following the U.S. ground stop order Friday.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
A nationwide ground stop in the U.S. ended around 8:15 p.m. Eastern Friday night and some flights to and from U.S. airports have taken off.

However, normalizing air traffic after the longest flight stoppage in 25 years will be slow, authorities warned, and chaos continues at airports across Canada and the U.S.

Fernandes and Griffiths were expecting an easy flight to Orlando, Fl. when they arrived at Pearson International Airport Friday evening. Instead, they were met with uncertainty about whether or not they would make it to their destination.

“We met another couple that’s going to Miami, but we’re going to Orlando. Their flight is not grounded but ours is and we’re flying out at the exact same time with the same flight company,” Fernandes told Global News Friday.

She said when they arrived at the airport they spoke with an Air Canada agent.

“He said ‘I don’t know. The situation seems a bit dicey.’ But we can’t really leave because we could miss our flight,” Fernandes said.

The couple waited for a couple hours before deciding to go home and have only received a cancellation from the airline.

Other passengers across the country said they were looking into other options, such as renting a car and driving to their destination.

In a statement to Global News, Air Canada said it cancelled approximately 250 flights on Friday, affecting around 27,000 customers.

“This was a significant disruption, and its effects have carried over into today, with additional cancellations as aircraft and crews are out of position across our network,” Air Canada spokesperson Yasmine Mehdi told Global News on Saturday.

According to the flight tracker platform Flight Aware, 9,155 flights within, into or out of the U.S. were cancelled Friday. The same platform showed more than 4,000 flights cancelled by midday Saturday.

Forty-seven cancellations were recorded at Calgary International Airport Friday and approximately 48 departing flights were delayed, a spokesperson said, adding that they could not confirm all disruptions were related to the ground stop.

A spokesperson for Porter Airlines told Global News that it will likely take through the weekend for schedules to return to normal.

“Passengers have been rebooked on the next available flight. If the new itinerary does not meet the passenger’s needs, they will be refunded to the original form of payment,” the spokesperson said.

In a statement on social media, West Jet said it was offering guests travelling to and from continental U.S., Mexico or the Caribbean, with travel scheduled between Friday and Sunday, the opportunity to make a one-time change, or cancellation at no fee.

In an update Saturday, Bryan Bedford, administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration, said 41,000 flights within, into and out of the U.S. were scheduled for Saturday and the public could expect that between 4,000 and 5,000 of those would be cancelled.

“We will still have delays and cancellations today, but that will set us up for a full recovery tomorrow and based on everything that we’re hearing from our airline partners, they believe that they’ll be able to have full schedule integrity by the close of business on Sunday,” he said.

Bedford said every passenger would either be re-accommodated or will receive a refund but said “everyone should reach out to their air carriers directly.”

In an update Saturday, Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said officials see “zero evidence” the disruption was caused by a cyber attack or related to any AI systems.

He said the disruption was caused during “routine maintenance” to shift the network from copper wires to fibre.

“It’s pretty straightforward work that we were doing yesterday at a very remote location. So what we’re working to determine was whether we had incompetence, meaning was it user error or installer error from L3Harris or did they install a faulty router?” he said.

L3Harris owns and operates the FAA air traffic control communications system.

Duffy said the FAA has been working for some time to replace antiquated equipment that will bring its communications systems up to date with the latest technologies.

The FAA already replaced thousands of old copper wires with fibre optic lines and upgraded hundreds of radio systems as part of the overhaul that began last year after Congress approved $12.5 billion in funding. Duffy said he is pushing for $30 billion more to complete the work.

“The number one mission at the FAA and our air traffic organization is to fly people to their destinations safely and we will air on the side of safety. We’ll keep airplanes on the ground unless we are 100 per cent confident we’ve got the stability and the resiliency to operate safely,” Bedford said.

“I’m confident, very, very confident that the system is operating as safe today as it was two weeks ago,” he added.

Friday’s halt was the second nationwide ground stop of all departures since the Sept. 11, 2001 terrorist attacks. The other happened in January 2023, when the FAA paused all domestic departures for less than two hours.

– With files from Global News’ Colin D’Mello, The Canadian Press and The Associated Press

stories.title: Canada-U.S. trade deal must include viable auto sector, Carney says
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney says trade talks with the U.S. are making progress, but Ottawa won't accept a deal that doesn't allow for a viable auto sector.
stories.author: Dylan Robertson
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney says trade talks with the U.S. are making progress, but Ottawa won’t accept a deal that doesn’t allow for a viable auto sector.

“Lots of people think that we should just go and take whatever deal,” Carney said Saturday in Manila.

“This government will not settle for a deal with the United States that is not consistent with a viable Canadian auto sector.”

Carney was speaking at a news conference, three months after Canada pulled out of trade talks with the U.S., saying there had been last-minute demands from Washington that included a hit to Canada’s auto sector.

“This is one of the fundamental issues in our trade negotiation, and we are making progress toward that,” he said of the auto sector, adding it was also “one of the most challenging issues” in the talks.

Carney revealed he had “quite a long, substantive conversation” this week with U.S. President Donald Trump, in which both U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and Trump’s chief of staff Stephen Miller were on the line.

Carney said the American automotive market relies in part on Canadian manufacturing, and the continental industry is challenged by speed of production and by electrification.

“The sooner that we can get to a stable trading relationship under the new trade policy of the United States for the auto sector, it’s absolutely in the interest of course of Canadian workers, Canadian auto sector, but very much the U.S. as well,” he said.

Carney also said that Chinese investment in Canada’s auto sector is restricted to a set timeline and amount of vehicles, and will be reassessed based on multiple factors including the state of Canada’s integration into the U.S. automotive sector.

Carney also reiterated that Ottawa feels automaker Stellantis has not met obligations it took when accepting federal funds as it signed a deal to sell its Brampton, Ont., assembly plant to defence contractor Roshel.

“We’re not satisfied in any way with the current situation and the partial approach that Stellantis has taken here,” Carney said.

“The expectation is that Stellantis fully respects its engagements to the workers and to Canada.”
