stories.title: Expert insight: We found rare dinosaur tracks from the Coniacian age in British Columbia
stories.summary: The Coniacian dinosaur tracks were first found in Canada in 1988 but the remote nature of the site delayed further investigation until 2022.
stories.author: Special to Western News
stories.content:
Imagine the Western Plains of North America, from Texas to Alaska, submerged under a broad, shallow seaway. To the west lay the ancestral Rocky Mountains. To the east were low-lying plains traversed by large, sluggish rivers.

This was the landscape of North America in the mid-Cretaceous period – a geological age with a time span of 105 to 75 million years ago – when the global sea level was around 100 metres higher than it is now.

A high concentration of atmospheric carbon dioxide, due to massive volcanism, created a “greenhouse” climate such that Earth lacked significant polar ice caps. Alaska and Antarctica enjoyed temperate climates.

The record of dinosaur bones and tracks from this time in North America is sparse, especially from the Coniacian age – a sub-stage of this Cretacious period, spanning 89.75 to 86.5 million years ago.

We have discovered the first Canadian dinosaur tracks from this Coniacian age, in the Tumbler Ridge area of northeastern British Columbia.

One of us, Guy Plint, first noticed these tracks in 1988. However, the remote nature of the site, best accessed by helicopter, delayed further investigation until 2022 when, together, we were able to begin a more comprehensive study. The findings were recently published in Historical Biology.

The authors explore the Tumbler Ridge area of northeastern B.C., searching for dinosaur tracks. (Guy Plint)

North America has yielded an abundant record of dinosaurs, both skeletal material and tracks. Because dinosaur tracks can only be made and preserved in non-marine, terrestrial sediments, most North American tracks are found in sedimentary rocks laid down by rivers that drained the Rocky Mountains.

Their sediment load gradually built deltas and coastal plains along the Western margin of the Interior Seaway.

Over millions of years, the sea level slowly rose and fell, alternately narrowing and widening the coastal plain.

The late Cenomanian, Turonian, Coniacian and Santonian stages of the Cretaceous period – between about 95 and 84 million years ago – were times of exceptionally high net sea level when shorelines were pushed to the west, lapping against the foothills of the Rocky Mountains.

In Western Canada, Coniacian rocks are entirely marine with the exception of the small Tumbler Ridge area of northeastern British Columbia.

Ornithopods, or duck-billed dinosaurs, could stand on their hind legs. Here, the skeleton of a Hadrosaur duck-billed dinosaur is displayed in the Royal Ontario Museum in Toronto. (Wikimedia Commons/Thomas Quine)

Here, a river system built a delta that protruded eastward into the seaway. The deposits of that ancient delta are called the Marshybank formation, which, critically, includes some terrestrial strata that preserve the tracks we found.

In addition to these rocks of Coniacian age, the Tumbler Ridge area includes terrestrial deposits spanning much of the Cretaceous period. These have yielded an abundant and diverse record of other fossil vertebrate tracks.

These include traces of giant crocodiles, birds and pterosaurs, as well as abundant dinosaur tracks.

The Tumbler Ridge Museum is a repository and exhibition area for many examples of such tracks. The area was designated the Tumbler Ridge Unesco Global Geopark in 2014.

The Marshybank delta was very low-lying with shallow lakes, mires and floodplains traversed by sluggish, sinuous rivers. Abundant fossil roots attest to dense vegetation, and preserved tree stumps indicate stands of large trees, probably conifers like the dawn redwood.

River floods washed sand beyond the river banks to form thin sand sheets called crevasse splays.

The bottom surfaces of these splays preserve, as natural casts, a variety of dinosaur tracks, originally impressed in soft mud. The sandy banks of ancient river channels were also pervasively trampled by dinosaurs.

The most common tracks we found have three broad blunt toes and are typically 30 to 50 centimetres wide. These are ornithopod, or “duck-billed dinosaur” tracks. These large herbivores could walk on their hind legs, or shift to a quadrupedal gait.

The second most common track type has three, narrower and more elongated toes, tipped with claw impressions; we believe these to be carnivorous theropod dinosaur tracks.

We also found some rare rounded tracks with four or five indistinct digits, which might belong to ankylosaurian (“armoured”) dinosaurs.

The dinosaur tracks from the Marshybank Formation near Tumbler Ridge, which are mostly ornithopods, resemble a similar discovery from the contemporaneous Frontier Formation in southwestern Montana. They also have many elements in common with dinosaur fauna from the overlying Wapiti Formation (from 84 to 66 million years ago).

However, the ornithopod-dominated tracks of the Marshybank Formation differ markedly from those of the underlying Dunvegan Formation (97-95 million years ago) and Gates Formation (109-107 million years ago), which are dominated by ankylosaur tracks.

Fossil plants in the Marshybank strata include gymnosperms (for example conifers, cycads and ginkgos), ferns and horsetails. Most of the flora, however, are angiosperms (flowering plants) that May be distantly related to modern plane, poplar and willow trees, plus laurel, buckthorn, soapberry and low-growing shrubs and herbs.

Angiosperms evolved in tropical latitudes about 130 million years ago and spread rapidly to high latitudes, appearing in Alaska about 30 million years later.

Flowering plants provided a more nutritious and easily digested source of food than conifers, cycads and ferns. They were also faster-growing and better able to recover from cropping by dinosaurs.

The proliferation of the Coniacian herbivorous dinosaurs, particularly ornithopods, and the sustenance of the carnivores that preyed on them, is therefore related to the diversification and dispersal of flowering plants.Image 3: The Conversation

Guy Plint, Professor Emeritus, Earth Sciences, Western University and Charles Helm, Research Associate, African Centre for Coastal Palaeoscience, Nelson Mandela University

stories.title: Politics Insider: Stelco recalling 175 workers
stories.summary: Also, thoughts on why Eby lost and an update on the Darlington nuclear station
stories.author: Ian Bailey
stories.content:
Hello, welcome to Politics Insider. Let’s look at what happened today.

Stelco Inc. is recalling 175 laid-off steel workers effective Dec 1., seemingly ending a faceoff that started in early fall between Ottawa and the company’s parent, Cleveland-Cliffs Inc.

Niall McGee reports that Hamilton-based Stelco announced in a statement today that sufficient demand from customers for its steel made the recall possible.

The restart of operations will take several weeks. All affected employees will be compensated retroactively for any pay missed while off the job, the company said.

Stelco announced on Sept. 28 that it was laying off up to 500 workers at its plants in Hamilton and Nanticoke, Ont., because of its inability to make money in its galvanized-steel business. Ottawa almost immediately alleged that Cliffs had violated a legally binding commitment to maintain employment levels in Canada after it acquired the Canadian steelmaker in 2024.

This is the daily Politics Insider newsletter, curated by

. It is available exclusively to our digital subscribers. You can sign up for more than 20 other newsletters on

Eby seemed inauthentic during failed election campaign, former minister says: Brenda Bailey, who served as finance and jobs minister under David Eby, called last month’s crushing defeat of the NDP government in British Columbia a “harsh judgment” on the outgoing Premier’s leadership and his decision to call the snap vote.

Ottawa to invest $200-million in Woodfibre LNG project, source says: Owners Enbridge and Singapore-based Pacific Energy designed Woodfibre to produce 2.1 million metric tons of liquefied natural gas a year, all of which is contracted to BP.

Ontario spent nearly $13-billion and 20 years refurbishing the Darlington nuclear station. Why has it struggled?: Ontario Power Generation and Ontario’s government promised the refurbishment would position Darlington for 30 years of reliable service. It’s too early to know whether its recent unplanned outages amount to teething pains or indicate deeper reliability challenges of the sort that have plagued other refurbished stations featuring Candus, the country’s homegrown reactors.

Parliamentary break: Both the House of Commons and the Senate are on a break this week.

Prime Minister’s Day: Mark Carney was scheduled to arrive in Manila on Saturday for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit, which he is attending as a guest of the chair. He is to meet with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., and hold a news conference. Carney is on a trip that began Wednesday and also includes stops in Dublin, Phnom Penh and the Chinese city of Shenzhen (for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Economic Leaders’ meeting). His trip concludes Thursday.

Party Leaders: In Ottawa, Green Party Leader Elizabeth May is scheduled to attend Saturday’s announcement of the results of the party’s contest to pick a new leader. No schedules released for other party leaders. On Saturday, NDP Leader Avi Lewis will be in Winnipeg to address a convention of the Manitoba NDP.

Ministers on the Road: With the House of Commons on a break, ministers continue to travel Canada, talking about the federal budget.

In the St. John’s-area municipality of Mount Pearl, Fisheries Minister Joanne Thompson visited Solace Power . In the rural Nova Scotia community of Gaspereau, Justice Minister Sean Fraser talked about budget support for the Canadian wine sector.

In Thunder Bay, Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree talked about budget measures to advance reconciliation with Indigenous Peoples. Northern Affairs Minister Rebecca Chartrand did the same in Winnipeg.

In Woodbridge, Ont., Industry Minister Mélanie Joly, accompanied by Ontario Economic Development Minister Vic Fedeli, talked about the budget during an event. In Toronto, Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne participated in a armchair discussion hosted by the Empire Club of Canada.

Two ministers were out in Calgary. Crown-Indigenous Relations Minister Rebecca Alty attended an event at the Mini Thni Subdivision at the Bearspaw First Nation and Emergency Management Minister Eleanor Olszewski talked about the operation of the Productivity Mega deduction .

And in Vancouver, Energy Minister Tim Hodgson and B.C. premier-designate Lorne Doerkson made a funding announcement for a liquefied natural gas project.

New job for Merrifield: Katy Merrifield, the campaign director for the B.C. Conservatives, is joining GT & Company as a partner for the public affairs consultancy. An announcement on LinkedIn said Merrifield will lead GT’s practice across British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan while advising clients on federal matters.

“You look at how the world sees Canada today, and I would say the most sought-after currency today is trust. Who can you trust in this world today where you have extreme volatility?” – Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne , in Toronto today.

The Green Party of Canada is set to name a new leader this weekend, succeeding Elizabeth May. How many leaders has the party had since it was founded in 1983?

Scroll to the bottom of this newsletter for the answer.

Ottawa should adopt B.C.’s orphan port

For more than a century, private players have seen the advantages offered by the port of Prince Rupert. It is time Ottawa does the same. — The Globe and Mail Editorial Board

For an Anishinaabe jurist, the Canadian Museum for Human Rights’ Nakba exhibit gets a failing grade

The Canadian Museum for Human Rights has received piles of feedback about its small exhibition “Palestine Uprooted: Nakba, Past and Present” – both positive and negative. Perhaps the most surprising critique has not yet made it to its inbox. It’s a report by Anishinaabe scholar and retired justice Harry LaForme and his wife Janice LaForme, a lawyer, written for the Network of Engaged Canadian Academics (NECA), a non-partisan group of university and college faculty concerned about campus antisemitism. — Marsha Lederman, Columnist

Ottawa’s plan to sharpen oversight of banks’ anti-money-laundering efforts might work

Ottawa’s plan to designate OSFI as the primary supervisor of major banks’ anti-money laundering and anti-terrorist financing obligations could stem the rising tide of dirty money – but only if it does it the right way. — Rita Trichur, Columnist

Got a news tip that you’d like us to look into? E-mail us at tips@globeandmail.com . Need to share documents securely? Reach out via SecureDrop .

The answer to today’s question: The party has had 14 permanent and interim leaders, starting with Trevor Hancock.

stories.title: Shaping Saskatchewan: Naomi Lendvay
stories.summary: At just six years old, Naomi Lendvay was diagnosed with Rhabdomyosarcoma and was told she had just 12 months to live. Unexpectedly, a testing drug ended up killing her cancer.
stories.author: Chris Carr
stories.content:
At just six years old, she was in a battle for her life. Naomi Lendvay was diagnosed with Rhabdomyosarcoma and was told she had just 12 months to live.

Doctors started her on a ‘testing drug’ they hoped would extend her life. Unexpectedly, it ended up killing her cancer.

“Still to this day, we don’t know why, but I am very grateful it did, because I am still here to share my story,” said Lendvay.

Today, spends part of her time raising awareness and money for childhood cancer research. “Now I get to use my voice and inspire others to and help give others hope and make it, so others know what to fight for,” added Lendvay.

Lendvay recently shared her story with hundreds of people at the Synergy 8 Community Builders Drive for Kids Golf Tournament and Banquet. She said a mom reached out to her following the event to share her story about her child getting sick.

“When they went to the doctor, they were dismissive and not really taking in… the mother’s intuition. They knew something was wrong with their child. And that they were really sick,” said Lendvay. “She said she wouldn’t have fought as hard if she hadn’t have heard our story,” said Lendvay.

So, what does Lendvay think about the positive impact she’s having on others?

“I’m just glad we decided to take action and get the word out that kids get cancer too because it has probably really changed people’s lives, probably more than we know.”

Lendvay has since help raise more than $350,000 for cancer research.

stories.title: ‘How does space smell?’ Halifax students connect with Canadian astronaut aboard ISS
stories.summary: High school students in Halifax enjoyed the rare opportunity to chat with Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk, direct from the International Space Station.
stories.author: David Murdock and Rebecca Lau
stories.content:
High school students in Halifax enjoyed the rare opportunity to chat with Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk , direct from the International Space Station.

Kutryk, a former CF-18 fighter pilot, is serving as a mission specialist during a six-month mission , as part of Nasa’s four-person Crew 13.

On Friday, students at École Secondaire du Sommet had the chance to quickly connect with the crew.

“I thought it was amazing to have an opportunity like this to talk to an astronaut. It’s not something I thought I’d ever see in my lifetime,” said student Marie Gooding.

The school had a small window of time to chat: just 10 minutes as the station whizzed overhead at 25 times the speed of sound.

“I think the most interesting answer would be the reply to how does space smell and from what I remember, he said it smelled like iron or metal, which is very interesting, I hadn’t expected that,” said Gooding.

“It has pushed me really to go into the sciences and now it makes me want to be like a doctor. So while I might not be going into the space domain, it does make me want to learn a lot more about how space works and the planets that surround us in our universe.”

The Ariss, or Amateur Radio on the International Space Station, program is run internationally by volunteers and lets students speak directly with astronauts in orbit using ham radio.

The program aims to inspire students to explore science, technology, engineering and math through hands-on radio projects.

“Science is not just in their classroom, it’s not just what they learn out of a textbook, it’s really bigger than that. So to see if they can start making connections between what they learned and what they see outside in the real world,” said science teacher, Karen Scarcella.

For students, the chance to connect with a real-life astronaut was eye-opening.

“This inspires me to enter in like a space agency of some kind but not actually going into space, maybe working like a scientist at Nasa or something similar,” said student Christopher Succar.

stories.title: Montreal Trudeau International Airport says all flights to and from U.S. suspended
stories.summary: Montreal - Montreal Trudeau International Airport says all flights to and from the United States are suspended.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A countrywide grounding of aircraft in the United States on Friday afternoon was lifted about five hours after being ordered, but travel plans had already been disrupted for many Canadians hoping to head south of the border or come home.

The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration had issued a so-called ground stop order at around 4 p.m. eastern time, citing communications issues affecting the nearly two dozen air traffic control centres that direct planes en route between airports across the country.

Airports across Canada suspended flights to and from the United States. Air Canada said late Friday that it was cancelling the rest of those flights for the rest of the day.

Airports across Canada suspended flights to and from the United States after a U.S. officials issued countrywide ground stop order, though it was lifted hours later. At Toronto’s Pearson airport, passengers stood with their luggage, repeatedly refreshing their phones and looking for answers from airport staff. (Nov. 13, 2026)

The Calgary Airport Authority said after the ground stop order was lifted that it was making a similar move.

“All flights bound for the lower 48 states have now been cancelled out of YYC for Friday, Nov. 13, and some delays are still possible across other routes,” it said in a statement.

The Vancouver Airport Authority said continued cancellations and delays were expected, especially for flights to the continental United States and Mexico, as airlines worked to restore their networks.

Nav Canada, the privately run non-profit corporation that operates Canada’s civil air navigation system, said it would continue to ensure air traffic remains safe and efficient in Canadian airspace.

“Some delays May continue while operations return to normal and backlogs are cleared,” it said on social media. “Passengers are encouraged to check the status of their flight with their airline.”

Toronto Pearson International Airport said arriving and departing U.S. flights continued to experience disruptions and cancellations.

Earlier in the evening, passengers at Pearson stood with their luggage, repeatedly refreshing their phones and looking for answers from airport staff.

For Kelly Adenike, who was trying to get to Punta Cana in the Dominican Republic, the question was whether she would make it out of Pearson at all or end up back home in Kitchener, Ont.

“This really sucks,” she said. “Do they expect me to go home? Could they call it off soon? Maybe let us know if we can wait until midnight?”

Brenda Zhou and her daughter, Athena Guan, were supposed to fly to Miami, where Athena was scheduled to attend a college soccer identification camp.

The Toronto residents had checked in at Pearson and cleared the initial steps before U.S. customs processing was abruptly shut down, Zhou said.

“They just shut down everything and sent everybody out,” she said.

Air Canada rebooked them on a flight to Tampa for Saturday night, meaning her daughter would miss a camp session that morning.

Zhou said she had already paid for a hotel, a rental car and the camp registration fee, and did not know whether she would be able to recover those costs. She said they would head back home and were now hoping to make the camp on Sunday.

One Canadian trying to head back north of the border said the airplane doors had just closed on her flight from Nashville to Toronto when the captain announced that the plane would not be able to take off due to an unforeseen issue with air traffic control.

Samantha Chowen, who lives in Regina, said passengers were asked to deplane after about an hour.

She said she was told not to expect to fly home to Canada on Friday but to get a hotel and wait for further notice.

“They said they will be emailing us shortly with a rerouted flight but that right now they can’t guarantee when that will be,” said Chowen. “Kind of just sit and wait I guess.”

Chowen, who had been on a weeklong trip, said she tore her ACL on the third day of her vacation.

“I’ve been hobbling around just trying to get home,” said Chowen. “As long as I’m home by Monday to make my MRI, this is fine.”

U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters at the White House that nobody was in any danger during the communications failure.

“There was never any lives at risk,” Mullin said. “There was no flights at risk. FAA was able to handle it. We did it out of an abundance of caution.”

Mullin said the aviation agency was installing new equipment and it was “overwhelming the older system.” There appeared to be no indication of a cyberattack, Mullin said.

U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said there was no guarantee the scenario wouldn’t repeat itself.

“Is this exact thing going to happen again?” he said. “I don’t — I don’t know that this exact scenario will happen.”

Duffy also repeatedly called on Congress to authorize billions of dollars in spending to modernize federal aviation safety.

This was the first countrywide ground stop in the United States since January 2023, when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned. The last such shutdown before 2023 happened after the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.

stories.title: Nova Scotia gives family doctors a dedicated billing code for menopause care
stories.summary: Move recognizes the time proper consultations require, advocates say
stories.author: Kristy Kirkup
stories.content:
Family physicians in Nova Scotia who have recognized expertise in women’s health can now apply a dedicated code for compensation when they offer reproductive and sexual health services, including perimenopause care.

After Manitoba, Nova Scotia is the second province in the country to create a distinct billing code for specialized women’s health services, a change some health experts say is necessary to recognize the added time and expertise required to support patients navigating hormonal transitions.

Doctors do not require a certificate of added competence in family medicine to bill the code.

“Previously it wasn’t feasible, I think, financially to do the care, which is a huge problem in and of itself,” said Sarah Fraser, a family doctor based in Halifax. “Now it’s actually possible, and I think it’s encouraging.”

Doctors across Canada have traditionally used general assessment and consultation codes for perimenopause and menopause care, rather than a specific billing code.

But advocates say dedicated codes recognize that this kind of care often requires longer appointments to allow doctors to review patient history, address a wide range of symptoms and discuss a treatment plan.

“When we have a billing code, it allows us as physicians to be appropriately compensated but, more importantly, to be able to give women the time to ask their questions, and for us to be able to provide enough time to make them feel validated and heard,” said Shafeena Premji, a Calgary-based menopause specialist and medical advisory board member of the Menopause Foundation of Canada.

In Alberta, more than 300 physicians and menopause practitioners signed a petition last December calling for a menopause-specific billing code under the province’s public insurance plan. The petition described the absence of the code as a “major barrier” preventing equitable care access.

“This is a dire issue,” Dr. Premji said. “The sooner we do it, the sooner we’re going to be able to support half of our population.”

Women typically reach perimenopause and menopause in their 40s and 50s. While these hormonal changes are considered a natural part of the aging process, some women struggle with debilitating symptoms – including hot flashes, mood disturbances and trouble sleeping – and face barriers when trying to obtain care.

The new code in Nova Scotia took effect in July. Previously, family physicians could apply a consult code for providing menopause care, but many felt the fee was not clearly defined, creating confusion about when it could be used.

In October 2023, Manitoba became the first Canadian jurisdiction to create a billing code to compensate doctors specifically for menopause visits. Since then, Doctors Manitoba says, tens of thousands of such appointments have been covered.

Physicians in Manitoba can claim $93.66 for each assessment and additional tests; follow-up care is also covered.

Doctors Manitoba says this coverage stands in contrast with the hundreds of dollars patients are often charged for assessments when they turn to health care providers outside the public system.

Omolayo Famuyide, a certified menopause practitioner who founded the Layo Clinic in Winnipeg, which offers women’s reproductive health care, described Manitoba’s menopause billing code as “groundbreaking,” saying it’s been beneficial for both doctors and patients.

Manitoba is also one of only two Canadian provinces, along with British Columbia, that publicly fund menopause hormone therapy.

In Ontario, Sheila Wijayasinghe is among the family physicians who support creating a dedicated code.

“We can do comprehensive care in the public system. It’s just that we are often stretched for time,” said Dr. Wijayasinghe, who practices in Toronto.

“If you give us a designated code that allows us and acknowledges that it takes extra time, this could be very helpful.”

This sentiment was echoed by Aimee Debow, a Toronto-based menopause coach whose company, Menovate, works with corporations supporting employees through menopause.

She believes a dedicated menopause billing code could have been “life-changing” and spared her several years of suffering.

In her early 40s, she experienced perimenopause symptoms, including sleep challenges and brain fog, but felt dismissed by doctors. After countless medical appointments, she turned to the private system, which she knows many women cannot afford.

“It’s not just a code. It’s a code that actually gives the doctor enough time to help the person,” Ms. Debow said.

stories.title: Manitoba May need to spend far less on new power generation: Kinew
stories.summary: Winnipeg - Manitoba's premier says the province May need to spend far less than previously thought on new power plants.
stories.author: Ian Bickis The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Wab Kinew says the Manitoba Public Utilities Board has concluded that one natural gas-fired turbine is needed for now, at a cost of about $1 billion.

The Crown corporation Manitoba Hydro has maintained that three turbines, costing $3 billion, are needed to meet peak demands within a few years.

Article continues below

Angine de Poitrine debut third member in Toronto

The utilities board submitted its findings in a report to the government earlier this week, following lengthy hearings over the summer.

Kinew says Manitoba Hydro hasn’t seen the report yet, and he didn’t say when the government would make it public.

He says the news is good for both the province’s finances and the environment.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 13, 2026.

stories.title: U.S. grounds flights nationwide after air traffic control communication outage
stories.summary: The ​US Federal Aviation ‌Administration on Friday issued a national ground stop "due to ​extraordinary circumstance and ​reasons for safety."
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) grounded all departing flights nationwide after a communications failure hit air traffic control centres across the country, resulting in thousands of disrupted flights.

“The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following communication issues impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centres,” the FAA told Global News in a statement.

It said technicians are investigating the issue and it will provide updates as they become available.

The ground stop order is affecting flights between the U.S. and Canada’s major airports.

In a statement posted to social media, Toronto Pearson International Airport said flights were “impacted” and “there are currently no scheduled U.S.-bound departures or arrivals at this time.”

Vancouver International Airport told Global News it was aware of a “nationwide technology issue” that forced the ground stop.

“As a result, YVR is seeing delays for U.S. bound departures as well as some international flights that would fly over the U.S. Domestic flights within Canada are not impacted,” it said.

Edmonton International Airport told Global News in a statement that it has seven flights bound for the U.S. set to depart by the end of the day. It said these flights could be impacted.

“As this is an evolving situation, passengers travelling to the United States today should check directly with their airline for the latest information on their flight before coming to the airport,” a spokesperson said.

Montreal-Trudeau International Airport said on social media that “all flights to and from the U.S. are suspended until further notice.”

A spokesperson for Calgary International Airport told Global News all U.S. bound flights are being held.

Spokespeople for Saskatoon International Airport and Regina International Airport told Global News they have no scheduled direct flights to the U.S. for the rest of the day Friday.

A spokesperson for Air Canada told Global News that flights to and from the Caribbean and South America May also be impacted.

“Any flights currently airborne have been advised they are permitted to continue,” they said in an email.

The disruption ​is the latest sign of strain on the US air traffic ​control system, which has been beset by equipment failures, communications problems and shortages of ‌controllers ⁠while the FAA tries to replace aging infrastructure.

Congress approved $12.5 billion for the overhaul last year, and the FAA and White House asked lawmakers on Friday for another $30.1 billion.

Shortly before the announcement, the FAA halted traffic ​in Chicago due to ​air traffic ⁠control communications issues. The agency said, “All departing traffic should remain groundstopped until further notice.” The FAA said it ​would manage international flights on a case-by-case basis.

Friday’s halt ​was the ⁠second nationwide ground stop of all departures since the September 11, 2001, attacks. The other happened in January 2023, when the FAA paused all domestic ⁠departures ​for less than two hours.

With files from Reuters

stories.title: With no age requirement, Sobey Award recognizes well-established artists
stories.summary: The work of the six regional finalists is displayed at the National Gallery of Canada
stories.author: Kate Taylor
stories.content:
It has been five years since the Sobey Art Award eliminated its 40-and-under age requirement, a bold move then followed by an eventual suppression of the word emerging in its criteria. You can see the results at the National Gallery of Canada in this year’s exhibition of work by the six regional finalists, five of whom are in their 40s and 50s. It’s a tight show, smaller than in some years, including several works produced by what are clearly long-standing careers.

Although the marketing now sometimes talks about artists at “a critical juncture in their careers,” this is not an exhibition that gives the viewer any new clues as to what the 24-year-old Sobey Award is actually recognizing. Is it a prize for mid-career artists? Or underrecognized artists? On the positive side, the show in Ottawa is full of convincing work.

First up, as you enter, is Caroline Monnet, representing Quebec. The child of a French father and Anishinaabe mother who made their living renovating houses in Gatineau, Monnet is already well known for her work using construction materials to create patterns inspired by her Indigenous heritage. There is a strong selection here of her wall pieces created by embroidering or marking on various housing membranes – one provocative work uses mould to create a pattern on gypsum board – as well as a ceramic sculpture, a striking black and white geometric shape, technically an icosahedron, or an object with 20 triangular faces.

Monnet works intelligently with issues of Indigeneity and modernity – she enjoyed a large retrospective at the Canadian Museum of History this summer – and should have been on the Sobey short list before she hit her 40s, so this is something of a catch-up. There she is getting well-deserved recognition; better late than never.

Right across from her work is a large piece by Audie Murray, the candidate for the Prairies and the only artist here still in her 30s. So, she’s less well known and the tight show weighs against her because she is only represented by one piece. (Thankfully, the Sobey judges assess the whole career, not the exhibited works alone.)

For the show, Murray has marked the wall with ashes from a smudging, as though a fire had smoked it. Pleasingly minimalist, it’s a powerful gesture at the intersection of Indigenous spiritualism and Western art practice, where charcoal is a traditional drawing tool. However, it’s also a work that could use some space so that viewers could stand back and let its ideas breathe. Instead, it’s shoehorned into the gallery.

The New Brunswick artist Shane Perley-Dutcher, a member of the Tobique First Nation representing the Atlantic region, also mixes Western and Indigenous artistry to reflect on distinctions between art and craft in different traditions. He uses the materials of a metalsmith – copper, brass and silver – to produce sculptural versions of the ash-splint baskets of the Wolastoqey (Maliseet).

He is well-established in his practice. So too is Samuel Roy-Bois, a Quebecker who teaches at the University of British Columbia, Okanagan and represents the Pacific region. His highly intellectual art considers our relationship in space with both sculpture and architecture. He is represented here by two photographs featuring red aluminum ladders against a snowy landscape and an installation that reproduces, as fragile skeletons balanced on plastic pails, sections of the balloon framing used in domestic architecture.

Lotus L. Kang of Ontario is also no neophyte. She showed at the Venice Biennale this year, filling the pavilion of corporate sponsor Bulgari with her evocative installations of celluloid and light. Perhaps the most intriguing thing about her use of film is that it does not project any image; it only reminds you that it contains images. In Ottawa, she is showing Azaleas II , a giant spinning drum of a kind once used to dry developed photographic film where the strips mounted on it project faint moving patterns yet always decline to become a video. Fragile sculptural pieces – coloured glass bottles, an open notebook – are scattered on the ground beside it.

Meanwhile, Melaw Nakehk’o, a Dene/Denesuliné artist from Fort Simpson, NWT, who is representing the circumpolar region, is still at a stage in her career where she seems to be shopping around for the right medium and right motif. Her works here include semi-abstract paintings showing patterns created by strings of sinew, figurative paintings of a young woman and of a two-headed reindeer, and, more interestingly, a soft sculpture of caribou hide in which four tattooed hands fan out from a single wrist. The title is Mostly Human and suggests the artist’s most promising theme is metamorphosis.

Her work is like that of the Sobey nominees of old – emerging but not yet there. On Saturday, the Sobey judges will reveal whether they are choosing achievement or potential.

The 2026 Sobey Art Award Exhibition continues at the National Gallery of Canada in Ottawa to Jan. 3.

content_blocks.text: He is well-established in his practice. So too is Samuel Roy-Bois, a Quebecker who teaches at the University of British Columbia, Okanagan and represents the Pacific region. His highly intellectual art considers our relationship in space with both sculpture and architecture. He is represented here by two photographs featuring red aluminum ladders against a snowy landscape and an installation that reproduces, as fragile skeletons balanced on plastic pails, sections of the balloon framing used in domestic architecture.

content_blocks.text: Lotus L. Kang of Ontario is also no neophyte. She showed at the Venice Biennale this year, filling the pavilion of corporate sponsor Bulgari with her evocative installations of celluloid and light. Perhaps the most intriguing thing about her use of film is that it does not project any image; it only reminds you that it contains images. In Ottawa, she is showing Azaleas II , a giant spinning drum of a kind once used to dry developed photographic film where the strips mounted on it project faint moving patterns yet always decline to become a video. Fragile sculptural pieces – coloured glass bottles, an open notebook – are scattered on the ground beside it.

Her works here include semi-abstract paintings showing patterns created by strings of sinew, figurative paintings of a young woman and of a two-headed reindeer, and, more interestingly, a soft sculpture of caribou hide in which four tattooed hands fan out from a single wrist. The title is Mostly Human and suggests the artist’s most promising theme is metamorphosis.

stories.title: Alberta seeks to dismiss First Nation challenge of Premier Smith's sovereignty act
stories.summary: Edmonton - Alberta's government is asking a judge to strike down a First Nation's constitutional challenge of its sovereignty act, arguing the law hasn't had any impact on treaty rights.
stories.author: Lisa Johnson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Edmonton - Alberta’s government wants a judge to throw out a First Nation’s constitutional challenge of its sovereignty act, arguing it hasn’t shown any impact on treaty rights.

Lawyers were in Edmonton court Friday to argue over the government’s application to have the court strike the claim from Onion Lake Cree Nation and stop it from proceeding to trial.

Court of King’s Bench Justice Grant Dunlop reserved his decision.

Premier Danielle Smith won leadership of the United Conservative Party with the sovereignty act as her signature proposal in 2022, and it became her flagship first law.

Smith said the Alberta Sovereignty within a United Canada Act was needed to push back against federal encroachment into provincial jurisdiction.

When she invoked it for the first time, Smith conceded she didn’t need the law to implement new measures to fight against Ottawa’s energy regulations and that the act’s use was symbolic.

Onion Lake Cree Nation, which straddles the Alberta-Saskatchewan boundary, argues the act is unconstitutional because it goes against the Treaty 6 relationship with the Crown.

It has asked the court to declare it unenforceable.

Chief Pete Chief said the law was passed without meaningful consultation and raises serious questions about treaty rights and the limits of provincial authority.

He said those questions deserve to be heard by the court.

“Our treaty rights existed long before Alberta was created, and those rights did not disappear when the province came into existence,” Chief told reporters outside Court of King’s Bench.

The province argues the act doesn’t authorize anything that would go against the Canadian Constitution or federal law, and that the First Nation’s claim doesn’t show the act has affected any treaty rights.

Government lawyer Heather Campbell said Onion Lake didn’t provide any facts or evidence in its claim to show treaty rights have been infringed upon.

“On its face, it’s not unconstitutional,” she said of the law.

Campbell said the First Nation’s challenge amounts to premature, abstract speculation and unsupported hypotheticals.

The province’s application to strike the claim, filed in July 2025, also seeks legal costs, saying Onion Lake’s claim is an abuse of process.

Campbell said the government had no legal obligation to consult with First Nations before passing the law.

Onion Lake Cree Nation disagrees.

Lawyer Robert Hladun said that under the Constitution, governments have a duty to consult if legislation could possibly affect treaty rights.

“This isn’t rocket science or something that is speculative,” he said.

He also pointed to regulations related to the enforcement of federal firearms policy enacted by Smith’s government under the sovereignty act last year.

Hladun said because Treaty 6 guarantees rights to hunting, trapping and fishing, many rules regulating firearms are up to the nation, not the province.

Michael Marchen, another lawyer for Onion Lake, said Alberta declaring federal legislation unconstitutional, through legislature motions under its sovereignty act, creates a problem that demands the court step in.

“There’s a live legal issue to be determined,” he said.

Onion Lake also filed a similar court claim in Saskatchewan in 2023 over the Saskatchewan First Act, which asserts provincial jurisdiction over non-renewable resources, ON similar grounds.

In Alberta, the four-year-old legal challenge last made headlines in early 2025, as the long-simmering debate over separatism bubbled over.

Smith’s government tweaked provincial law, lowering the threshold for citizen petitions to prompt a referendum, including on the issue of secession. That drew protest from Indigenous leaders across the province.

At the time, Onion Lake Cree Nation Chief Henry Lewis said the moves signalled that Smith was pushing a separatist agenda, disregarding treaty rights.

Smith has maintained she wants Alberta to remain in Canada but that she supports giving Albertans a say through direct democracy.

On Oct. 19, Albertans voted overwhelmingly against beginning the legal process to hold a second, binding referendum on separating from Canada.

On Friday, Justice Minister Mickey Amery’s office declined to comment on the Onion Lake challenge because the matter is before the courts.

“The Alberta Sovereignty within a United Canada Act helps ensure Alberta’s voice remains firm on our priorities and gives us a way for our province to take strong and effective action against destructive federal policies,” it said in a statement.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 13, 2026.

stories.title: Organized crime suspected in rash of high-end car thefts in Sarnia
stories.summary: Sarnia Police believe organized crime is behind a recent rash of high-end Toyota and Lexus thefts in the city.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
Sarnia Police believe organized crime is behind a recent rash of high-end Toyota and Lexus thefts in the city.

Police say there were five thefts or attempted thefts in two days. Car thieves targeted Toyota Highlanders, Toyota Tundras, and various Lexus models – each typically valued at between $60,000 and $100,000.

Acting Inspector Kent Jamieson says they’re stolen from driveways or taken off the street from in front of homes.

“So, anybody who is scouting in the area can see that they’re there. Can see how readily available they are. How vulnerable they are to being stolen,” said Jamieson.

He also says the thefts are connected to organized crime involving suspected culprits from outside the area. Once a vehicle is taken it can be difficult to trace.

“There’s various ways that they can be sold. They can be re-identified. They can be shipped to other countries where any type of theft that happened over here, there’s no real accountability measures over there,” he explained.

Western University tech expert Apurva Narayan says thieves are becoming more technologically sophisticated, and can now use artificial intelligence to their advantage. He says they can enter and start a car without leaving a mark on it.

“When you unlock your car you send a signal to the car. That’s basically your security unlocking signal that goes to the car and they can actually monitor that. That allows them to replicate and do some type of signal attack. Then once that hits, they know what the vulnerability is and now they can unlock all these cars,” he explained.

In the meantime, police say prevention is the best protection. The Sarnia Police Service officers a security consult at no charge. You can have officers come to your home and do a full security check. It’s called Crime Prevention through Environmental Design.

“We have trained officers here. You can schedule an appointment and they will come visit you at your home, and actually go around the property with you and provide their suggestions based on their experience and training,” explained Jamieson.

Sarnia Police Service shared the following list.

Theft Prevention Tips

Residents can reduce their risk of vehicle theft by:

Parking vehicles inside a locked garage whenever possible.

Using a visible steering wheel lock, such as a “Club” style device. Physical anti-theft devices remain one of the most effective deterrents, as they require additional time and effort to defeat.

Installing an aftermarket immobilizer approved by insurers or vehicle manufacturers.

Parking another vehicle behind the targeted vehicle when parked at home.

Parking in well-lit areas and ensuring residential security cameras are operational.

Keeping keys and key fobs secured inside the home. While the current thefts do not appear to involve relay attacks, protecting keys remains an important theft prevention measure.

stories.title: ‘Intent is to try to appeal’ encampment cleanup order, Saskatoon organization says
stories.summary: Station 20 West says it received a notice to remove the encampment in front of its 20th Street facility from the City of Saskatoon but will not comply until the two parties meet.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
A Saskatoon organization said it will not follow an order to remove an encampment on its property until it can discuss the implications of that move with the city.

In the order to remedy the contravention, which is dated Oct. 30, the City of Saskatoon instructed Station 20 West to clean the encampment by Nov. 30. The notice states that more than 15 tents and structures are in front of the 20th Street facility, which is creating a nuisance for people in the neighbourhood.

The site is also in “an unsightly condition” and May provide a home for wildlife, according to the city’s notice.

Wanda Martin, the director of Station 20 West’s board, said that the city delivered that notice without any prior consultation on Sunday, when the building was closed. The community enterprise works to improve the wellbeing of those living in the city’s core and helps connect people with services – including those that can help find housing or employment.

“Our intent is to try to appeal the bylaw contravention, and to really support people as well as we can,” Martin said, speaking with Global News at the encampment site Friday.

In a news release shared earlier that day, the organization said it would not voluntarily dismantle the encampment without a conversation with the city about the expected consequences of that move on its residents.

Those discussions with the city would involve safety concerns and ensuring that appropriate, permanent solutions will be available for displaced encampment residents. If not, the problems that residents are facing would be shifted, not solved, the board director said.

Martin acknowledged the various safety concerns associated with encampments but said that removing the site does not provide a long-term solution for the people who live in it.

“While we don’t believe this is a great idea, for people to live like this, we do believe that just simply displacing them back to homelessness in another area only just moves the problem around,” she continued, adding that the people who live at the site have developed relationships with one another and Station 20 West staff.

In response to a request for an interview, the City of Saskatoon provided the following statement to Global News on behalf of Deputy Chief of the Saskatoon Fire Department (SFD) Yvonne Raymer.

“Station 20 West is privately owned and responsible (for) complying with The Property Maintenance and Nuisance Abatement Bylaw. The SFD does not publicly discuss operational plans when bylaw enforcement May be involved,” the emailed statement reads.

The bylaw cited by the city says that properties in Saskatoon must not negatively affect the safety, health, or wellbeing of those around them. It also bars nuisances on properties. The city’s definition of “nuisance” included “untidy or unsightly property.” The bylaw puts the onus of managing issues on private property on the land’s owner.

Mavis Daniels, 49, has lived at the encampment site at Station 20 West for a few weeks after another encampment, across 20th Street, was dismantled . She said the organization has helped provide her and other residents with food, clothing and washrooms.

“I tried finding homes everywhere; I’ve been on all of the housing sites,” she said. “I put my name down everywhere just to apply, but with my budget so low, it’s really, really difficult.”

“Winter is coming and I don’t know where we’re going to go if we get kicked out of here. Where is everybody going to go? We’re going to have to just post up anywhere and it’s just not going to work.”

Daniels said she hopes that the City of Saskatoon will work with the advocates to allow the encampment residents to stay at their homes.

stories.title: London art teacher recognized nationally for lasting impact on students
stories.summary: A longtime art teacher at H.B. Beal Secondary is one of five educators across the country to win a prestigious...
stories.author: Samantha Luis
stories.content:
A longtime art teacher at H.B. Beal Secondary is one of five educators across the country to win a prestigious art award.

Kim Davy, is the only teacher in Ontario to win the Rita L. Irwin Art Teacher Dissemination of Knowledge Award , through the Canadian Society for Education through Art.

Kim Davy (Credit: Thames Valley District School Board)

The nomination came from a former student, who is now enrolled at the Nova Scotia College of Art and Design.

“It’s so lovely,” said Davy, who has taught at Beal for 17 years.” I think because it comes from a student, it’s very heartwarming,” she said. “That a kiddo would think of me … because I had an impact on how they’re living their lives now or helping them find a direction that’s well suited, and they’re happy, healthy humans. That’s just perfect. It’s beautiful. It’s very affirming, right? It tells me that I’m doing the right thing, which I love.”

As Davy walked around Beal’s art department Tuesday, she took pride in her school and how much freedom and unique projects those that enroll have access to.

Students said Davy leaves a positive impact on everyone she has the opportunity of educating, “I love Mrs. Davy. She’s taught me a lot about how to explore my own style, and how to actually protrude the voice of the artist that I am,” said Kade Campbell, one of Davy’s post-secondary students.

Davy is a fixture in the Beal Art Program, which is a specialized program designed to help students move toward a career in fine arts. While it starts in Grade 9, the program offers students two years beyond Grade 12.

Ace Clements said Davy is always there for her students beyond the classroom.

“If there’s something that you need, she’ll be there,” said Clements. “If you have personal things going on, she will relate and help you through those.”

The Rita L. Irwin award is named for a University of British Columbia art professor who is deeply committed to the arts. It is meant to recognize art educators who foster “ meaningful learning through the visual arts ,” according to the Thames Valley District School Board news portal .

Davy’s students recalled inspiring sentiments the passionate educator has shared with them. “(Davy would say) ‘You really don’t have to be scared about talking about your art, because you’re a really great person, and I think that people should be happy to talk about you,'” said Campbell. “That made me feel really happy, because I’m not very great at talking about myself, and I’ve always struggled with that,” said Campbell.

Davy took great pride in boasting about the art around her.

Beal Art classroom (Credit: Sam Luis/ XFM News)

Amber Wallace said Davy’s encouragement “sparked (her) interest more in ceramics and being able to make forms freely.”

Davy was once a Beal Art post-secondary student herself. She then went to the Nova Scotia College of Art and Design, and 11 years later got her Bachelor of Education from Western University.

After finding out about her award, Davy was especially excited to her mom, who encouraged her to go into education as a past educator herself. “She’s very proud that I’m a teacher. She was very proud and very supportive that I would be recognized in this way and at a national level, which is so lovely,” Davy said

While students say they’ve learned so much from Davy, she said she’s also learned from them.

“I can honestly say that who I am as a teacher has been greatly impacted by the Beal art program,” said Davy. “We have this wonderful cycle of young people. They’re sensitive, they’re emotional, they’re figuring life out. I learn as much from them as I think they do from me.”

stories.title: Halifax council backs long-term strategy for fire services as population grows
stories.summary: The Halifax Professional Fire Fighters Union is praising Halifax council for taking steps to develop a long-term service and resource strategy.
stories.author: Angela Capobianco
stories.content:
The Halifax Professional Fire Fighters Union is praising Halifax council for taking steps to develop a long-term service and resource strategy.

The union says the service has been underfunded since amalgamation, and that it needs to keep up with significant population growth.

“I say the mountain continues to grow if we don’t continue to climb,” said Brendan Meagher, the union’s president.

“And so the deficits that we’re looking at now in our capabilities are due to the first 20 years after amalgamation of contracting our service. So it’s time to build.”

Coun. Janet Steele brought two motions to council on Tuesday to ask staff to develop a long-term strategy for Halifax Regional Fire & Emergency, noting that since she’s been on council, the department has come to budget meetings asking for more staffing and resources every year.

She hopes her motion will help with future planning.

“This is about more predictability for council, more transparency, a little more planning ahead, and I think it gives residents a better idea of what’s coming up as well as firefighters who serve all of us,” she said.

Coun. Tony Mancini says insufficient resourcing is part of the broader issue of rapid growth in the municipality.

“We have to add to that concern of infrastructure, in my opinion, our emergency services, both police and fire,” he said.

“Do we have enough as it is right now? And fire (and) emergency (services are) a very expensive business.”

Meagher says this work is a long time coming and hopes to see a significant increase in staffing as part of the strategy, as well as improvements to firefighting training for high-rise fires.

But he warns this can’t be a one-time endeavour and will require years of work that could be potentially expensive.

“I would suggest that if a good objective look is taken at the fire service, that the economic impact of not investing properly in emergency response is potentially catastrophic,” he said.

The motion passed at council unanimously.

stories.title: How Microsoft outage shows risk of tech monopolies: ‘We were just helpless’
stories.summary: Many businesses and consumers were unable to communicate through digital channels as a global outage of some Microsoft services left people scrambling.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
Many businesses and consumers were unable to communicate through digital channels as a global outage of some Microsoft services left people scrambling, and experts say this event further highlights the need for Canada to adopt more sovereign digital tech.

“The fact that Canada basically closed for business because one U.S. company had a glitch on some servers shows how dependent we are, how vulnerable we are,” says Joshua Pearce, who holds the Thompson Chair of Innovation at Western University.

On Thursday, the outage hit a wide range of Microsoft 365 offerings that interact with its Exchange Online and email services.

Services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot were reported by users to be down. As of publication, Microsoft said most services had been restored but fixes were still ongoing and there was no timeline for full restoration as of 3:00 p.m. Friday.

The full extent of the fallout from the outage is unclear, but regions spanning North America to the Asia Pacific were included in Microsoft’s updates, and the company reported its 365 suite of services had nearly half a billion paid subscriptions as of January.

“I was just shocked how much white collar work depends on the single Microsoft product, and when it’s down, really lots of people weren’t able to do their jobs,” says Emily Osborne, a policy research associate at the Canadian Shield Institute.

“There was nothing we could do to sort of address the outage as it was happening — we were just helpless to Microsoft’s control,” she added.

“We depend on so few providers, and when the services of one of them stops working that has a huge impact on our economy.”

Even the federal government said they were impacted by the outage, according to a statement in response to a Global News request Friday.

“The Government of Canada experienced impacts from the Microsoft service outage. Ensuring government digital services are secure, reliable and resilient is a priority, and we continually assess our systems and dependencies with that objective in mind,” said AI and Digital Innovation Minister Evan Solomon in a statement.

Diversifying reliance on different providers and expanding beyond some of the big American names can give businesses and consumers more options when a problem arises, experts say.

Osborne says having more sovereign digital providers is something that Canada could work on.

“There’s also certainly a role for the government to play. We’ve seen lots of governments in the EU making the very active and strategic choice to move away from products delivered by American firms. So that’s certainly something that Canada could consider doing to increase our resilience,” says Osborne.

“It would be hard to switch everything all at once, but there’s certainly an argument to be made for starting somewhere small with some sort of government communication platform that is a sovereign alternative — a privacy-preserving alternative to Microsoft products.”

Global News sent a request for comment to Shared Services Canada (SSC), the federal government’s IT provider, asking if a form of sovereign digital communications software is being developed or considered for use. A SSC spokesperson acknowledged the request, but did not provide a response by publication.

In the EU, a service known as Euro-Office is a suite of cloud-based digital sovereignty initiatives launched this year to serve as an alternative to American platforms like Microsoft 365.

“This is the actual data sovereignty or digital sovereignty we need to talk about is the physical infrastructure and the software that we use,” says Evan Light, associate professor at the faculty of information at the University of Toronto.

“It’s an open source office suite that does everything Microsoft Office does, but it’s developed by the European Union. It’s open source, it’s free, and it’s meant to be a project to sort of decouple the European Union from these tight, vulnerable things to American software.”

Light says these systems can be tailored and scaled to individual organizations, which can help limit the impact of an outage.

“So I could run a server here at U of T for my faculty, and if we need to reboot that thing, we’d reboot that thing and it affects a hundred people rather than millions.”

Experts says businesses and consumers should also have backup plans for technology failures, including maintaining alternative communications services to help limit disruptions.

“Thinking in terms of multi-homing and then having sort of multimodal forms of communication at your disposal rather than just getting into the habit of using one service all the time over and over and over again,” says Brett Caraway, associate professor of media economics at the University of Toronto.

“Institutions, I think, need to think more carefully about what they would do if they lost something. You’ve got to game that out.”

“There’s a lot of convenience and a lot efficiency that comes out of having a centralized coordination system, but it also exposes you to a great deal of risk.”

– with files from Global News’ Uday Rana

stories.title: Vancouver police investigating after local mosque vandalized with graffiti
stories.summary: Vancouver - Police in Vancouver are investigating after graffiti was discovered on the front doors of a local mosque.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver police say the case was reported by a maintenance worker, who flagged down patrolling officers in the area of West 8th Avenue on Friday morning.

The worker from the Al Masjid Al Jamia Mosque told police that graffiti that read “UK blood is on your hand” was spray-painted across the mosque’s front doors.

Article continues below

Angine de Poitrine debut third member in Toronto

No suspect has been identified or arrested.

Police say they have increased patrols in the area of the mosque and are asking anyone with information to come forward.

Investigators are also actively collecting evidence, and say police would like to assure Vancouver’s Muslim community that the crime will not be tolerated and May be pursued as a hate crime if evidence supports it.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 13, 2026.

Alberta implementing new oil royalty payment system to encourage production

stories.title: Alberta implementing new oil royalty payment system to encourage production
stories.summary: Calgary - Alberta's government is introducing a new royalty payment program that it says is aimed at incentivizing development in the oil industry.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Calgary - Alberta’s government unveiled a new royalty payment program Friday that it says is aimed at incentivizing development in the oil industry.

The application-based framework would give companies a guaranteed 10-year royalty schedule for new projects or eligible expansions.

They would pay two per cent of revenues for the first five years then see one per cent hikes annually until reaching a maximum six per cent.

Premier Danielle Smith said the goal is to stimulate investment and boost long-term oil production. It comes as her government is trying to fill Pacific Link, the pipeline the province is trying to build to the West Coast.

“To meet our goal of doubling oilsands production in the coming decade or so, we need hundreds of billions of dollars in new investment,” Smith told reporters, adding that Alberta needs to compete with the United States and Venezuela.

“Investors have choices about where they put that money, and we want them to put it here in Alberta.”

The premier also touted the benefits for Albertans when increased royalties are collected down the road from higher levels of production.

“Although royalty revenues from these new projects will be modest to start, eventually it means tens of billions of additional royalty revenues for the public programs and infrastructure that Albertans rely on,” she said.

The new royalty program is expected to be in place next year.

Earlier this month, several major players in Alberta’s oilsands posted multibillion-dollar profits in their latest quarterly reports.

The heads of those companies and others stood behind the premier as she made the announcement.

Kendall Dilling, president of a conglomerate of major oil producers called the Oil Sands Alliance, acknowledged the “optics” of the new program’s timing but said companies aren’t making expansion decisions based on today’s oil prices.

“We’re trying to predict what oil prices are going to be five, 10 years down the road. We can’t control that. So what we can control is things like predictable royalty rates for the first 10 years of a project,” he said.

“Those are the things that allow us to make the decision (to grow) that’s forward-looking like that.”

Rich Kruger, chief executive officer of Suncor, said Smith’s United Conservative Party government should be applauded for the new program.

“Make no mistake, when this industry does well in Alberta, Alberta does well,” he said.

“Record profits for the industry this year, record royalties, record taxes,” he said, “and that goes beyond Alberta, it goes federally as well.”

Janetta McKenzie, with the clean energy think tank Pembina Institute, criticized the new program, saying it hands more of the value of Alberta’s oil to corporate shareholders rather than Albertans.

“At a time when the industry is amassing billions in windfall profit due to the conflict in the Middle East, the private sector is absolutely capable of financing production expansion if they believed in sustained long-term oil demand,” she said in a statement.

Under the new program, the province said a project would fall back under the existing royalty payment system once its 10-year period expires.

Oil companies currently pay rates on a sliding scale, depending on the benchmark price of oil and whether a company has recouped the capital it puts into building a project.

If a company is still in what’s called the pre-payout phase, it pays rates between one per cent and nine per cent of gross revenue depending on the price of West Texas Intermediate, with the maximum taking effect when oil hits US$120 per barrel.

As of Friday afternoon, West Texas Intermediate was trading at about US$88 per barrel.

Finance Minister Jason Nixon, as well as government officials who briefed reporters, were unable to say exactly how much oil companies could save under the new program.

The officials said it would depend on the individual project and unpredictable factors outside the government’s control.

Only projects that plan to produce 5,000 barrels of oil per day would be eligible for the new program.

Nearly five million barrels of oil are produced per day in the province, said Smith.

Prime Minister Mark Carney designated the Pacific Link pipeline as a project of national interest last month.

The pipeline, with a price tag between $35 billion and $44 billion, would carry upwards of one million barrels of crude oil per day from Bruderheim, Alta., to a port near Delta, B.C.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 13, 2026.

— By Jack Farrell in Edmonton

stories.title: Students showcase their artistry at 25th Annual Juried Exhibition
stories.summary: Visual arts students showcased their creations Thursday at Western University. The visual arts department's 25...
stories.author: Callum Contursi
stories.content:
Visual arts students showcased their creations Thursday at Western University.

The visual arts department’s 25th annual Juried Exhibition included paintings, sculptures, videos and printmaking created by students in all levels.

“It’s my passion. It’s something I can’t live without,” said student Prinda Sudhikam, who won two awards at the exhibition.

Sudhikam’s work titled “Thai sweet mung bean rice-skin dumpling that looks like a zebra,” won the People’s Choice Award.

At the end of the event, which was held at Western’s John Labatt Visual Arts Centre, a jury of art professionals judged the works. Students could win up to $300 in cash prizes, subscriptions and gift cards.

“This is the first time I’ve ever won anything, this is a huge honour for me.” Sudhikam said.

Sudhikam said she used “pointillism” in her work inspired by her experiences scuba diving

Prinda Sudhikam photographed with her artwork at the Annual Juried Exhibition at the John Labatt Visual Arts Centre on Nov. 12 Callum Contursi/XFM News

For other students, having their art included was an achievement in itself.

“As soon as I got chosen, I felt very grateful and happy. It made me feel very valued and appreciated,” said Maya Dugas, a student whose work was featured in the exhibition as well.

“I would like to become a high school art teacher,” Dugas said when asked why she began studying art.

“That is my dream as of right now because my favorite teacher growing up was my high school art teacher.”

The exhibition will continue showcasing the students’ artwork from Nov. 12 to Dec. 3.

Maya Dugas photographed with her artwork titled “& we still met” at the 25th Annual Juried Exhibition at the John Labatt Visual Arts Centre on Nov 12. _mayadugas/Instagram

stories.title: Three plead guilty in connection with 2025 Best Defence Conference protests
stories.summary: Four people charged with mischief in connection with protests at a defence conference in London last year appeared in court Friday.
stories.author: Bailey Shakyaver
stories.content:
Four people charged with mischief in connection with protests at a defence conference in London last year appeared in court Friday.

The group was charged following demonstrations at RBC Place in October 2025. Police alleged that paint was thrown at staff, protesters barricaded the parking garage, and one person used a hammer to break locks on the building.

One defendant pleaded guilty to mischief and obstructing a peace officer and was sentenced to three years of house arrest, followed by a three-month curfew.

Two others pleaded guilty to mischief and received conditional discharges, while charges against the fourth defendant were withdrawn.

stories.title: OpenAI loses appeal to dismiss major copyright lawsuit by Toronto Star, other media
stories.summary: A coalition of media organizations, including the Toronto Star, alleges OpenAI illegally used news articles to train its generative AI software ChatGPT.
stories.author: Jacques Gallant
stories.content:
A lawsuit brought by Canadian news organizations against OpenAI can move forward in Ontario, the province’s top court ruled Friday, dismissing the tech giant’s argument that its lack of a physical presence in Ontario means the lawsuit should be heard in the United States.

The copyright lawsuit , filed by a coalition of media organizations including the Toronto Star, alleges the tech giant illegally used news articles to train its generative AI software ChatGPT and is now profiting unjustly.

California-based OpenAI had been looking to overturn a decision made last year by Superior Court Justice Jessica Kimmel, who concluded that the case was “sufficiently connected to Ontario” with three OpenAI-affiliated companies named in the lawsuit — OpenAI OpCo, LLC, OpenAI, LLC, and OpenAI, Inc. — being identified as doing business in the province.

Writing for a unanimous three-judge appeal panel, Justice Bradley Miller said Kimmel did not err in her findings, including that at least some of the affiliated companies “either made contractual arrangements in Ontario, advertised to users including in Ontario, or licensed their tools to customers either directly or through third parties.”

In other words, Miller wrote, the lower-court judge had found multiple instances of the companies carrying on business in Ontario.

The companies relied “heavily” on the argument that they didn’t have a physical presence in Ontario, Miller noted, but he said the case law cited by the appellants didn’t support their argument. He said Kimmel was not wrong to find that “there was a good arguable case that the appellants carried on business in Ontario for the context of assumed jurisdiction, even without a physical presence.”

“This decision matters well beyond the news media industry,” said lawyer Sana Halwani of the firm of Lenczner Slaght LLP, which represented the news media organizations. “Digital businesses earn money from Canadian content and users, and their activity reaches into Canada. When disputes arise, they must answer to Canadian law in Canadian courts.”

The media companies welcome technological innovations; however, all participants must follow the law, Lenczner Slaght LLP said in a written statement.

“Canadian journalism is created by Canadians, for Canadians, at significant cost. We look forward to having our clients’ claims decided on their merits by a Canadian court,” the firm said.

NEW York (AP) — A coalition of online safety and consumer advocacy groups on Thursday sued five of the world’s leading artificial intelligence…

OpenAI can still choose to ask the Supreme Court of Canada for permission to hear its appeal, although the country’s top court only agrees to hear a small number of cases from the Ontario Court of Appeal.

OpenAI did not respond to the Star’s request for comment by publication time.

The outcome of this case could have widespread implications for “a big range of copyright rights holders in Canada,” said Alissa Centivany, an associate professor of information and media studies at Western University.

“The issues at stake are significant; they’re huge,” she said, explaining that the scraping of online content for commercial purposes is a “global issue.”

Most jurisdictions allow content scraping for noncommercial or research purposes, said Centivany, “but we don’t have any jurisdictions that have said it’s OK to do this for commercial reasons or for reasons that involve creating expressive outputs that compete with the originals.”

“I hope and believe that courts will find that to be an infringing use,” she said.

The Court of Appeal ordered OpenAI to pay $100,000 in legal costs.

ChatGPT and other popular AI models have become the subject of litigation on a number of fronts.

Similar copyright infringement lawsuits are ongoing against OpenAI in the U.S., including one filed by the New York Times in 2023. According to the Times , 11 other publishers have joined the suit, which remains before a U.S. court in New York.

In a California court on Thursday, a coalition of online safety and consumer advocacy groups sued a group of leading AI firms, including OpenAI, to halt development, alleging the giants are unable to prevent the risk of “catastrophic” harm caused by their advancing AI models.

stories.title: Flu activity 'high' in several provinces including B.C., Alberta and P.E.I.
stories.summary: Toronto - Health Canada says flu activity is on the rise and expected to continue trending upward in the coming weeks.
stories.author: Hannah Alberga The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The federal health agency says several regions are seeing a ‘high’ percentage of cases testing positive including British Columbia, Alberta, Prince Edward Island and the Yukon.

The latest national data released Friday shows more than 4,200 influenza cases detected in the first week of November.

Article continues below
