stories.title: Remembrance Day ceremonies to honour CFB Wainwright fire victims
stories.summary: Wainwright - Four soldiers killed in a fire during a training exercise are among those being honoured today at a Remembrance Day ceremony in Wainwright, Alta.
stories.author: Bill Graveland The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Wainwright - Hundreds in a hockey arena stood for a moment of silence before Rev. Mokwadi Basele led them in prayer.

His thoughts were of the four soldiers killed more than three weeks ago in a wind-propelled grass fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright.

And he hoped for a quick recovery for the many others still in hospital with severe burns.

“God, we come closer to home, we come to Wainwright, as we remember the tragedy that befell this small town,” said the minister with Grace United Church at Wednesday’s Remembrance Day service in the town southeast of Edmonton.

“We lift up those who were injured and all who continue to heal in hospitals and at home, as well as comrades from the base and friends who live with shock and grief.”

The four who died were honoured at ceremonies across Alberta and Canada.

Pte. Shaun Farrell, 23, of Prince Albert, Sask.; Pte. Aidan Goulding, 23, of North Vancouver, B.C.; and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, 19, of Langley, B.C.; and Sgt. Morgan Wong, 26, of Edmonton died in the Oct. 17 blaze.

A few blocks from the Peace Memorial Multiplex, some left flowers and wreaths at the base of a historic, century-old fieldstone tower commemorating Canadians who died in the First and Second World Wars.

“We come every year,” said Wainwright resident Reimer Nielsen.

“This (Remembrance Day) is a little more sombre and more important to be here for the four.”

Veteran Sean Hansen said Remembrance Day is always special in the town, but it feels different this year because of the fire.

“Unfortunately, some paid with their lives and some are horribly scarred,” he said.

About 84 soldiers with the Charlie Company unit of the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry were taking part in attack training on Oct. 17, when a windstorm shot flames from a grass fire and onto the troops.

Thirty-nine others were injured. As of last week, the military said 25 were still recovering in hospital.

“These young people literally ran into balls of fire to save their brothers and sisters in arms,” federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said after attending the Wainwright ceremony.

He represents the riding of Battle River-Crowfoot, which includes the base.

“We think of their mothers, their fathers, their sisters, their brothers, their friends, and there are dozens of others who recovering from the most horrendous wounds imaginable,” he said.

“Third-degree burns on 80 to 90 per cent of their bodies. We reflect on the courage of the people on that day.”

Northwest of Edmonton, at least 2,000 lined a road leading to the St. Albert Cenotaph, a war memorial for local soldiers who died in combat.

Roughly 300 members of the same regiment caught in the Wainwright fire marched to the site.

Farrell’s family was also there, and they laid a wreath in his honour.

“We May not know much about the lives of the people who were recently killed or injured in Wainwright, yet each one of them lived and breathed among us,” Rev. Ken MacRae, a retired Armed Forces chaplain, told the crowd.

“They had or still have dreams of their own. They had or still have friends and family who love them.”

He said the names of the four killed in Wainwright are to be added to some cenotaphs and memorial sites across the country.

“God has not forgotten them, nor should any of us forget these individuals.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney, at a ceremony in Ottawa, honoured those in Wainwright.

He has called the deadly fire at the base one of the worst tragedies for the Armed Forces on Canadian soil during peacetime. Three investigations are looking into what happened.

Rabbi Idan Scher gave the benediction at the Ottawa service. He said Canadians united after the fire.

“Canadians lined up to donate blood, prepared meals for emergency crews, opened their homes and worked tirelessly to care for the injured,” Scher said.

“At a time when our world feels increasingly divided, these Canadians reminded us of what truly matters. They did not ask what their neighbours believed, where they came from, or whether they saw the world the same way.

“They simply asked, ‘How can I help?’”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 11, 2026.

— With files from Jack Farrell in St. Albert, Alta.

stories.title: Toronto ceremonies at Queen's Park, Old City Hall among those marking Remembrance Day
stories.summary: Toronto - Provincial and municipal dignitaries are set to join veterans and their families today at Remembrance Day ceremonies in Toronto.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - As John Anderson prepared to lay a wreath at a Remembrance Day ceremony in Toronto, the retired Canadian Navy lieutenant said he would be thinking of people who were part of his service “brotherhood.”

The Cambridge, Ont., resident who was in the navy for more than 40 years said taking part in the solemn ceremonies every year is a particular honour.

“It honours the people who served to give us what we have today and the current people that are serving,” he said. “You bring them together, it’s like one big brotherhood.”

The 79-year-old, who said he helps connect veterans with the services they need, was in the large crowd gathered around the Old City Hall Cenotaph on Wednesday to honour the sacrifices of Canada’s veterans and soldiers.

Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow also commemorated the Legion on its 100th anniversary during her remarks at the event.

“The Legion shows us the city we can be. A city where no one carries the burden alone. A city where we take care of each other and stand up for each other,” she said.

About two kilometres away, many more joined a ceremony outside Queen’s Park, where Ontario Premier Doug Ford said this Remembrance Day “is especially poignant” after the devastating fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta that killed four soldiers and injured dozens of others.

“I want to thank all the heroic Ontario health-care workers who were deployed to support recovery efforts and continue to pray for those impacted by the fire,” he said.

“Whether it’s a family member or a friend who answered the call to serve, or someone who came home with wounds, visible and invisible, Remembrance Day holds a special meaning for each of us.”

Brig.-Gen. Éric Landry, who has served in Afghanistan in leadership roles, thanked every member of the Canadian Armed Forces who has chosen to defend the country.

“We are a very reliable ally. We are the neighbour every country (wishes) they had,” he told the crowd at Queen’s Park.

Landry spoke of Canada’s role in the U.S.-led war in Afghanistan, 25 years after it began.

“We deployed 40,000 troops to Afghanistan over 15 years; 158 of us never came back. And all of us who did come back were changed forever,” he said.

“So I want to thank everybody, but I want to tell them also that this is worth it. Canada is worth defending.”

Landry also honoured the four soldiers who died in the Wainwright fire, saying they will never be forgotten.

Other Remembrance Day ceremonies were also held in Toronto, including at the Fort York National Historic Site and the Toronto Zoo.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 11, 2026.

stories.title: From activist to academic, Bessie Borwein never stopped connecting people
stories.summary: Her family remembers her as a fierce, brilliant, loving woman who made lives better by her presence in them
stories.author: The Globe and Mail
stories.content:
Bessie Borwein: Matriarch. Scientist. Communicator. Connector. Born March 17, 1927, in Johannesburg, South Africa; died June 9, 2026, in London, Ont., of natural causes; aged 99.

Bessie Flax – not short for Elizabeth or Beatrice, just Bessie − grew up under the dual shadows of apartheid and the Holocaust, danced with Nelson Mandela in her student activist days, married at 19 and spent the next 75 years building a life defined by a relentless impulse to make the world a better place.

Bessie and David Borwein grew up together in the Johannesburg Jewish community. David was three years older and tutored her in math when she was an undergrad at University of Witwatersrand in Johannesburg. They married in 1946.

The couple left South Africa two years later to live in London where David pursued a DPhil in mathematics and Bessie started a PhD in botany. After the Nationalist Party came to power in 1948, David used to say that they could never go back as Bessie would have spent her life in jail – a statement he made with equal parts pride and genuine assessment of the risks.

David’s first teaching position was at the University of St. Andrews in Scotland. Bessie cried when she heard the news – she did not want to go somewhere so cold and dark and small. In the end, they loved it and spent 15 happy years there, welcoming three children, Jon, Peter and Sarah. Bessie and her family also became British citizens.

Ever adventurous, in the 1960s, the family of five immigrated to Canada – to London, Ont., a place they had never heard of – for a one-year sabbatical at Western University. They decided to make Canada their home and became Canadian citizens in 1982.

In London, Bessie began working as a lab technician and a professor at the university encouraged her to pursue graduate work. She completed her PhD in anatomy in 1973. Bessie studied the eyes of Anableps anableps , a quirky fish that swims at the water’s surface and thus sees two worlds at once. This was something that her daughter always found fitting.

Bessie was the answer to anyone who ever said it was too late to start. She had an extraordinary, illustrious career that didn’t start until she was nearly 50. She became an associate professor at Western University then associate dean of medical research. She served on the Research Ethics Review Board, founded a non-profit that educated the public on science, worked with the Alzheimer’s Society in Ontario, the Ontario Breast Screening Program, Madame Vanier Children’s Services and the Youth Science Foundation, among other gigs. She also won a list of awards and recognitions too long to recount here.

Bessie was a do-er. If there was a problem, she needed to help solve it. In 1968, when a neighbourhood child went missing, she spearheaded the Block Parent program, a network of safe homes each marked by a sign in the window. London was the first city in Canada to have it and it spread across the country.

She never stopped connecting people to each other – spotting the invisible thread between two people and pulling until they met. Bessie often sent packages of random newspaper clippings to her children, simply to say she was thinking of them. She signed every note “YDM” (for Your Devoted Mother). She also took in a cousin’s daughter and rewrote two futures in a single act of kindness – hers, and Sarah’s, as they became as close as sisters.

Bessie took infectious joy in her grandchildren and became a devoted and loving grandmother to all nine of them. Her home was a haven, full of warmth, heated political argument and David’s dry wit. He used to say their 75-year marriage worked because of the division of labour: He did the division, she did the labour.

She outlived her sons Jon and Peter, and David. Bessie carried those profound losses in her body and over the years, slipped away from the world. But the Bessie her family remembers was a fierce, brilliant, loving woman who made lives better by her presence in them.

Bessie was close to 100 before she died. Had she been a little more present, she might have held on for that telegram from the king.

Sarah Borwein is Bessie Borwein’s daughter.

stories.title: ‘Normal is back’: Federal Conservatives get a lesson in unity from their B.C. cousins
stories.summary: 'The biggest lesson you can take away from B.C. politics is that things can change quickly, and expect the unexpected,' MP Aaron Gunn said
stories.author: Sarah Ritchie
stories.content:
Ottawa — When Aaron Gunn first walked into the House of Commons after the provincial B.C. Conservatives won their election last month, he was met with high-fives and claps on the back from his colleagues.

The victory offered a morale boost to a federal Conservative caucus that’s had few of those in the last year.

Gunn said the win is evidence the Conservative brand is “alive and well” in Canada, but the B.C. MP isn’t convinced the federal party can draw much from the success, given the strange set of circumstances that preceded the election.

“The biggest lesson you can take away from B.C. politics is that things can change quickly, and expect the unexpected,” Gunn said.

B.C. Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson rose from being a backbench MLA to the office of British Columbia premier in a matter of weeks, after NDP premier David Eby gambled an early election call on the turmoil within the conservative movement.

Doerkson’s first order of business after learning his colleagues had chosen him to succeed ousted leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay — after flying home from South Africa — was to get everyone into the same room.

After months of vicious infighting, Doerkson’s party pulled together in a hurry.

That happened, in part, because everyone knew an election was coming whether they were ready or not. It was also a deliberate strategy: unity was campaign director Katy Merrifield’s “biggest priority.”

“We in B.C. on the centre-right are very accustomed to doing exactly (that): focus on the 70 per cent of things you can agree on, drop egos. Everyone get inside the tent and work together,” she said.

That’s a lesson Merrifield said can apply to any political party.

Gunn, a first-time MP who was a key part of building the current version of the B.C. Conservatives, was “very close” to running for the provincial party leadership last winter. He had to sit back and watch as the party’s spring leadership race turned nasty.

B.C. Conservative Party Leader Lorne Doerkson on election night in Vancouver on Oct. 24, 2026. Arlen Redekop / Postmedia

Findlay won narrowly at the end of May, but bitterness lingered between her supporters and those who’d backed her primary opponent, Caroline Elliott.

Federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre waded into the fray over the summer by taking a verbal shot at the “Liberal lobbyists from out east” who’d worked against Findlay (a shot intended for Ontario Premier Doug Ford and his former campaign manager, Kory Teneycke, but one that landed hard among the rest of Team Elliott).

Elliott responded with a social media video calling on everyone to “unite, not divide.”

The fractures cracked wide open in the early fall, with a chaotic stretch of staff hirings followed swiftly by firings and the departure of 13 MLAs. It became clear Findlay couldn’t continue.

When the election was called and Doerkson was chosen as leader, many of those recently departed MLAs were brought back into the fold.

“Everybody showed up, and it’s like, ‘Let’s see if we can put Humpty Dumpty back together again,’” Gunn said.

Anthony Koch, who was a senior adviser on Doerkson’s campaign, was among those who jumped back into the fray after working on Elliott’s leadership run. A key takeaway for him is that tone matters.

“Yes, you need to motivate your people. Yes, you need to be a real conservative. But you also need to present yourself in such a way that no one’s scared by the prospect of you forming government,” said Koch, who was communications director for Poilievre’s 2022 leadership campaign.

Doerkson’s Conservatives didn’t compromise on principles, Merrifield said. The party pledged to get rid of Dripa, the controversial NDP law to enact the UN Convention on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, and end the sexual orientation and gender identity policy in education.

“I can’t point to any policy that Kerry-Lynne Findlay announced that Lorne Doerkson came in and reversed and abandoned,” said Gunn.

“But the tone and how those issues were communicated, I think, did change significantly.”

Insiders describe Doerkson as a “happy warrior,” a consensus builder and a regular guy.

Merrifield said she thinks his appeal, similar to that of Prime Minister Mark Carney, demonstrates that the era of anger-driven politics is out, at least for the moment.

“Normal is back,” Koch said.

Politicians like Justin Trudeau, who energized progressives, or Donald Trump, who ignited the Maga base, are falling out of favour with an electorate that’s now looking for “more calm, competent, normal, adult-like politicians,” he said.

Merrifield, who was Poilievre’s communications director last year, was credited with encouraging the Tory leader to change his strategy and tone after losing the 2025 election. For a brief period during her tenure, he spoke more with mainstream media and sat down with popular podcasters like Joe Rogan. But the party continues to struggle in the polls.

Gunn acknowledged Poilievre has tried to shift his tone — a number of times, in fact — over the last two years, but maintains that another adjustment is not what’s needed.

“What I think we need to continue focusing on is staying true to your values, principles and beliefs, while also trying to be as welcoming to as many Canadians as possible,” he said.

Koch is still firmly in the camp of those who believe Poilievre is the best person to lead right now. He has the support of caucus, and earned the support of delegates at this year’s leadership review.

But caucus morale took a series of blows over the last year as four MPs crossed the floor, and a fifth joined the Senate. Two others have left, and byelections to replace them in Yorkton-Melville and Brantford-Brant South on Dec. 7 are being closely watched.

Poilievre already weighed in on the Ontario race, installing a candidate instead of allowing an open nomination, and in the process blocked a local party organizer who had the backing of outgoing MP Larry Brock. Dave Carrol is now running as an independent in what’s expected to be a tight race.

With polls continuing to place the Conservatives a distant second to Carney’s Liberals, losing Brantford-Brant South could be another mark against Poilievre.

Koch said there is another cautionary tale for federal Conservatives in all of this: if you rewind the clock to early September, British Columbia’s centre-right looked like it had been cleaved into at least three parts.

For some Tories, the disastrous outcome the B.C. Conservatives narrowly avoided is just as instructive as the party’s electoral triumph.

Sarah Ritchie joined National Post’s politics bureau after four years covering breaking news on Parliament Hill for The Canadian Press, where she worked as a reporter and editor. Before that, she was an anchor and investigative reporter at Global News in Halifax and covered the Nova Scotia legislature for CTV Atlantic.

stories.title: House unanimously passes Conservative MP’s bill honouring son who died by suicide
stories.summary: Ottawa — The House of Commons has unanimously adopted a bill introduced by Conservative MP Luc Berthold, in memory of his son, that aims to help young people struggling with addiction.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
OTTAWA — The House of Commons has unanimously adopted a bill introduced by Conservative MP Luc Berthold, in memory of his son, that aims to help young people struggling with addiction.

The Quebec MP, who also serves as deputy House leader for the Official Opposition, has been championing the legislation while grieving the loss of his son David, who died by suicide after struggling with addiction and encounters with the justice system.

Bill C-231 was given the alternate title “For the Friends of David Law.” It would allow youth courts, in certain circumstances, to delay sentencing for a young person found guilty of an offence, allowing them to participate in a substance abuse treatment program or another type of treatment program.

The bill would amend the Youth Criminal Justice Act to give courts that option.

Shortly before the Commons unanimously adopted the bill on Monday, Berthold addressed his son during an emotional speech that noted it would have been David’s 30th birthday.

“Today, David, the House of Commons is unanimous. Your life, your experiences, your joys, your sorrows, none of it will have been in vain,” he said.

“Your life will serve as an example to perhaps help other young people avoid going through all the hardships you went through, perhaps make different choices, and help young people choose a path that will allow them to be here for their 30th birthday.”

Before Bill C-231 can become law, it must pass through the Senate and receive royal assent from the Governor General.

Speaking to reporters alongside his wife, Caroline, and daughter, Justine, Berthold said he was taking his grief “one day at a time,” with some days more difficult than others.

Berthold, a former mayor of Thetford Mines, Que., was first elected to Parliament in 2015.

“I think we started out with the idea of doing something, of giving meaning to something that makes no sense, in order to help other people,” Caroline said.

Both of David’s parents said that during a period when he was doing better, their son had expressed a desire to help “his friends.”

“He even had plans with his father to give talks to help young people, so I think this bill is, in a way, making the help David wanted to provide a reality,” Caroline said.

Berthold said he hopes the Senate will move more quickly than the House of Commons in advancing Bill C-231.

At the same time, the Conservative MP welcomed the collaboration among lawmakers from all parties during the bill’s consideration.

He also thanked public servants, noting that his original proposal had been broadened to give young people access not only to addiction treatment but also to other forms of care, including mental health treatment.

“We really had great collaboration from everyone to make this bill something that will, I hope, change the lives of many young people,” Berthold said.

Asked what would be needed to ensure provincial and municipal governments have the resources to provide appropriate addiction treatment programs, the Quebec MP said the bill was a first step.

“Our goal is to raise awareness among people, but also among governments, so that when a judge tells a young person to go to a treatment centre, there will be one available to them, and access won’t depend on their parents’ financial means,” he said.

Berthold criticized what he described as a “two-tier system,” in which lower-income families struggle to help their children access the resources and support they need.

He said raising awareness would be “the next step once we’ve completed all the stages of the legislative process here.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 17, 2026.

Émilie Bergeron, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Cadet captain paralyzed from waist down after Hamilton attack
stories.summary: Police have said the Nov. 8 attack stemmed from a confrontation over the harassment of young cadets selling Remembrance Day poppies.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A cadet leader who underwent spinal surgery after a violent attack says he is currently paralyzed from the waist down and will require months of physical rehabilitation.

Capt. Kenneth Kunkel provided an update on his situation last week in a statement shared online by a Hamilton member of Parliament.

Kunkel says he is in continual pain and his doctors cannot give him a prognosis at this time, but he remains “hopeful and positive.”

He thanked those who have reached out to express support or donated to an online fundraiser set up for his family.

Police have said the Nov. 8 attack stemmed from a confrontation over the harassment of young cadets selling Remembrance Day poppies.

They said two youths approached young air cadets who were selling poppies in front of a restaurant on Barton Street East and blew an air horn “directly into their ears.”

Investigators said a man who was supervising the cadets followed the youths into the restaurant to confront them, leading to a struggle.

They allege a woman jumped in to help the youths and assaulted the air cadet leader, who fell to the ground. One of the boys allegedly hit the man multiple times.

A 12-year-old boy and a 48-year-old woman were charged with aggravated assault in the incident.

In his statement, Kunkel said he wanted to clarify some details of what happened that day.

He said he confronted a youth in the restaurant about assaulting one of the cadets and told him they needed to go to the front and call police. The youth “immediately tried to run away,” Kunkel said, adding he grabbed the youth’s backpack and started walking toward the front of the restaurant while asking staff to call police.

The youth started punching him, he said, and a woman intervened on the youth’s behalf. Kunkel said he told her the boy had assaulted a cadet and they needed to speak with police.

While his attention was on the woman, the boy grabbed the lanyard holding Kunkel’s car key and ripped it off his neck, he said. When Kunkel reached to grab it back, the woman “blindsided” him, slamming him into a concrete pillar, he said.

“My legs buckled beneath me and I collapsed,” he said. “While I was lying on the ground helpless, the young male proceeded to violently punch me directly in the face numerous times.”

Kunkel was taken to hospital and underwent surgery that night, he said.

A GoFundMe page set up on behalf of Kunkel and his family said he is the commanding officer of 826 Gryphon Squadron Royal Canadian Air Cadets, and has been with the cadets for 20 years.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 17, 2026.

stories.title: National Congress of American Indians calls on Trump to reverse Lake Ontario change
stories.summary: The National Congress of American Indians is calling on U.S. President Donald Trump to walk back his August executive order renaming Lake Ontario as Lake America.
stories.author: Alessia Passafiume
stories.content:
The National Congress of American Indians is calling on U.S. President Donald Trump to walk back his August executive order renaming Lake Ontario as Lake America.

The organization, which represents American Indian and Alaska Native tribal governments in the United States, says the order demonstrates disrespect for Indigenous geographic names and Indigenous cultural, spiritual and historical relationships with lands and waters.

A resolution rejecting the name change, passed at the organization’s October assembly, was introduced by the Seneca Nation of Indians, a community based in western New York.

Trump directed all arms of the federal government to start calling the body of water Lake America in August, to the dismay of Haudenosaunee communities on both sides of the border whose languages are the source of the name “Ontario.”

Lake Ontario is known in Seneca as “sga:nyodai:yoh,” meaning “beautiful lake,” and in Wendat as “ontari:io,” meaning “the lake is beautiful, the lake is big.”

The resolution says unilateral efforts to rename geography risk erasing Indigenous history and calls on the U.S. federal government to suspend its use of the term “Lake America.”

“The National Congress of American Indians opposes the removal, replacement, or erasure of Indigenous names of lakes, rivers, mountains, and other geographic features and calls upon federal, state, and local governments, geographic naming authorities, and public and private entities to preserve and respect those names in consultation with affected Tribal Nations,” it says.

“Lake Ontario is one example of the enduring Indigenous relationships with geographic features that this resolution seeks to protect, having been known to and used by the Seneca and other Haudenosaunee peoples since time immemorial for travel, trade, diplomacy, subsistence, and cultural practices, and bearing a commonly used name derived from Indigenous linguistic roots.”

Wendat Nation Grand Chief Pierre Picard told The Canadian Press his nation was “shocked” to hear about Trump’s renaming of Lake Ontario. He called it an attempt to eradicate their history in the region.

The Wendat occupied parts of the St. Lawrence Valley up to the Great Lakes and the area was rich with both pre- and post-contact trade routes.

The name Lake Ontario predates the founding of both Canada and the United States.

Trump’s move was ridiculed by Wisconsin Gov. Tony Evers, a Democrat. He posted a video of himself at a McDonalds restaurant, signing a fast food napkin to decree that Lake Michigan would now be called “Lake Wisconsin.”

“See, I can sign napkins that say things, too,” Evers wrote on X at the time.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has said the lake remains Lake Ontario “then, now and always.”

stories.title: Ontario secondary teachers vote 96% in favour of strike mandate
stories.summary: The vote by teachers represented by the Ontario Secondary School Teachers' Federation comes before central bargaining has fully started, with negotiations beginning next week.
stories.author: Allison Jones
stories.content:
A second public high school union now has a strong strike mandate, raising the risk that the Ford government could be facing widespread teacher walkouts across the province if contract negotiations are not ironed out.

The Ontario Secondary School Teachers’ Federation (OSSTF) announced Tuesday that the public high school teachers it represents have voted 96 per cent in favour of giving their union a strike mandate if necessary.

Those results come one day after Ontario Catholic teachers voted overwhelmingly in favour of a strike mandate, with 98 per cent voting yes.

“(Teachers) working in publicly funded high schools are sending a clear message to this minister that they cannot continue to do more with less,” said OSSTF president Martha Hradowy.

OSSTF’s education worker members also voted 92 per cent in favour of a strike mandate. The vote comes before central bargaining has fully started, with negotiations beginning next week.

“Our members have given us a clear mandate that they want investments in public education. They want supports for their students, and quite frankly, they want respect restored to the teaching and education profession. And that’s what we’re going to get to the table,” she told reporters Tuesday.

1:47 Ontario Catholic teachers deliver strong strike mandate

A strike mandate does not mean a strike will happen, with additional legal steps required before one could take place.

Hradowy said teachers have been pushed to the brink in their profession due to the Ford government under-funding education.

She said teachers across the province have been concerned about ballooning class sizes, less support for students and less respect for educators as the system is buckling due to staff shortages.

“Ontario parents are having to keep their children at home because there isn’t enough support for their child in classrooms, and that is not unique,” she said.

Cuts to staffing for educational assistance, speech language pathologists, professional supports and social workers, she said, have left teachers responsible for dealing with complex student needs without assistance and vulnerable to workplace violence.

“We should not be going to the bargaining table, just asking for the basics in public education,” Hradowy said.

Ontario teachers have been left with no contract since August. Bargaining has been delayed as the government and major education unions were at an impasse on what issues should be negotiated centrally and what should be left to local unions and boards.

OSSTF and the other education unions have said they encouraged the government to begin negotiations early in the spring, but they were ignored.

Education Minister Paul Calandra said the recent union votes are not unusual to the bargaining process and it’s an indication that members are urging the unions and the government to negotiate a fair agreement.

“These numbers aren’t surprising or shocking to me. I mean, you go back over 30 years, the numbers remain consistent no matter who’s in office,” he said.

He said it’s the unions who took their disputes to the Ontario Labour Relations Board, while the government has been “open” for negotiations.

The government can’t “give them anything that they want,” he said. “I have to balance taxpayers.”

NDP Leader Marit Stiles said Calandra is wrong to view the strike mandate vote results as an indication of support for his ministry.

“It’s saying very clearly that this minister has failed,” she said. “All you have to do is listen to a parent, a student, any education worker right now and they will tell you firsthand that this is unsustainable.”

OSSTF and the other education unions have said they encouraged the government to begin negotiations early in the spring, but they were ignored.

Education Minister Paul Calandra said the recent union votes are not unusual to the bargaining process and it’s an indication that members are urging the unions and the government to negotiate a fair agreement.
“These numbers aren’t surprising or shocking to me. I mean, you go back over 30 years, the numbers remain consistent no matter who’s in office,” he said.
He said it’s the unions who took their disputes to the Ontario Labour Relations Board, while the government has been “open” for negotiations.
The government can’t “give them anything that they want,” he said. “I have to balance taxpayers.”
NDP Leader Marit Stiles said Calandra is wrong to view the strike mandate vote results as an indication of support for his ministry.

“It’s saying very clearly that this minister has failed,” she said. “All you have to do is listen to a parent, a student, any education worker right now and they will tell you firsthand that this is unsustainable.”

stories.title: Ford government moves to shield itself from lawsuits related to Osap fraud probe
stories.summary: Nolan Quinn, Ontario’s minister of colleges and universities sidestepped questions in the legislature Tuesday about the government looking to grant itself legal immunity.
stories.author: Olivia Bowden
stories.content:
Facing mounting pressure over a growing private career college loan scandal, the Ford government is moving to shield itself from lawsuits tied to its decision to freeze student funding over fraud allegations.

The province has introduced an indemnity clause, folded into Bill 148, to modify existing career college legislation.

If passed, the new legislation will completely eliminate the right to sue the Ontario government including its ministers and other officials, for financial damages, negligence or other civil claims stemming from any specific regulations the Ford government passes.

“We’re holding these institutions accountable,” said Nolan Quinn, the colleges and universities minister, in the legislature Tuesday. “These are very serious criminal allegations and that is why we had to put a (Ontario Student Assistance Program) pause because one dollar going out towards fraudulent use is one dollar too many,” he said.

NDP Leader Marit Stiles fired back, stating that Quinn “didn’t do his job.”

“Now they’re trying to pass legislation to protect themselves from lawsuits. And it’s retroactive, so shame on you,” she said.

“To all of the students and the families that are watching this today, let me tell you this government cares more about protecting themselves in court over a mess that they made, than they do about your future,” she said.

2:02 Online petitions ask Ontario to restore OSAP for private college students

The Ford government is currently cracking down on private career colleges over alleged student loan fraud. In October, the government implemented a sweeping student loan freeze across all 242 private career colleges as it said it was investigating “serious concerns” raised by the federal government, advocacy groups and internal audits and inspections.

The province has said it’s examining allegations of third parties completing student coursework within minutes, thousands of OSAP applications submitted from the same IP addresses and students who could not identify their school, program or courses.

The government has also introduced legislation that will cap OSAP growth at private career colleges, limit OSAP funding to in-person and hybrid programs at those institutions and require them to have a physical location, and prohibit them from operating unrelated businesses on campus.

But the blanket OSAP freeze that remains in place has meant many students are now struggling to pay for rent, food and childcare costs. Many report having to drop out of their programs.

The indemnity clause would specifically bar anyone from suing the province for financial damages resulting from fraud investigations, school registration revocations or any decisions on the student Training Completion Assurance Fund, which is a provincial program that protects students enrolled in registered private career colleges if their institution closes unexpectedly.

Several career colleges have said they are now in a financial freefall and are having to lay off staff for the first time due to the OSAP freeze.

Interim Ontario Liberal Leader John Fraser called the proposed indemnity legislation “window dressing.”

“This government is always doing something to protect itself rather than protect Ontarians. They’re covering their asses,” he told reporters Tuesday.

“If you can take money away from people that you’ve committed to, like they did with all these students, all these moms and dads, then you can do what they’re doing in that bill with the same powers that you have,” he said.

“They just need to come clean.”

In a statement to Global News, Quinn’s office said “through our legislation, we are strengthening accountability to ensure anyone who intends to abuse our OSAP system for personal gain is held to the full extent of the law.”

“With this legislation, our government would better protect OSAP from misuse, enforce stronger penalties against wrongdoers, and stop bad actors in their tracks. We will pursue all avenues to return fraudulently used funding to the taxpayers,” said Bianca Giacoboni, Quinn’s press secretary.

stories.title: Trillium College students disappointed at selective return to classes
stories.summary: Students at one career college are decrying its approach to the Osap pause, with the school allowing only those who can pay without the financial aid to continue learning.
stories.author: Allison Jones
stories.content:
Students at one career college are decrying its approach to a provincewide pause on Ontario Student Assistance Program payments, with the school allowing only those who can pay without the financial aid to continue learning.

Lorraine Eaton, who is in the law and security program at Trillium College, was supposed to graduate in January and had a security guard job lined up. Now, because she was relying completely on Osap loans and can’t pay tuition out of pocket, she has been told she can’t attend class.

“I am frustrated to all hell,” she said.

“I’ve actually had a couple of my classmates tell me they’re in class right now and … (our teacher) has this list of how many people can go into the class and there’s a lot of people not on that list anymore.”

Trillium College, with five campuses around the province, announced last month that it was suspending classes due to uncertainty created by the provincial government’s Osap pause. For many career colleges, Osap-funded tuition makes up a sizable portion of their revenue, and many say they are struggling, having to lay off staff or even consider closing.

Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn announced in early October that Osap would not flow for students at private post-secondary institutions during a government-commissioned audit of the sector that Quinn says has uncovered serious and widespread concerns.

He has not offered a timeline for resumption of Osap for career college students other than saying it would be in the new year, and low-interest, third-party bank loans Quinn said he was trying to arrange have not yet materialized.

Now, nearly a month after Trillium paused its classes, they are starting to resume, but only for some students.

Certain cohorts started returning last week, but some students told the school they couldn’t afford a payment plan without their Osap loan.

“Those students will remain on temporary academic pause and will not return with their cohort unless an eligible funding source or approved payment arrangement is confirmed,” Trillium wrote in a note to students.

Students on a payment plan have to pay weekly in advance of the following week’s classes and if a payment is missed, the student’s attendance May be “temporarily paused,” the school wrote.

A spokesperson said in a statement that Trillium is focused on resuming instruction “wherever this can be done responsibly and on helping as many students as possible complete their education.”

“Students and cohorts that are not included in the initial phases of the return will remain on temporary academic pause,” Jennifer Miles wrote.

“They have not been automatically withdrawn from Trillium College. The pause will continue while the college and affected students await an accessible government funding solution or establish another viable arrangement that supports the responsible completion of their programs.”

Jennifer Koster is in Trillium’s law clerk program and was supposed to graduate in February.

She said she could not pay the full amount Trillium had proposed for a payment plan and offered lesser instalments, but the school did not accept that so she remains on academic pause while some classmates have returned.

“I just want somebody to help,” she said. “There’s a lot of students just like me that are stuck in the same position, and we’re not getting what was promised. … It’s us taking responsibility for a mess that we didn’t create.”

Marina Whitehead, a student in Trillium’s community developmental service worker program, is in her program’s placement right now, so she is not attending classes.

But she does still owe the school nearly $6,000 from earlier in the term that Osap was supposed to cover, and she worries she won’t be able to graduate as planned in February if Osap doesn’t come through. Whitehead’s placement involves working 40 hours a week unpaid.

“We’re working for free,” she said. “Where would you like me to pull that much money out of?”

content_blocks.text: Students at one career college are decrying its approach to a provincewide pause on Ontario Student Assistance Program payments, with the school allowing only those who can pay without the financial aid to continue learning.

Lorraine Eaton, who is in the law and security program at Trillium College, was supposed to graduate in January and had a security guard job lined up. Now, because she was relying completely on Osap loans and can’t pay tuition out of pocket, she has been told she can’t attend class.
“I am frustrated to all hell,” she said.

“I’ve actually had a couple of my classmates tell me they’re in class right now and … (our teacher) has this list of how many people can go into the class and there’s a lot of people not on that list anymore.”

Trillium College, with five campuses around the province, announced last month that it was suspending classes due to uncertainty created by the provincial government’s Osap pause. For many career colleges, Osap-funded tuition makes up a sizable portion of their revenue, and many say they are struggling, having to lay off staff or even consider closing.

Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn announced in early October that Osap would not flow for students at private post-secondary institutions during a government-commissioned audit of the sector that Quinn says has uncovered serious and widespread concerns.

He has not offered a timeline for resumption of Osap for career college students other than saying it would be in the new year, and low-interest, third-party bank loans Quinn said he was trying to arrange have not yet materialized.
Now, nearly a month after Trillium paused its classes, they are starting to resume, but only for some students.
Certain cohorts started returning last week, but some students told the school they couldn’t afford a payment plan without their Osap loan.

“Those students will remain on temporary academic pause and will not return with their cohort unless an eligible funding source or approved payment arrangement is confirmed,” Trillium wrote in a note to students.
Students on a payment plan have to pay weekly in advance of the following week’s classes and if a payment is missed, the student’s attendance May be “temporarily paused,” the school wrote.
A spokesperson said in a statement that Trillium is focused on resuming instruction “wherever this can be done responsibly and on helping as many students as possible complete their education.”
“Students and cohorts that are not included in the initial phases of the return will remain on temporary academic pause,” Jennifer Miles wrote.

“They have not been automatically withdrawn from Trillium College. The pause will continue while the college and affected students await an accessible government funding solution or establish another viable arrangement that supports the responsible completion of their programs.”
Jennifer Koster is in Trillium’s law clerk program and was supposed to graduate in February.

She said she could not pay the full amount Trillium had proposed for a payment plan and offered lesser instalments, but the school did not accept that so she remains on academic pause while some classmates have returned.

“I just want somebody to help,” she said. “There’s a lot of students just like me that are stuck in the same position, and we’re not getting what was promised. … It’s us taking responsibility for a mess that we didn’t create.”
Marina Whitehead, a student in Trillium’s community developmental service worker program, is in her program’s placement right now, so she is not attending classes.

But she does still owe the school nearly $6,000 from earlier in the term that Osap was supposed to cover, and she worries she won’t be able to graduate as planned in February if Osap doesn’t come through. Whitehead’s placement involves working 40 hours a week unpaid.
“We’re working for free,” she said. “Where would you like me to pull that much money out of?”

stories.title: National Congress of American Indians calls on Trump to reverse Lake Ontario change
stories.summary: The National Congress of American Indians is calling on U.S. President Donald Trump to walk back his August executive order renaming Lake Ontario as Lake America.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — The National Congress of American Indians is calling on U.S. President Donald Trump to walk back his August executive order renaming Lake Ontario as Lake America.

The organization, which represents American Indian and Alaska Native tribal governments in the United States, says the order demonstrates disrespect for Indigenous geographic names and Indigenous cultural, spiritual and historical relationships with lands and waters.

A resolution rejecting the name change, passed at the organization’s October assembly, was introduced by the Seneca Nation of Indians, a community based in Western New York.

Trump directed all arms of the federal government to start calling the body of water Lake America in August, to the dismay of Haudenosaunee communities on both sides of the border whose languages are the source of the name “Ontario.”

Lake Ontario is known in Seneca as “sga:nyodai:yoh,” meaning “beautiful lake,” and in Wendat as “ontari:io,” meaning “the lake is beautiful, the lake is big.”

The resolution says unilateral efforts to rename geography risk erasing Indigenous history and calls on the U.S. federal government to suspend its use of the term “Lake America.”

“The National Congress of American Indians opposes the removal, replacement, or erasure of Indigenous names of lakes, rivers, mountains, and other geographic features and calls upon federal, state, and local governments, geographic naming authorities, and public and private entities to preserve and respect those names in consultation with affected Tribal Nations,” it says.

“Lake Ontario is one example of the enduring Indigenous relationships with geographic features that this resolution seeks to protect, having been known to and used by the Seneca and other Haudenosaunee peoples since time immemorial for travel, trade, diplomacy, subsistence, and cultural practices, and bearing a commonly used name derived from Indigenous linguistic roots.”

Wendat Nation Grand Chief Pierre Picard told The Canadian Press his nation was “shocked” to hear about Trump’s renaming of Lake Ontario. He called it an attempt to eradicate their history in the region.

The Wendat occupied parts of the St. Lawrence Valley up to the Great Lakes and the area was rich with both pre- and post-contact trade routes.

The name Lake Ontario predates the founding of both Canada and the United States.

Trump’s move was ridiculed by Wisconsin Gov. Tony Evers, a Democrat. He posted a video of himself at a McDonalds restaurant, signing a fast food napkin to decree that Lake Michigan would now be called “Lake Wisconsin.”

“See, I can sign napkins that say things, too,” Evers wrote on X at the time.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has said the lake remains Lake Ontario “then, now and always.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 17, 2026.

Alessia Passafiume, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Toronto sees another stretch of warm weather with temperatures in mid-teens
stories.summary: Toronto - Toronto and the surrounding areas are getting another stretch of unusually warm weather in the middle of fall.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - Toronto and the surrounding areas are getting another stretch of unusually warm weather in the middle of fall.

Environment Canada is forecasting clear and sunny weather and temperatures hitting 13 degrees on Tuesday in Toronto.

A Toronto non-profit is launching a tech week for the city, filling a hole created by the recent departure of the annual Collision conference. The Toronto skyline is seen on Monday, Aug. 5, 2024. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Chris Young

stories.title: Trillium College students disappointed at selective return to classes
stories.summary: Students at one career college are decrying its approach to a provincewide pause on Ontario Student Assistance Program payments, with the school allowing only those who can pay without the financial aid to continue learning.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Students at one career college are decrying its approach to a provincewide pause on Ontario Student Assistance Program payments, with the school allowing only those who can pay without the financial aid to continue learning.

Lorraine Eaton, who is in the law and security program at Trillium College, was supposed to graduate in January and had a security guard job lined up. Now, because she was relying completely on Osap loans and can’t pay tuition out of pocket, she has been told she can’t attend class.

“I am frustrated to all hell,” she said.

“I’ve actually had a couple of my classmates tell me they’re in class right now and … (our teacher) has this list of how many people can go into the class and there’s a lot of people not on that list anymore.”

Trillium College, with five campuses around the province, announced last month that it was suspending classes due to uncertainty created by the provincial government’s Osap pause. For many career colleges, Osap-funded tuition makes up a sizable portion of their revenue, and many say they are struggling, having to lay off staff or even consider closing.

Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn announced in early October that Osap would not flow for students at private post-secondary institutions during a government-commissioned audit of the sector that Quinn says has uncovered serious and widespread concerns.

He has not offered a timeline for resumption of Osap for career college students other than saying it would be in the new year, and low-interest, third-party bank loans Quinn said he was trying to arrange have not yet materialized.

Now, nearly a month after Trillium paused its classes, they are starting to resume, but only for some students.

Certain cohorts started returning last week, but some students told the school they couldn’t afford a payment plan without their Osap loan.

“Those students will remain on temporary academic pause and will not return with their cohort unless an eligible funding source or approved payment arrangement is confirmed,” Trillium wrote in a note to students.

Students on a payment plan have to pay weekly in advance of the following week’s classes and if a payment is missed, the student’s attendance May be “temporarily paused,” the school wrote.

A spokesperson said in a statement that Trillium is focused on resuming instruction “wherever this can be done responsibly and on helping as many students as possible complete their education.”

“Students and cohorts that are not included in the initial phases of the return will remain on temporary academic pause,” Jennifer Miles wrote.

“They have not been automatically withdrawn from Trillium College. The pause will continue while the college and affected students await an accessible government funding solution or establish another viable arrangement that supports the responsible completion of their programs.”

Jennifer Koster is in Trillium’s law clerk program and was supposed to graduate in February.

She said she could not pay the full amount Trillium had proposed for a payment plan and offered lesser instalments, but the school did not accept that so she remains on academic pause while some classmates have returned.

“I just want somebody to help,” she said. “There’s a lot of students just like me that are stuck in the same position, and we’re not getting what was promised. … It’s us taking responsibility for a mess that we didn’t create.”

Marina Whitehead, a student in Trillium’s community developmental service worker program, is in her program’s placement right now, so she is not attending classes.

But she does still owe the school nearly $6,000 from earlier in the term that Osap was supposed to cover, and she worries she won’t be able to graduate as planned in February if Osap doesn’t come through. Whitehead’s placement involves working 40 hours a week unpaid.

“We’re working for free,” she said. “Where would you like me to pull that much money out of?”

stories.title: Ontario's medical regulator pauses safer supply drug changes after legal challenge
stories.summary: Toronto - Ontario’s medical regulator is hitting pause on implementing a host of changes to the ways doctors prescribe safer supply drugs after it was served with a legal challenge.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - Ontario’s medical regulator is hitting pause on implementing a host of changes to the ways doctors prescribe safer supply drugs after it was served with a legal challenge.

The College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario says it was served Friday with the legal action, which includes a motion for an injunction to prevent the regulator from enforcing the new safer supply rules.

stories.title: Milton, Ont., to swear in first new mayor in 46 years as Gord Krantz leaves office
stories.summary: Milton - The town of Milton is set to swear-in a new mayor for the first time since 1980.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
MILTON - The town of Milton is set to swear-in a new mayor for the first time since 1980.

George Minakakis and eight regional and town councillors will take their oaths of office at the council’s inaugural meeting Monday night.

Minakakis takes the reins from Canada’s longest-serving mayor, Gordon Krantz, who held Milton’s top job for 46 years before being defeated in October’s municipal election.

First elected to the town’s council in 1965, Krantz helped steward Milton’s transformation from agricultural community to rapidly growing suburb, negotiating the “Big Pipe” project that brought the town fresh drinking water from Lake Ontario in 2000 and sparked a population boom.

During Krantz’s tenure as mayor, Milton’s population more than tripled and the town was Canada’s fastest-growing municipality for a 10-year stretch.

The 89-year-old told The Canadian Press in an interview before October’s election that he was running again for mayor because he still felt he had more to do.

But ultimately, voters rewarded Minakakis, who ran on a platform of strengthening Milton’s economy and attracting more businesses to the bedroom community to spur local job growth.

The former business executive had served as a Milton town councillor for a year after winning a 2025 byelection.

Krantz told The Canadian Press in October that pragmatism guided his long political career.

“Separating out your wants from your needs for your community is important,” he said of the “delicate” balancing act of expanding services while keeping taxes low as Milton grew.

“As I will often say, there really is no free lunch. You pay me now or you pay me later,” he said.

Krantz said he correctly predicted that Milton would one day be home to highrise buildings when he was a town councillor back in 1965, an idea “way out in left field” at the time.

His next prediction for Milton’s future? Urbanization and a move away from cars.

“You’re going to find places like Oakville, Burlington, Milton, and the region of Halton, York and Durham be part of one great metropolis 100 years from now. Urbanization is here to stay in this part of the world,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 16, 2026.

stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
ST. JOHN’S - An airport in a Newfoundland town known for its care of stranded plane passengers was on the ready Friday as flights were grounded for several hours in the United States.

Reg White, chief executive of the airport authority in Gander, N.L., said he called the local hotels for vacancy numbers and made sure the restaurant could stay open if planes were diverted to the town.

stories.title: Busy day at Canadian airports as airlines scramble to recover from U.S. flight stop
stories.summary: Toronto - One of Canada's largest airlines says it will likely take the weekend for schedules to return to normal after officials temporarily grounded flights across the United States on Friday.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - Dale Flood had booked what he called a once-in-a-lifetime 50th birthday trip with his family to New York City to watch his beloved Buffalo Bills play on Sunday.

After a four-hour freeze on U.S. air traffic resulted in his Saturday morning flight being cancelled, the Vancouver man jumped into action, hoping to salvage the trip for himself, his wife and his 11-year-old son.

But after staying up until 4 a.m. trying to get his family on any flight that could get them to New York on time, he had to concede defeat. Instead, his family will fly on Sunday, landing too late for the much-anticipated NFL game.

“It’s sad,” Flood said in a phone interview. “It’s hard to watch an 11-year-old cry. It’s hard to go through all of October and November really looking forward to this, to that time in New York.”

The ripple effects of a four-hour freeze on U.S. air traffic continued across Canadian airports on Saturday, as airlines issued flight notices and travellers spent hours tethered to their phones waiting for updates.

Airports from Vancouver to Halifax posted on social media that they were facing delays, and the one in Toronto said it even called in more staff to help out.

“A busy day of travel is underway,” said Toronto Pearson International Airport.

Flood acknowledged that the disruption was unforeseen, and that there was likely nothing that could have been done to get him from the West Coast to New York on time. But he’s frustrated by his inability to get through to an agent over the phone.

“You do wish you could at some point talk to Air Canada, like actually talk to a human being,” he said.

Traveller Edward Langer, who is in New York with his 15-year-old daughter, said his Saturday flight back home to Edmonton was postponed by about four days due to the freeze.

He said he and his daughter are facing several missed days of school and work, as well as thousands of dollars in extra hotel costs.

He had not been able to reach Porter Airlines as of Saturday afternoon despite spending hours on hold.

“When you go on some of the travel sites to book hotels, (the price) is just doubling and tripling,” he said.

“It’s crazy.”

Global travel chaos began after the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration issued a so-called ground stop order on Friday that brought air traffic in that country to a halt for more than four hours.

The U.S. government said new technology being added to the nation’s air traffic control system overloaded antiquated equipment and caused intermittent communications and radar gaps. The matter was under investigation.

Air Canada said Saturday it cancelled approximately 250 flights after the order, which affected some 27,000 passengers.

“This was a significant disruption, and its effects have carried over into today, with additional cancellations as aircraft and crews are out of position across our network,” said Yasmine Mehdi, an Air Canada spokesperson.

“Returning to normal operations will take some time.”

Porter Airlines and WestJet said it would likely take the whole weekend for its flights to return to normal schedules.

Porter said it would refund its customers who can’t accommodate rescheduled flights while Calgary-based WestJet said its policy allowing flexible rescheduling was activated.

Isabelle Rochefort said she had been standing in line at Montreal’s Trudeau International Airport to board her Air Canada flight to Cancun, Mexico, around 5 p.m. Friday when she received word that it was cancelled.

She said the situation was initially confusing because her plane wasn’t touching down in the United States.

“We didn’t know what to do, of course,” she said in a series of Facebook messages.

“The Air Canada staff had no information on what was next except that we had to wait for news.”

She was able to retrieve her bag after leaving the line and call someone to drive her home to Sorel-Tracy, more than an hour-and-a-half away.

She’s since been rebooked on a new flight leaving Sunday, though she’ll have to pay for yet another expensive ride to the airport.

Rochefort believes that both the airport and airline are managing as best as they can.

“The real question now is, will it be possible to be compensated?” she asked.

“That remains to be seen.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 14, 2026.

—- By Morgan Lowrie in Montreal, Sarah Smellie in St. John’s, and Fakiha Baig in Edmonton, with files from The Associated Press

stories.title: One person arrested, other suspects at large after overnight home invasion in Mt. Brydges
stories.summary: One person is in custody, and others remain at large after a home invasion in Mt. Brydges, Ont. west of London.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
One person is in custody, and others remain at large after a home invasion in Mt. Brydges, Ont. west of London.

Around 3:55 a.m., officers from the Middlesex County OPP, and officers from Strathroy-Caradoc Police Service (Scps) responded to reports of a break and enter involving possibly armed individuals in the area of Edinburgh Road, Adelaide Road, Parkhouse Drive and Ferne Drive.

“We had a police officer that was on scene within one minute,” said Staff Sgt. Jason Cartwright of the Scps.

“The officer, when she arrived, actually was confronted by one of the suspects who was exiting the residence (on Parkhouse Drive) at that time. She got into a short-foot pursuit with the suspect, at which time the suspect did get away. She returned to the residence and called for more assistance and continued the investigation.”

While the person on foot did get away, an officer who was in the area was able to locate what was believed to be a suspect vehicle.

“He attempted to stop that vehicle, but the vehicle did not stop for police,” said Cartwright.

Police say they don’t have much information on the two outstanding suspects other than they are still searching for two black males between the age of 20 and 30 who were wearing dark clothing.

Hours after the home invasion, police tape surrounded a home on Parkhouse Drive, where a couple was home at the time of the break in.

A contractor was rebuilding the front door which was kicked in and Scps officers along with K9 were searching the area near the residence.

CTV News spoke with a couple of neighbours along Parkhouse Drive who wished to remain anonymous. They said the incident is “very unnerving” and one even went as far as to track down OPP officers and ask them to come double-check the area around her home and under her porch.

Another neighbour told CTV News he plans to upgrade from a doorbell camera to a full security system.

“This is unnerving for sure,” said Cartwright.

“This is a a serious incident that occurred. There will be police presence in Mt Brydges today in the area. We are potentially looking for one or more suspects still. If there’s anything suspicious in the area, call 911 or our emergency line and we will certainly have somebody come out and see them.”

Police say despite early reports, there is no evidence that the suspects had a firearm.

stories.title: Lawyers unsure if extra funding can reduce massive caseload at Federal Court
stories.summary: Ottawa — The recent federal budget included $58 million in additional funding court administration but the Federal Court still doesn't have a clear picture of how it can be used to reduce a massive caseload that has grown rapidly since 2020.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
OTTAWA — The recent federal budget included $58 million in additional funding court administration but the Federal Court still doesn’t have a clear picture of how it can be used to reduce a massive caseload that has grown rapidly since 2020.

“At the moment, the Federal Court doesn’t have additional details on how the funding confirmed will be distributed among the stated purposes,” Chief Justice Alan Diner told The Canadian Press in an emailed statement on Thursday.

The Federal Court hears immigration-related issues such as visa applications, refugee claims, admissibility cases and removals. It has responsibility for upholding the law in other areas related to federal jurisdiction, like intellectual property, national security and Indigenous rights.

The court asked for additional resources to handle a caseload that’s ballooned to nearly 31,000 proceedings commenced as of Sept. 30 this year — up from about 7,600 in all of 2020.

More than 27,000 of the proceedings started this year are immigration cases.

Diner told The Canadian Press in an August interview that judges and court staff have had to work evenings, weekends and vacation days to handle a caseload that has been growing in large part because of immigration matters.

The budget says the money is earmarked for the Courts Administration Service, which serves the Federal Court, the Federal Appeal Court, the Tax Court of Canada and the Court Martial Appeal Court of Canada.

The single mention of it in the documents published Nov. 5 says the new funding is meant to address the Federal Court caseload and to help the Courts Administration Service with Official Languages Act compliance, a translation backlog and the need to modernize court infrastructure.

The extra $58 million in funding is set to begin in the 2027/28 fiscal year and continue for four years, averaging $14.5 million annually.

Joannie Fogue, spokesperson for Justice Minister Sean Fraser, said the funding is meant to “strengthen the national courts,” respond to resource challenges and build workload efficiencies. But exactly how it will be allocated aren’t yet known.

“We are continuing to work through the details and implications of the funding commitment and are awaiting further information on the how allocation will be distributed,” she said in a media statement.

While the court awaits more details, immigration lawyers question whether the additional money from Ottawa will do much to move cases through the court more efficiently, given how the demands have grown.

“Any increase in funding is positive, but it’s a modest increase and the increase in the Federal Court’s immigration caseload has been anything but modest,” said Jacqueline Bonisteel, an Ottawa-based immigration lawyer.

While Bonisteel said the additional funding is welcome, she doesn’t see how $58 million spread over four years will be enough, given the spike in the caseload.

“It’s not going to be enough to cope with the issues that the court’s seeing right now, a 600 per cent increase in immigration caseload since 2020,” she said.

“The current compliment of judges and the current resources that the court has just simply aren’t enough to deal with that magnitude of an increase.”

Bonisteel said it can take “upwards of two years” now to get an immigration case through the court.

Zeynab Moayyed, a Toronto-based immigration lawyer, agreed the problems at the Federal Court go beyond what $58 million could fix.

Moayyed cited a shortage of registry staff in the court and said routine paperwork that used to take about a day to process — like a filing for a judicial review — now takes weeks.

Moayyed attributed the increase in caseload in part to more people filing mandamus applications meant to force a decision from the Immigration Department when people are facing long delays.

But both Moayyed and Bonisteel said the quality of Immigration Department decisions has declined since the feds adopted artificial intelligence tools and new software in a bid to review and process applications more quickly.

The lack of human interaction at the department is turning small problems into large ones and pushing them onto the court’s plate, they said.

“Previously, (lawyers) could reach out to (Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada), to program managers, to visa office managers and so on. And … if it was a mistake they would receive a reconsideration and that matter would be reopened, and if it wasn’t a mistake, (the applicant) would understand what they did wrong,” Moayyed said.

“But with the coming into effect of those tools, at the same time we had the shutting down of informal ways of addressing areas that happen in the system, and applicants started turning to Federal Court.”

Bonisteel said the department could ease the Federal Court’s workload by finding a way to streamline requests for reconsideration before they get shunted to the court.

“These are very multi-faceted problems and they need multi-faceted solutions. So it’s not just about court funding. It’s about addressing the systemic issues that are leading to the increase in the court’s caseload,” she said.

The Immigration Department has said it uses AI and advanced analytics tools under human oversight at all times. The department says these AI tools do not make decisions and are meant to assist with tasks like triaging applications, identifying routine cases, generating case summaries and answering client questions through chatbots.

The department’s first AI strategy, released earlier this year, says the goal is to get the technology to reduce application backlogs and wait times.

Moayyed said those long delays are causing “a great deal of distress” for people stuck in the system.

“Our job, in addition to being immigration lawyers, has become confidant and the therapist for a client, listening to them talk about having their life on hold and in limbo until they get a decision,” she said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 14, 2026.

David Baxter, The Canadian Press

stories.title: CFB Wainwright incident casts spotlight on reserve pay disparities: former bureaucrat
stories.summary: Ottawa — A former director general for the Canadian military's reserves and cadets says the tragic incident at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright casts a spotlight on disparities in pay and benefits for reservists.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
OTTAWA — A former director general for the Canadian military’s reserves and cadets says the tragic incident at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright casts a spotlight on disparities in pay and benefits for reservists.

John Milne, a retired major-general, told The Canadian Press reservists on short-term contracts get less compensation than the regular force members they train with. He said the recent training accident at CFB Wainwright shows those short-term reservists face the same risks as their regular force colleagues.

Four soldiers died and 39 others — including several reservists — were injured when a fire suddenly overtook a training area at CFB Wainwright last month.

Military pay is not a straightforward matter and is calculated based on a range of factors.

Unlike regular force members, reservists usually study or work at full-time civilian jobs while they serve under one of a number of different service classes for the military. Those service classes affect how their benefits are determined.

Milne — who has written academic papers on military pay structure — said the formula the federal government uses to calculate daily reservist pay has amounted to an earnings penalty of roughly 32 per cent for part-time reservists compared to the regular force.

He said it’s a “matter of equity” and the daily rate for reservists should be made the same as what regular force members get. He also said the policy governing their benefits should be rewritten to be more fair.

“As the government grows and increases its military commitments and has intentions of using reservists in more dangerous and more complex environments, then it’s a matter of equity that the daily rate for the reservists should actually be the same as the daily rate for the regular,” he said.

Reservists injured in training also normally receive lower-tier compensation and benefits during their recovery, Milne said. He added he believes the military has reclassified the Wainwright reservists’ contracts from short to long-term service classes to improve their access to benefits.

The Department of National Defence did not respond to questions about the reclassification of injured reserve members’ contracts by deadline.

Official information about the Wainwright tragedy has been limited. Three separate investigations are taking place.

Milne sent a submission to the House of Commons national defence committee in the hopes that Parliament would take up the matter. In it, he writes that there is “no justification” for the earnings penalty, which affects other benefits such as disability payment amounts.

He also wrote directly to Defence Minister David McGuinty. A response letter he received from the minister’s office said the military’s pay structure is complex and involves “specific military considerations” different from civilian pay, and denied that Milne had identified pay inequities.

Prime Minister Mark Carney announced a military pay hike last year, which included a 13 per cent boost for some reserve force ranks. It did not address how pay is structured.

The Canadian Armed Forces Ombud has flagged for years systemic financial inequities and administrative delays with reservist pay as major problems the government must fix, but has reported little progress.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 14, 2026.

Kyle Duggan, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Saturday Sports: Knights lose in shootout, High School Sports Roundup
stories.summary: Ryan Kaczynski scored the only goal of the shootout as the Sault Ste. Marie Greyhounds beat the London Knights 5-4 Friday.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
Ryan Kaczynski scored the only goal of the shootout as the Sault Ste. Marie Greyhounds beat the London Knights 5-4 Friday.

One week after the Knights beat the Greyhounds 5-4 in overtime, it was the hosts this time who earned the extra point.

Caleb Mitchell scored twice for London who let a 4-2 lead slip away before going to overtime and then the breakaway contest.

Goaltender Arvin Jaswal, who was acquired by the Knights in late October, made his first start after missing time due to injury. He stopped 24 of 28 shots.

Marcus Nordmark and Ryan Brown were the other goal scorers for London. The Knights are in Saginaw Saturday to face the Spirit who made a trade Friday to acquire St. Thomas, Ont. native Parker Vaughan.

South lions win aa football championship

The Lions, ranked #21 in the Ontario Coaches Poll, will now head to Richardson Stadium in Kingston for the Ontario Championship after the victory at 1Password Park in St. Thomas, Ont.

Crusaders to meet oaks in aaa football final

The championship matchup is set in Tvra AAA Football. Catholic Central will face Oakridge for a berth in Ofsaa.

Oakridge advanced in double-overtime after a wild contest at CityWide Field. The Oaks surrendered a lead late in the fourth quarter and survived a wild sequence of events in extra time.

The Spartans blocked an Oaks field goal in overtime, so they just needed a single point to win. They tried to punt the football out of the endzone but the Oaks fielded the punt, and punted it back out of the endzone to force a second OT.

After a defensive stop, the Oaks marched down the field to the 15, Oakridge tried to punt for a rouge.

The punt was fielded by the Spartans, but when they tried to punt it out, it was blocked out of the endzone by Kaden Kheav for the 22-21 win.

In the other contest, the Catholic Central Crusaders, ranked #1 in the country, beat the Lucas Vikings 20-10 to move onto the final.
