stories.title: Grey Cup game bids farewell for now to iconic Snowbirds aerial team
stories.summary: Calgary - The national anthem is set to ring through McMahon Stadium on Sunday and herald across the sky nine Snowbirds jets, in a fitting show retiring the planes of Canada's military aerial ambassadors.
stories.author: Dayne Patterson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
CALGARY - The national anthem is set to ring through McMahon Stadium on Sunday and herald across the sky nine Snowbirds jets, in a fitting show retiring the planes of Canada’s military aerial ambassadors.

The CFL’s Grey Cup championship game will be the last time the Snowbirds fly in their CT-114 Tutor jets for a scheduled public spectacle.

Capt. Marc-André Plante, who flies as Snowbird 8 on the team, says it’s the perfect sendoff.

The Canadian Football League’s Grey Cup championship game — the most important annual contest for the league’s fans — will be the last time the Snowbirds fly their CT-114 Tutor jets for a scheduled public spectacle before they are retired for a replacement. (Nov. 14, 2026)

“It is Canada’s demonstration team. It’s Canada’s football league. It’s like all these things just kind of make sense, when you look at it where we just celebrate Canada as a whole,” he said in an interview.

The Snowbirds, based out of the 15 Wing Air Force base at Moose Jaw, Sask., have never flown anything but the Tutors.

They have performed roughly 2,700 times for more than 140 million people across North America in more than a half-century of service.

At the end of the year, the Tutors are to be retired and will eventually be replaced by the CT-157 Siskin II. The team is expected to be temporarily grounded until the early 2030s.

But on Sunday, the team will soar.

The jets are to set off from the Calgary International Airport and zoom over the stadium as close to their minimum flight height of about 150 metres from the tallest point that they’re flying over, creating a memorable chorus of ooohs and ahhhs.

As celebrated Canadian musician Sarah McLachlan finishes her final note of O Canada, the jets are to roar over the stadium one last time.

Plante and his squadron will then return to the airport, tuck the planes into a hangar and bus to the stadium to watch the rest of the game.

The team will later head home to Saskatchewan on Monday.

“Of course, as we’re flying back to Moose Jaw, if we have sufficient gas, we’ll probably do a little flyover of our hometown as we are coming in.

“But as far as an invited assembly of persons, (the Grey Cup) would be our last.”

The official retirement plan, and the future of the planes, is outside of the crew’s control, Plante added.

He said the federal government’s announcement in May hasn’t changed his last few months flying with the squad.

If anything, the team has tried to fly over as many towns and cities as gas and time allowed, he said.

Flying with the Snowbirds has been the highest honour so far in his military career, said Plante.

“Being able to inspire hundreds, thousands of Canadians across Canada to pursue their own forms of excellence — whatever that may be, whether or not it’s joining the military or doing anything else that’s contributing to Canada — I think is an amazing thing to do.”

For Snowbirds enthusiast William Gilson, the flyover will be historic and memorable.

“This flight over the Grey Cup on Sunday is really going to be, I feel, the end of a very important part of my life and an important chapter in Canadian military history.”

It’s a shame the team will be grounded for the next several years, he said.

“So I want to be there.”

Gilson, from Calgary, is a full-time teacher and a military aviation photographer. He estimates he has taken about 10,000 to 15,000 photos of the Snowbirds and expects to add another few hundred to his photo library Sunday.

He said he’s skeptical that Snowbirds will return after being grounded. Petitions have also been circulating to keep the Snowbirds in the sky, including one brought to the House of Commons with more than 2,000 signatures.

Gilson’s love of aviation was born out of his family’s military background and the high-flying stunts of the Snowbirds.

He was 11 when he saw them perform at the airport in Abbotsford, B.C., in 1972. He went to shows every year after, until just recently.

“They’re not overly powerful but demonstrate the true thing to be Canadian: calm, cool, collected, thinking with a smart head.”

Gilson said his camera is going to be perched Sunday on a toboggan hill just southwest of the stadium when the red-and-white birds fly overhead.

He expects to be joined by several hundred other aviation enthusiasts — and maybe some of his family.

His daughter recently called him and asked when he started to become interested in airplanes. His three-year-old granddaughter has said she loves them too.

“It’s just in my blood and it’s in the family’s blood, I guess.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 14, 2026.

stories.title: Rains ease but storm surge heads for southwest B.C., posing new flood risk
stories.summary: Vancouver - Deluged residents of coastal British Columbia face a new flooding risk as rains ease, with warnings of a storm surge that could raise sea levels.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
SQUAMISH - The waters of the Squamish River roared under rainy skies Friday, as search and rescue crews recovered the bodies of three people who died when a boat overturned in the swollen waterway north of Vancouver, following days of heavy rain and flooding in the region.

Insp. Robert Dykstra, the officer in charge of the Sea to Sky RCMP, said there were originally about eight people aboard the boat Thursday, and police said no one is unaccounted for.

But Dykstra wasn’t sure why they were on the water or what caused the boat to overturn.

Three people are dead after a boat overturned Thursday in the Squamish River, which is swollen from days of heavy rain. RCMP Insp. Robert Dykstra says it’s believed eight people were aboard, and none are unaccounted for. (Nov. 13, 2026)

“I do believe that they ran into something. That’s all I really know at this point,” he told reporters on Friday.

Dykstra said he believed the boat was local to Squamish and he wasn’t aware of any injuries among the survivors of the incident.

The tragedy came after southwest British Columbia was drenched by a series of storms that brought more than 300 millimetres of rain to some areas this week.

The Sea to Sky corridor, including Squamish and Pemberton, was among the areas hardest hit.

Dykstra said police got the call at around 1:50 p.m. on Thursday but it took time for responders to gain access to the area because of a road washout and the state of the raging river.

Police initially said two people had died and a third was missing, but a third body was recovered by Friday afternoon.

Two people have died and one other is missing after a boat overturned Thursday in the Squamish River which is swollen from days of heavy rain. Nils Robinson, manager with Squamish Search and Rescue, says search efforts are continuing. (Nov. 13, 2026)

Three full white body bags were unloaded from a helicopter at the airport in Squamish around 1:30 p.m., as low-lying clouds rolled in.

Police have not released any details about the victims or survivors.

Dykstra called the situation “tragic.”

“You never know exactly why people are doing what they’re doing sometimes,” he said, adding that “there could be any number of reasons” for the boat being on the water.

Dykstra said the best thing for people to do during major weather events is stay home and stay safe, especially around rapidly moving waters.

“These waters are unforgiving when they’re going fast.”

All of the rainfall warnings that had blanketed the region over the past week were lifted by Friday, but as weather conditions eased, effects of the deluge were still being felt.

The entire village of Pemberton, about 90 kilometres north of Squamish, remained under an evacuation alert. Evacuation orders imposed by the nearby Lil’wat First Nation, and in Zeballos on Vancouver Island, also remained in place, although an order for parts of Pemberton was downgraded to alert status.

A shelter-in-place advisory issued Thursday for some residents about 16 kilometres north of Squamish was lifted Friday. Still, residents were advised not to drive across flooded roads, and RCMP told residents to stay out of flood zones.

BC Emergency Health Services said it received a call at 2:48 p.m. on Thursday about the boat incident near the 15900 block of Squamish Valley Road. No one was taken to hospital, it said.

At the Squamish airport earlier Friday, a white pickup truck pulled an RCMP boat into the parking lot as members of the local search and rescue team gathered inside their headquarters before deploying to recover the third victim.

Legislator Jeremy Valeriote, who represents West Vancouver-Sea to Sky, said he was “devastated” and his thoughts were with the victims’ families.

Valeriote, who was re-elected as the riding’s Green legislator last month, said the Sea to Sky region “is a strong and resilient community.”

“But no one should have to navigate this alone.”

Valeriote said he and his team would support people however they could as the community begins recovering.

At an unrelated event on Friday, B.C. premier-designate Lorne Doerkson called the situation “very serious” and said he intended to visit the area.

“It’s pretty serious in our province right now. So (my) heart goes out to those families that are dealing with the losses. Of course the communities as well. These are small communities and everybody is going to feel the pain in those communities,” he said.

Wilson Williams, chairperson of the Squamish Nation, said at the same event that he was “calling upon Mother Nature” to protect those in areas dealing with the hazardous weather.

The province’s River Forecast Centre downgraded warnings it had issued for the south coast to a lower-level high streamflow advisory. It also ended flood watches for Fraser Valley north, the central coast and east Vancouver Island.

Meanwhile, residents of coastal areas of southwest B.C. were facing a new flooding risk, even as rains eased, with warnings of a storm surge that could raise sea levels.

Environment Canada said the surge could hit low-lying and exposed coastal areas of Metro Vancouver, southeast Vancouver Island and the southern Gulf Islands.

It said elevated water levels surpassing tidal predictions were being driven by high winds and “enhanced wave activity,” and could last into the weekend.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 13, 2026.

stories.title: Fatality reported after October collision in Morris-Turnberry
stories.summary: The lone occupant of the passenger vehicle suffered serious injuries and was airlifted to a London hospital for treatment.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A 68-year-old Huron-Kinloss Township man has died from injuries sustained in a two-vehicle collision last month in Morris-Turnberry, provincial police say.

Huron County OPP, Huron County Paramedic Services and the North Huron Fire Department responded to the crash on Amberley Road between Currie Line and Helena Street on Oct. 14.

Police said the collision involved a passenger vehicle and a van.

The lone occupant of the passenger vehicle suffered serious injuries and was airlifted to a London hospital for treatment.

OPP said the 68-year-old driver died on Nov. 10 as a result of injuries sustained in the collision.

No further details were released.

stories.title: Ontario to cap Osap growth at career colleges following massive increases
stories.summary: Toronto - Career colleges in Ontario could soon be subject to limits on the growth of students funded by financial aid, following explosive increases in the sector that prompted the government to call in the police.
stories.author: Allison Jones The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - Career colleges in Ontario could soon be subject to limits on the growth of students funded by financial aid, following explosive increases in the sector that prompted the government to call in the police.

Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn announced that legislation will be introduced on Monday, saying the significant concerns around Ontario Student Assistance Program usage in the sector are far more widespread than first suspected and the bill is intended to increase oversight and accountability.

“What we have found here are not minor administrative concerns, but rather co-ordinated, sophisticated efforts to take advantage of students and taxpayers for personal gain,” he said Thursday at a press conference.

Career Colleges Ontario, which processes OSAP applications for the schools, has removed 24 more campuses from their membership, with an additional 13 under review, Quinn said. The association has also identified concerns about backdating applications at 33 additional campuses, he said.

“This behaviour is despicable, and it must be stopped,” Quinn said.

The legislation is set to include the as-yet undefined cap, limit OSAP funding to in-person and hybrid programs at those institutions and require them to have a physical location, and prohibit them from operating unrelated businesses on campus.

Quinn has said that concerns about career colleges being co-located with immigration and recruitment firms are among issues raised by an ongoing KPMG audit of the sector. As well, the legislation would allow the province to more easily recover OSAP funding from career colleges by holding them liable for students’ loans.

Critics say the problem is one of the government’s own making, allowing online-only programs to qualify for OSAP in the first place during the COVID-19 pandemic and not watching closely enough as growth skyrocketed.

“If the minister is indicating that this is so systemic, how come they let it get this bad?” Liberal critic Tyler Watt said.

NDP critic Peggy Sattler said oversight measures proposed in the bill are important, but it never should have come to this.

“This bill is a classic case of closing the barn door after the horses are gone,” she said.

Between 2023-24 and 2024-25, the amount of provincial OSAP grants to career colleges nearly doubled, to about $1 billion in the latter year. That was largely due to activity at a small number of career colleges, according to data obtained by The Canadian Press through a freedom-of-information request.

The ministry alleges that some of those schools were unable to verify students were attending class or completing their own coursework, allegations the schools deny.

While the KPMG audit is ongoing, Quinn has paused OSAP payments to all private post-secondary institutions, causing some students to drop out and some colleges to consider closing their doors.

Quinn has said the government is working on securing low-interest loans for students through banks until the pause is lifted in the new year, but he has so far not indicated a timeline for that.

Colleges and students are calling on the government to weed out any bad actors in a way that doesn’t also penalize institutions and students who follow the rules. Premier Doug Ford has said KPMG auditors have been tasked with clearing low-risk schools first.

Career Colleges Ontario said it will review the details of the legislation once it is actually introduced, but in the meantime the announcement does nothing for the compliant institutions affected by the broad pause.

“Innocent students continue to bear the consequences of the sector-wide pause, and we continue to call on the government to reinstate OSAP for students attending compliant institutions,” the association wrote in a statement.

Interim Liberal leader John Fraser said the government is holding innocent students hostage with the OSAP pause.

“The rent doesn’t wait,” he said. “The grocery bill doesn’t wait. The kids’ clothes don’t wait, and this government’s saying, ‘wait,’” Fraser said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 12, 2026.

stories.title: Impacts from B.C. drenching mount as water levels rise
stories.summary: Vancouver - The impacts of the drenching on British Columbia's south coast have been increasing as heavy rain triggers evacuation orders and alerts, flood warnings and the shutdown of a water treatment plant.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
VANCOUVER - Peter Spitzer is among residents of Paradise Valley Road who are sheltering in place north of Squamish, B.C., after their homes were cut off by river waters swollen by drenching rains and a dam discharge that followed.

He’s been at his property near the confluence of the Cheakamus River and Culliton Creek for nearly 40 years and has seen floodwaters break their banks before.

Spitzer and his neighbours in the flood zone about 16 kilometres from Squamish know the drill.

“We all stay put and help the neighbours out if somebody needs anything. We usually have food and water for quite a few days before we run out,” he said Thursday.

A procession of storms has drenched parts of southwest British Columbia with more than 300 millimetres of rain in 48 hours leading to multiple evacuation orders and alerts, as well as the shelter-in-place decree that was issued by the District of Squamish on Thursday morning.

The entire village of Pemberton, population 3,400, is under an evacuation alert “out of an abundance of caution.”.

But rains have eased for most of the province, including Metro Vancouver.

Environment Canada had lowered most rainfall warnings by Thursday, although yellow warnings were still active for west and inland Vancouver Island, where heavy rains were forecast to last into Friday afternoon.

But the impacts of the deluge continue. Spitzer said parts of Paradise Valley Road were flooded and water under the now-closed Bailey Bridge out of the community is “very close to the top.”

“At the moment there’s no way out of the valley,” he said.

Spitzer said the water hadn’t reached his home but others were surrounded or their basements were flooded.

Video posted online shows trucks driving down roads covered in fast-flowing water. Another shows a resident standing at the front door of his home, which is under several feet of water, while a friend on the opposite bank calls across the water to make sure he is OK.

The District of Squamish said in a statement Thursday that the spill level from the Cheakamus Dam at Daisy Lake peaked at approximately 5 a.m. and was expected to decrease slowly throughout the day.

The district said that would create room in the reservoir for more rain, and eventually allow for roads to be reopened, adding that river levels were also expected to peak Thursday.

The flooding came after the rate of water flowing into the dam’s reservoir more than tripled expectations, due to back-to-back storms.

Whitney Deane, a spokesperson for B.C. Hydro, said forecasters were originally expecting the rate of water flowing into the reservoir to peak at a manageable 235 cubic metres per second by midday Thursday.

But at 11 p.m. on Wednesday, the hydro company issued a flood warning and about an hour later, flows into the reservoir peaked at 735 cubic metres per second, she said.

“That’s roughly three times the forecast coming at a much shorter window,” she said.

The string of weather systems that slammed southwestern B.C. since last week brought 306 millimetres of rain to Port Mellon in the Howe Sound region since Tuesday, while 261 millimetres fell at Kennedy Lake on Vancouver Island.

The rain forced evacuation orders for parts of Vancouver Island, the Lil’wat First Nation in the central Interior, and parts Pemberton, about 150 kilometres north of Vancouver.

Pemberton’s evacuation order covers properties on Airport Road, including the community’s airport, wastewater treatment facility, wildland fire management base and a public golf course. The B.C. Ministry of Transportation’s DriveBC website says Highway 99 east of Pemberton has been shut in both directions.

The Lilʼwat Nation has expanded an evacuation order and alert for the area from Kwetsa7 along the Lillooet River corridor to Lillooet Lake.

Elsewhere, the Strathcona Regional District issued a water conservation notice for the village of Sayward on the northeast coast of Vancouver Island, as high flows in Newcastle Creek led to extra sediment in the water, and an evacuation order due to flooding and landslide risks remains in place for about 30 properties in the village of Zeballos on northwest Vancouver Island.

“A strong frontal system over the area will weaken today. Rain will continue to ease as the front weakens,” Environment Canada said Thursday.

Environment Canada said several locations reported more than 100 millimetres of rain in the last 48 hours, including Kennedy Lake on Vancouver Island (248 mm), Port Alberni (123 mm), Porteau Cove on the Sea to Sky Highway (140 mm), Whistler (138 mm), and Squamish (134 mm).

The storms have been associated with a spike in temperatures which saw daily records fall in more than 30 locations on Wednesday, including Abbotsford, where the mercury reached 20.1 Celsius, smashing a 45-year-old record by three degrees.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 12, 2026.

Note to readers:This is a corrected story. An earlier version misidentified data provided by B.C. Hydro as being the rate of discharge from the dam. In fact, those numbers represent inflow.

stories.title: Canadians gather for Remembrance Day ceremonies across the country
stories.summary: Ottawa - Canadians across the country are gathering today to reflect on the legacy of war and remember the men and women who served and died defending this country.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OTTAWA - Guns boomed, bagpipes wailed and CF-18 Hornets thundered overhead as Canadians paused at the National War Memorial in Ottawa on Wednesday to remember those who served and died defending this country.

This Remembrance Day comes just weeks after a deadly training accident at Canadian Forces Wainwright left four dead and dozens of other soldiers with burn injuries.

Sgt. Morgan Wong of Edmonton, Pte. Shaun Farrell of Prince Albert, Sask., Pte. Aidan Goulding of North Vancouver and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark of Langley, B.C., were killed at the Alberta training base last month.

They died and dozens of others were injured when strong winds suddenly swept up a grass fire that was burning on the automatic grenade launcher range and carried it across the training area.

“We mourn their loss, stand with those recovering from their injuries, and hold their families and fellow service members in our thoughts,” Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a media statement.

Gov. Gen. Louise Arbour said Canadians’ thoughts “remain with the soldiers we lost, those who were wounded, as well as the families, friends, comrades and all others affected by this tragic event.”

National Defence has said that, as of Nov. 4, 14 of the 39 injured had been released from hospital while another 25 remained in hospital.

Thoughts for Wainwright victims poured out from people across the country.

A prayer for the victims was read at the ceremony in Place du Canada in Montreal, as cannon fire rang in the air. In Toronto, Mayor Olivia Chow said she wished the injured “strength and healing.”

Hundreds gathered at an arena in Wainwright, Alta. for the local ceremony. They included Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre, whose riding includes the training facility.

South of the border, Rear-Admiral Kristjan Monaghan spoke at the Canadian Embassy on Pennsylvania Avenue in Washington, D.C., about those who died in Alberta last month.

“The loss experienced there has been felt across the Canadian Forces family, across the nation and beyond,” Monaghan said.

“It reminds us that sacrifice is not defined solely by geography. Service members accept risks, not only when deployed overseas but also while preparing themselves to serve their country.”

Canadians are also marking a quarter-century this year since the Afghanistan war began. The war — the longest in Canadian history — stretched on for more than 12 years and involved some 40,000 Canadian Armed Forces members.

Veterans Affairs Canada said 158 Canadian Armed Forces members and seven Canadian civilians — a diplomat, four aid workers, a government contractor and a journalist — lost their lives in Afghanistan.

Ian Moffat, a retired Royal Canadian Navy commander who served for 41 years, said Wednesday he was thinking about a soldier who died in Afghanistan.

“When I was in Afghanistan, there was a young armoured soldier in her very early 20s who was killed by an [improvised explosive device],” he told The Canadian Press at the ceremony in Ottawa.

“If you saw her picture, you’d swear she wasn’t any older than 17. I was at the ramp ceremony when she was loaded on board and I’ve never forgotten that.”

Ray McGill of Courtice, Ont. came to Ottawa so he could proudly watch as his son marched in his first Remembrance Day parade after joining the military last year.

McGill said his job during the Afghanistan war was to notify next of kin when soldiers were killed.

“It’s a pretty powerful day and gives us an opportunity to come out and pay tribute to those who can’t be here today,” he said. “Those guys gave their todays for our tomorrows.”

Kyle Scott, a Canadian Army veteran of the Afghanistan war who travelled to Ottawa from Alberta, said he was thinking about the comrades he served with who never made it home — and those who died after their return.

“I think of my own family and the troubles they faced when they returned from the First and Second World Wars,” he added.

“Life after service is often harder than when you are serving, so today has a lot of meaning.”

Marcel Huot, a Second World War veteran wounded twice in Normandy, was one of several veterans of that war who came out to the national ceremony.

He said he remembers a heavy barrage of artillery fire, “sand everywhere” and live fire directed at him. He recalled dropping to the ground to avoid the shelling before being hit in the back by a piece of shrapnel.

Huot said his thoughts are of his wife, who enjoyed coming out to the national remembrance ceremony.

“She died of Alzheimer’s. I’m lonely sometimes,” he said.

Veterans Affairs estimates the population of living Canadian veterans from the Second World War and the Korean War has dropped to approximately 4,306 people.

This year also marks the 100th anniversary of the founding of the Royal Canadian Legion — created in 1926 to serve as the main advocacy group for veterans’ benefits — and the 150th anniversary of the Royal Military College.

Hundreds of cadets came out to celebrate RMC’s anniversary.

“The cadets here and across Canada have grown considerably. There’s almost 70,000 cadets in the organization now across Canada,” said Dave Edwards, who works with the Connaught Cadet Training Centre in Ottawa. “It’s a great thing to see.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 11, 2026.

— With files from Nick Murray, Alyssa Wheeler and David Baxter in Ottawa, Charlotte Glorieux in Montreal, Jordan Omstead in Toronto, Kelly Malone in Washington and Bill Graveland in Wainwright
